63.title: Bean Coordination
63.content: Skill bean-coordination: Pointer to the bean-based session work-plan system (the beans CLI flat-file issue tracker, data under beans/). Operational usage lives in todo-manager.md / session-intent.md; this file is the canonical copy of the coordinator logic that downstream repositories sync from. Named by: DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring, SMART Guideline end to end . The bean-based work-plan system — the beans CLI, a flat-file issue tracker storing issues as markdown under beans/ — is how every session tracks its work-plan and how agents hand off across sessions.

64.title: A bean is never deleted
64.content: beans delete exists in the CLI. Do not use it — not on a sibling’s work item, and not on your own. Work that turns out not to be wanted is scrapped: status: scrapped, with a section saying why. That is also what “disable” means here; the CLI’s status vocabulary is draft, todo, in-progress, completed, scrapped, and there is no disabled state. A scrapped work item records that something was considered and rejected, and on what grounds, which stops the next agent re-entering the same dead end. A deleted work item leaves a sibling session unable to tell abandonment from accident. Archiving is a VIEW, not a third way out . beans/defs/archive/ is not a terminal state. An archived work item keeps its status and is still part of the store, moved aside rather than closed. Archiving is a file move, not a status change, so it records no reason and is not a way to make unwanted work go quiet. bun run cat check:bean-archive holds the rule: the archive node must be declared in beans/beans.json — check:declared-dirs and check:harness-dirs compare declarations against disk, not the reverse, so they cannot see an undeclared directory — and every work item in it must be completed or scrapped. If you want a work item out of the way, scrap it with its reasons first, then archive if you like. readBeans reads the active store and readArchivedBeans the archive. They share the graph typology bean-defs, so anything resolving by KIND gets whichever is declared first; resolve the archive by its id. A work item count that reads only the active store does not fall when work is archived. Claiming and closing are separately scoped. Claim before you work, so two sessions do not pick the same item (§”Claims are global via the branch store”). Closing is governed by evidence, not by authorship: read §”Closing a bean whose work has already landed” before you close anything — it carries the three obligations, and the ready-to-close tag for the case where you cannot re-derive the measurement yourself. What stays off limits is a work item a sibling is mid-flight on: a claim naming a branch, a recent note, an open PR. Closing that loses work the sibling had not finished reporting. Full cycle, as a diagram: Work items and todos. Operational spec (read these): . | todo-manager.md — work item lifecycle: beans create / update / list, parent/child epics, status transitions. This is the authoritative local usage spec. | session-intent.md — session-start intent + session-end results protocol against the master ledger and the work item queue. | pending-show.md — read-only “what is this session working on?” display. | idle-backlog.md — pull right-scoped work items while idle. | . Install the CLI: cat-harness-tools/scripts/install-beans.sh (idempotent; go install github.com/hmans/beans@latest).

65.title: Claims are global via the branch store
65.content: Claims are written immediately to the work-plan store (work-plan-store) by bun run cat beans:claim <id>. The claim (update(id, { status: "in-progress" })) and its holder note (note(id, ...)) are persisted directly to the shared store, so: . | Immediate global visibility: sibling sessions see your claim as soon as beans:claim finishes. | Atomic write with collision detection: if two sessions race to claim the same work item, the store Tool detects the conflict and rejects the second claim (state: "conflict"). | . Always claim with bun run cat beans:claim <id>. Do not use beans update --status in-progress, which writes no holder note and does not persist to the shared store. A claim is not gated by the code pre-push hook (prepare-merge step 6), which judges only the checked-out code commit. How the git state-branch Tool pushes claims and state commits to refs/heads/cat/... is in work-plan-store-git-branch. If a claim is ever refused as a gate failure, that is a bug in the hook — report it, and do not bypass the claim. When several agents drain at once, or the store has more than one copy, the claim is bean-drain step 2 instead: check recent history and open PRs first, then claim across every store copy (the bean-claim-check Tool). beans:claim writes one copy and reads status only. Linking PRs to beans with Closes-bean: and recording closure evidence . Code changes on main and work-plan state in the work-plan store (work-plan-store) are separate. To link them: . | In your PR body, include: Closes-bean: <bean-id> . | On closure, record the landed merge commit SHA from main, the branch, and verifiable evidence in the work item body (update / note in work-plan-store; when the store is on a git state branch, push with bun run cat state:push per work-plan-store-git-branch). | . A DECISION bean you will not land soon — put the question where a person reads . A decision work item exists to get a ruling, and its value is that somebody with the authority to rule sees it. A work item left on a branch merely gets duplicated; a decision left there sits unanswered while every branch downstream of it waits. If you open a decision work item on a branch you will not land soon: set status: draft in front matter (or beans create "<title>" --status draft), post the question where the owner already reads — the issue — and say ON THE WORK ITEM where you posted it. All three parts. The comment is what reaches a person; the line on the work item stops the next session re-asking and tells them where the answer will appear; and status: draft lets automated checks find an unanswered ruling request. draft is already in the status enum and otherwise unused, so it needs no new vocabulary. A decision work item stays status: draft until ruled on or landed. --- status: draft ... --- . Prose is not a signal. Recognisers over work item prose (Recommendation, Options, safe default, ruling, an unticked box) disagree by two orders of magnitude, and also match work items that record a ruling. So a check reads the STATUS, never the prose. bun run cat check:draft-beans (scripts/check-draft-beans.ts) finds any ruling request that never landed, reporting with a denominator. The trigger is STARTING WORK, not claiming . Run the open-PR check before you start work on a topic — not only before you claim a work item. A cause inside a work item you already hold, a fix an owner just asked for, a gate you are about to unbreak: each is a unit of work a sibling can already have a PR up for, and none of them involves claiming anything. Search the subject as well as the id: the file you are about to edit, the gate you are about to turn green, the symbol you are about to add. A search keyed on a work item id finds nothing when the sibling’s work has no work item of its own, or its work item is only on an unpushed branch. A duplicate-detecting test punishes whoever merges second, not whoever duplicated. Merging first does not mean you were first. Starting any new unit of work runs the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work”, scaled to its blast radius and recorded in the workplan work item before the first edit. And ASK AGAIN before you open the PR — looking once is not enough . Re-run the open-PR search immediately before you open your PR, not only before you start. A search at the start finds nothing when the sibling’s PR does not exist yet, and no relation between work items can fix that: the second session to arrive cannot know it is second. Only asking again later finds it. These do not replace the second check: . | alternative | why it fails | . | a describes: edge between work items | the second session to arrive cannot know it is second, so nobody is in a position to write the edge | . | a label or line on the PR carrying work item ids | only helps once a PR exists, which is exactly the window these collisions open in | . Same commands, same widened search terms — the subject as well as the id. The cost is one call at a moment you are already stopping to write a PR body. Two independent implementations of one fix produce two sets of observations, and the weaker implementation’s observations look like findings about the subject — and you cannot tell which set you hold until the other lands. So the second check also stops a measurement taken against your own artefact from being reported as a property of the system. bun run cat beans:claim <id> — how it behaves . scripts/claim-bean.ts builds the status change as a commit of its OWN and pushes it, so a sibling sees the claim immediately instead of when your PR opens. bun run cat beans:claim <bean-id> # store defaults to the CURRENT directory's checkout bun run cat beans:claim <bean-id> --dry-run # say what would happen . Run it from the checkout doing the work. The command resolves the checkout’s top level, prints claiming from <tree> (branch <b>), and refuses with exit 5 when that checkout is on the default branch or detached — the signature of the wrong tree — naming the tree it was about to write to. Pass --repo <worktree> from elsewhere; --any-branch overrides for a claim that really is made from there. It is a claim only — never your work: a claim bundled with work cannot be pushed until the work is ready. It also writes the same status into your copy of the work item, so a branch still carrying todo does not revert the claim at merge time; it does not commit that. It builds the commit in a detached git worktree, so a session mid-edit is not asked to accept a checkout, and removes it on every path including failure. Read the outcome, because three of the seven are refusals: . | outcome | exit | what it means | . | pushed | 0 | claimed; every session sees it | . | already-claimed | 0 | a sibling holds it, and is named. Nothing written — pick another item | . | held-unknown | 4 | in-progress there, and nobody recorded a holder. Nothing written. It cannot tell a live sibling from a claim abandoned days ago, so it refuses and says so — read the work item and the open PR list before taking it | . | already-closed | 0 | it is completed or scrapped there. Not claimed, deliberately — reviving finished work, and especially a scrapped work item whose purpose is recording a rejected approach, is a decision rather than a side effect of asking to claim | . | new-on-branch | 0 | the work item is not in the shared store yet, so nobody can see it and there is nothing to race over. Claim locally and open the PR early | . | fell-back | 3 | the push was REJECTED. The work item is not claimed anywhere a sibling can see — claim on your branch and open the PR at your first commit | . | unknown | 2 | the store could not be read. Never “the bean is free” | . held-unknown is common: any work item set in-progress with beans update instead of beans:claim, or hand-edited, carries no holder. Its exit code is 4, distinct from 0 (which already-claimed uses to say pick another item) and from 2 (the store was read perfectly well). fell-back is to be expected. Whether a direct push is accepted cannot be determined from inside an agent session (GET /branches/main/protection answers 403, and git push --dry-run does not run receive hooks), so the tool attempts and handles the rejection, loudly. A non-fast-forward is retried — another claim landed first, and the retry may discover the work item is now theirs, which is the correct answer rather than a conflict to force past. Two sessions choosing the same work is a different failure from two concurrent PRs going green alone and red together; the latter is about merging concurrent work.

66.title: Lifecycle of a coordinated work item
66.content: Several agent sessions run in parallel against the same repo, each in its own claude/* branch and ephemeral container. Without discipline they duplicate work, clobber each other’s queues, or resolve items a sibling is mid-flight on. Work items are the shared substrate. | Prime — at session start read the current work-plan (beans prime + beans list, or the CLI-independent fallback that parses beans/ directly). Know what is open and what siblings are touching. | Declare intent + claim — before starting, claim the work item via bun run cat beans:claim <id>, which records your holder note and updates the work-plan store (work-plan-store) immediately so siblings see it globally. When the work item is for a process step (code-change-review, merge-train, crdm-requirements, etc.), start or resume its workflow instance with workflow_start (--bean <id>) so the work item is placed on its current BPMN step (process-state.md). | Work — keep the work item current; advance the workflow instance with workflow_complete as each step finishes; append status notes as you go to a work item only your branch is changing. When other open pull requests are adding to the same work item, write a note instead — §”Adding to a bean — a note, not an append” below. Do not fork it into a parallel todos/*.json queue — link to any bulk queue from the work item instead. | Hand off or finish — on landing, close the work item, complete its workflow instance (or run bun run cat workflow:instances --sweep to close stale instances on closed work items), and update any cross-repo ownership note. If you stop mid-flight, leave the work item in-progress with a note saying where you got to, so the next session resumes instead of re-deriving. A work item abandoned silently is indistinguishable from one nobody started. | . An unclaimed work item is fair game for any session; a claimed one is not. Respect sibling claims. Agents create and set in-progress; they do not take over the work another session is mid-flight on. Complete it in the PR’s own last commit . Mark the work item completed in the last commit of the PR that does its work. Do not wait for the merge: a completion committed after the merge, on a branch then re-created from the new main, is in no PR and is orphaned, so the work item still reads open and the next session is offered finished work. If the PR is abandoned, the work item reads done only on a branch that never lands. | The ## Done when items are ticked in that same commit, with the evidence, so the work item shows why it is complete, not just that it is. When the work item delivers requirement statements, those items ARE their success criteria, copied when the work item was made (todo-manager §”Working with Beans” 4), and the work item is in its requirement set’s workPlan — so ticking them is judging the criteria, and closing the last work item of a set is what moves the set toward delivered. | A work item whose Done-when is not yet all met stays open in that commit, with a note saying what is left; completing it to avoid an orphan would be the opposite error. | . bun run cat beans:landed reports what slipped through: open, non-epic work items named in a merged PR’s title on main, those with every Done-when item ticked listed first. It reports and never closes; closing is still on evidence, per the next section.

67.title: Adding to a bean — a note, not an append
67.content: When more than one open pull request has something to add to the same work item, each writes a NOTE, never an append to the work item. bun run cat beans:note <bean-id> --title "Finding 3: ruling and after state" --body "…" git add beans/notes/ # the note AND the regenerated index . That writes <bean-id>--<YYYY-MM-DD>--<branch>.md in the declared notes directory of beans/beans.json, and rewrites the generated index beside it (README.md). The work item itself is not touched. Appending from several PRs puts every other open PR in conflict on that one file, and the merge-main bot refuses a work item conflict on purpose: two sessions editing one work item is a coordination question, not a regeneration, so the shared write is what has to go. The branch is the key, and that is the rule that must not drift. Two open pull requests never share a branch, and the branch is known at the first commit, which a pull request number is not. A second note from the same branch is a new ## section in that branch’s own file — found by its front matter, not by today’s date — so only that branch ever writes it. A date-plus-finding name would collide when two sessions work the same finding on the same day. Reasoning in full: cat-harness/schemas/sdlc/bean-note.ts. What still conflicts, and why that is acceptable. The index is rewritten by every pull request that adds a note, so two of them conflict on it. Its rows all sit inside one <!-- bean-notes:begin --> region, so the declared readme-generated-regions pattern resolves it without a person and regen rewrites it from the merged notes. The notes themselves never conflict. cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/bean-notes.test.ts merges two real branches to show both halves, and fails when the branch is dropped from the name. What beans:notes:check judges (in CI): every file in the directory is a folio-bean-note/v1 note naming a work item that exists, under exactly the name its own front matter derives (a hand-named note is the first step back to two pull requests writing one path), and the index is current. | The work item’s own body stays the owner’s. Re-scoping it, ticking its ## Done when, or closing it are still edits to the work item, made by whoever holds it. | A note does not move the work item’s updated_at, because bumping it from every pull request is the one-line conflict notes remove. A reader asking “is anyone working on this?” reads the index’s dates as well as the work item’s. | Sections appended before the convention stay where they are. Moving them would rewrite the region every still-open pull request is appending to. | .

68.title: Closing a bean whose work has already landed (STRICT)
68.content: A work item verified done and left open is as misleading as one abandoned silently: an agent that picks it up re-derives work already on main. A rule that says only who may not close a work item leaves nobody able to discharge it. So: a work item closes on EVIDENCE, not on authorship. You may close any work item — whoever opened it — when you have re-run the measurement yourself and it passes. You may not close one because a note in it says somebody else measured it. Three obligations come with that: . | Re-derive, never quote. The note claiming resolution is the thing under suspicion; reading it is not verification. Run the check, then record the command and its result in the work item, because notes claiming resolution do fail re-verification. Where a note gives a line number or a count, verify the fact — line numbers rot. | A Done-when only a person can satisfy is not yours to discharge — for example “the issue can be closed by its author”; an agent never closes an issue on its own say-so. | Mid-flight is still off limits. This governs work that has landed. A work item a sibling is actively working — a claim naming a branch, a recent note, an open PR — is theirs, finished or not. | . Verified-done and still not closable? Say why, with an expiry, in the shape bean-blocking.md requires of a block: an exception that carries no way to re-derive it is indistinguishable from an oversight. Stopping because you are blocked is a different state with its own requirements — what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff: bean-blocking.md. Reconciling closes in bulk — and an owner’s reopen outranks your evidence . A sweep that closes many work items on evidence (patch-ids on main from branch-archaeology, a gate that now passes, commits naming the work item) is these same three obligations applied per row. It adds one of its own: the owner may have moved work items from completed back to todo or in-progress because the earlier close was not good enough, and those work items can still carry a close(<id>) commit on main. Before closing, read the work item’s own status history (history(id) in work-plan-store, plus the archive; see work-plan-store-git-branch for the git state-branch form). If it was closed and later reopened, it is not closable on any evidence that predates the reopen. Read the reopen note. Close it only with evidence that answers that note’s reason and is newer than it. If there is no such evidence, list it as “reopened by the owner — evidence does not answer the reopen” and leave it. The same holds in reverse: evidence that a completed work item did not land (its commits absent from main under every test in branch-archaeology §1) is a finding to report, not a licence to reopen it on the agent’s own say-so, unless the owner has asked for that sweep. Re-derive from the REMOTE, never from your checkout (STRICT) . Where you read the evidence from is part of the evidence. Getting it wrong produces a finding that is confident, specific and false — for example “this file has no such code” read from a checkout branched before the commit that added it. A branch older than the claim. Grepping the working tree answers “is this in MY base”, which is a different question from “does this exist”. Ask the remote: git show origin/main:<path>, git log origin/main -- <path>. Never grep over the checkout to prove an absence. A fetch in the same compound command is not a barrier. git fetch -q origin main && git cat-file -e origin/main:<path> looks airtight and is not: sibling sessions merge every few minutes, so the ref can be stale when read. Fetch, then read in a separate command, and re-read before publishing. A file that exists only on an open PR’s head. When the claim is “nobody has built this”, check the open branches too, with the open-work-lookup Tool: a path, a prefix or a work item id, against main and every open PR head (see also bean-drain). The cost is asymmetric, which is why this is STRICT. A missed finding is a work item that stays open one more day. A false one about a sibling’s work is a correction, a retraction, and a reader who now trusts the next finding less. When you cannot re-derive it yourself — ready-to-close . Re-derivation is not always available: the measurement may need a running deployment, a branch this container does not have, or a judgement the owner reserved. Without an exit, leave it open is what an agent picks every time, and the work item costs a session of confusion on every sweep. The third state: tag the work item ready-to-close, quote under a ## Evidence heading what you DID verify, and say in one line what you could not re-derive and why. The owner confirms the batch. It is a tag, not a status, because the status vocabulary belongs to the third-party CLI: . $ beans update <id> --status ready-to-close Error: invalid status: ready-to-close (must be in-progress, todo, draft, completed, scrapped) $ beans update <id> --tag ready-to-close Updated <id> . and BeanStatusSchema in schemas/tools/tool-types.ts is defined as “exactly what beans update --status accepts”, so a sixth status here would desync the schema from the tool it documents. bun run cat check:ready-to-close lists every tagged work item with its evidence, so the confirmation is one read. It reports and never acts — deletion-requires-confirmation.md — unless the owner has waived the bean-close gate for this session or process run, in which case the batch closes under that waiver and the turn report names it: confirmation-waiver.md. It is not a parking space. ready-to-close says re-derivation is beyond this session; it never says I would rather not. Where you can run the check, run it and close the work item.

69.title: Where a sibling session is visible from (STRICT)
69.content: Sibling sessions can be listed (list_sessions gives each one’s id, title, branch and a task summary), which is enough to see WHO overlaps you before you write anything. They cannot reliably be reached: each sibling is its own cloud container, and messaging one may be refused. Seeing a sibling is not reaching one; what you commit is the only thing that arrives. A session is an ephemeral container, and nothing about it survives the container except what it committed. The Claude-Session: trailer on a commit is therefore the ONLY durable session identity this repository has, and a branch tip is the only durable statement of where a session got to. A sibling’s state is INFERRED, and the inference has a boundary . | what the trailer and the branches DO tell you | what they do NOT | . | which commits a session authored | whether it is running now | . | when it started and stopped committing | whether it is blocked, thinking, or gone | . | which branches carry its work, and its latest subject | what it intends to do next | . “Stopped committing” is not “finished”, and it is not “abandoned”. Treat a recent tip as a live claim, treat silence as a question, and ask — never as licence. One command, not a procedure . bun run cat sessions --since 4h . The sibling-sessions Tool node (tools/sibling-sessions/) does this, so every session counts the same way. It reads all branches, because a sibling’s work is on ITS branch. A window with no commits exits non-zero rather than reporting “no siblings”: a sweep over nothing has not found anything. Before creating or claiming, look . | The checkout is a snapshot. A container fetched main when it started, and everything merged since is invisible until it fetches again. | beans create is not idempotent and dedupes on nothing. The existence check in todo-manager §”Check before you create” reads the LOCAL store, so it cannot catch a duplicate a sibling created since, and the cost of not looking is duplicates somebody scraps one at a time. | . So before creating a work item for a decision, or claiming one, do both: . git fetch origin main bun run cat sessions --since 4h . The second is the one that gets skipped, and it answers who else is on this right now.

70.title: A quiet claim — what in-progress does NOT tell you
70.content: blocked has an expiry (bean-blocking.md); in-progress has nothing, so it carries no information about activity, and a reader cannot tell a stalled agent from a claim nobody has thought about since a bulk edit. The signal is liveness, not elapsed time . A claim is LIVE when something outside the work item says so: an open PR naming it, an unmerged branch touching it, or a note since. A claim with none of those has announced nothing to anybody — and a claim that announces nothing does not reserve anything. Elapsed time is the fallback, not the rule, because it is what a tool can compute offline. bun run cat health reports bean-quiet-claims at 72 hours since updated_at, alongside bean-claimed as the denominator. Its count is an upper bound: a work item it lists may have an open PR the sweep cannot see. Read it as “check these”, never as “take these”. Who may act . | Any session may TAKE a quiet claim — check for a liveness signal first; if there is none, work it, and say in the work item that you took it and what you found. This is the unclaimed case, reached by a different route. | Nothing re-statuses it automatically. The check reports; a person or the session taking the work acts. A tool that flipped in-progress back to todo would destroy the one record of who was where. | Quiet is not evidence of completion. Closing is governed by §”Closing a bean whose work has already landed”, and staleness is not evidence. A quiet claim on unfinished work goes back to the pool; it does not get closed. | . A stale claim is reset to todo, and the reset keeps the record . A claim untouched for weeks is not one anybody is honouring, but it still tells every sibling “taken”. A claim with no liveness signal (§”The signal is liveness”) AND no commit naming the work item or touching its branch in 14 days may be reset to todo by a sweep, provided the sweep appends a note recording what it reset. beans update <id> --status todo --body-append - <<'NOTE' _<UTC timestamp>_ — claim reset by stale-claim sweep: was `in-progress` since <date>, held by <branch / session from the holder note, or "no holder recorded">; no open PR, no unmerged branch naming it, no commit in 14 d. Re-claim with `bun run cat beans:claim`. NOTE . This does not contradict “nothing re-statuses it automatically”: the note keeps the record. The sweep is run by a session or the owner who has checked the network half (bun run cat check:quiet-claims), never by an unattended job. 14 days is the bean-stale-in-progress threshold in bun run cat health, so the two never drift apart. The reset never moves a work item to completed or scrapped, never touches an epic whose children are moving, and runs as one batch with a summary, under work-plan-restructure when it is more than a handful.

71.title: The branch store is the one every sibling reads (STRICT)
71.content: Work items live in the shared work-plan store (work-plan-store; on git, the dedicated state branch in work-plan-store-git-branch), not committed to main or held on unmerged feature branches, where a review of the store sees none of them. | Write work items directly to the work-plan store. Newly created work items, epics and Done-whens are written (create / update in work-plan-store; bun run cat state:push on the git state-branch Tool) as soon as the plan exists, so the work plan is immediately visible to all agents. | A sweep reads the work-plan store, and also sweeps open branches that still carry work item files from before the shared store, so no session is blind to current goals and claims. | .

72.title: Each bean has one home (STRICT)
72.content: Each work item lives in exactly one store, because copies of one work item written separately drift apart: . | Work item | Its one home | . | cat-tools-*, and the work items the tools layer took when it split off | beans/defs on main of https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools | . | folio-core-*, and the work items the core content layer took | beans/defs on main of https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant-core | . | every other work item | litlfred/folio-assistant, branch cat/cat-harness/beans | . litlfred/cat-harness’s own cat/cat-harness/beans branch keeps its notes, queue, surveys and workflows, but no work item files. Write a work item change once, to its home, and nowhere else. From a cat-harness checkout that means fetching the folio-assistant branch, not this repository’s. The tools hold the rule too: state:push refuses to write a work item file to the retired branch (deleting one is allowed), beans:claim there names the home instead of reporting the work item missing, and bun run cat check:bean-one-home fails when any work item id is in two stores or in the retired one. Run it after editing work items by hand. The table it reads is https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools/blob/main/scripts/lib/bean-homes.ts.

73.title: Which copy is canonical — work-plan/skills/work-plan/
73.content: This file. LOCAL_PACKAGES (built in scripts/skill-packages.ts) is the table skill_fetch serves from, so an agent asking for this skill by name receives this file. When this skill or the installer changes, work-plan/skills/work-plan/ is what a downstream repo syncs from, and the generated mirror under the docs site follows it automatically. On landing a coordination change that affects a downstream repo, update that repo’s ownership note and close the tracking work items.

74.title: Issues are a third todo source — queryable issue: link
74.content: beans/ (agent work plan) and todos/ (human items and feedback) are the two stores declared in the repository. GitHub issues are a third source, carrying external tracking, stakeholder adjudication, cross-repo visibility, and human decisions. A work item can link directly to its corresponding GitHub issue via the front-matter issue: field: . --- title: 'ISSUES ARE A THIRD TODO SOURCE: queryable bean-issue link' status: in-progress type: feature issue: 730 --- . The issue: field is typed as z.union([z.number().int().positive(), z.string().min(1)]).optional(), supporting numeric issue numbers (issue: 730), issue shorthand (issue: "#730"), or fully-qualified issue URLs (issue: "https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/issues/730"). When an issue is owed . Work items representing substantive roadmap scope or human adjudication owe an issue: . | Features (type: feature): features deliver user-facing capabilities or major roadmap changes, so they require an external tracking issue for stakeholder visibility and acceptance. | Stakeholder adjudication: any work item requiring human adjudication, policy rulings, or cross-team consensus (flagged via issue-required or needs-issue tags, or explicit adjudication requirements in the body) owes an issue link so the discussion and ruling remain discoverable. | . The check bun run cat check:bean-issues audits the work item store to verify that work items owing an issue provide either an issue: front-matter link or an issue reference in the work item body (#<number>, issue #<number>, or issue URL). It reports compliant work items alongside findings for unlinked items under 3-state reporting (0 = pass, 1 = finding, 2 = could not determine).

75.title: Disambiguation (do not conflate)
75.content: . | work items = the agent’s session work-plan (beans/, this skill). | todos = the human work-plan items (todos/). | issues = the third todo source (issue: front-matter field), carrying human/stakeholder adjudication and external tracking. | sidecars (*.qa.json, *.witness.json) = content state tracking. Work items ≠ sidecars. Do not convert QA / witness queue items into individual work items (see todo-manager.md disambiguation block). | A sibling session sharing this store (this skill) ≠ an agent in another environment you hand ONE task to, which you cannot see and which a person may relay to: agent-handoff. That covers who writes which work item, where the receiver reports, the one line the person pastes, and why the receiver’s own measurement is evidence rather than the close. | .

76.title: bean-coordination (skill)

77.title: /before-after-preview — show the reviewer the change, not a description of it
77.content: Skill before-after-preview: Make a reviewer-facing BEFORE/AFTER preview of a change to anything that is rendered — a docs site, a paper’s PDF, a FHIR IG, a slide deck, a website — and put it where the review and feedback processes expect it. Covers one build with one variable, stable capture, pairing every picture with a measured count and its method, the viewports and colour schemes to shoot, an honest status line, publishing with alt text, a section per content type naming this repository’s own build and render tools, and how reviewer feedback on the preview becomes work items. Use before asking anyone to review a rendered change, at the HCI validation gate, and whenever a reviewer asks “what did it look like before”. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: before-after-preview · Package: sdlc-core · Worked example: the Folio tab . continual-progress holds that a human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. rendered-verification adds that the agent that wrote the change cannot either. This skill is about what goes to the reviewer: a before/after preview that is a fair comparison, carries a number, and can be read without opening anything else. It covers every content type this platform renders.

78.title: How this sits beside its neighbours
78.content: This skill does not replace any of these. It tells you which one to use. | skill | what it answers | use it for | . | rendered-verification | does it work? — the agent checks in a browser | the tools: computed style, hit tests, pageerror, and asserting that the page actually loaded its styles | . | visual-diff | how much of this figure changed? | automatic pixel pictures of changed blocks on a folio’s review page | . | staging-review | where do I look? | the before (main) and after (staging) URL pairs, and what to review at each | . | this skill | is the reviewer’s comparison fair, measured and findable? | the preview itself, for any content type, and where it fits in the processes | . If the change is a folio block and the staging job already made its pictures, link to those. Use this skill for everything the job cannot make: page chrome, behaviour on scroll, a PDF page, an IG page, a slide. A staging “after” is not permanent. gh-pages keeps at most ten branches/<slug>/ previews and rotates the least recently updated off, so a link in a preview can 404 days later while the PR is still open. The next push to the branch re-stages it. Where the comparison must outlive that, publish the captures themselves (§6) rather than only the staging URL. Detail: staging-review §”The cap”. Which pages to picture. For a Change Set, the pages come from its rendered list (skill rendered-impact), so the “k of n pages changed” count is the list’s count, not one made by hand. Its unconfirmed content pages (bytes unchanged, content loaded in the browser) are exactly the ones a screenshot settles.

79.title: The rule
79.content: A reviewer is shown a rendered change as a before/after pair. Each pair comes from ONE build with ONE variable, is captured stably, is paired with a measured count and its method, and has a status line saying what it is and what was not checked. Each pair is introduced by a narrative: a sentence or two, in plain words, on what a reader will now see or do differently and why. The narrative comes first, above the pictures. A pair without it makes the reviewer play spot-the-difference, and the difference they find first is not always the one that changed: a re-render shifts anti-aliasing, a merge brings in somebody else’s edit. Name the change so the reviewer looks for it, then let the pair confirm it. If any part is missing, say so in the preview. Never drop a missing part silently. Build only the cone. For any rendered kind, the “after” build need only cover what the change can reach: its own files, its generator’s import closure, and what is derived from those. That is the general rule, written once in feature-staging §7. Anything the cone leaves out is identical to the “before” by construction, so leaving it out loses no comparison.

80.title: 1. One build, one variable
80.content: The only difference between the two pictures should be the change under review. In order of preference: . | The same build, with the change toggled. Render once and make “before” by switching the change off in place. The usual way is injected CSS that hides the new element, reverts a rule, or removes a class. Everything else stays identical, including the build, the theme, the fonts, the data and the viewport. | Two builds made with identical tooling, one of the base commit and one of the head commit. Use this when the change cannot be toggled, for example generated markup, a different PDF, or a new IG page. Use git worktree add <dir> origin/main --detach and symlink the installed dependencies (see rendered-verification §”A before/after pair beats an after”). Say in the preview that there are two builds, with both SHAs. | A local build against a published one. Only if nothing else is possible, and the preview must say so in its first line. The published side used different tooling. On the docs site, for example, the pinned remote_theme differs from the local theme gem. Any difference in the pictures may come from that and not from the change. | . Record which of the three you used. It is the first line of the status line in section 5.

81.title: 2. Stable capture — load everything, then check the two shots line up
81.content: A pair captured while the page is still settling compares two moments, not two versions. Do all of these before either shot: . | Force lazy media to eager: document.querySelectorAll('img[loading=lazy],iframe[loading=lazy]').forEach(e => e.loading = 'eager'). | Scroll the whole page once, top to bottom and back, so anything that loads on intersection has loaded. | Wait for network idle (page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')) and for document.fonts.ready. | Turn smooth scrolling off: document.documentElement.style.scrollBehavior = 'auto'. Otherwise a scrollTo returns before the page has moved. | Assert the shots line up: scrollY must be equal in both, and so must the getBoundingClientRect().top of a reference element outside the change, such as a heading. If either differs, the shots are invalid. Retake them. Do not caption around the mismatch. | . Lazy images that load between the before and after shots move the text, so the two pictures show different content at the same scroll offset and still look plausible. The reference-element check catches this; looking at the pictures does not.

82.title: 3. Measure, don’t just show
82.content: A picture shows one position. A count shows all of them. Send both, and name the method so the reviewer can repeat it or dispute it. | Choose a question that has a yes/no answer at one position. For example: “is body text visible beside the handle?”, “does the caption overflow the slide?”, “is this IG table wider than the viewport?”. | Ask it at many positions: scroll steps, pages, slides, or viewports. Report the result as k of n, before and after. | Measure from the rendered geometry. For text overlap, collect Range client rects of the text nodes, intersect them with the element’s getBoundingClientRect(), and confirm each hit with document.elementFromPoint at the overlap. A rect intersection alone counts text that is painted underneath. | State the step size and the viewport with the numbers. | . Folio tab, platform.html, 19 scroll positions at 1280×900: text visible beside the handle at 16 of 19 positions before, 0 of 19 after. At 390×844: 18 of 20 before, 0 of 20 after. A second table used 97 px steps across four page and viewport pairs: platform 1280 9/21 → 0, platform 390 32/39 → 0, index 1280 25/50 → 0, cat-harness/index 390 36/60 → 0. Treat a count the same way as any other measurement. Validate the method on a known positive and a known negative before trusting it (rendered-verification §”A COUNT over the built site needs its instrument validated first”).

83.title: 4. Several viewports, and both schemes when colour is involved
83.content: At least: . | viewport | size | why | . | desktop | 1280×900 | the layout most authors write in | . | phone | 390×844 | fixed and sticky elements, narrow columns, overflow | . Add light and dark whenever the change touches colour, contrast, a border or an image with transparency. Switch the scheme with the real control (on the docs site that is jtd.setTheme, not an attribute set by hand) and check that the switch took effect before shooting. Show a pair for each combination that matters. Give the count for every combination you measured.

84.title: 5. Honest status — one line, at the top
84.content: Status: <committed | pushed | in PR #N | merged> at <sha> · Build: <one build, toggled | base <sha> vs head <sha>, same tooling | local vs published> · Not checked: <what, and why> . “Not checked” is required and is never empty without a reason. Typical entries: . | local theme gem vs the pinned remote theme; | dark mode; | a browser other than Chromium; | print CSS; | the IG Publisher’s full build (only sushi ran); | the PPTX was not rendered, only its geometry was reconstructed. | . A preview that looks complete but hides an unchecked axis is a false green.

85.title: 6. Publishing — a private page, updated in place
85.content: . | Where: a private web page. Use the Artifact tool when it is available. It holds the pairs, the counts, the method, the status line and links to the PR and the issue. Update the same page as the work moves on, so the link in the PR body stays current. Do not post a new page for each round. Where no page can be published, attach the images to the turn and to the PR comment instead. | Alt text on every image, saying what the reader should see. For example: “Before, phone, scrolled 1200 px: the Folio tab covers the first three words of each line”. Do not write “before screenshot”. A preview without alt text cannot be used by a reviewer with a screen reader. | Label each pair in words, not only with position or colour: “Before” and “After”, then viewport and scheme. | Committed evidence: do not commit screenshots to the repository. The page and the PR are the record. visual-diff’s pictures are built by CI and are not committed either. | . The Folio tab preview was published this way as a private artifact page, with the before/after pairs, the counts above, the method and the PR link.

86.title: 7. By content type
86.content: The discipline above is the same for every type. What changes is how you build it, what one “position” is, and what you toggle. Docs site (Jekyll, just-the-docs) . | Build: bun run cat preview:site. Its header explains how its output differs from CI’s: the local theme gem, not the pinned remote_theme. | Serve under the baseurl. Symlink <serve>/folio-assistant -> <build> and serve the parent directory. Served at /, every stylesheet returns 404 and the page still renders, unstyled. | For theme chrome, take the real CI build from gh-pages (rendered-verification §”The REAL build is reachable”). | Toggle: inject CSS into the one build. | Position: a scroll step (for example 97 px) or a page. | . The worked example is the Folio tab. The fixed “Folio” handle covered body text as the page scrolled. The capture used one preview:site build of commit 438268976. “Before” was made by injecting .fa-glass-band{visibility:hidden!important}, so the new strip was the only difference. The capture forced lazy images to eager, scrolled the page once, turned smooth scrolling off, and checked that scrollY was equal in both shots. The counts are in section 3. Papers (LaTeX → PDF) . | Build: the paper render path. See build-pdf (the science layer) and the paper_render_pdf tool, or document_render_pdf for a document folio with no TeX. Build base and head with the same TeX Live and the same class files. A PDF cannot be toggled in place, so this is always case 2 of section 1. | Page images: rasterise with pdftoppm -r 110 -png or mutool draw when present (check with command -v). Otherwise render the pages with pdf.js in Chromium. paper_preview opens a rendered PDF or HTML for a person to look at. It is for a human looking, not for capture. | Position: a page. Align pages by anchor, not by page number. An added paragraph shifts every later page. Pair the page that holds the changed label in each build. | Measure: changed pages k of n, overfull boxes and warnings from the log before and after, and page count. | A changed block’s own picture comes from visual-diff on the HTML render. Link it rather than taking it again. | . FHIR IGs (sushi, IG Publisher) . | Order: sushi must pass first. A red sushi run has no IG to preview. Then run the IG Publisher, and compare the rendered output/ pages (ig-publication (the FHIR IG layer), fhir-validation (the FHIR IG layer)). | Build: two builds with identical tooling. The Publisher jar floats to the latest release on every run, so record its version for both sides. If the versions differ, some differences in the pictures may come from the tool and not from the change. ig-incremental-build.bpmn’s restored-state assembly is fine for an authoring preview but is not the full build. Say which one you used. | Position: an output/ page such as StructureDefinition-*.html, a pagecontent page or artifacts.html. Pick the pages from the changed resources, not by browsing. | Measure: pages changed k of n. Also compare qa.json errors and warnings before and after. A preview that looks right with more QA errors is not an improvement. | . Slide decks (PPTX, ODP) . On a slide, layout carries meaning. What overlaps, what is cut off and what sits next to what is part of the message. | Render if you can. soffice --headless --convert-to pdf, then use the paper route for page images. Check with command -v soffice. The session that worked out this route had no LibreOffice in its container. | If you cannot render, reconstruct the geometry from the package XML. A .pptx is a zip file. | ppt/presentation.xml <p:sldSz cx cy> gives the slide size. | Each ppt/slides/slideN.xml shape has <a:off x y> and <a:ext cx cy>, in EMU (914400 per inch). | A shape with no <a:xfrm> inherits its geometry from its placeholder in slideLayoutN.xml, then from slideMasterN.xml. Follow the chain or the shape is missing. | For .odp, read content.xml svg:x/svg:y/svg:width/svg:height, which use units such as cm. | Draw the boxes as SVG with their text, before and after. Measure overlaps and boxes past the slide edge as k of n slides. | . | Status must say “geometry reconstructed, not rendered”. Fonts, autofit and text wrapping are not modelled, so text overflow inside a box is unchecked. | . Websites in general . | The docs-site method, without the Jekyll parts. Build base and head with the site’s own build, or toggle with injected CSS or JS in one build. Serve under the same path prefix the site is deployed at. | Everything in rendered-verification applies: styles actually loaded, pageerror count zero, and hit tests at the centre of controls. | Position: scroll steps, routes, or interaction states such as a menu open or a form in error. List the states you covered. | .

87.title: 8. In the review and feedback processes
87.content: When it is required. A preview is required before a rendered change is handed to anyone to judge: . | when the PR is opened for review; | at each round of author feedback; | at the HCI validation gate’s review. | . A non-rendered change needs none. Say so in one line, rather than attaching an empty preview. Who makes it. The agent that made the change, in its own lane. The reviewer’s lane reads the preview and does not build it. A reviewer who must build their own before/after has been handed a chore, not a review. Only the producing activities carry the skill ref, because a skill ref says the lane PERFORMS the skill and the lane’s role must carry it (role-carries-activity-skill). The reading activities name the preview in their documentation and carry no ref. | process (cat-harness/processes/) | activity | role | . | content-change-review.bpmn | Task_CommitPush | agent produces it with the first push (skill ref) | . | content-change-review.bpmn | Task_Iterate | agent refreshes it with each revision push, which bypasses Task_CommitPush (skill ref) | . | content-change-review.bpmn | Task_ReviewStaging | author reads it beside the staging URLs | . | content-change-review.bpmn | Task_CompareBeforeAfter | review committee reads it beside visual-diff | . | code-change-review.bpmn | Task_CommitAndOpenPR | agent produces it for a change to a rendered surface (skill ref) | . | code-change-review.bpmn | Task_Review | reviewer reads it | . | editing-hci-validation.bpmn | Task_DraftEdit, Task_ReviseEdit | agent produces it with the proposal, before Gateway_ValidationFork, so it exists when review starts (skill ref) | . | editing-hci-validation.bpmn | Task_SmeReview | human or SME reads it as an input to judgement | . Where it is linked. | PR body: the preview link and the status line, near the top. Also any count that settles the question. | Issue comment: each round’s summary on the issue carries the same link (issue-working). | Update the page in place, so both links stay current. | . Asking the reviewer. The question follows interaction-modality: context first, then options, then the recommendation, then the question. The choices are structured and easy to select, because some reviewers find typing hard. Put the preview link and the counts in the context, so the reviewer can answer without opening anything else. Recommended first: . | Looks right. Approve this preview. (recommended when the counts went to zero and nothing is unchecked) | Something is wrong at a position. Pick the pair by its label, for example “After, phone, 1200 px”. Adding a note is optional. | Check something not covered. Pick from the “Not checked” list. | Not now. | . Say what happens if they give no answer: the PR stays open and nothing merges. Merging still needs the explicit confirmation the processes require. How feedback becomes work. | A choice of 2 or 3, or a comment on the preview, becomes a work item with the pair’s label, the status line’s SHA and the position (todo-manager; check before you create). | On a folio, a comment tagged block: <label> on the PR becomes a review-comment/1.0.0 todo (review-comments). | Feedback on published content goes through content-feedback. | The next round’s preview answers each item. Take the same pair again and update the count. | .

88.title: What this does NOT do
88.content: . | It does not decide whether the change is right. It makes that decision possible to take at a glance. | It does not replace the gates, rendered-verification’s checks, or visual-diff’s pixel job. It uses them. | It is not a merge approval. A reviewer choosing option 1 has approved the preview, and the merge still needs its own confirmation. | .

90.title: Blocked build dependencies — read the refusal before you work around it
90.content: Skill blocked-build-dependencies: A build or a model download fails from an agent container. Read which of three different refusals it is before doing anything — a policy denial (403 on CONNECT), an upstream rate limit (429), or a host that is simply down — because each has a different remedy. Covers the Maven Central mirror that gets a Gradle or Maven build through a 429, which hosts were measured open and shut, and when the work belongs to an agent with different network access instead. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . Outbound HTTPS from an agent container goes through a proxy. A failed download looks the same from a build log whatever caused it, and the three causes have nothing in common: . | what you see | what it is | what to do | . | CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403, curl 000 | policy: the environment’s network settings deny the host | nothing in the container fixes it. Say which host, point the person at the environment’s network settings, or hand the step to an agent that has the access (below) | . | HTTP 429 Too Many Requests | the upstream is rate-limiting the shared egress address | use a mirror of the same content (below). Retrying the same host usually fails again | . | timeouts, 5xx | the host, or the route to it | retry with backoff, then try a mirror | . Ask the proxy, not the log. curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status" lists recentRelayFailures with the host and the kind of refusal; a connect_rejected there is policy, full stop. Never disable TLS verification or unset the proxy to get past any of these.

91.title: Maven Central through a 429
91.content: Measured 2026-10-06, building Grobid from source: . | host | result | . | repo.maven.apache.org | 429 — Gradle’s default mavenCentral(); the build failed in 28 s | . | repo1.maven.org | 200 (intermittently 429 earlier the same hour) | . | maven-central.storage-download.googleapis.com | 200 — Google’s mirror of Maven Central | . | plugins.gradle.org, services.gradle.org | 200 | . Gradle: pass the init script, which repoints every repository and plugin lookup at the mirror without touching the project’s build files: ./gradlew build --init-script cat-harness-tools/scripts/gradle-maven-mirror.init.gradle . With it the same Grobid build succeeded in 3 min 45 s. -Dmaven.mirror=<url> picks another mirror. Maven: the equivalent is a <mirror> in ~/.m2/settings.xml with <mirrorOf>central</mirrorOf> and the same URL. Do not commit the mirror into a project’s build files. The 429 is a property of this egress path, not of the project; CI runners reach Maven Central directly.

92.title: Hosts that are policy, not load
92.content: Measured from the same container on the same day — re-check before relying on it, because the policy is the environment’s and can change: . | huggingface.co: denied (403 on CONNECT). Model weights live there (Nougat, most transformer checkpoints). The code installs from PyPI; the weights do not. | codeload.github.com archives: denied. github.com release assets were denied on 2026-10-06 and answered 200 on 2026-10-09 — re-check, and prefer finding-software’s pinned, checksummed release rung when it is open. git clone over HTTPS works either way. | PyPI and npm: open. | . A change to the environment’s network settings may not reach a container that is already running. When it does not, hand the step to an agent that has the access rather than stall: open a work item whose steps run end to end without this session (install, run, the exact scoring command, where the result goes), and give the person a one-line instruction of the form “do bean X on branch Y of repo Z” (agent-handoff). Code the step needs, such as a reader for the tool’s saved output, lands first, in this session, so the other agent only runs the tool.

93.title: Running code from outside the repository
93.content: Cloning and building a third-party project is running code nobody here wrote. Do it only when the person has asked for that tool by name, keep it under the scratch directory rather than the repository, and commit only what reads its OUTPUT. A session’s permission check may refuse the clone until the person says to go ahead.

95.title: bpmn-authoring
95.content: Named by: DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: bpmn-authoring · Package: workflow · Named by l2-dak-authoring.bpmn (Business processes · BPMN 2.0, Business analyst lane) and crdm-requirements.bpmn (Phase 2: Map current workflow (BPA), Agent lane). Author BPMN 2.0 business process diagrams — both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn.

96.title: Inputs and outputs
96.content: schemas/skills/bpmn-authoring/: . | in — processName (required), sourceWorkflow, existingBpmn, participants | out — bpmnFile, diagramFile, taskCount, gatewayCount, participantCount | . graphviz is a declared capability with degradation: skip — layout help degrades, authoring does not stop.

97.title: Diagram Interchange is not optional
97.content: A .bpmn with no DI section — no explicit x/y on its shapes — parses and renders blank, although the XML looks complete. bun run cat render:bpmn renders every diagram to docs/assets/img/workflows/ with bpmn-js in headless Chromium; bun run cat render:bpmn:check fails when an SVG is stale. Run the renderer and look at the SVG before you call a diagram done.

98.title: Readable at 100%: check it before and after (author check)
98.content: Every diagram you write or touch must, when you are done: . | fit 1400 × 900 in diagram units, so its 16px text reads at about 14px in a 1200px band without zooming; every task a fixed 120 × 120 square: boxes never grow to fit their names, and a name that does not fit is shortened (TASK_SIZE in the tools layer); | have no label on another label, on a flow (its own included), on a box or across a lane line: a gateway’s question above the diamond, its answers beside their flows, every label inside one lane; | have right-angled flows and every name inside its box, pool and lane names inside their strips; | have no crossing flows, and the lane order that keeps flows between lanes shortest: each lane sits next to the lanes it exchanges flows with, so no flow crosses a lane it does not stop in. A lane that talks to only one other lane, such as an owner who only approves the merge steward’s card, goes on the outside, next to that lane (owner, 2026-11-07: “swap owner lane down to reduce arrows across non interacting actor lanes”). | . bun run cat bpmn:detangle <file> reports all of it, and --write fixes what it can (lane order, right angles, box and lane sizes, label places). Run it before and after, and put both counts in the PR. Zero findings on every diagram you touch, or it does not merge (owner, 2026-11-02, after 63 of 80 harness diagrams were found with findings: “improve bpmn authoring process/skills so doesnt happen again”). A report nobody has to act on is how they piled up. Run bpmn:detangle <file> --check last; a finding you leave needs a reason in the PR, and only diagram-too-wide / lane-order may be left that way. Then look at the render: the check cannot yet see a box drawn across a lane line or outside its own lane, two flows drawn on top of each other, or a flow that wanders through a lane it does not stop in. Those are found only by looking. The same findings are in render:bpmn’s warnings and the process’s QA report, so a reviewer sees what the author left. The procedure, and why the budget is 1400 × 900, is bpmn-detangle.

99.title: In this repository, a diagram is executable
99.content: processes/**/*.bpmn are not pictures. workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete run them, and workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. That has consequences for how you author: . | Every activity carries <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="…"/> naming the skill that implements it, and <cat-harness.processes:bean store="beans/"/> where it touches the work plan. bun run cat check:workflow-refs fails on a ref that resolves to nothing, and bun run cat kg:audit additionally fails when the named skill exists but no package can serve it. | Every lane names a role. Declare the role once as a top-level <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> (before the collaboration and the process), and set partitionElementRef="<role id>" on the lane; the id is the role’s in scenarios/roles.json, verbatim. Lane names are free text; an explicit ref is the join that does not depend on spelling. <bootstrap.processes:role ref> is the deprecated form. A diagram using any bootstrap.processes: element declares the namespace as the first child of <bpmn:definitions>: <bpmn:import namespace="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns/" location="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns.jsonld" importType="http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld"/>. | A store is not a lane. Lanes are for people and agents, the roles that act. A place where things are kept, such as the work plan (work items), a corpus, a session record, an activity log or a published bucket, is a <bpmn:dataStoreReference>. The tasks that read or write it point at it with data associations, and each task sits in the lane of whoever does it. A “Work plan — beans” lane holding “Open the bean” says the store does the work, when the agent does. | The process’s own bpmn:documentation opens with what it is for. Its first sentence is the diagram’s row on the publication-workflow page. kg-export carries it on the Process node as summary (the whole text as description), the page reads it from the published named-subgraph JSON-LD (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) rather than from anything written by hand, and check:process-index fails when a declared diagram’s node has none. So that sentence says what the process does or answers — not who asked for it, which work item or issue it came from, or where the work got to. Those belong later in the documentation, or in the work item. | A gateway may be computed rather than chosen — see dmn-authoring. | Policy is declared on the process. <cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement="strict"/> means workflow_gate refuses a step that is not enabled; absent policy means strict. Steps marked relaxable="false" may never be relaxed by any package. | .

100.title: Readable diagrams: what the research supports
100.content: These rules are what holds up from the BPMN comprehension research, checked mechanically. kg:audit reports each rule below per process (src/workflow/diagram-quality.ts in the tools layer). The sources, and how strong each rule’s evidence is, are in the process-model-quality methodology. | Separate routing from work. A task never has two outgoing flows: put an exclusive or parallel gateway after it, or a reader must guess fork vs choice (activity-implicit-split, major). A loop-back INTO a task is fine. A gateway either joins or splits, not both (gateway-mixed). A question is a gateway, never a task: a box named “Should it leave now?” or “Separate this graph?” is a decision drawn as work. If someone must judge first, draw that as a task (“Judge whether it should leave”) or a call to Process_AskThePerson, then the question on the gateway after it. | Keep it small. Split by phase into call activities past 20 flow nodes (process-size). That 20 is house style. The only threshold with evidence is 7PMG’s 50 (process-decompose, major), and it predicts modelling errors such as deadlocks, not reading speed. | One start event per process level (process-single-start). Several named end events are fine, and the work item CLOSE pattern needs them. | A decision is a question, its branches are the answers (decision-label-question). | Label activities verb-object: imperative verb, then its object (Review the draft, not Draft review) (activity-label-verb-first). The evidence is one study of how ambiguous labels felt (29 students), so this is reported, never gated. | A name says the step, nothing else. No trailing [skill] slug: the skill is in <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>, and the page links it from there. No step numbers (“1 ·”, “Phase 2:”, “P1.1”): the flows already give the order, and a number in front breaks verb-first. A number that cites a section of a source document goes in the task’s documentation. A list of numbered steps is a sign the diagram copies a document’s outline; group the steps into phases instead. | . Split by phase: how . A diagram can be right in every step and still unreadable on its page. When process-size fires, or a diagram has a start event per lane, split it like this: . | The top-level process shows the phases. Each phase is a <bpmn:callActivity calledElement="…"> to its own process. Keep at the top only what moves the work between phases: who hands off to whom, and the decisions that send it back (rejected → revise). A loop that crosses phases is drawn at the top; a loop inside a phase stays in that phase. | A phase lives in its own file, <parent>-<phase>.bpmn, next to the parent, with its own process id (Process_<Parent><Phase>) and a first documentation sentence that says what the phase does. It becomes the phase’s row on the publication-workflow page like any other diagram’s. | A phase that ends two ways ends in two named end events, and the caller’s gateway right after the call reads which one it reached, as GW_BeanYours reads Process_BeanOpen’s. | Keep the node ids when you move nodes into a phase. A test, a schema or a skill that points at Task_X then changes only its file and process, not its id. | Open and close the work item at the top, once. A process that is only ever called runs on its caller’s work item, so a phase calls neither Process_BeanOpen nor Process_BeanClose (check:bean-calls). “Once” holds for the top as well: a process with several outcomes routes them all into one Process_BeanClose call, which decides itself whether the work item is completed, scrapped or blocked, and only then branches to its named end events. One close per outcome repeats the same box and makes the diagram wide. | A caller’s adjudication accepts looks one level down. If the judgement moves into a phase, put accepts on the call to that phase, and take it off any caller further up. | Name a call activity for the phase, verb-object like any activity (“Review the change”), not for its file. | . A phase that only one parent calls is still worth its own file: the point is the page a reader opens, not reuse. Untangle every diagram you touch . The same discipline as ArchiMate views (archimate-models §”Untangle every view you touch”), and the same geometry: a change never adds a tangle. Run bun run cat kg:audit before and after, and compare edge-crossing, edge-through-node and edge-rectilinear for the diagram, and check that no shape has a flow in and a flow out on the same point and that each lane’s rows sit at k/(n+1) of its height (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”). Say both counts in the PR. Route loop-backs in the channel below the lane (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”), then look at the rendered SVG. What the evidence does NOT support . Do not import these from style guides or model output; each was checked: . | Mandatory left-to-right flow. Figl & Strembeck 2015 (44 people) found no significant difference in accuracy or time across four directions. Lay out left-to-right for consistency, not because it reads faster. | A word cap on labels, a gateway fan-out cap of 4, and a fixed colour palette. No study behind them. Colouring matching split and join gateways made novices more accurate and experts faster, not more accurate (Reijers et al. 2011). | OR-gateways need no rule: the process model refuses inclusive gateways at load. | .

101.title: If it has actors, activities and a control flow, it is BPMN
101.content: Not a Mermaid fence. Mermaid stays for the things that are not processes — component maps, lattices, navigation graphs. The audit of which is which is on the publication workflow page, which the content core authors.

102.title: Why this skill is in a platform package
102.content: It covers both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn, and platform processes such as crdm-requirements.bpmn name it, so it cannot live in a content-type package: a platform process depending on a content-type package crosses the boundary the platform-boundary-guard subagent keeps. Its DAK material stays here rather than in a second skill, because a generic skill naming a domain worked example is ordinary, and two skills that must be read together to author one diagram are not.

103.title: When a layer above transforms it
103.content: A layer built on this one may transform an authored business process into another artefact — FHIR Shorthand, for instance — and then the BPMN is a source artefact rather than documentation of one. Author it knowing it will be transformed: names and ids you choose here appear in what is generated. That layer’s own tooling skill has the mechanics; this one names no layer above it.
