380.title: Directory conventions — what a layer declares it scans
380.content: Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . Every layer carries a declaration at its repository root — a *.json whose name field equals its own filename stem, found with findDeclarationFile and never composed from a path. It declares the directories the layer scans for content, and what kind of graph each one holds. Schema and resolution: schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts. It is the harness’s schema, not folio-assistant’s. agentic-harness is the layer that defines Roles, Skills, Tools and these conventions, and every other layer inherits from it — so a layer need not be a folio-assistant to carry one. A Tool repo or a Test repo carries the same declaration.

381.title: Why directories rather than a content type
381.content: The obvious reading of “an instance holds zero or more content instances” is a list of instances under one contentType. That shape does not survive a multi-repository split: . The things agentic-harness holds are not folios. They are Tool definitions, a knowledge graph of skills and workflows, and a schema graph. None renders as a document and none has a contentType in the document | paper sense. A model that gives every layer a content type forces the harness to claim one it does not have. So the general object is a layer with directories, each holding a graph. folio is one graph typology among several.

382.title: Node Kinds are declared: nodeSchemas
382.content: A layer lists every $schema value its files carry, and the published schema that defines it, in its declaration’s nodeSchemas — a path relative to the declaration, or an IRI for a published standard. It is bootstrap’s field (KnowledgeGraphDeclarationSchema in graph.ts), so a reader with nothing installed can go from a file’s $schema to its Node Schema without knowing any harness. The graph-typology registry’s nodeSchemas is a different, harness-side table: it maps a tag to a TypeScript validator or shape, which only a harness can run. graph.test.ts fails on a bootstrap file whose $schema is not declared, and on a declared local schema that does not fix that very tag.

383.title: The graph typologies
383.content: The vocabulary is open, and split across two layers. A kind answers two questions, and only one of them is here. renderable — does this become a website — is below. The other is what a running process does with the graph: produces it, reads it, or writes it, and content-context-and-state-graphs owns it. Read it before adding a kind — holds is required, so a kind that has not decided does not compile. An old kind spelling still reads . The cat-harness kind was once spelled kg. Renaming a kind is a CROSS-INSTANCE breaking change: a downstream layer declaring graphs: ["kg"] would resolve nothing silently — scanning, finding nothing, reporting a clean run. So GRAPH_TYPOLOGY_ALIASES in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts maps kg → cat-harness, resolved once at the registry boundary and nowhere else. resolveGraphTypology reports WHICH spelling was used, so a caller can warn — an alias that resolves silently is an alias nobody ever removes. A directory id survives a rename of anything else. An id is the layer’s own handle. A Subgraph id is its name inside its Harness, and the Harness name qualifies it (cat-harness.skills). RENAMED_DIRECTORY_IDS reads an old id as the new one, so an older declaration still overrides the entry it meant. The JSON-LD projection canonicalises. toJsonLd emits the type IRI, not the spelling, so reading a projection back yields cat-harness whatever was written. kg:audit, kg-export, kg-qa sidecars and the kg QA family keep their names: those are command and file-format names, not the graph typology, and renaming them would touch hundreds of references for no change in what a declaration means. The layer is not a column here. holds is the FIELD on GraphTypologyDef that carries the content/context/state layer; the live answer is graphTypologiesOfLayer() in content-context-and-state-graphs, and a hand-maintained copy would drift from the registry. The table of every kind is a published page, not this skill. Each row is a kind’s description, and the rows span every layer in the checkout. The table is built at publish, by bun run cat kind:table, at <base>/cat-harness/kind-table/ (docs/cat-harness/kind-table.md, declared in cat-harness’s builtAtPublish), because a table kept in this skill goes stale at every re-pin that brings a layer’s new kind. To change a row, edit the kind. test/ is the one test tree . This layer declares qa at test/results/ and health at test/health/results/, and everything a test runner reads is under test/: the Playwright *.e2e.ts specs, their support/ fixtures, and the health sweep’s own *.test.ts. When two trees compete, move the cheap side. An id in a declaration is the expensive thing to move; a path reached by one line of one config file is cheap. Change a directory’s path and keep its id, so an inheriting layer’s override still matches: resolveDirectories matches on id, never on path. Move a declared directory in a change of its own: relocating one as a side effect of adding a graph typology is how a directory quietly goes missing. Verify a move like this positively, never on a green test run. A consumer that now scans nothing reports clean, which looks identical to success. Constants that compose a path from segments (join("tests", "health", "results")) are invisible to a grep for the moved path. Ask each tool to name its subjects: bun run cat harness:dirs:check, bun run cat health:list, and Playwright’s spec count. A rendered translation is not its own graph typology — the FILE declares its language. docs/fr/index.md carries lang: fr and translation_source: index.md in its own front matter, so it is the same kind of thing as the page it translates: renderable content, differing by a field. pipeline/translation-index.ts discovers the locale subtrees by reading those fields and never matches a directory name against a list of language subtags — that inference is wrong in both directions, silently hiding a no/ chapter (Norwegian, or the English word) and silently showing a pt-BR/ or translated-fr/ one. Translatability is a property of a format within a content type, which the owning layer declares under contentTranslations (collected by schemas/library/translation-tools.ts) and isTranslatable answers — not a property of a directory. A kind per locale subtree would restate what every file already says and grow as O(locales x subtrees).po catalogues are the genuine exception, and that is what translation-sources is for: they are not content in any language, so no file inside them can declare one. uploads and library are two kinds, not one, and the split is load-bearing. They are the two stages of the document-ingestion pipeline, and the corpus-grep checklist searches library/ only — so a source still sitting in uploads/ does not merely go unread, it makes a clean grep read as “nobody has done this” while the file is on disk. An un-ingested source is worse than an absent one, because it produces false confidence rather than a gap. One sources kind covering both would erase exactly the distinction the pair exists to state. They are also the reason materialiseDirectories exists. Declare only what exists: absent and empty are indistinguishable to a consumer, so declaring a directory without creating it converts a real gap into a false pass. bun run cat harness:dirs creates every directory a layer declares or inherits; the session-start sweep and init-folio both call it, so a declaration is never left without the directory it names. todos is not a second work plan, and the distinction is the one AGENTS.md already draws. beans/ is the AGENT work plan and no second store may be stood up beside it. todos/ is the other thing that document carves out — “the content-review feedback workflow … a separate domain feature, not the agent work-plan” — and it is content: a todo records that a person has something outstanding, and it is owned and authored by the folio. A todo carries the four coordinates of the role model, because they are already declared and inventing a fifth vocabulary for them would be the drift this file exists to prevent. AGENTS.md: an actor performs a task in a process as a role. A todo is that sentence left unfinished, so it is tagged by roles, processes, tasks and identities (schemas/sdlc/todo.ts). Two things about those tags are load-bearing rather than incidental: . | A task reference carries its process. A BPMN activity id is unique only within its process, so a task tag is the pair { process, task } and never a bare string. Same lesson as the subprocess interpreter: a step id without its phase is not an address. | An identity is provider-qualified, and its link to an actor is optional. litlfred is not an identity; github:litlfred is. The link to a declared actor is absent whenever the person is not in scenarios/actors/ — and somebody who comments on a pull request is a real person with a real outstanding item whether or not the registry has heard of them. Absent means not linked, a third state; never anonymous, and never defaulted. | . resolveTodoTags reports each tag as resolved, dangling or not-checked, and the third is the one that matters: a checkout with no skills/ must report every role tag as unchecked, never as dangling. A wall of false findings is how a check gets switched off. todos/ is not a machine-queue directory. Bulk machine-generated JSON (audit output) goes under build/, and scripts/tests/audit-output-paths.test.ts pins that none lands in todos/. That guard forbids machine output there; it does not forbid the declared content graph described here. bean-defs and workflow-state are two nodes of one beans graph. WHAT IS BEING WORKED ON carries judgement and is edited by hand; WHERE A RUNNING PROCESS GOT TO is a token the interpreter owns. A consumer asking for the work plan must not be handed BPMN instance state. Why the work plan is the harness’s and not core’s. The test is whether the harness has one, and it does: a layer has work whether or not it has content, and agentic-harness carries a beans/ store for its own. A Tool repo and a Test repo have work plans too. That is a different test from the one that sent folio to core, which is about capability — only core can render. One beans kind, with the distinction carried by its nodes. beans/ is a graph with named nodes, declared by beans/beans.json (schema: schemas/sdlc/bean-graph.ts): defs holds the work plan, workflows holds running-instance state. Two sibling directory entries for a parent and its child would misrepresent a containment relation and tell the two apart only by file extension. So the harness says which directories exist and what kind of graph each holds, and the work item graph says what its own nodes are. One fact, one place, at each level — and a consumer asks for a node by name instead of inferring it from a file extension. Nesting is not inheritance. A consumer scanning a declared directory must not assume it owns everything beneath it — check whether a deeper path is declared, here or in a graph’s own node list.

384.title: An unavoidable duplicate is fine; an unchecked one is not
384.content: The declaration is meant to be the single statement of the layout, and mostly it is — fields that restated it elsewhere were removed rather than kept in sync. Two copies survive because neither can be removed, and both are checked: . | a third-party tool’s own config, which will never read this schema; | a constant on a hot path, where re-reading a JSON file to learn one’s own directory would cost more than the duplication saves. | . The rule is not “never duplicate”. It is: an unavoidable duplicate is fine; an unchecked one is not. In this layer bun run cat check:harness-dirs is what makes the difference. The dot-prefix guard tests every segment, not just the first . A node path resolving under a dot-prefixed directory is rejected, and the guard checks every segment of the resolved path. A node declared .defs under a visible root resolves to a hidden directory and is exactly as invisible as the stores this convention exists to surface — so checking only the head would have made the guard unfireable. Why invisibility is worth a guard at all: a dot-prefixed directory is absent from a plain ls, from most file browsers, and from a forge’s web tree, which hides the artefacts a person looks for first.

385.title: The conventional layout
385.content: cat-harness/ <content-core>/ cat-harness.json <content-core>.json tools/ → tools folio/ → folio skills/ → skills (inherits tools/, skills/, schemas/, …) schemas/ → schemas . cat-harness declares tools/, skills/ and schemas/ among its directories. The content core declares only folio/ and inherits the rest. Where a NEW layer puts its code: <stub>/src . A new layer puts its source under <stub>/src/ and declares it as code. One directory, one declaration. (Stated here as well as in the code kind, because somebody starting a layer reads the layout, not the kind table.) . The existing layers are the exception. schemas/ is already a declared graph of its own kind, and adding code to it would give one directory two kinds; pipeline/ is core’s subject, not the harness’s; and scripts/ hold entry points named by path from package.json and the CI workflows, which check:ci-invocations and check:command-paths guard, so moving them is a large invocation surface for nothing the declaration does not already buy. They are declared where they are. <stub>/src binds what has no history yet. Being declared is not being reached. Those are two questions and bun run cat check:code-accounting reports them apart — never averaged, because a rise in one can hide a fall in the other. A sub-sub-graph — one RESERVED name inside a declared directory . A vendor-specific override of a voice goes in a nested family, voices/vendors/, not a sibling graph voices-vendors/: a second declared graph for one concept is a declaration inside a declaration. So: . A family within a graph is a RESERVED SUBDIRECTORY NAME inside the one declared directory — never a second declaration, and never a rule about arbitrary nesting. Three properties, each load-bearing: . | One declaration. Every consumer that already asks for the graph gets the family with no change, and there is one answer to “where does this live”. | One level, under a name the reader states. “Any directory, any depth” is a rule nobody can check, and it would silently make an unrelated nested directory — a notes/, a scratch draft — part of the graph. | The directory is where a PERSON looks; the file is still the contract. A vendor voice declares what it overrides in its own extends field (extends, not overrides — the obvious name is the wrong one), exactly as one sitting flat would. Nothing downstream may infer a relation from a path — the same rule as everywhere else here: extension and location are coincidences, a declaration inside the file is the contract. | . Adding the name to the convention is not enough; the READER has to descend. vendors/ holds no voice.json of its own — its children do — so a reader that scans one level would skip every override in silence and report a clean read over real content. voices-viz.test.ts asserts both directions: a voice under vendors/ loads, a voice under any other nested directory does not. VOICE_VENDORS_DIR in schemas/content/voices.ts is the one spelling of the name.

386.title: Assets sit at <stub>/<asset> — no declaration reaches down (ENFORCED)
386.content: A declared directory never sits inside another declared directory. An layer’s assets hang directly off its stub — cat-harness/skills/, the IRIS replica’s library/, the DAK layer’s methodologies/ — and a package inside one of those is a package, not a second graph. Read this with §”Nesting is declared FROM WITHIN” below, which governs: nesting is permitted when described by a node in the first subdirectory. What is forbidden either way — and what check:layout-norms measures — is a ROOT DECLARATION enumerating a path it cannot verify. When a from-within node describes a nesting, check:layout-norms must not report it. Depth is not the test, and reaching for it produces false findings. A library two segments from the repository root is right, and test/results/ is right because test/ is not a graph. What is wrong is containment: a declared directory inside another declared directory, which forces a consumer scanning the outer one to decide whether the inner one’s nodes are also its own. The part that is easy to get wrong . When you relocate a buried asset, remove its declaration rather than repointing it. A package subdirectory of an already-declared graph needs no entry of its own, and adding one declares the same directory twice — the same defect, one level down from where it was. Repointing a buried package’s entry while keeping it makes discovery find the one directory twice (for skills, gen-skill-docs then demands a category under both the basename and the declaration id). How it is enforced . bun run cat check:layout-norms, a ratchet rather than a corpus-wide gate. The nestings that exist today are baselined in scripts/layout-norms-baseline.json; a pair not in the baseline fails. A layer with no baseline entry cannot regress, while the layers with outstanding work do not turn CI red. Removing a nesting prints as FIXED and never fails: a guard must not punish the fix it exists to encourage. --update shrinks the baseline, so the diff a reviewer sees is the progress. Ask the baseline for the list, never this page.

387.title: Inheritance
387.content: A layer inherits its dependencies’ directories, walked depth-first through dependencies.folioAssistant — the same order schemas/kg/harness-config.ts uses for skills and translations. Deepest dependency first, root last, so the root wins. Overrides match on the directory’s id, never on its path. A layer that wants a graph somewhere else redeclares its id with a different path: . { "id": "kg", "path": "graph/knowledge/", "graphs": ["kg"] } . Matching on path instead would make two knowledge graphs out of one relocation, and every consumer would scan a directory that is not there. An override also keeps the inherited position in the scan order rather than moving to the end — a relocation should not reshuffle what is scanned first. A subgraph is declared ONCE; every layer that has it is a MEMBER . If a layer depends on one where docs/ is a declared subgraph and has a docs/ of its own, the viewer detects it: that layer is a named member of the docs graph, with no per-entry field to set. So inheritance is automatic. resolveDirectories returns, for every instance-scoped entry, one member per layer in the chain whose <root>/<path> exists — ResolvedDirectory.member names it. The declarer’s member comes first, so a consumer looking a subgraph up by id is handed the same directory as before; the rest follow in chain order. Existence-filtered (declare only what exists); a repository-scoped entry has one location by definition and gets no members. Whether an inherited directory is CREATED is a fact about its graph typology, GraphTypologyDef.perInstance, stated once in the registry rather than per entry: . | perInstance: true — part of the SHAPE a folio has: uploads, library, docs, qa, beans, todos, voices, folio, glossary, translation-sources, external-schema. materialiseDirectories creates the dependent’s own, empty, with a keep marker. | absent — merely where a layer’s content lives: schemas, tools, code, processes, methodology. A dependent that HAS one is a member of the subgraph; one that does not gets nothing created. | . Creation is a property of the kind, stated once, because a per-entry field disagrees with itself across entries. A layer always materialises what it declared itself, whatever its kind. A legacy dependents key still parses and is dropped. A nested entry that is a subgraph of the LAYER (skills.json’s voices, as opposed to beans.json’s defs, which is part of its parent’s graph) says so with "subgraph": true. The checkout aggregates — no layer declares another’s directory (STRICT) . A platform that named its dependents’ directories (so a corpus-wide tool could ask it for “every library”) would be naming its users, and those entries drift from the owners’ own ids. The rule now: . | The checkout’s root layer aggregates. folio-assistant.json needs every layer the checkout stages, and declares the checkout-level state it physically holds (beans, todos, memory, interaction, issue-marks, fsh-guts, root-docs). | Only that layer declares at the checkout’s scope. A scope: "repository" entry anywhere else is a MIRROR, and check:instance-graph refuses it (repository-mirror), as it refuses an layer the root does not reach (unstaged). | A corpus-wide question is asked of the checkout, not the platform. checkoutDirectories / checkoutDirectoriesForGraph in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts resolve every staged layer through its OWN chain and union the members — per layer, because one long chain would override sibling ids (the DAK layer’s processes would replace the harness’s). A tool shipped BY a layer asks corpusDirectoriesForGraph(instance, kind): that layer plus everything stacked on it, never its own dependencies (those are its overlay). Known-skills callers say which question they ask: CorpusScope ("instance" | "checkout"), and corpusScopeFor(root) gives the rule — the platform’s own run is corpus-wide, --instance <x> is that layer alone. | Falsifier, kept as a test: the platform resolved ALONE sees nothing above it. A split checkout running against one folio sees that folio and its dependencies — what it contains, not what the platform remembers having been next to. | .

388.title: Nesting is declared FROM WITHIN, by a node in the first subdirectory (STRICT)
388.content: Nesting is allowed only one way: a (Sub)KGraph node within the first subdirectory labels the other subdirectories within it, and that structure is inherited. A declaration never reaches down a path. A layer declares a directory; that directory’s own contents are described by a node inside its first subdirectory, which names the sibling subdirectories present there. Depth is carried one level at a time, by the level that can see itself. What this forbids, and it is the shape everything currently reaches for: . // WRONG — the root declaration enumerating a path it cannot verify { "id": "docs", "path": "cat-harness/content/docs/", "graphs": ["folio"] } . The root cannot tell you what is under docs/; it can only assert it. A node that lives there can be wrong in a way somebody notices, because it sits beside the thing it describes. And the structure is INHERITED. A dependent layer gets the nesting the same way it gets the directory — through the overlay, resolved by id, in scan order. It does not re-describe a dependency’s interior, and it does not have to: the describing node came with the directory. A from-within entry can be a LAYER directory . A kind’s declarationFile names the node. What an entry in it IS depends on one field: an entry marked "subgraph": true is a layer directory, and resolveDirectories lists it exactly as if <instance>.json had declared it. It carries within (the id of the directory that declared it), and check:layout-norms treats that pair as the sanctioned shape. An entry without the marker (beans.json’s defs, docs.json’s proposals, voices.json’s vendors) is a part of one graph and stays out of the layer list. skills/skills.json is the worked case. It is one node with two lists: topics (subdirectories that hold skill packages) and directories (layer directories inside skills/, such as voices/, and lean/ in the science layer). Three rules the resolver holds: . | Never through a mirror. A scope: "repository" entry points at ANOTHER layer’s directory; following its declaration file would resolve that layer’s subgraph as one’s own. The guard stays for a downstream folio that still carries a mirror. | A declaration beats a default. skills/voices is also a built-in default; a from-within declaration replaces that convention, while an instance-level declaration with the same id still wins over both. | A MEMBER’s own declaration file is read, not only the declarer’s. A member’s from-within entries are members of the chain too, named member: "<instance>", within: "<subgraph id>". | . Concern groups — a sub-subgraph in every grouping kind . Eight groups — sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct — are built into location, split across schemas, skills, uml, processes, library and tests. The same from-within rule, one more use of it: . | Which kinds group is a fact about the kind: GraphTypologyDef.concernGroups, with the kind’s declarationFile as where groups are named — skills/skills.json (topics), processes/processes.json, schemas/schemas.json, library/corpus/library.json, uml/uml.json, a test directory’s code.json (groups, "$schema": "concern-groups/v1"). | A group is a CODE of code-lists/concern-group.json, which carries its title and definition once; its directory is the code (sdlc/processes/). A ninth code is a ruling, not an edit. | Declared once, inherited as members — option A one level down. The harness declares a group; each higher layer’s same-named <dir>/<group>/ is a member (core’s skills/library/ of the harness’s library). A higher layer adds no group of its own; content-type work goes in as PACKAGES under content/. | Declare only what exists. A group is declared in the PR that first fills it; a declared-but-absent group throws. | One walker: scripts/concern-groups.ts (groupedChildrenIn, resolveGroups); packageDirsIn delegates to it. check:concern-groups holds the four rules and prints each group with its members. | . Applied: docs/source/ . The documentation source lives at docs/source/, inside the docs graph it renders, and is declared FROM WITHIN by the docs graph’s own node, docs/docs.json (entry docs-source, carrying the existing docs kind). Readers ask docsSourceDirFor(root) rather than spelling the path. Adding it to the root declaration instead would be a root declaration reaching down. A directory that holds live content and is declared nowhere is the worse twin of declared-but-absent: present-but-undeclared, with a clean run over content that is really there. What is ruled, and what is open . Do not settle an open naming question in the corpus to proceed (deletion-requires-confirmation, surprise-to-corpus). |   |   | . | ruled | nesting is described from within, by a node in the first subdirectory, naming the others present there; and that structure is inherited | . | ruled | a root declaration reaching down a multi-level path is not allowed | . | open | the node’s kind and name in general — SubKGraph, a reused kind, or something else. One case is ruled: docs/docs.json’s docs-source reuses the docs kind | . | open | whether existing multi-level declarations are grandfathered or must migrate | .

389.title: Making a field REQUIRED is a change other branches pay for
389.content: A required field with no default is right when its wrong value is invisible either way, but the cost lands on other branches: entries added on main while the field is in review do not carry it, and on the merged tree every readDeclaration throws. So when you add a required field to a declaration several sessions are editing at once: . | Write the error before the field. readDeclaration names the offending entries and gives the valid values with a one-line test for choosing between them — not a raw Zod dump. | Expect to pay it more than once, and land quickly. Every day the branch sits open, another entry arrives without the field. | A conflict-free merge is not a passing merge. Git has nothing to reconcile when main adds entries and a branch adds a field, and the result can still be unparseable. Verify the merged tree, never the merge. | .

390.title: Where a subgraph gets its content — source
390.content: A subgraph declares where it gets its content: mounting a directory, mounting a branch, and later perhaps a graph database. The harness layer config can override it. A “directory subgraph” and a “branch subgraph” are one thing with two sources, so there is one field and one resolver, never a branch concept beside a directory concept. Schema schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts. | source on a directories[] entry is a discriminated union on kind. { "kind": "directory" } — the default, so absent means it — says the content IS the checkout at path. { "kind": "branch", "branch": "cat/cat-harness/todos", "keyedBy": "tip" } says the content lives on a declared repository branch and path is where a mount of it lands. A later kind (a graph database) is a new member of the union: additive, and a compile error at every consumer that has not decided what to do with it. | The branch NAME is declared once, on the directory entry that owns it: its storage (or source). There is no central table. A script that resolves a family’s branch reads the folio’s declaration first and keeps its built-in names only as a fallback (cache-family-fallbacks.test.ts keeps those in step). A branch no declaration names is a finding (subgraph-source.test.ts), never a guess at what to fetch. | The layer config overrides it, by id. "subgraphSources": { "<dir-id>": <source> } inline on the instance’s index.config.json entry (index-config; a legacy <instance>.config.json is still read). subgraphSources moves a declared directory’s content. Bringing in a whole layer from another repository is the entry’s source.remote, which is a different field. The declaration says what the subgraph IS; the config says how THIS instantiation is set up, and where content is mounted from is that kind of fact. Matched on id, never path — §”Inheritance”. The checkout root’s config has the last word. | One resolver, and every consumer asks it: declaredSubgraph(start, id) in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts, through resolveSubgraphSource. Precedence: config override → source → a legacy storage → directory. The answer carries declaredIn, so an override is never silent. Never read source off the declaration yourself — that skips the override. | storage maps exactly: storage: { branch, keyedBy } is source: { kind: "branch", branch, keyedBy }. The resolver reads either and refuses an entry carrying both — two answers to one question. A qa subgraph keyed by tip is refused whichever field says it. storage is the LEGACY spelling: write source in a new entry. The presence checks (materialiseDirectories, check:declared-dirs, audit:coverage) ask contentIsOffCheckout, which honours both. | Mounting dispatches on the kind, and the process is processes/kg/mount-subgraph.bpmn: directory is the checkout path in place (a write is a commit); branch + tip is mounted from the tip and spliced back without force (branch-store mount/push); remote is another repository’s tree at a full 40-character pin, laid down and locked by mount:remote and never written back (the remote-mount skill); a kind with no flow is refused with its own exit code rather than read as an empty directory. A remote mount’s effective path must not collide with downstream declared directories, reserved root/route names (RESERVED_ROOT_AND_ROUTE_NAMES), or sibling mounts (checkMountPathCollisions). | The KG export publishes the resolved source on the Subgraph node, as contentSource — dcterms:source, with kind (dcterms:type), branch (dcterms:identifier), keyedBy and declaredIn scoped inside it. A GitHub-hosted branch gets an @id that is its tree URL. | . Which layer a kind is in does not follow from its source. todos is state on main and still state on cat/cat-harness/todos; a context graph could be mounted from a branch and stays read-only. See content-context-and-state-graphs. Where a NEW layer’s state lives — on its own branch, by default . This subsection owns the rule. The scaffold skills (getting-started, folio_init) point here and do not restate it. A scaffold that writes beans/ and todos/ on main without declaring them leaves nothing able to say where its work plan lives, so the scaffold asks the source resolver. | The default is a property of the KIND, read once at scaffold time. A graph typology may carry newInstanceSource: { kind: "branch", keyedBy: "tip" }, beside perInstance. beans, todos and fsh-guts carry it (fsh-guts so a new layer’s first cutover has somewhere to deposit — see the main half below). It is a storage fact and says nothing about holds: fsh-guts stays context. It has no branch, because a kind has no branch name to give. folio_init composes the name and writes a complete source into the new layer’s own <instance>.json. After that the declaration is the one answer. The resolver never reads newInstanceSource, so it is not a second place answering where the content lives. It also cannot move an existing layer whose entry declares no source. | The branch name is cat/<instance>/<directory-id>, built by instanceStateBranch in schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts. For example, the dpi-h-ra layer’s branches are cat/dpi-h-ra/beans and cat/dpi-h-ra/todos (the cat/<harness>/<name> convention applied to a folio). One name does three jobs: . | it names the declaration (<instance>.json); | it prefixes the work item ids (.beans.yml → <instance>-); | it names the state branches. | . The last segment is the directory id, the key that branch-store mount --id and state:seed --id use. | folio_init resolves each state graph through the one resolver (after writing the declaration and config, so a subgraphSources override is honoured), and acts on the resolved source: . | resolved | what folio_init does | . | branch | Declares the graph. Does not write it into the checkout. Adds /<path>/** to .gitignore so a mount is never committed. Prints the seed command. | . | directory | Writes the graph and declares it. | . | Seeding is printed, not performed. No platform command creates a new state branch: . | branch-store refuses to (“seeding … is a steward act”); | state:seed only refreshes an existing seed. | . So folio_init prints a self-contained shell block. Run it once from the new repository. It pushes an orphan tip branch holding: . | a state-manifest/v1 manifest marked authoritative: true, because a new layer has no main copy; | a README; | the graph’s starting files. For beans, those are beans/beans.json and beans/defs/, and the seed must carry them: beans:claim reads beans.json from the branch and refuses to guess where defs is. | . Then state:mount puts each branch at its declared path. | Cutting an EXISTING layer over is two halves, and both have a command. Run both from the layer’s own repository. Every default is the cwd’s git toplevel, and --repo-root <dir> overrides it. | The branch half: state:seed --id <id> --authoritative. The branch becomes the store. | The main half: state:seed --id <id> --cutover. It is a dry run that reports files and bytes and the deposit it would make. Add --commit to deposit, then stage git rm -r <path> and a /<path>/** ignore line as one commit naming the branch, the tree id and the deposit. It never pushes main. It refuses unless all of these hold: . | the manifest says authoritative: true; | the manifest says keyedBy: "tip", or the mount would be corrupt; | a declaration keeps the path on that branch; | nothing under the path is uncommitted; | HEAD:<path> and the branch’s <path> are the same tree id, so the two copies are byte-identical; | the directory’s own layer declares a fsh-guts graph kept at a branch tip, and the deposit into it lands and re-reads verified. | . | . What a cutover removes goes to fsh-guts first — the one rule for it. Before any git rm, --commit packs <path>/ at HEAD with git archive, checks the pack extracts to the same tree id it is about to remove, and splices the existing retired/ pair onto the trashcan’s tip through branch-store (never a force push, expect: null so it never overwrites): retired/cutover-<instance>-<dir>-<tree12>.tar.gz plus a same-basename .md declaring folio-fsh-guts/v1, kind: cutover-snapshot, movedFrom, movedOn, reason: cutover, the layer, sourceCommit, tree and authoritativeBranch. It re-reads the tip, and only if both blobs are there does it make the removal commit. No trashcan declared, a trashcan not on a tip, a branch that is not there, or a push that did not land: refused, main untouched, with the fix named. This is not a second disposal of work items — the branch is still the live store; the deposit is the copy main last held. deletion-requires-confirmation still governs: the dry run is the report, and --commit is only run on the owner’s explicit go. Then run state:mount. | A state directory nobody declared is a finding: undeclared-state in check:declared-dirs. Every other check there compares declarations to disk. This one runs the other way, for the conventional state paths only (DEFAULT_DIRECTORIES entries whose kinds all holds: "state"). It reports and never removes anything. Whether to move the content off main is the owner’s call (deletion-requires-confirmation). | .

391.title: What a derived subgraph is computed FROM — derivedFrom
391.content: source and storage say where a directory’s content is kept. derivedFrom says what it is computed from: the declared directory ids of the graphs whose change can invalidate it. { "id": "smart-trust-docs", "path": "docs/", "graphTypologies": ["docs"], "derivedFrom": ["smart-trust-artifact-index"] } . Three rules: . | The edge sits on the DERIVED side. The writer of a derived graph is what knows its inputs, so the edge points down the stack: an IG’s pages name its artefact index, and the index never lists the pages. A source-side edge would make upstream graphs name graphs above them. | Generated pages and ingested indexes are in the derived layer, as library/ is, so a QA finding against them goes to their generator. | An edge across a missing needs path is a RATCHET, not an error. Example: an IG’s pages are styled by the DAK layer’s chrome, but the IG does not need the DAK layer. The gate holds such an edge as a baselined layering gap with a reason. The dependency stays declared and the gap stays visible. | . Data graphs only. A generator is code. The staging cone reaches it through its import closure, so code is not declared a second time here. Rendering order is a topological order over derivedFrom. Until the gate computes it, the order in which directories are declared is the rendering order, and a consumer declared before its source is flagged. Absent means “not declared”, not “derived from nothing”. A directory in the derived layer either names its sources or says why not: a library/ is derived from an external publication, which is not a declared graph. Silence is not an answer. The gate is check:derived-from. The storage clock — a derived artefact is kept no closer to main than its inputs (STRICT) . A derived artefact can be current in a commit only if every input it is computed from is kept in the commit. Follow derivedFrom upstream; if any input is kept on a BRANCH (a source that is not a directory, or a storage), that input moves without a commit, and a committed copy of the artefact is stale on main and on every open PR the moment somebody writes there. No :check gate can hold it current, because the check and the input are on different clocks. A visualisation is a derived artefact of the directory it shows. The edge is implicit: a viewer of X is computed from X by definition. So the rule covers viewer pages as well as derived directories (caches, auto-docs, IG pages). | inputs, transitively | where the artefact is kept | what holds it current | . | all in the checkout | committed | its :check gate, at every commit | . | any on a branch | built at publish, never committed — gitignored | derive:publish, which runs its declared writer after state:mount | . What is declared: . | the visualisation (or derived directory) names its writer — the script derive:publish runs. A visualisation built at publish with no writer is refused (publish-without-writer): nothing would build it; | nothing else. Which artefacts are built at publish is DERIVED from the edges and the inputs’ storage, never listed — not in a workflow, not here. The next graph moved onto a branch (work items, todos) carries its viewers with it by declaring their writers. | . What is checked, by check:derived-from: . | a tracked artefact with a branch-kept input is refused (committed-from-branch), naming the chain to the input; | --list on derive:publish prints what will be built and why. | . What the readers do: a visualisation built at publish resolves by its writer, not by the disk (visualisationResolves in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts). Subgraph coverage, harness tiles and viewer declarations all ask that one function, so the generated docs/_data/harness.json is the same whether or not a checkout happens to hold a locally built copy. Asking the disk would emit one answer locally and another in CI. The failure it prevents. A viewer committed on main while its input is kept on a branch goes red on main and on every open PR at once the moment somebody pushes to that branch, and each PR has to regenerate and commit the page. A take-base merge pattern only makes the collision cheap; building at publish removes it. Publishing a subgraph’s contents — the declared Subgraph node is the container (STRICT) . A declared subgraph is a Subgraph node plus its content nodes. A generator that publishes the contents of a declared subgraph (a todos.jsonld, a work items graph, a library index) does NOT mint its own collection node for them. It: . | uses the declared Subgraph node’s IRI as the container @id — <doc dir>/directory/<id>, from declaredSubgraphNode in kg-export.ts, which is the same function the node itself is minted by — typed Subgraph, with hasPart to each member (kg-export §”Subject IRIs — a path, not a #fragment”). Take the IRI from declaredSubgraphNode, never by composing it; | gives every member inSubgraph → that IRI (dcterms:isPartOf, the same term the KG export uses for the same edge); | carries the subgraph’s resolved contentSource, so a branch-sourced subgraph names its branch; | mints nothing parallel — no schema:Collection, no <Kind>Graph. | . The helpers are subgraphContainer and memberOf in scripts/subgraph-node.ts, and subgraphPublicationFindings is the check: subgraph-node.test.ts runs it over every adopting publisher. Converting a publisher adds its row there. The declaring layer’s document must be published for the @id to dereference. Which documents are published, and where: instance-publication §”What each layer publishes”. Do not restate the subgraph’s name on a container written to <dir>/<id>.json. A file whose name equals its stem is what findDeclarationFile reads as a LAYER declaration, and the site directory becomes a layer root that hides the checkout from every resolver. A consumer never spells a declared directory’s path (ENFORCED) . Because a subgraph’s source can move — from a directory to a branch, and then somewhere else, overridable per layer — a literal "fsh-guts/…" or join(root, "beans", "defs") breaks on the move, or goes vacuous and reads nothing. So read the location through its resolver (directoryForGraph, fshGutsDirectory, beanDefsDir, declaredSubgraph, …). Two ratchets enforce this, and neither fails just because a count goes down: . | gate | what it scans | baseline | . | check:declared-paths | a layer’s literals into its OWN declared directories | cat-harness-tools/scripts/declared-path-baseline.json | . | check:foreign-paths | a layer’s literals into ANOTHER layer’s directories, across the whole checkout | cat-harness-tools/scripts/foreign-path-baseline.json — empty | . | Classify a hit by what it READS, not by how it is spelled. A name counts as foreign only if the scanning layer does not declare the same name. A docs/ joined onto a STAGED layer’s root, or matched inside that layer’s own declaration, belongs to that layer even though the name coincides. | A site that cannot read a declaration says why, on the line above: // declared-path-literal: <reason>. The reason is required. A marked site is still reported, just not counted. Legitimate cases: the convention fallback for a layer that declares nothing, an ignore file, and a path inside another layer’s declaration. | A file that exists today is not a stable path. The move is the expected case, so literals naming an existing file are a one-way baseline: a NEW literal naming an existing file fails the gate, and --update may drop a witness but refuses to add one, so the list only shrinks. Accepting a literal because its file exists would fire only once the file moves. | The known blind spot: only the first literal of a path call is read, so resolve(opt("todos") ?? "todos") hides its default. Review such a default by hand. | .

392.title: Three states, as everywhere else here
392.content: . | No declaration → readDeclaration returns undefined. An layer not yet migrated is ordinary, and callers fall back to today’s conventions. Not an error. | Present but unreadable → throws. A declaration nobody can parse leaves every consumer scanning the wrong directories, which is strictly worse than not having one. | An unknown graph typology → rejected, not accepted and ignored. | .

393.title: Declare what exists
393.content: A directory that is declared but absent is worse than one that is missing: every consumer scans nothing and reports a clean run over it. This repository’s own declaration is the worked example, and no count is given here on purpose: <name>.json is the list; a number in prose is a claim nothing checks. Ids are stable across a relocation, paths are not, and it declares nothing it does not have.

394.title: storage — a directory kept on a branch
394.content: A ContentDirectory may declare where its contents are KEPT when that is not the checkout (schema DirectoryStorageSchema in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts, or its modern source: { kind: "branch", ... } spelling in schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts): . // Derived / QA: commit-keyed { "id": "qa", "path": "test/results", "graphTypologies": ["qa"], "storage": { "branch": "qa-reports", "keyedBy": "commit" } } // State / work-plan: tip-keyed { "id": "beans", "path": "beans/", "graphTypologies": ["beans"], "storage": { "branch": "cat/cat-harness/beans", "keyedBy": "tip" } } . A graph on another ref is still a declared directory, mounted at the declared path. Declaring storage or a branch source does not make it a separate concept from a directory. The layer still accesses the graph at its declared path (beans/, todos/, test/results/), whether via a working mount (e.g. worktree mounted by state:mount at session start) or an in-memory branch store. | keyedBy: "commit" (derived/QA): Writers write the declared working copy path, and bun run cat qa:publish carries it to the branch under main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/. Readers go through qa-store (readQa, bun run cat qa:fetch), which answers hit / miss / corrupt / unknown. | keyedBy: "tip" (state graphs: work items, workflow instances, todos): Represents a single living tree where the branch tip IS the state. Writers write to the mounted path and push via BranchStore (branch-store.ts push or bun run cat state:push), which splices changes onto the remote tip and pushes without force (-f), retrying if the tip moved. Claims and updates are immediately visible globally. | Presence checks stop expecting unmounted files on main: a stored directory absent from the checkout tree on main is not “declared but absent”, and harness:dirs does not create it empty. audit:coverage reads its kind as stored via contentIsOffCheckout. | . Every qa directory declares storage. Each stored working copy is ignored by version control, one line per declared directory, kept equal to the declarations by directory-storage.test.ts. A directory whose every kind may leave main (qa, health — mayLeaveMain in scripts/qa-results.ts) may be absent from a checkout without that being a finding. Judgements never move: they are the attestations kind at test/attestations/, on main, because a regenerated file cannot reproduce them. Flip a directory to storage only after every reader has migrated; flipping it earlier tells the presence checks to stop looking while readers still read the checkout. A branch’s README is rendered, not written . Every special branch says what it is at its root, and a reader cannot recover three of those facts from its files: its status (the store, a seed, or retired), its provenance (the commit it was seeded from, and when) and how it is written. A branch without them cannot be told from an abandoned one. They are KG already, in two places, and the README is rendered from both by bun run cat branch:readme (cat-harness-tools): . | the declarations — every directories[] entry whose storage or branch source names the branch, read where each layer declares it. Never a central table of branches: each harness (and each layer) declares its own; | the branch’s root manifest.json, state-manifest/v1, whose field set is schemas/kg/state-manifest.ts: one shape for a tip-keyed branch (seed commit, graphs) and one for a route-keyed branch (writer, gate). | . branch:readme:check reports each declared branch current, stale (absent, hand-written, or behind its sources) or unknown (the branch or its manifest could not be read, or the manifest does not parse); --push <branch> replaces the README with a describing write, the one write that may touch it. The commit-keyed QA branch carries no manifest and is described as derived from its declarations alone. A family (branchPrefix) has one README per member, rendered from the family’s declaration and the member’s manifest, and a branch a declared Tool publishes (gh-pages) is that Tool’s to describe.

395.title: Authoring an entry — the checklist
395.content: The rules are argued elsewhere in this skill and its neighbours; this is the list to run down when you add or edit a directories[] entry, with where each one is argued. | id, path, graphTypologies — required. Refer to the entry by id everywhere else; ids are stable, paths are not (§”Declare what exists”, §”Inheritance”). Pick each kind by what a process does with it (content-context-and-state-graphs). | title — a short noun phrase a reader would put on a tab. It is the directory README’s heading; absent, the heading falls back to the id and subgraph-readmes records a no-title finding. | description — one or two sentences for a reader: what the directory holds and what it is for, 60 words at most (DESCRIPTION_WORDS, finding long-description). It is printed under the README heading. History, rulings, measurements and argument go in a _description_comment on the same entry (the _<field>_comment convention the entries already use) — _ keys are annotations every loader drops (§”Node schemas, one per $schema family”). | Declare only what exists, or say why not with absent: { reason }. Where its content comes from is source — omit it for the checkout directory; a branch source names its branch on the entry itself (§”Where a subgraph gets its content”). | coverage — the skill that governs it and the docs that say what it is for; an opt-out carries its reason (SubgraphCoverageSchema). Without a skill the directory is unreachable by an agent even where a person can read it. The visualiser is NOT declared here: the harness declares it, at its own level, in visualisers — covers this directory’s id (or coversKinds its kind), renderedBy a Tool — and it is published at <base>/<harness>/<visualiser>/[<sub-graph>/], computed by visualiserRoute (harness-tiles §”Where a tile goes”). A directory never names its page, and a page never claims a directory; two declarations on one route fail check:visualiser-routes. The visualiser is where a node’s RENDERING IRIs are derived from; the node never names them — kg-viewer §”The asset and its rendering are two resources with two IRIs”. | The files inside declare what they are — front matter, a $schema, a leading comment — never an extension or a location (§”A sub-sub-graph”, §”Every other marker”). The README’s “what it is” column reads exactly that, so a file that says nothing shows as a gap. | Generated or authored — say which, in the file. A generated file carries the markers of the region it owns (readme-sections) or a header naming the command that wrote it, is never hand-edited, and has a --check twin in CI. | A missing fact is a QA finding, never a blank or a guess — the three states of §”Three states, as everywhere else here”. Record it as a QA result under test/results/ (the working copy qa-publish stores on the qa-reports branch); do not fill it with a plausible default. | Then regenerate: bun run cat readme:subgraphs renders the directory’s README from this entry (liquid-templates), and bun run cat kg:export publishes the entry as a Directory node (kg-export). | .

396.title: Naming — a self-identifying declaration, stub-named artefacts (STRICT)
396.content: The declaration carries three publication fields beside name: . | field | meaning | . | stub | filename stem of every artefact this layer publishes. Defaults to name. | . | canonicalUrl | where those artefacts live — the base every @id/$id is minted against | . | previewUrl | where CI previews are served, when that differs | . Modelled on WHO’s SMART Base repository’s dak.json (ours is the dak section of index.config.json’s contentTypes), which carries canonicalUrl, publicationUrl and previewUrl and derives its stub by stripping the repository’s prefix (smart-<stub> → <stub> → https://smart.who.int/<stub>), so stub, directory and published path are one word. The rule, and it is enforced by test: . | Every published artefact is named <stub>.* — <stub>.jsonld, <stub>.schema.json. Never a generic kg.json. Compute it with artefactStub(), never by re-deriving it, so two exporters cannot disagree about what this layer is called. | The declaration file is <name>.json — named for the layer’s name, NOT its stub. It is the one file here not computed with artefactStub(): instanceDeclarationFilename() spells it, and instanceConfigFilename() spells the <name>.config.json beside it. artefactStub() is stub ?? name, so the two coincide for every layer declaring no stub. A coincidence in the data is not the rule: a layer declaring a differing stub publishes <stub>.jsonld beside a <name>.json, and composing either from the other resolves to nothing. | The renderable site lives at docs/<stub>/. Compute it with siteDir(d) or siteDirFor(root), never by writing the path out. | . Where each <stub>.jsonld is served, which base its @ids are minted against, and what is stripped from it are not naming rules: instance-publication §”What each layer publishes — graph, address, schema, and what is stripped”. Identity: repository and livesAt . name is what needs edges and filenames resolve against, but it is not an identity outside the layer: it names no forge or owner, and two owners may each publish a layer of the same name. So the declaration also says which repository the layer is: . | field | meaning | . | repository | owner/name: the planned home, e.g. litlfred/cat-harness | . | livesAt | { repository, path }: where it sits today, when not at the root of repository | . It is planned rather than current because IRIs are keyed by it and must survive a split. Where the layer sits before the split lives in livesAt (for example, a directory of a monorepo). Leaving livesAt out asserts that the layer already sits at its own repository’s root. Never keep an owner/repo table by hand. instanceRepositories(checkoutRoot, folioRoot?) in schemas/kg/instance-repositories.ts derives the owner/repo ↔ name ↔ root map. It reads the declarations in the checkout and in the folio’s dependency overlay, and it throws when two layers claim one repository. instance-repositories.test.ts is the gate. It checks three things: . | every layer declares repository; | every livesAt.path is where the layer actually sits; | every livesAt names one host. | . A reference to another layer names its repository, never its name. The instance field of a voice rule’s source, a voice’s sources[], a RoleRef, a ThemeRef and an AssetSource is typed RepoFullName, so a bare name does not parse. Every resolver matches the reference through declaresInstance, which accepts either form, because needs edges and internal callers still speak in names. instance-repositories.test.ts checks that every committed reference resolves. The owner/repo → IRI map is derived too. repositoryNamespaces() gives each repository’s vocabulary namespace. One rule, instanceNamespace, produces it, and the glossary uses the same rule: . | a layer that declares iriBase mints under its own release’s major, <iriBase>v<major>/ns#; | one that declares none mints under the platform site, <stem><stub>/ns#. | . code-lists/own-namespaces.json still lists these namespaces, because code reads them by code. The gate fails when the list spells one differently from what the declaration derives. So moving a layer’s IRIs is one edit, to its declaration’s iriBase, and the list follows. cat-harness and the content core declare an iriBase on their planned repositories’ hosts, versioned as bootstrap’s is: . | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/ | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/ | . Their namespace documents are published beside the site, as bootstrap’s are. Every other marker: THE TYPE DECLARES ITS OWN FILENAME (STRICT) . The rule above covers the root declaration and published artefacts. For every other marker — the files by which a repository asserts what it is — there is no uniform spelling and there cannot be one: . | marker | who owns the name | . | sushi-config.yaml | SUSHI reads that exact name, and it is YAML | . | index.config.json contentTypes.dak | ours. It is a SECTION, not a file: the content type declares { indexSection: "dak" } (IndexSectionMarker). WHO’s SMART Base still writes and reads dak.json; an IG’s build reads that file into the index for one build, with a warning, until the IG moves it | . | index.config.json contentTypes.ig | The FHIR layer’s. A repository declares itself the source of a FHIR IG with this section, registered as { indexSection: "ig" } by https://github.com/litlfred/fhir-harness/blob/main/schemas/ig-content-type.ts. Carrying sushi-config.yaml alone does not declare an IG. The section’s include lists the paths the harness reads. See “A marker declares what is read”, below | . | <name>.json, <name>.config.json | ours | . | beans.json, todos.json | ours, and named after the graph TYPOLOGY | . One of those is not ours to rename — sushi-config.yaml, whose name SUSHI owns — so any rule claiming to cover the set would be false. So the type declares its filename, and the convention is that rule rather than a spelling. What a new type copies is say what your marker is called, not a pattern to imitate. <slug>.config.json everywhere would rename what WHO owns. The declaration file identifies itself. findDeclarationFile admits a *.json only when its name field EQUALS its own filename stem, and findInstanceRoot calls it rather than testing a word agreed in advance. So beans/beans.json, which shares the {name, directories} shape but declares "name": "folio-assistant" against the stem beans, is not a layer root — refused by what the file says it is, not by a path exception. Discovery still works, because a consumer matches on the file agreeing with itself. At the graph-typology level this is GraphTypologyDef.declarationFile. A nested declaration’s filename is named by its kind, not computed as ${basename(path)}.json: a relocation (beans/ to work/) must not make the walk look for work/work.json while the file is still work/beans.json. BEAN_GRAPH_FILE and TODO_GRAPH_FILE derive from the kind, and the directory-name convention remains only as a fallback for a kind that declares none. A marker declares what is read, and nothing else is . A harness can point to a repository without taking in all of its content: the harness declares what it pays attention to. A content-type section is the harness’s explicit statement of which parts of the repository it reads. It is not a flag that brings in the whole repository. contentTypes.ig is the first section to carry such a statement: its include is a list of repository-relative POSIX paths, where an entry ending in / covers a directory. The rules: . | The FHIR layer’s assertIgDeclares refuses any path that is not on the list. | A section with no include, or an empty one, declares nothing. It is never read as “everything”. | The list bounds this harness only. SUSHI and the IG Publisher still read their own inputs. | A repository that declares no contentTypes.ig is a legacy IG: the FHIR layer reads it whole, as before, and warns once per repository per run that the section is missing. The warning is the prompt to declare it, not noise to silence. | Every IG reader in the FHIR layer asks its scripts/ig-read-scope.ts before it reads a path. To make one see a path it skips, add the path to include; that layer’s ig-build-pipeline skill, §”What this layer reads”, says how: https://github.com/litlfred/fhir-harness/blob/main/skills/fhir-ig-base/ig-build-pipeline.md | . A new section-shaped type should follow the same pattern: declare the paths it reads beside the marker, and read nothing else. docs/<stub>/ — the site is packaged for the split (STRICT) . The stub that names <stub>.jsonld also names the directory holding this layer’s renderable site: docs/<stub>/, not docs/. Each layer is its own repository, so under its own stub a split is a directory move rather than a file-by-file sift, and two layers can be checked out side by side. No published URL changes, because Jekyll is pointed at the stub directory as its source root (source: ./docs/<stub>), leaving the site’s internal layout untouched. It is not the folio graph-typology declaration. Declaring docs/ with the folio kind in the harness makes readers that do not load core’s registration throw unknown graph typology "folio", because folio is contributed by core. siteDirFor throws rather than defaulting when a layer declares neither stub nor name — a guessed site root writes the whole site where nothing serves it, and “could not determine” is not an answer. scripts/tests/site-dir-single-answer.test.ts fails on any new docs/… literal in a path-resolving position (prose is left alone), including in a clean merge from a branch cut before a move.

397.title: The declaration is itself a graph
397.content: toJsonLd() projects a declaration into the folio namespace: each directory is a node with an @id and an @type. The set of directories a layer scans is then queryable by the same machinery as anything else in the knowledge graph, rather than being configuration only one module understands. The authored form is the stored one and the graph form is derived — one truth, not two. readDeclaration accepts either, and a round-trip test pins that: the projection emits @type instead of graph, so reading the published form back without the reverse lookup silently loses the one field that says what a directory holds.

398.title: Skills are KG content
398.content: The skills graph is where skills live, and that is why they are addressed through the declaration rather than by path. An agent asks skill_list / skill_fetch for a skill; it does not open skills/<something>.md from memory. A layer may site its skills anywhere — this repo’s skills id points at skills/ — and a downstream layer inherits its dependencies’ skills through the same inheritance rules above. A hardcoded path breaks on the first relocation, which is the whole reason overrides match on id. Roles, processes and decisions are KG content too . The knowledge graph is not only skills. It holds the whole actor → role → skill → task model: . scenarios/roles.json the ROLE GRAPH — a role is a BPMN swimlane skills/ ← this instance's `skills` graph requirements/*.json conformance obligations pointing at the rest permissions/permissions.json the actions an actor may be permitted (the ODRL profile; who holds them is policies/) <group>/<pkg>/*.md skills <group>/<pkg>/package-manifest.json which skills a package publishes . and the processes those roles act in — processes/**/*.bpmn and processes/**/decisions/*.dmn — are reached through the skill that describes them, not as standalone artefacts. A BPMN activity names the skill that implements it (<bootstrap.processes:skill ref>); a lane names the role its tasks are performed in (partitionElementRef → a <bpmn:resource> whose id is the role id); a role carries the skills its lane’s activities need. bun run cat kg:audit checks every one of those joins and writes a sidecar per node. Model and resolution rules: role-model.md; schema: schemas/process/role-graph.ts.

399.title: Layering — a harness module must not import the content vocabulary
399.content: The declaration schema needs the platform’s IRI namespace to mint @type values. It lives in schemas/kg/namespaces.ts, a leaf that imports nothing, classified to the harness — not in schemas/kg/jsonld.ts, which is the content core’s content vocabulary (block kinds, DoCO structural types, SPAR citation terms), because importing that would make the harness depend on the content model for its own type IRIs: a harness → core edge. The direction only works one way round — core may import the harness; the harness may not import core — so a constant both layers need lives at or below the harness. Do not duplicate the constant with a test asserting the copies stay equal: a drift guard is an admission that there are two definitions. Extract instead, and re-export from the old home so existing importers are untouched. cat-harness.test.ts pins the property structurally — it asserts the module does not import ./jsonld or ./block-kinds. Reach for that test when adding anything else at the harness layer.

400.title: What lives in the schemas graph — one authored form, many renderings
400.content: The schemas directory holds schema definitions, and the convention for every one of them is the same: the Zod schema in .ts is authoritative, and every other form is generated from it. schemas/<thing>.ts (tools layer) ← AUTHORED. Zod + the inferred type. ├─→ schemas/kinds/<kind>.schema.json JSON Schema (validators, editors) └─→ a JSON-LD projection KG node (queryable) . The TypeScript type is z.infer<typeof Schema>, never declared alongside the schema — two declarations of one shape drift, and the drift is invisible until something reads the stale one. Both renderings have their mechanism, so adding a schema introduces no new machinery: bun run cat kind:json-schemas generates the JSON Schemas through Zod 4’s native z.toJSONSchema (schemas/README.md), and toJsonLd() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts is the worked example of the graph projection. Why Zod — the grounds, and what kind of ground each is . The choice is a JUDGEMENT on what the tool does — functionality and pragmatism, not a preference for .ts — and stating its grounds is what lets a later reader tell whether they still hold. Three are functional and checkable: . | It produces both renderings the graph needs — JSON Schema natively and the JSON-LD projection from the same definition — so there is one source. | Validation is easy, at author time (tsc, the editor) and at run time (.parse), with the TypeScript type inferred rather than restated. | A large, active community — a maintained library, so a converter change is a version bump, not a rewrite. | . One is a HOUSE RULE, and is labelled as one. In trials, agents hallucinated less authoring schemas in .ts than in the alternatives tried. A guess is that .ts is easier to digest, or costs fewer tokens. That is an observation, not a measurement, and it must not be quoted as evidence that .ts is better. It is a tie-breaker between options that pass the three functional grounds, never a reason on its own. What would reopen the decision: another carrier that meets all three functional grounds and measurably beats this one on something that matters here. “.ts is what we use” is not a ground, and nor is the house rule by itself. Keep the two kinds of ground apart when you argue it either way — running a preference and a measurement together is how a judgement comes to look like a fact. Generate as many renderings as have a consumer, and no more. JSON Schema because validators and editors speak it; JSON-LD because the KG query path does. A third — SHACL, an OpenAPI fragment, Turtle — is added when something needs it, not in anticipation: each is another file to regenerate and another chance for a stale artefact to be read as current. A rendering is never where a fix lands. If a generated .schema.json is wrong, the .ts is wrong; edit that and regenerate. A --check mode in CI — the pattern gen-skill-docs.ts --check already uses — is what makes that enforceable rather than merely asserted. Why not author the rendering and validate backwards . The tempting inversion is to hand-author the JSON-LD node, because it is the form the KG consumes, and validate it against Zod in CI. That is the same two artefacts with the authority pointing the wrong way, and it is worse for one reason: a hand-authored node is unchecked until CI runs. With Zod authoritative the schema is the type, so a malformed definition fails at tsc, in the editor, before it is committed. Validation-after-the-fact catches the same error strictly later and only if CI runs the suite. This holds for the Tools schema and for everything else in the schemas graph. Worked through in docs/concepts/architecture/cat-harness-minimum.md §”Carrying it”.

401.title: Adding a graph typology
401.content: Decide which layer owns it first — if it renders, it is not the harness’s. | A harness kind: one entry in BASE_GRAPH_TYPOLOGIES (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts). | A kind belonging to a layer above: a module like schemas/kg/folio-graph-typology.ts that calls registry.register(name, def) at import, so the harness never learns the name until that layer is loaded. | . Either way the definition is @type IRI + renderable + holds + summary, and the JSON-LD projection and the reverse lookup both derive from it. A kind added without deciding either axis will not compile. holds is the content/context/state one, and content-context-and-state-graphs is where you answer it — including the bar for adding a value at all, why there is no “could not determine”, and why it is compared by sameKind so two layers cannot register one name on different layers and have the first silently win. Note the declaration’s graphs field is validated against the registry at read time, not by a closed Zod enum. An enum would be built at module load — before core has registered folio — so it would reject the one kind the entire rendering pipeline depends on. Node schemas, one per $schema family . A kind says what shape its nodes have in up to three fields on GraphTypologyDef, and they answer different questions: . | field | answers | form | . | schema | where is the shape written down? | a module path, or an external-schema record | . | validator | what can I RUN against a node? | one Zod module#Export | . | nodeSchemas | which shape does THIS node have? | $schema tag → { validator } | { shape } | { writtenBy } | . nodeSchemas exists because one directory can hold several families, and a single validator then names one of them and says nothing true about the rest. qa holds seven. A node already says which family it is (its $schema tag), so the tag is the key. The three reference forms record three different facts: . | validator: a Zod schema. Runnable. | shape: a TypeScript interface, module#Name. Its fields can be read from source (readShape in schemas/kg/kind-validator.ts), but nothing can check a node against it. | writtenBy: nothing types the family. Name the module that writes it (or, for an authored file, the one that consumes it), so the gap is recorded as data rather than left out. | external: the node conforms to a specification nobody here types, such as a JSON Schema document (https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema). This is named rather than restated, and it is not a gap. | . A reference may name the harness that owns the module: folio-assistant-core:schemas/catalogue.ts#CatalogueSchema. It resolves through the layer that declares that name, never through ../. An escaping path is still refused, because it resolves into whatever checkout sits next door. This is how a harness kind whose node shapes live in core (catalogue, uploads, external-schema) says so honestly. Top-level _ keys are annotations (_comment, _note). The sweep drops them before parsing, as every loader here already does. The kinds without a node schema, and why — recorded so they are not re-opened: . | code: its nodes are TypeScript source, so the language is the schema. | methodology: its nodes are Markdown prose. | folio: core’s renderable kind. Its block manifests are typed by the content adapters, not by the registry. | bean-defs: Markdown in the third-party beans CLI’s layout. That CLI’s own GraphQL type Bean is drawn in uml/harness-object-model.puml. | cat-harness: on a directory beside another kind it is the umbrella, not a node kind. | . Declaring nodeSchemas claims the map is COMPLETE. check:kind-validators routes every JSON node in the kind’s declared directories by its tag. It fails on a tag the map does not name, on a reference that does not resolve, and on a node that fails its family’s Zod schema. kg:validate routes the same way. gen-uml-overview.ts draws one class per family.

402.title: Pinning a reference — a SHA may stage, only a version may publish
402.content: Downstream must align to FHIR and SUSHI — a hard constraint. A SHA is for staging; a published reference is a semver. A preview is staging, not published. Two tiers, and the tier is decided by whether a consumer may DEPEND on the artefact — not by whether they can reach it. That is why an externally reachable PR preview is staging: it is provisional, and nothing should pin to it. | tier | a reference may be | . | staging — working checkout, PR preview, branch under review | a submodule SHA, a git ref, a pre-release, or a version | . | published — anything an external consumer may depend on | semver only | . A SHA is an excellent pin and a useless published reference. It names a commit in a repository the downstream consumer may not have and may not be able to fetch — and in FHIR’s vocabulary cannot be stated at all: dependsOn carries packageId and version, and there is no field a SHA belongs in. A published artefact carrying one is not a stricter pin, it is an unresolvable one. Exact versions, never ranges. This is the FHIR rule, not the npm one, and it follows directly from the alignment constraint: a downstream that must resolve like SUSHI cannot be handed a range. No ref at all is the same defect, reached by default. An unpinned reference is current by omission — the pre-release choice made by nobody. current and dev are FHIR’s real pseudo-versions and belong in the staging tier with a SHA, deliberately chosen and written down. A REFERENCE is not PROVENANCE . The distinction is what makes this checkable, and both look identical in a published document — a hex string. |   | what it is | example | . | reference | a consumer must RESOLVE it to obtain another artefact | a dependency’s ref/version, an asset’s source | . | provenance | a record of where THIS artefact came from | the build stamp’s sha, sourceCommitSha | . A stamp saying “produced from commit abc123” asks nobody to fetch abc123. So classification is by KEY, declared in PROVENANCE_KEYS, never by the look of the value — a regex over the published JSON fails on the build stamp, which is the exported graph’s only 40-hex string. bun run cat check:published-refs enforces this; advisory, --strict to fail. It reports each carrier’s count even when that count is nought, because a gate that silently covers nothing and exits 0 is the most expensive recurring defect. Full scheme, including what a layer’s version means and what makes it go up: docs/proposals/instance-versioning.md.
