554.title: ig-artifact-ingestion
554.content: Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: ig-artifact-ingestion · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Covers fhir-harness’s fhir-artifact-index graph typology (schema fhir-harness/schemas/fhir-artifact-index.ts). The artefact index of a FHIR Implementation Guide is a knowledge graph keyed by the IG’s own canonical URLs, linking each artefact to its JSON, JSON Schema and JSON-LD representations. No IG publishes such an index itself, so it is always assembled, and it records what each part was built from. This skill says how an index is assembled in this harness; it does not judge whether an IG’s content is correct (that is fhir-validation’s job).

555.title: Which IGs carry the IG API overlay
555.content: Every IG gets an index; the JSON Schema and JSON-LD links come only from an IG API (WHO calls it the DAK API): the per-artefact sidecars and the enumeration schemas (ValueSets.schema.json, LogicalModels.schema.json) that dak-postprocessing steps 3–6 produce. The index’s sidecarApi says which: . | present — sidecars were found and bound to artefacts; | absent — the source was read and held none; | unknown — nobody looked. unknown is not a kind of absent: only absent is a reason to stop. | . An IG with no IG API is a thin index, not an error.

556.title: Where the index is built: at publish, from the AST
556.content: An IG instance does not commit its fhir-artifact-index/. fhir-harness’s ig-index:build (fhir-harness/scripts/build-ig-indexes.ts) writes it at publish: . | document | schema | built from | . | index.json | folio-fhir-artifact-index/v2 | the IG’s cached AST, by ast-to-artifact-index.ts; its manifest says authority: "cache" | . | menu.json | folio-ig-menu/v1 | the IG’s own sushi-config.yaml menu:, at the commit the checkout’s lock pins (buildMenu) | . | releases.json | ig-releases/v1 | the repository’s GitHub releases, as pointers to their assets; a failed read writes no file, because no list is not an empty list | . | package.tgz | — | the AST’s resources, as package/<Type>-<id>.json, with a package/package.json from sushi-config.yaml | . | sidecars/ | — | the IG API sidecars a layer above writes (ig-site:sidecars), bound to the artefacts | . | contexts/ | — | each .jsonld under input/images/ whose only key is @context | . ig-identity.json (folio-ig-identity/v1: id, canonical, version, status, read from sushi-config.yaml) sits beside them when present. An IG with no identity file has no status this pipeline can state and draws no watermark; that is not “published”. Each document has a different source, so each carries its own provenance. Folding two together would give one file two answers to “where did this come from”. The menu is the IG’s own ordering of itself . sushi-config.yaml’s menu: is a nested map, and order is the file’s order. Never sort it: that would re-navigate somebody else’s IG. Read it from the source config, never from a screenshot: a picture carries no hrefs, and a closed dropdown looks like an empty one. The chrome comes from a chain, and only part of it is the IG’s own . An IG declares its appearance in no file it owns: it comes from the fhir.template chain its ig.ini names, for example . local-template → who.template.root 0.5.0 → fhir.base.template 1.0.0 . So the chrome (folio-ig-chrome/v2) is keyed by the chain’s top template and lives once, in smart-base’s themes/chrome.json, worn by every IG on that chain. It carries layers base-first, and every token records which package won it and what it overrode, which is how to answer whose value is this? For example who.css styles no #publish-box, so the yellow box is HL7’s: the token comes out from: "fhir.base.template" with overrides: []. An overlay is not a merge. --toc-box-border is 1px solid navy in HL7 and navy in WHO — each right in its own layer, but together they make HL7’s rule resolve to border: navy, which is invalid. Every layer parses on its own, so a naive merge ships a broken rule silently. Upstream defects are recorded, never corrected . The chrome mirrors its sources, defects included, and records whose each defect is: . | shape — one token name carrying different kinds of value across layers, as above. | malformed — a value that is not valid CSS on its own terms, such as --breadcrumb-text-color: ##555555 (a doubled # in HL7’s project.css). | . A carried defect shows up in generated pages looking exactly like an ingest bug, which is why the record names its owner. The detector matches one narrow pattern: a false positive would accuse someone else’s stylesheet of a fault it does not have. ingest:ig-chrome:check compares the committed chrome with the template chain. CI cannot fetch the template repositories, so with no source it exits 2 (could not determine), never 0, and it is registered as a report, not a gate. Run it by hand after cloning the IG and its templates.

557.title: What the AST does not carry
557.content: . | Category. The Publisher assigns editorial categories when it writes artifacts.html, after the AST is taken. The index uses the Publisher’s default grouping by resource type and names every artefact where a published grouping differs (--keep-published-grouping keeps the grouping of a committed index still on disk). | Where it is published. A canonical URL is an identity, not an address. The published base is the committed copy’s source.of when that names a published site, else the instance declaration’s iriBase, else none, and the run says which. Never derive either the published base or canonicalBase from the other. | . AST-built artefacts are materialized with purpose compiled, and carry the gates of folio-assistant-core/schemas/materialization.ts. sourceLoss and copyright stay unknown until someone establishes them; a permitted there would claim “no restrictions known” without having looked.

558.title: What is never invented
558.content: . | canonical is optional. Examples and instance resources have no canonical URL and are most of a large IG. Minting one produces an identifier that resolves to nothing while looking authoritative. | category absent never means “Other”. The IG’s own artefact page has a literal Other section; a second one would make the word mean two things. | A lossy field is left absent, not repaired. An absent field is a fact; a repaired one is a guess. | .

559.title: When the source is a published site
559.content: The schema also accepts an index read from a published IG (source.kind gh-pages, output or url), with provenance naming the published file each part came from. These are different evidence: output/ is a local build, gh-pages is what the world can see; never label one as the other. A published IG offers four partial views, none sufficient alone: . | file | holds | misses | . | canonicals.json | canonical URL, version, name | every artefact without a canonical | . | package.tgz → package/.index.json | every artefact’s type and id | titles, categories, canonicals | . | artifacts.html | the editorial category and human title (per-row title is ResourceType/id) | anything machine-readable | . | package.manifest.json | package id, version, FHIR version, build date | — | . Traps: . | Read the source, not the page about it. dak-api.html links the enumeration schemas under schemas/, but they sit at the published root. | openapi/openapi.json is not the IG API. On the WHO SMART Trust IG it is the DDCC Gateway API, subject matter that lives there. Key the overlay off each artefact’s own stem (<ResourceType>-<id>.openapi.json), never a directory scan. | .index.json is lossy (Organization entries can carry a truncated "type": "["). canonicals.json is the spine for anything canonical; a field seen only in .index.json stays absent. | .

560.title: Running it
560.content: bun run cat ig-index:build -- [--only <instance>] [--work <dir>] [--plan] . --plan prints what would be built and touches nothing. Exit 0: every IG found was built; 1: one or more failed (each named); 2: usage. An IG instance is found, with no declaration of its own, when it needs fhir-harness (directly or through a layer above), declares a repository, and that repository carries an AST branch family. An instance missing any of the three is skipped, and the run says which and why. To add an IG, give it those three; never commit or hand-edit the index it produces.

562.title: ig-ast-delta
562.content: Skill ig-ast-delta: List and view what changed between two IG ASTs, check whether an AST is still valid for the IG’s current inputs, and render the delta as just-the-docs pages that carry the provisional mark. Read before trusting a cached AST, before reviewing an incremental IG build, and before rendering anything from a cache. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: ig-ast-delta · Package: fhir-ig-base · Layer: fhir-harness . An instance of the general compiled-artefact-cache pattern; the shared contract is cat-harness’s compiled-artefact-cache skill. The AST’s cache is declared once, as the cache/1.0.0 node caches/fhir-ast.cache.json: its verify is validity below, and its staleness is computed by caches:viz (see ig-build-pipeline §”The AST cache lifecycle”). An IG AST is a per-resource dump of what one IG Publisher build held in memory. It is written by the ast-export library, which is built on top of the Publisher rather than inside it (litlfred/fhir-ig-publisher@claude/ast-export, ast-export/). This skill is the consumer half: listing an AST, checking it, diffing two of them, and rendering the result for a reviewer.

563.title: The one rule: a cache, never an authority
563.content: Every AST manifest says "authority": "cache" and lists what is provisional until a full Publisher run: indices, dependency edges and versions. Anything rendered from an AST, or from a delta between two, shows that mark to the reader, on the page itself (ig-publisher-reduction P3). A mark that exists only in a log or a JSON field does not count.

564.title: Where the files come from
564.content: | file | written by | says | . | manifest.json (ig-ast/v1) | AstExportCli, AstMerger | every resource with its key, the toolchain, the inputs the AST is valid for, and, on an incremental AST, mixed: true and builtAt per resource | . | dependencies.json (ig-ast-dependencies/v1) | same | every edge, resolved to a resource in this IG or null when the target is elsewhere | . | fsh-index.json | SUSHI (copied by AstExportCli) | the authoritative mapping from source .fsh file to output resource filename, with source line ranges. SUSHI writes it to fsh-generated/data/fsh-index.json; the copy lets a later delta map a file that has since been deleted | . | plan.json (ig-ast-plan/v1) | AstPlanCli | what a delta of changed files means: rebuild, load from cache, remove, or a full build and why | . | delta.json (ig-ast-delta/v1) | ig-ast.ts diff (here) | what changed between two ASTs | . The formats are declared once, and published as JSON Schema . The three ig-ast* formats are declared in Zod in fhir-harness/schemas/ig-ast.ts, and readAst validates through it. The JSON Schemas (draft-07) and a JSON-LD context are generated from that declaration and committed beside it: . | ig-ast.schema.json | ig-ast-dependencies.schema.json | ig-ast-plan.schema.json | ig-ast.context.jsonld | . bun run cat ig-ast:schema regenerates them and ig-ast:schema:check is the CI gate. The Java writer and any downstream consumer validate against these files. Every object is open to fields the writer adds first; authority is the literal "cache", and a manifest claiming anything else is refused. A resource’s key is canonical|version, or Type/id when it has no canonical. Two ASTs are compared by key. An incomplete AST is refused: a missing dependencies.json or a missing or unparsable resource file stops the command, because an empty substitute would diff as “no change”.

565.title: Commands
565.content: All of them live in fhir-harness/scripts/ig-ast.ts, and each is declared as a Tool: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/ig-ast.ts list <ast> bun run fhir-harness/scripts/ig-ast.ts validity <ast> --ig <root> [--toolchain "<ig-publisher X / core Y>"] [--at <rev>] bun run fhir-harness/scripts/ig-ast.ts digest --ig <root> [--at <rev>] bun run fhir-harness/scripts/ig-ast.ts diff <base-ast> <head-ast> [--plan plan.json] [--json delta.json] [--site <dir>] bun run fhir-harness/scripts/ig-ast.ts render <delta.json> --site <dir> bun run fhir-harness/scripts/ig-ast.ts jsonld <ast> > ast.jsonld . validity: is this AST still the IG I have? . It reuses folio-assistant-core’s compiledValidity, the staleness check the Lean .olean cache uses. The Java side writes inputs in exactly CompiledInputsSchema’s shape: toolchain, sourceRevision, and inputDigest as 64 hex characters. validity recomputes the digest and the revision from the checkout and compares. | valid (exit 0): built from these inputs. | stale-inputs (exit 1): names which input differs. A changed input/ file is inputDigest; a newer Publisher is toolchain. | cannot-tell (exit 2): never a pass. A manifest without usable inputs, or with a digest in the older sha256:<hex> form, lands here. | . The digest is computed in two languages, Java when writing and TypeScript when checking. A golden vector (58871352384745e1d7fd68f7ea918b0e2febbd86cf36a9cb5f0c7ce9d13a82f1) is asserted by both test suites. If you change the algorithm, change it and the vector in both places; a drift makes every AST read as stale, or a stale one read as valid. A later commit that changes no input is the same source. If the recorded sourceRevision is an ancestor of HEAD and the recomputed inputDigest equals the recorded one, the revision counts as unchanged (sameSourceAs), so a README merge does not make the cache stale. A recorded commit the checkout cannot see (a shallow clone, another branch) stays stale. After a build, check the commit, not the work tree: --at <rev>. The Publisher writes under input/ during a build: it renders input/images-source/*.plantuml into input/images/*.svg, overwriting tracked files and adding untracked ones, so a work-tree digest taken after the build is not the commit’s and a freshly built AST fails its own check. validity --at HEAD (and digest --at HEAD) hashes the inputs as committed (inputDigestAt); in a clean checkout this equals the work-tree digest and the exporter’s. ig-ast-refresh.yml instead restores input/ with git before its check. The toolchain cannot be read from a checkout. Without --toolchain it is assumed unchanged, and the result’s current says so. When the Publisher you would run is known, pass it. diff: list what changed . Resources are added, removed, changed or versionChanged. A version move (same canonical, different version) is paired, not reported as a removal plus an addition. Each changed resource carries a differential: JSON paths whose value was added, removed or changed, capped at 200 rows per resource, with the overflow counted rather than dropped. Edges are listed as added or removed. --plan folds the incremental plan’s decision in. The differential is structural, over the dumped JSON, not FHIR-semantic: reordering a repeating element shows as a change at every index, and a narrative regenerated with a new timestamp shows as a change. Read it as “these bytes moved”, and judge meaning yourself. render: view it in the pipeline . --site <dir> writes just-the-docs pages: index.md (the list, grouped by resource type, with counts, the plan, and edge changes) and one page per changed or version-changed resource (path, op, base, head). | Every page opens with the provisional mark. Do not remove it to make a page look finished. | Liquid in values is neutralised, not merely wrapped. FHIR narratives carry Liquid output and tag delimiters (double braces, brace-percent). A raw block around the page is not enough: a value containing the raw block’s own closing tag would end it. So every value gets a word joiner (U+2060) inside each opening and closing delimiter; the text reads the same, and Jekyll parses nothing. This skill names those delimiters in words because its own reference page is rendered inside a raw block by gen-skill-docs; do not write the closing tag literally here. | One page per key, not per Type/id. Page names carry a hash of the key, as the AST’s own files do, so two versions of one resource are two pages. | Table cells escape |, which a key contains (canonical|version). | . Put the pages under the IG’s own just-the-docs site (see ig-render-jekyll) as a child section, so the reviewer keeps the site’s navigation.

566.title: Where this sits in a process
566.content: The review is drawn as its own subprocess, fhir-harness/processes/content/ig-ast-delta-review.bpmn. In fhir-harness/processes/content/ig-incremental-build.bpmn it belongs between Task_Merge (restored and rebuilt records merged) and Task_Qa (QC gates on the aggregate), which that diagram does not yet show: it is what the QC reviewer reads to decide whether the incremental result is what a full build would have produced. The steps, in order: . | validity on the base AST. stale-inputs or cannot-tell means no incremental build; run a full one. | AstPlanCli for the delta of changed files. The planner uses two maps: . | Forward (fsh-index.json, from SUSHI): which .fsh file produces which FHIR resource. This is the authoritative answer. | Reverse (fsh-file-users/v1, from fsh-cone --file-users): which files depend on a given file. This is how a changed RuleSet- or Alias-only file (which produces no resource itself) reaches the resources it affects. | . | IncrementalBuildCli (or a full build, if the plan says so). | diff base head --plan plan.json --site <site>/ast-delta/. | The reviewer reads the rendered delta. A difference they cannot explain is a missed coupling in the cone rules, not a curiosity: file it as a work item and run a full build. | .

567.title: Which rendered pages a source change reaches
567.content: Before any build, fhir-harness/scripts/ig-rendered-impact.ts predicts the rendered files a change to .fsh, .cql or input/pagecontent alters, through fsh-cone and SUSHI’s fsh-index.json, as a rendered-impact/v1 (skill rendered-impact in cat-harness). An AST diff afterwards confirms it: a resource the delta reports changed whose page the prediction did not name is a cone defect. bun run fhir-harness/scripts/ig-rendered-impact.ts --ig <root> --base origin/main --head HEAD [--ast <output-ast>] --out impact.json .

568.title: Do not
568.content: . | Do not treat a clean validity as a correct AST. It says the AST was built from these inputs, not that the build was right. | Do not diff a merged (mixed: true) AST against a full build and call every difference a bug. Check builtAt first. A resource carried from the base was not rebuilt, and the difference may be the change itself. | Do not render from an AST whose validity you did not check. | Do not re-implement any of this in a CI workflow. CI calls these same scripts and tools, so a CI result and a local result are the same measurement.github/workflows/ig-ast-refresh.yml (ig-build-pipeline §”The AST cache lifecycle”) does exactly that: ig-cache.sh, ig-ast.ts validity and AstExportCli. | .

571.title: index-ig
571.content: . This WHO Implementation Guide for Immunizations details how to use Health Level 7 (HL7) Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) for consistent digital representation of Immunization services. This implementation guide and set of artifacts are still undergoing development. Content is for demonstration purposes only. Summary . This implementation guide includes a machine-readable representation of WHO guidelines for Immunizations, as documented in the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for Immunizations (link forthcoming) and explicitly encodes computer-interoperable logic, including data models, terminologies, and logic expressions, in a computable language to support implementation of Immunization use cases by WHO Member States. The guide is part of the WHO SMART Guidelines approach to support countries to integrate WHO global health and data recommendations into digital systems accurately and consistently. It defines a series of FHIR Resources, Profiles, Extensions, and Terminology based on the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for Immunizations. Supporting guidance, recommendations, resources, and standards are included in the Bibliography and Dependencies. About this implementation guide . This implementation guide is broken into the following levels of knowledge representation: . | Home - contains references to the guidance, guidelines, policies and recommendations underpinning this implementation guide. | Business Requirements - contains the requirements for this implementation guide including the definition of key concepts, use cases, and a data dictionary. | Data Models and Exchange - contains the data models and data exchange protocols with actors and transactions defined. | Deployment Guidance - contains relevant technical specifications and guidance, testing resources, reference implementation materials, and supporting guidance for adaptation to local contexts. | . This guide is prepared to facilitate digital implementation of WHO Immunization guidelines by providing FHIR-based computable representations of and implementation guidance for using the key components of the WHO Digital adaptation kit (DAK) for immunizations: . | Health Interventions & Recommendations | Generic Personas | User Scenarios | Business Processes & Workflows | Core Data Elements | Decision Support Logic | Indicators & Monitoring | Functional & Non-functional Requirements | . This guide is a companion to the Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) and should be used side-by-side with it. Implementers are strongly encouraged to make use of the Digital Adaptation Kit. The focus of this guide is on the explanation and use of the computable artifacts. This guide assumes use of the following resources: . | IPS Patient | CPG ActivityDefinitions . | For a complete listing of the artifacts defined in this implementation guide, refer to the Artifact Index. | A complete offline copy of this implementation guide can be found on the Downloads page. | This Implementation Guide makes use of Clinical Quality Language for the decision support artifacts including the PlanDefinitions and Measures. They are used to express how a calculation should occur and can be used with a CQL engine in order to process the decision or indicator directly from the applicable FHIR resources. Links to this specification, the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Speciciation, and other helpful resources can be found in the Support dropdown. | . Disclaimer . This draft is provided without warranty of completeness or consistency and the official publication supersedes this draft. 573.title: l1-extractions/9789240116191-eng/ (l1-extraction-9789240116191-eng)
573.content: Not inside a library entry. Scroll horizontally to see all columns → . | locale | catalogues / templatesQ1: availability | entriesQ2: strings | translated | fuzzy | untranslated | officialQ3: signed off | . | ar Arabic | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 120 | 120100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | es Spanish | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 120 | 120100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | fr French | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 120 | 120100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | ru Russian | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 120 | 120100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | zh Chinese | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 120 | 120100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . Two questions, not one. catalogues / templates asks whether a .po exists at all for each extractable .pot; the string columns ask how much of the catalogues that DO exist is done. A locale can be near 100% translated across a handful of catalogues while most of its templates have none — which is why the first column is not folded into the rest. “no basis” is not zero. A share over an empty denominator is undefined, and rendering it as 0% would report a measurement this run did not make. One directory per table, each named. translation-sources is a graph KIND, and more than one instance may declare it; the first table measures the directory named in the subtitle, and each instance below it gets its own table for its own declared directory. They are never summed: two instances' catalogues answer two questions. A catalogue sitting in an instance that has not declared the directory is invisible here — which is a gap in that declaration rather than a locale with no work done, and the two must not read the same. Fuzzy is counted apart from translated. A fuzzy entry has a translation and needs review; adding it to translated would flatter exactly the entries a reviewer must look at.

726.content: . | All instances | smart-base | smart-immunizations | . A document kind is a named structure of sections that a document authored with a harness follows: fixed (exactly these sections) or semi-fixed (these required, others allowed). Every kind and section names its sources.

727.title: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) dak
727.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . Sources: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099456 — WHO DAK guidance; https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085138 — WHO DAK guidance; https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant/issues/1614 — owner ruling 2026-09-30: ten components . 728.title: Digital Transformation Handbook (DTH) dth
728.content: A WHO guidance publication on digitalising one area of a health system — an L1 publication whose body is a planning method rather than recommendations. It sits within the DIIG process and should use the DPI-H Reference Architecture (owner, 2026-10-01). Its domain sections map onto smart-kg L2 (DAK) classes: a DTH states for a health-system area what a DAK states for a guideline. Structure read from the three DTHs ingested in smart-base/library; a section is required only where all three have it. The Reference Architecture for DPI-H calls itself "A Digital Transformation Handbook for DPI-H" and is cited here as the architecture the others should reference. semi-fixed structure · 22 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dth.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Audience and how to use this handbookaudience-and-how-to-use | required | Target users/roles per chapter and the stepwise reading path through the handbook.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng, 2. 731.title: L2 Digital Transformation Handbook (DTH) l2-dth
731.content: An L2 Digital Transformation Handbook folio authored on top of an L1 WHO Digital Transformation Handbook and the DPI-H Reference Architecture (smart-ra). 734.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . 738.title: Digital Transformation Handbook (DTH) dth

It sits within the DIIG process and should use the DPI-H Reference Architecture (owner, 2026-10-01). Its domain sections map onto smart-kg L2 (DAK) classes: a DTH states for a health-system area what a DAK states for a guideline. Structure read from the three DTHs ingested in smart-base/library; a section is required only where all three have it. The Reference Architecture for DPI-H calls itself "A Digital Transformation Handbook for DPI-H" and is cited here as the architecture the others should reference. semi-fixed structure · 22 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dth.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Audience and how to use this handbookaudience-and-how-to-use | required | Target users/roles per chapter and the stepwise reading path through the handbook.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng, 2. 739.title: WHO guideline (L1) l1-guideline
739.content: An L1 publication containing recommendations for clinical practice or public health policy, structured as the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd ed.) §12.1 "Guideline format" requires, with the SMART additions Mehl 2021 names: uniquely identified recommendations and data recommendations. Cataloguing by reference means recording that something exists without holding it, so a small number here is the design rather than a shortfall.

846.title: DIIG — the investment path from a health system bottleneck to a costed plan

847.title: What it is, in one sentence
847.content: A nine-chapter sequence taking a health programme from we have a problem to we have a budgeted, governed, monitorable digital implementation, in which each chapter’s output is the next chapter’s input.

848.title: The nine chapters, as the Guide numbers them
848.content: |   | chapter | what it produces | . | 1 | Introduction | scope, key terms, and when the Guide applies | . | 2 | Form the team and establish goals | roles and responsibilities; a shared statement of the programme’s needs and goals; an understanding of operations across levels of the health system | . | 3 | Identify health system challenges and needs | a map of the current state, bottlenecks confirmed and prioritized, and those bottlenecks mapped to generic health system challenges | . | 4 | Determine appropriate digital health interventions | selected interventions, an enabling-environment assessment, functional requirements and user stories, a future-state workflow | . | 5 | Plan the implementation | infrastructure; legislation, policy and compliance; leadership and governance; workforce and training; services and applications | . | 6 | Link the digital health implementation to the enterprise architecture | an assessment of the architecture, the common and enabling components (the digital health platform), and the investment linked to both | . | 7 | Develop a budget | phases of implementation, cost drivers, a budget matrix | . | 8 | Monitor the implementation and use data effectively | a logic model, an M&E plan, a culture of data use, adaptive management | . | 9 | Value proposition and next steps | the case made to whoever pays | . Chapters 4 and 8 close with a progress check, the Guide’s own gate.

849.title: It builds on CRDM, and this platform already carries CRDM
849.content: Chapter 3 says so in its own words: . This process builds on the Public Health Informatics Institute’s Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM), a commonly used approach for defining the problem, identifying how it could be improved, and describing how the improved process would need to function (50). — library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-043.md (PDF page 43, printed page 31), introducing Fig. 3.1. Adaptation of CRDM approach for defining health system challenges . CRDM’s three areas of concentration, verbatim from the same page: . | Business process analysis | Business process redesign | Requirements definition | . cat-harness runs CRDM (skills in cat-harness/sdlc/skills/crdm/, processes including cat-harness/processes/process/crdm-needs.bpmn and crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn), so DIIG Chapter 3 and the platform’s requirements process descend from one published method. DIIG adapts CRDM for health system challenges; it does not restate it. Where the two disagree, neither overrides the other and they are not merged (methodology-adoption: never blend two methodologies). Pick one per decision, name it, follow it.

850.title: Where this adoption stops
850.content: . | The annexes are named, not rendered. DIIG’s fourteen worksheets and templates (the planning and implementation charter, the persona worksheet, the process matrix, the budget template, the logic model template, the adaptive management checklist, and more) are instruments a programme fills in, not steps an agent performs. They are cited to the ingested sections. | Figures are cited, not described. The Guide’s figures are in the ingested entry as figures/vfig-p<PDF page>.png (Fig. 3.1 is vfig-p043; Fig. 1.1.1 also as SVG, by smart-base:diig-figure); where this file mentions a figure it quotes the text around it. | Chapter 5’s country-specific and intervention-specific considerations (Annexes 5.3, 5.4) are a reference table of scale, not a method. Left in the library. | .

851.title: Refusals
851.content: methodology-adoption’s refusals bind. The first has a concrete target in this method. Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. DIIG Table 3.3.1, Formula for scoring and ranking bottlenecks (sections/page-050.md, PDF page 50, printed page 38), scores each bottleneck on three criteria, each 1–3: . | How much impact does this bottleneck have on the process? | What is the likelihood of overcoming this bottleneck? | Is this important to a wide range of stakeholders? | . — and combines them into a Score and a Prioritized Ranking. This platform adopts the three criteria and refuses the arithmetic. Three ordinal judgements on incommensurable scales, summed with equal weight, give a number whose precision is invented. An agent applying DIIG Chapter 3 records each criterion’s answer and its reason, and orders the bottlenecks by argument; it does not print a score. The summed score is kept as an alternative: the DTH for health supply chain architecture repeats the tally in its Annex 3 (9789240101197-eng, sections/page-068.md: “Adding the scores yields the prioritized ranking.”), and DIIG Table 3.3.1 and SC Annex 3 are both recorded beside this refusal in smart-base/findings/dth-terms.md. The refusal still governs what an agent applying this method does. Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. DIIG Chapter 4 selects interventions against prioritized challenges. The interventions considered and not chosen are part of the output, with why. Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A DIIG citation with no rendered step is an appeal to authority no reader can check. Never blend DIIG with CRDM, MAPS or the M&E guide. All touch digital health implementation; they are parallel tracks selected by context, not a toolkit to assemble from.

852.title: Its neighbours in this library, and what each is for instead
852.content: |   |   | . | Classification of Digital Health Interventions (v1.0, v2.0) | the controlled vocabulary DIIG Chapter 4 selects from; not a method | . | Digital transformation handbooks (primary health care; substandard and falsified medical products) | DIIG applied to one domain — worked instances, not the method | . | The MAPS Toolkit | assessment and planning for scale, which begins where DIIG’s first implementation ends | . | Monitoring and Evaluating Digital Health Interventions | the full treatment of what DIIG Chapter 8 compresses into one chapter | .

853.title: DIIG — Digital Implementation Investment Guide
853.content: ← All methodologies . diig — declared by smart-base — source held . Applies when. Planning, costing and monitoring a DIGITAL HEALTH IMPLEMENTATION inside a health programme — from forming the team through to the budget and the monitoring plan. It is a programme-investment method, not a judgement method: it does not grade evidence (that is grade), does not choose between design options (kepner-tregoe), and does not constrain how a decision is recorded (madr). Reach for it when the question is what shall we build, with whom, at what cost, and how will we know it worked — and specifically when the answer has to survive a funder. Origin. World Health Organization, International Telecommunication Union and the United Nations Foundation Digital Health Initiative, Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG): integrating digital interventions into health programmes (2020), ISBN 978-92-4-001056-7. Ingested at who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/; every citation below resolves to a section there. Ingested sources: . | library/9789240010567-eng | . Node file: diig.md .

854.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
854.title: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
854.content: The method behind classify-and-code-content, recommendation-extraction, and recommendation-scenarios. It joins the platform’s generic ontology and glossary rules — ontologist, glossary-terms, vocabulary-authority, and code-lists — with the WHO Family of International Classifications (WHO-FIC) and SMART Guidelines DAK component conventions.

855.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
855.title: 1. The scheme for each slot
855.content: Every classifiable slot in an L1 extraction or L2 DAK component has an authoritative primary scheme and a local fallback or code list. Coding a slot means resolving a concept in the scheme designated for that slot, never picking an arbitrary string or borrowing a code from an unrelated axis. | Slot | Where it sits | Authoritative scheme(s) | Local representation in this stack | . | Condition / disease / health problem | L1 recommendation.population / condition; L2 data dictionary (C5) & DMN inputs (C6) | ICD-11 (WHO International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision; MMS & foundation URI) | KGTerminologySystem (#ICD11, http://id.who.int/icd/release/11/mms); DAK C5 ICD-11 binding column | . | Intervention (clinical, public-health or digital) | L1 recommendation.intervention; L2 user scenarios (C3), business processes (C4), data dictionary (C5), indicators (C8) | ICHI (International Classification of Health Interventions) for clinical and public-health interventions; CDISAH / CDHI v2.0 (library/9789240081949-eng, input/fsh/codesystems/CDHIv2.fsh, CDSCv2.fsh) and CDHI v1.0 (library/who-rhr-1806-eng, CDHIv1.fsh) for digital health interventions and system categories; WHO UHC Intervention Compendium for service packages | input/fsh/codesystems/CDHIv2.fsh, CDHIv1.fsh, CDSCv2.fsh, CDSCv1.fsh; KGTerminologySystem (#ICHI, #SNOMEDCT, #LOINC) | . | Persona / actor / occupational role | L2 generic personas (C2), user-scenario involves edges (C3), BPMN swimlanes (C4) | ISCO-08 (ILO International Standard Classification of Occupations) and CDISAH / CDHI health-workforce categories | Target guide’s personas.md (l1-scenario-vocabulary/v1), then smart-base generic personas (input/fsh/actors/*.fsh, DAK.Persona.*, input/fsh/codesystems/ISCO08.fsh), then local glossary-terms candidate | . | Medicine / vaccine / health product | L1 recommendation.intervention; L2 data dictionary (C5), scheduling logic (C7), product catalogues (library/9789240116191-eng) | WHO ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification) and ICD-11 medicaments/vaccines extension | KGTerminologySystem (#ATC, http://www.whocc.no/atc); product-catalogue attributes per library/9789240116191-eng | . | Guideline / scenario domain | L1 intake classification; L2 user-scenario domain property | SMART Guideline domain scheme (clinical | public-health | health-system-strengthening) | folio-assistant-core/glossary/guideline-domain.glossary.json (folio-glossary/v1, SKOS ConceptScheme guideline-domain) | . | Business process | L2 business processes (C4); business-process realises user-scenario edge | Target SMART Guideline’s C4 business process catalogue (business-processes.md); domain process catalogue where published | l1-scenario-vocabulary/v1 processes[]; could-not-determine with a structured warning when absent | . | Normative statement strength, direction & certainty | L1 recommendation (strength, direction, certaintyOfEvidence); EtD frameworks | GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) and RFC 2119 / BCP 14 requirement levels | smart-base/code-lists/grade-*.json (grade-recommendation-strength, grade-recommendation-direction, grade-certainty, grade-etd-criterion, grade-rating-down, grade-rating-up) and folio-assistant-core/code-lists/rfc2119-requirement-level.json | .

856.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
856.title: 2. The reuse-first precedence
856.content: An agent or terminologist coding any slot walks the four-rung ladder and stops at the first rung that yields an exact or well-scoped match: . | Rung 1 — Target guide’s own declared vocabulary (exactMatch in guide). The target guide’s own personas (personas.md), business processes (business-processes.md), data dictionary (C5) and local code lists. If one defines the concept and its scope covers the statement, reuse its identifier verbatim. | Rung 2 — Layer base vocabulary (smart-base generic personas, FSH CodeSystems, and shared code lists). When the target guide does not declare the concept, or declares it more narrowly than the statement needs (an immunization guide’s health worker cannot be stretched to cover inpatient clinical management): . | smart-base generic personas (DAK.Persona.* in input/fsh/actors/, extracted in smart-base-generic-personas.json); | smart-base FSH CodeSystems (ISCO08, CDHIv2, CDHIv1, CDSCv2, CDSCv1, KGTerminologySystem and KG*); | shared folio-code-list/v1 lists (smart-base/code-lists/*.json, folio-assistant-core/code-lists/*.json) and SKOS glossaries (folio-assistant-core/glossary/guideline-domain.glossary.json). | . | Rung 3 — External authoritative standard (WHO-FIC / ILO / HL7 / W3C). A standard clinical, occupational or ontological term not in Rungs 1–2 is resolved against the external authority in vocabulary-authority and §1 above (ICD-11, ICHI, CDHI, ISCO-08, ATC, SNOMED CT, LOINC), recording the mapping predicate (skos:exactMatch or skos:closeMatch) per ontologist. | Rung 4 — Local candidate or explicit third state (citing glossary-terms). When Rungs 1–3 hold no match: . | For a persona or domain concept: mint a local glossary entry in <instance>/glossary/<scheme>.glossary.json following glossary-terms with status: "candidate", source: "extracted" (citing the doc_id and section / quote), and emit WARNING <slot>-glossary-candidate. An agent writes only status: "candidate"; promotion to status: "authored" is a person’s, in the terminologist/ontologist lane. | For a business process: never invent a process. Record could-not-determine with WARNING process-not-determined and the basis quoting the statement. That warning is the work list for the guide or domain process catalogue. | . | .

857.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
857.title: 3. Provenance and review status on every coding
857.content: Every classification or coding link records two independent facts: . | How the coding was obtained (source): . | declared — a person acting in an authorised role explicitly stated the code or link (must carry by); | context — the printed section heading, table header, or structural container in the source document settles the classification without inference; | inferred — an agent or author read the statement text and matched it against the scheme’s definitions. | . | Where it sits in review (status): . | candidate — proposed by the authoring-agent (using terminology-lookup and classify-and-code-content); | reviewed / authored — checked and signed off by a person acting in the terminologist (or l1-extraction-reviewer) role in classify-and-code-content.bpmn. | . | .

858.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
858.title: 4. Adjudicating L1 coverage exclusions (l1-extraction-reviewer)
858.content: When l1-recommendation-candidates scans an L1 source, every sentence carrying a normative marker (should, shall, must, recommend*, may be …) must either become an L1 node (recommendation, implementation-practice, remark, or part-of) or be excluded with one of the five closed reasons (background-fact, manufacturer-statement, editorial, research-question, duplicate-of:<id>). An agent may propose an exclusion in exclusions.proposed.json ("signerRole": {"role": "l1-extraction-reviewer"}) and never signs it. A person acting as l1-extraction-reviewer, in classify-and-code-content.bpmn, reads each candidate sentence in place on the printed page (sections/page-NNN.md), checks that it is non-normative under the stated reason, and either signs it (signedOffBy) or rejects it back to extraction curation, so no guidance is silently dropped.

859.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
859.title: 5. Refusals
859.content: . | Never invent a business process to make coverage look complete. When no process in the target guide or a published domain catalogue realises a scenario, the only valid value is could-not-determine with a warning. | Never stretch a narrower code as exactMatch. If a guide’s persona or a code list entry covers only part of the concept, use skos:closeMatch (or skos:broadMatch / skos:narrowMatch per ontologist) or fall through to the next rung. | Never self-approve a candidate term or an L1 exclusion. An agent writes status: "candidate" on glossary terms and leaves signedOffBy absent on exclusions; only a person in the reviewer lane records sign-off. | .

860.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
860.title: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
860.content: ← All methodologies . terminology-coding — declared by smart-base — source held . Applies when. Classifying and coding L1 narrative content (guideline recommendations, implementation practices, remarks) and L2 Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) artefacts (personas, user scenarios, business processes, data-dictionary elements, decision-table concepts and indicators) against authoritative vocabularies and local code lists. Reach for it whenever a slot requires a code or SKOS concept (condition, intervention, persona/role, medicine, guideline domain, business process, or GRADE rating), or when deciding whether to reuse an existing term, fall back to a generic base concept, or propose a local glossary candidate. It does NOT grade evidence (that is grade), does NOT model BPMN/DMN control flow (bpmn-authoring, dmn-authoring), and does NOT plan programme investment (diig). Origin. World Health Organization, SMART Guidelines: Digital Adaptation Kits (DAKs) (Mehl et al., BMJ Global Health 2021;6:e004908, ingested at smart-base/library/mehl-2021-who-smart-guidelines/); Classification of digital health interventions, services and applications in health (CDISAH) v2.0 (WHO, 2023, ISBN 978-92-4-008194-9, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240081949-eng/, superseding CDHI v1.0 at who-iris/library/who-rhr-1806-eng/); Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture (WHO, 2024, ISBN 978-92-4-010119-7, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/); and Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue (WHO, 2025, ISBN 978-92-4-011619-1, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/). 897.title: Tools — fhir-harness
897.content: The Tool nodes fhir-harness declares in its tools graph — one instance’s slice of every instance’s tools. A skill states a capability generically: what an actor needs to know to perform a task. A Tool is one concrete way to exercise it, with an installation, an invocation and typed inputs and outputs. One skill may be satisfied by several tools, and one tool may satisfy several skills. They are separate graphs and this is the tools one. The relation between them is satisfies, and it runs from a tool to a skill — this tool is one way to do that, never this skill is a tool. 36Tool nodes 9skills satisfied 36invoked as a shell command 0reachable over MCP

901.title: Provenance
901.content: Who decided, when, and under which work item, for the 35 tool(s) whose provenance log has entries. Open a tool to read its record. agent-memory (1) tool.description . | bean bean 31niOther vendors (Gemini CLI, Copilot, Codex, Cursor) are beaned under 31ni and not generated. | . archimate-actors (1) tool.description . | owner-decision smart-ra#166 2026-11-01Actors come first (owner, 2026-11-01, smart-ra#166 D4): the IG's ActorDefinitions are written from the DAK's personas, and an ArchiMate model only points at them. | . bpmn-checklist (1) tool.io.outputs[0].description . | owner-decision 2026-10-14One committed <stem>.checklist.md per diagram in every instance, beside its .bpmn (owner, 2026-10-14: commit them). | . build-instance-site (1) tool.selection.limits . | bean bean 53rvA FHIR IG's site (the IG pipeline layer's stage-ig-sites) is not built here yet; it needs the IG's FHIR packages, which some environments cannot reach (bean 53rv). | . ci-health (2) tool.selection.when . | history bean xom7Before trusting ANY workflow's outcome, and at session start. A workflow's result is invisible from a checkout, which is how docs-site.yml failed 30 consecutive runs over two months with nothing in the repository saying so (bean xom7). | . tool.selection.limits . | bean bean 1xhcA REFUSED OR FAILING API CALL EXITS 2 AND IS NEVER GREEN: could-not-look must stay distinguishable from looked-and-it-was-fine, and bean 1xhc has a case where this printed green while main was red because an unsettled newest run was dropped. | . compose-docs (1) tool.description . | issue #2235--shell writes the CHROME only — the layers' Jekyll machinery and assets, no page, no instance, and the host's generated includes empty — which an IG repository composes its IG into so its own site wears the main site's chrome (#2235). | . declaration-resolution (1) tool.description . | proposal lesson 6Read every instance declaration in the checkout and resolve what it names: directories (and those declared from within) through check:declared-dirs, assets through check:declared-assets, visualisers[].renderedBy through check:visualiser-routes, needs through the instance-graph resolver, and visualisers[].coversKinds against the graph typologies registered IN THIS CHECKOUT — its own and those a mounted layer contributes, read from the checkout under inspection rather than from where the harness module sits (lesson 6). | . feature-staging (3) tool.io.inputs[1].description . | bean bean w2g5DELETION: the branches/<slug> to remove, instead of staging anything. It exists because the label path cannot reach the previews the health sweep reports — being findable as an orphan REQUIRES the pull request to be closed, so the close event has already fired with no label (bean w2g5). | . tool.selection.limits . | bean bean plj1The removal arm is guarded THREE ways, and the guards are the point rather than ceremony: workflow_dispatch is available only to an actor with write access; cleanup_confirm must repeat the slug exactly; and the removal is preflighted at removal time against the same liveness signals the health sweep uses. That is deletion-requires-confirmation applied to the tool most able to break it — bean plj1 is a workflow whose shape deleted every open pull request's preview without anybody deciding it. This node does not claim that skill, because implementing the discipline once is not the same as stating it. | . tool.selection.cost . | history bean xd1sConcurrency is keyed on the branch or the cleanup slug, NOT the shared ref, so two cleanups of different previews no longer cancel each other (bean xd1s). | . gates (1) tool.selection.when . | issue #363It matters most where CI is not: tools/ is an INHERITED declaration and .github/workflows/ is not, so a downstream instance gets this Tool and none of the gates it names. #363's self-sovereign topology has no CI at all. | . gates-merged (1) tool.selection.limits . | owner-decisionThe merge queue (merge_group: on the gating workflows, switched on by the owner) is what closes that last gap. | . gh-pages (1) tool.selection.limits . | bean bean plj1Pages cannot serve server-side redirects or custom headers, and a full-replace push to the gh-pages branch deletes what the build did not produce unless the caller restores it first (docs-site-publish, bean plj1). | . ig-folio-site-workflow (3) tool.selection.when . | history 2026-10-14 https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools/pull/202A pipeline that still carries folio-site.yml and builds on a runner rather than in the agent's checkout (smart-base's default branch carried it on 2026-10-14). Since https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools/pull/202 stage-local gives an IG the same site — theme side bar and search, served directories, stamp — so this is no longer the only route to them. | . tool.selection.limits . | owner-decision 2026-10-14The current agent pipeline does not use it (owner, 2026-10-14). | . tool.selection.cost . | history 2026-10-12One runner job, 8 to 15 minutes measured on 2026-10-12, plus GitHub's Pages deploy. | . ingest-extended (2) tool.selection.limits . | bean bean 68dt bean 5rfyIt adds nothing for archives, spreadsheets or metadata — ingest-stdlib already does those, and does them where this cannot run. Its PDF rungs ARE testable in CI as of 68dt, which installs the lean set; the table rung (pdf-tables.py, camelot) is the one part that still is not, and anything gated on THAT remains a path CI cannot exercise — the 5rfy defect. | . tool.selection.cost . | history 2026-09-20Measured 2026-09-20: the lean set is 144 MB and CI installs it, so the PDF rungs ARE exercised there now. camelot-py for pdf-tables.py is the part CI still skips — 912 KB itself, but 323 MB with numpy, pandas and OpenCV, more than the whole lean set. | . kg-validate (1) tool.selection.when . | history #363Whenever a node's shape matters and you are not in this repository's CI. That is the case the tool exists for: tools/ is an INHERITED declaration and .github/workflows/ is not, so a downstream instance gets this and gets none of the 41 gates. #363's self-sovereign topology has no CI to inherit from at all. | . mcp-capture (2) tool.selection.when . | bean bean ce65Also the source data for migrating src/tools/ into Tool nodes (bean ce65). | . tool.selection.limits . | historyINTROSPECTION, deliberately, not source parsing. The first attempt read server.tool(...) with a regex and produced wrong input lists — words followed by a colon inside a DESCRIPTION came back as parameter names, so skill_fetch appeared to take Examples and Local. Authoring a node's io from that would ship a contract agreeing with nothing, which is worse than no contract because a contract is what the next check trusts. | . merge-overlap (1) tool.selection.limits . | proposal requirements T3Paths, not semantics (requirements T3): two PRs that change different files can still interact, which the shared-declaration list only partly covers. | . merge-train (1) tool.selection.cost . | history 2026-10-02One merge-base.ts per member (seconds each), then one regen (5-13 min measured 2026-10-02) and the three checks; a second regen if main had generated conflicts. | . mount-from-lock (1) tool.selection.limits . | issue #2518It lives in cat-harness, which is itself a mounted layer once separated, so it cannot bootstrap a checkout that does not already hold cat-harness. The parent must carry its own dependency-free entry point that fetches this script at the pin (folio-assistant's .github/mount-from-lock.sh, #2518) — never call this path directly from a workflow in a repository that mounts cat-harness. | . narrative-queue (2) tool.selection.when . | historyTo find out what is waiting on a person, or to discover that this queue exists at all — which was the actual gap. Before this node, grep narrative tools/*.ts returned nothing, so an agent asking the graph how a person confirms a narrative got no answer, and that is exactly the population the command is for. | . tool.selection.limits . | historyThat refusal is load-bearing rather than defensive — driving the CLI in an agent container once wrote "rejected_by": {"kind": "human", "id": "Claude"}, because git config user.name is the agent's and the schema could not tell. 915.content: Who decided, when, and under which work item, for the 35 tool(s) whose provenance log has entries. 916.title: Tools
916.content: A skill states a capability generically: what an actor needs to know to perform a task. A Tool is one concrete way to exercise it, with an installation, an invocation and typed inputs and outputs. One skill may be satisfied by several tools, and one tool may satisfy several skills. They are separate graphs and this is the tools one. The relation between them is satisfies, and it runs from a tool to a skill — this tool is one way to do that, never this skill is a tool. 253Tool nodes 106skills satisfied 224invoked as a shell command 30reachable over MCP

918.title: Who declares each specification
918.content: A user declares the specification it depends on; the record names no user. That is data-modelling step 8 — the dependent holds the pointer — and it is why this list cannot drift from the code: a file that stops declaring stops being listed. Four forms are read: a @conformsTo tag, a conformsTo: front-matter list, an xmlns binding, and a graph typology whose typing module declares the spec (bean u63y). Every declaration names a record on this page.

Every namespace the corpus declares is covered by a record above. 2 declared and not in use. Not a defect on its own: a record may cover a namespace only some artefacts carry. 960.content: L1 extraction viewer: a hub and a page per instance with l1-extraction directories candidate, extracted For every visualiser an instance declares with renderedBy: l1-extraction-pages, write the hub at <locale>/<harness>/<id>/ and, with subgraphs: "instance", one page per instance that declares an l1-extraction directory. Each page shows, from what the files declare: the L1 statements (graph nodes with a statement, and an authored L1 source's recommendations); the candidate work list's counts, coverage and decisions; each graph document's nodes by type and edges by predicate (L2 scenario candidates included); counts of curation, mapping, vocabulary, exclusions and run context; and a link from every file to its published copy (cat-harness's library:viz), when the site has it, and to its source at the pinned commit. Given an agent's l1-recommendation-curation/v1, refuse a non-verbatim statement or an unknown location, and write the recommendations and remarks as an L1 3.0 graph (checked with kg/src/validate.ts) with coverage and proposed, unsigned exclusions. 988.title: Glossary: BPMN activities
988.content: Candidate terms extracted from every BPMN task and call activity: name as the label, its own <documentation> as the definition, the element id as the code. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: smart-base 153 (SKOS). Split by first letter. 153 terms are too many for one page within its budget of 1.0 MB, so they are on 3 pages by the first letter of the label. The ranges are fixed, so a term’s address does not move as terms are added. A label that does not start with a letter is on the first page. | A–D: 68 terms | E–Q: 41 terms | R–Z: 44 terms | .

990.title: Glossary
990.content: Every term the instances in this repository define or carry, as W3C SKOS. Terms link to the external concepts they match rather than copying them. 207 terms: 0 authored in 0 glossaries, one page per instance that owns them, and 207 extracted from knowledge-graph assets in 4 generated schemes, one page per asset type, plus the sources below. | state | what it means | terms | . | authored | A person wrote or approved the definition. | 0 | . | candidate, extracted | Lifted from a knowledge-graph asset's own title and description, verbatim, and not curated. The definition is the asset's text, the source links to the asset, and an asset with no description gives a term with none. A person promotes one by authoring it. | 207 | . | could-not-extract | The source names a term the extractor could not read, and says why. | 0 | .

991.title: Already somebody else’s concept?
991.content: Extracted candidates are minted from this repository’s own assets and are not, by themselves, checked against any vocabulary. check:term-mapping asks whether each already exists as a concept somebody is authoritative for — SKOS for what a term MEANS, FHIR for a clinical code’s operational semantics — and the two are separate questions with separate answers. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 4444 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 4444 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin.

992.title: Pages
992.content: Each term is on exactly one page. Authored terms are on the page of the instance that owns their scheme (owner, 2026-10-15), and extracted candidates are split by asset type (owner, 2026-09-24), so that no page is fetched at the size of all of them. | page | holds | terms | size | . | this page | counts and sources | — | 6 KB | . | smart-base | authored terms of smart-base | 0 | 2 KB | . | Skills | candidates, extracted | 27 | 28 KB | . | Tools | candidates, extracted | 14 | 16 KB | . | BPMN activities | candidates, extracted | 153 | 115 KB | . | DMN decisions | candidates, extracted | 0 | 2 KB | . | Schema fields | candidates, extracted | 13 | 27 KB | . Size: this page is 6 KB before compression, within its budget of 64 KB; each instance’s and each asset type’s page has a budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter on each page runs over that page, and its A–Z bar jumps within it. The SKOS files in the sources are the machine-readable form.

1044.title: Already somebody else’s concept? (sin traducir)

1073.title: WHO Immunization Implementation Guide
1073.content: . This WHO Implementation Guide for Immunizations details how to use Health Level 7 (HL7) Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) for consistent digital representation of Immunization services. This implementation guide and set of artifacts are still undergoing development. Content is for demonstration purposes only. Summary . This implementation guide includes a machine-readable representation of WHO guidelines for Immunizations, as documented in the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for Immunizations (link forthcoming) and explicitly encodes computer-interoperable logic, including data models, terminologies, and logic expressions, in a computable language to support implementation of Immunization use cases by WHO Member States. The guide is part of the WHO SMART Guidelines approach to support countries to integrate WHO global health and data recommendations into digital systems accurately and consistently. It defines a series of FHIR Resources, Profiles, Extensions, and Terminology based on the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for Immunizations. Supporting guidance, recommendations, resources, and standards are included in the Bibliography and Dependencies. About this implementation guide . This implementation guide is broken into the following levels of knowledge representation: . | Home - contains references to the guidance, guidelines, policies and recommendations underpinning this implementation guide. | Business Requirements - contains the requirements for this implementation guide including the definition of key concepts, use cases, and a data dictionary. | Data Models and Exchange - contains the data models and data exchange protocols with actors and transactions defined. | Deployment Guidance - contains relevant technical specifications and guidance, testing resources, reference implementation materials, and supporting guidance for adaptation to local contexts. | . This guide is prepared to facilitate digital implementation of WHO Immunization guidelines by providing FHIR-based computable representations of and implementation guidance for using the key components of the WHO Digital adaptation kit (DAK) for immunizations: . | Health Interventions & Recommendations | Generic Personas | User Scenarios | Business Processes & Workflows | Core Data Elements | Decision Support Logic | Indicators & Monitoring | Functional & Non-functional Requirements | . This guide is a companion to the Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) and should be used side-by-side with it. Implementers are strongly encouraged to make use of the Digital Adaptation Kit. The focus of this guide is on the explanation and use of the computable artifacts. This guide assumes use of the following resources: . | IPS Patient | CPG ActivityDefinitions . | For a complete listing of the artifacts defined in this implementation guide, refer to the Artifact Index. | A complete offline copy of this implementation guide can be found on the Downloads page. | This Implementation Guide makes use of Clinical Quality Language for the decision support artifacts including the PlanDefinitions and Measures. They are used to express how a calculation should occur and can be used with a CQL engine in order to process the decision or indicator directly from the applicable FHIR resources. Links to this specification, the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Speciciation, and other helpful resources can be found in the Support dropdown. | . Disclaimer . The specification herewith documented is a demo working specification and may not be used for any implementation purposes. This draft is provided without warranty of completeness or consistency and the official publication supersedes this draft. No liability can be inferred from the use or misuse of this specification or its consequences. ⟦not rendered: ip-statements.xhtml⟧ — the IG Publisher renders it from a source this build does not hold; no renderer was given to this build. Edit this page on GitHub .

1074.title: indicator-extraction
1074.content: Skill indicator-extraction: Extract the indicators an L1 source prints (indicator reference or metadata sheets: name, numerator, denominator, disaggregation, definition, data sources) as L1 indicator nodes with every printed field, then draft one L2 program indicator per indicator, derived from its L1 node. Read before adding a WHO handbook’s or guideline’s indicators to a DAK or a DTH, and whenever an L2 indicator has to trace to its source. Part of L1 → L2 extraction for every DAK and DTH, beside recommendation-extraction. Named by: DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . Skill id: indicator-extraction · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Follows dak-l1-library, which ingests the source. Sibling of recommendation-extraction: that one takes a source’s recommendations, this one its indicators. It is a step of L1 → L2 extraction for a DAK or DTH, bound to Task_Indicators in l2-dak-authoring and Call_Data in dth-authoring.

1075.title: Two layers, kept apart
1075.content: | layer | what | kind / model | written by | . | L1 | the indicator as the source prints it, verbatim | indicator block (folio type smart-base:Indicator; KG L1 indicator, kg/src/l1.ts) | scripts/l1-indicator-sheets.py → candidates.json → gen-library-jsonld | . | L2 | the DAK’s or DTH’s own operational measure, a draft that points back | program-indicator (sgkg-l2), logical model ProgramIndicator | scripts/l2-program-indicators.py | . sgkg-l2 keeps them apart: merging them would merge a WHO definition with a country’s implementation of it. The L2 record is a draft with derivedFrom its L1 node, and the L2 author adopts, edits or drops it.

1076.title: Rules
1076.content: . | Ids come from the source. number / indicatorId is the printed indicator number (“1-01”, “4-01.3”). A sheet whose header prints none is reported and skipped, never numbered by an agent. The L2 id is <prefix>.<number> (“NHWA.1-01”); the prefix only namespaces it. | Verbatim. Every field is the printed text: lines joined, letter-spacing artefacts closed up, nothing reworded. A printed list (glossary terms, data sources) is one string joined with “; “. | Every printed field, not only name, numerator and denominator. The L1 node’s meta holds indicatorId, module, abbreviatedName, name, numerator, denominator, disaggregation, definition, glossary, reportingFrequency, reportingFrameworks, dataSources, furtherInformation and dimension where printed; a sub-indicator adds parentIndicator and guidingQuestions. These are the keys the structured-block cards read. | No gap is filled. ProgramIndicator makes definition, numerator, denominator and disaggregation 1..1. Where the source prints none (a composite or self-assessed indicator), the L2 draft lists it in gaps and the L2 author decides. Nothing is copied from another source to fill it. | A composite indicator keeps its sub-indicators as their own L1 nodes; in L2 they are the parent’s components, not program indicators of their own. | Read the page layout, not the section text, when the source prints sheets as a label column and a value column: Stage A’s text reads side bars and columns out of order. | .

1077.title: Steps
1077.content: . | The source is in the library (dak-l1-library), with its PDF in uploads/<doc-id>/. | L1 candidates. From the library repository root: . python3 smart-base/scripts/l1-indicator-sheets.py --entry library/<doc-id> \ --pdf uploads/<doc-id>/<doc-id>.pdf --pages <first>-<last> --json # look first python3 smart-base/scripts/l1-indicator-sheets.py --entry library/<doc-id> \ --pdf uploads/<doc-id>/<doc-id>.pdf --pages <first>-<last> --write . --write merges into candidates.json as the indicators aspect, replacing an indicator candidate with the same number (re-runs are idempotent). Check the count against the source’s own list of indicators (NHWA: the synthesis table, 29 indicators). | L1 nodes. bun cat-harness-tools/pipeline/gen-library-jsonld.ts --entry library/<doc-id> writes blocks/indicator-<section>-NN.{jsonld,md}, each derivedFrom its section, provenance: ingested, with the fields in meta. Existing indicator IRIs do not change when the first candidate of a section stays the same indicator. | L2 drafts. python3 smart-base/scripts/l2-program-indicators.py --entry library/<doc-id> \ --prefix <PREFIX> --out <where the L2 author will review them> . | Into the DAK or DTH. The L2 author takes the drafts into the guide’s indicators component (DAK component 8; a DTH’s data elements, indicators and requirements), through the guide’s own review (l2-component-edit-review) and, for a DTH, a change set. | .

1078.title: Validated against
1078.content: . | NHWA handbook, 2nd edition (who-iris 9789240081291-eng): 29 indicators, 33 sub-indicators, PDF pages 51-91. | . Not yet run on a guideline whose indicator sheets use a different layout (HIV SI 2022’s reference sheets: “What it measures”, “Rationale”, “Method of measurement”). Those labels are in the script’s label list, but the header number pattern may need a per-source ID_PATTERN.
