1123.title: Knowledge Graph separation — the method
1123.content: Skill kg-separation: Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. The end-to-end method: the signals that trigger it, the preconditions, eleven stages each with the command that gates it, the owner’s decision points, how identifiers, QA and publication move, how the parent consumes the result, rollback, and the post-move sweep that a move between the pair owes before the parent re-pins. graph-detanglement owns stages 1–3; this skill owns the rest. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: kg-separation · Package: graph-management Process: kg-separation.bpmn . This is the replicable method for separating a Knowledge Graph that is too large to handle, or whose consumers differ, written from what the bootstrap separation did. graph-detanglement is the practice for stages 1–3 (declare in place, detangle, isolate). Read it for those; this skill points to it and does not restate it. Everything from “split the tools out” to “the parent’s copy is deleted” is here.

1124.title: When — the signals, and none of them alone
1124.content: Separate when the graph is too large to handle, or when a business reason separates it: “split only where consumers or cadences differ”. Size is often not the reason — bootstrap is 33 files and left because its readers and its release cadence differ from cat-harness’s. Record the signals in the work item before deciding: . | signal | how it is measured | . | files and bytes per layer | git ls-files \| cut -d/ -f1 \| sort \| uniq -c | . | clone cost | bun run cat health → repository-size | . | gate time a content change pays | bun run cat gates (the gate count and wall time) | . | merge contention | commits per day on main; PRs re-conflicted before merge | . | cohesion and cut of the candidate | bun run cat kg:detangle | . | wrong-direction edges within one layer — modules bucketed into the proposed repos by path rule | check:partition (its root is ONE layer; read the scope it prints) | . | wrong-direction edges between layers — checked against each one’s declared needs | bun run cat kg:detangle:direction, blocking in CI | . | wrong-direction references — the prose axis, not the import axis | check:reference-direction | . | what the tools would drag along | the import cone of the would-be tools package (check:tools-closure once it exists) | .

1125.title: An example pointing up is a mention, not a dependency
1125.content: check:reference-direction holds that nothing names a layer that depends on it. One kind of pointer does not break that rule: a lower layer citing a source as an example, where the one copy of that source lives in a layer above it. For example, a base IG layer’s document kind and voice quote a draft reference architecture whose library entry belongs to a folio above it; two copies of one key break the bibliography build, so: . | One copy. The source’s library entry lives only in the layer that owns it. The lower layer deletes its copy and never re-ingests it. | The lower layer keeps a pointer. A document-kind source’s ref is a URL to the owner’s published library page (DocumentKindSourceSchema allows “a library entry id or a URL”). A voice source names the owning repository in instance and adds its url. A quote keeps its libraryId and sectionId. | It is checked where the copy is. The lower layer cannot read the sections, so its quote check reports such a quote as “an example held by , not checked here". That is not a pass and not a failure (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-base/blob/main/scripts/gen-dth-term-findings.ts, `EXAMPLE_POINTERS`). | It is a mention. The lower layer’s build does not need the higher layer, and nothing it runs reads through the pointer. The URL form is already an address under check:reference-direction’s URL exemption (“a location is where a thing is, not a dependency on it”). A pointer that something would need to resolve in order to build is a dependency, and the content moves up instead. | .

1126.title: Preconditions
1126.content: . | Names agree before the cut — directory, declared name, package name. A rename after the cut is a cross-repository change. | One directory per layer, so extraction is one move, not a sift. | Every gate that guards the boundary has been watched failing — plant a violation, see it red, remove it. A boundary gate can pass while guarding nothing: unable to fail, blind to side-effect imports, or blind across layers. | The owner’s decisions are recorded in the work item (the list below). | “Generated output is the contract” is written down: what crosses the boundary is the generated file, and any tool may produce it. | .

1127.title: The pair: a content repository and a tools repository
1127.content: A separated Knowledge Graph is two repositories, not one. |   | content (<name>) | tools (<name>-tools) | . | holds | files to read — .md, .json, .bpmn, generated schemas, READMEs, diagrams | the code that writes and checks the content — Zod sources, generators, README/diagram writers, content checks | . | code | none (FR-7 — a reader needs nothing installed) | yes, with a declared, minimal dependency set | . | depends on | nothing | the content, and nothing above it — check:tools-closure | . | is used by | the parent harness, pinned | the content’s own checks, and the parent (a package) | . The rules of the pattern: . | The Zod source moves DOWN into the tools repository — not up into the harness. Zod in the harness makes a content release wait on the harness, which itself needs the content: a cycle. | The tools repository owns the content checks AND the README and diagram writers — one copy, which the parent harness also calls. It is not a second harness: a content Knowledge Graph declares no visualisers. It is one toolset over swappable content, so a different visualiser is a different toolset. | Every tool is a script an agent runs as the actor in a process step. Agentic first. A GitHub Actions workflow may be described, but ships disabled, and nothing that costs money runs unless the owner asks. | Harness output ABOUT the content stays with the harness (hosted): its QA verdicts (kgQaHomeFor), translation templates (translationsHomeFor), exported graph and glossary ledger. The content repository carries only what its own checks need. | . Staged content with no tools repository yet — the finding, not the silence . A layer can be planned as a content repository before its -tools pair is authorised. Declare it — separation: "content" in <name>.json; the content half of an existing pair is read from the tools layer’s supports and needs nothing — and kg:audit’s content-instance-holds-code records a finding naming every code file still inside it. It is a minor QA warning, not a failure, because the tolerated set is small; a warning still names each file, so the violation is never silent. The remedy splits by what the code is: generic code (it works for any instance of its kind — any DSpace catalogue, any PDF) moves into the platform and takes the layer root as an argument; layer-specific code waits for <name>-tools.

1128.title: The stages
1128.content: Each stage names its lane (a role in scenarios/roles.json) and the command that gates it. A stage is done when its gate is green, never when the work looks finished. | # | stage | lane | gate | . | 0 | Brief, measure the signals, claim | authoring-agent | signals in the work item; bun run cat beans:claim <id> | . | 1–3 | Declare in place, detangle, isolate | authoring-agent | graph-detanglement — all its gates | . | 4 | Identity: name, version, iriBase, needs, nodeSchemas in the declaration; move the base once | platform-authoring-agent | iri:sync -- --from <old base> then iri:sync:check; check:node-iris | . | 5 | Hosted outputs out of the content | platform-authoring-agent | the content leak test’s pending list is empty | . | 6 | Split content from tools: create <name>-tools/ as a sibling, move the code, cut its import cone | platform-authoring-agent | FR-7 (content holds no code); check:tools-closure; generated files byte-identical before and after | . | 7 | Publication plan: every identifier the content mints is a file some step publishes, at /v<major>/ | publication-manager | check:node-iris; the site layout in instance-publication §”The release site” | . | 8 | Rehearse standalone: copy content + tools alone into a temporary directory and run the tools’ checks there | build-pipeline | green with nothing else on the path; an empty tree exits non-zero | . | 9 | Authorise — report what moves, sizes, what breaks, and wait | administrator | the owner’s answer (deletion-requires-confirmation) | . | 10 | Seed: the owner creates the repositories; once the source has settled, seed main, then the content and tools as reviewed PRs, with history | administrator, then authoring-agent | bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse answers settled for each layer, at seed time; then the seeding PRs reviewed and green | . | 11 | Parent consumes, additively: pin (a SHA while staging, a version once released), repoint imports, keep the parent’s copy. After any move of files between the pair, run the post-move sweep first (below) | platform-authoring-agent | the parent green with the dependency declared; check:published-refs; every gate in the sweep table | . | 12 | First release: tag, publish /v<major>/ | publication-manager | check:version-bump; every identifier dereferences (publish-verification) | . | 13 | Cutover: the one commit retiring the parent’s copy into fsh-guts as a verified archive (the deposit state:seed --cutover makes: it must extract to the exact tree removed, with a provenance note), deposited into the PARENT’s fsh-guts before the removal, frozen, never refreshed or rendered: a relocation, not a deletion (sub-kg-lifecycle stage 13 has the steps) | administrator | only after 11 and 12 are green; DONE only when bun run cat separation:cutover:check --site, run in the separated repository, exits 0 (Tool separation-cutover-check: mounts, declarations resolve, no monorepo wiring, layer direction, the site builds from the mounts alone) | . | 14 | Independent refinement: each new release adopted by the parent as a reviewed step | authoring-agent | upstream-version-adoption | . Nothing is committed to the new repositories before stage 10, and stage 10 starts only when the owner says so. Until then the pair is staged as sibling directories in the parent (bootstrap/, bootstrap-tools/). Ready to seed? — asked at seed time, not at rehearsal . A seed is a snapshot: one commit that names the source sha, with no history. Every open PR whose diff touches the layer when the snapshot is taken is orphaned into the monorepo: after cutover its change is in neither the seed nor anywhere that reads it. Stage 8 asked whether the layer stands alone, but the tree has moved since. So GW_SeedReady sits between creating the repositories and seeding them, and asks again: . bun run cat seed:ready --layer cat-harness --rehearse --text # exit 0 settled, 1 not yet, 2 unknown . | criterion | not yet when | . | heavy movers | an open PR labelled heavy-mover touches the layer or the next one up | . | next layer | any open PR touches the next layer up, which imports this one | . | layer load | more than five open PRs touch the layer | . | moves | an open PR deletes a file in the layer, or renames one into or out of it. A generator’s own names do not count: an owned-tree path in merge-conflict-patterns.ts (content-hashed payloads, rail data) is renamed by every regen, so moving one changes what no seeded path means | . | standalone | bun test is red with only the layer and what it needs beside it, as sibling directories | . | upward paths | a path DECLARED in the layer — a Tool module, a QA criterion source, a render target — resolves only in a layer above it, so it breaks the day the layer stands alone | . A test about the WHOLE CHECKOUT lives at the top. A test that reads several sibling layers at once, or the aggregate root itself (.github/, .gitignore, the root declaration, beans/, todos/, memory/, fsh-guts/), is red in every layer it is placed in, so it goes in the root layer’s DECLARED test home — folio-assistant-tests in folio-assistant.json, at test/ — never in a layer and never at a path a runner hardcodes. Whatever names every layer belongs at the top, so each layer below stays standalone-green. Split a file when only some of its tests read the checkout, keep the fixture tests with their layer, compose the moved paths from ORIGIN_DIR (the directory the test was written in), and move a corpus describe whole when it carries a vacuity guard: a sibling left behind passes standalone over nothing. A test reading an UPPER layer’s files moves to that layer. It is red standing alone for the same reason, one level down: the file it reads is not in its layer’s closure. It goes in the upper layer’s DECLARED test home, which may import the lower layer — never the reverse — and it is split, pointed back to and composed from ORIGIN_DIR exactly as above. Check first that the file it reads really IS the upper layer’s: a path written from the checkout root (cat-harness/src/… read relative to the working directory) is red standing alone over a file the layer does hold, and the fix there is to resolve it from the test file, not to move it. A test that reads the checkout’s GIT asks which of two things it is. A standalone layer is a fresh clone with no origin and one commit, so a test handed this checkout’s remote, HEAD or origin/main fails there on a missing input. A test of LOGIC that merely reads git — address derivation, an upload URL’s shape, a commit IRI, resolving a short sha — builds a throwaway repository whose facts it sets (gitFixtureRepo in cat-harness’s test/support/git-fixture.ts) and passes that root, with every assertion exactly as strict; a function that resolves its root internally gains an optional root parameter defaulting to today’s. A check that THIS repository is configured right — its own Pages address, its committed pages’ banners — keeps its assertion verbatim and moves to the top-level test home above. upward paths counts what breaks, not what is out of sight. It counts declared paths that resolve above the layer, not dependents discovery cannot find: discovery is checkout-local on purpose, so a count of what it cannot see never reaches zero, and the risk is paths, not layers. A seeding pair is not upward. A higher layer’s Tool nodes may resolve into their implementer below through needs; the two are seeded in the same step, so none of those paths can break on seeding day. The HIGHER layer says so, seedsWith: [<lower>] in its declaration, because a lower layer naming one above it is the wrong direction. seed:ready states such paths in its note and does not count them; a path into any other layer above still counts. Four things to keep straight: . | The layer map is read off the declarations: livesAt.path is the directory, the longest needs chain is the depth, and the next layer is every layer one level up that needs this one. Nothing in the tool names a directory. | Every threshold is in the decision table, processes/kg/decisions/seed-readiness-gate.dmn. The script works out each criterion’s verdict by evaluating the table with the other facts at zero, so changing “five” is a one-line edit to the table. | heavy-mover is a label a person applies. With none on the layer, the criterion passes. If the label cannot be read, the answer is could-not-determine. | The rehearsal runs only on request, with --rehearse. It copies the layer and its needs into a scratch workspace (~150 MB and ~8,000 tests for cat-harness) and refuses to start with less than 3 GB free. Without --rehearse, the standalone criterion is could-not-determine, so seed:ready cannot answer settled until a rehearsal has run. That consequence is the one constant SETTLED_REQUIRES_REHEARSAL. | . Could-not-determine is never clean. GitHub lists at most 3,000 files per PR, so a criterion that the unseen files could change is undetermined, and the gateway answers unknown and stops. An unknown only withholds settled, though. It never hides a finding that is already certain, so the table tests the not yet rows first. not yet goes to Drain: land, close or re-target the PRs it named, then ask again. The tool only reports. It never seeds, labels or comments.

1129.title: The owner’s decisions
1129.content: An agent asks these; it does not settle them. | Separate at all, and where the boundary is — after the signals are measured. | The address base for the extracted graph’s identifiers: under the parent, or the new repository’s own. | Where verdicts about it live: hosted in the harness, or in the content. | What the tools repository owns, and how its checks run (agent, package, described workflow). | Authorise the extraction (stage 9). | Whether the first release is a draft with a tag, or the first formal publication (instance-publication). | The cutover (stage 13). | .

1130.title: Identifiers and versions
1130.content: One iriBase and one version in the declaration. Identifiers a program reads and pages a person reads are both <iriBase>v<major>/…; the exact release is the pin’s (bootstrap-tools/schemas/release-iri.ts). A base move is bun run iri:sync -- --from <old base>, once. A $schema tag carries its schema’s own semver. The exported graph’s own @id moves only when the new repository actually publishes. A published node’s identifier must be its file’s path (check:node-iris).

1131.title: Versions of the pair — same scheme, same start, then independent
1131.content: . | At the split, both start at the content’s current version, for simplicity — bootstrap was 0.1.0, so bootstrap-tools starts at 0.1.0. | After that each is versioned on its own, by the same rules: semver, the bump computed from the exported surface (check:version-bump). | Tags are plain v<major>.<minor>.<patch> in each new repository: a standalone repository holds one layer, declared at its root, so the tag needs no name. check:version-bump reads the plain form only there; a repository of several layers — the parent while the pair is staged — keeps <name>-v<major>.<minor>.<patch>, because a plain tag could not say which layer it released. | A tools release says which content versions it handles as a list of supported MAJOR versions (bootstrap: [0]), never a range expression — instance-versioning rule 2 forbids range syntax, and within one major a newer minor or patch only adds (tagCompatible). A tool asked to work on a content major it does not list refuses rather than guesses. | .

1132.title: How the parent consumes the pair
1132.content: No git submodules, ever (remote-mount.md). | mechanism | when | details | . | Remote mount (remoteMounts) | staging & development | A declared directory fetched at a pinned 40-character SHA with a committed lock (index.lock.json) and consent record. Downstream checkout .gitignore automatically ignores mounted directory trees. | . | NPM KG retrieval (kg-retrieve-npm) | packaged distribution | package.json declared in <instance>.json (role: "package-manifest"). Tarball packed via pack-tarball with a folio-binary-release/v1 integrity record, downloadable via npm install or GitHub binary releases (unhydrated source vs hydrated store). | . | Package import | published tools | The parent imports the tools’ Zod schemas and pipeline writers as an npm package dependency. | . | Upstream pins | maintenance | upstream-pins.json, maintained by upstream-version-adoption.bpmn. | . Separation lessons . | Downstream Gitignore Contract: When remote mounts populate a layer directory in the consumer repository, the consumer’s .gitignore must ignore the mounted paths. Otherwise, git treats external files as uncommitted local files. index.config.json automatically includes all remoteMounts paths in the generated .gitignore. | Folded Layer Aliases: When a layer or subgraph is folded into another (e.g. cat-openapi folded into cat-harness as named subgraph openapi), external forks or dependencies may still carry needs: ["cat-openapi"]. schemas/kg/harness-config.ts maintains FOLDED_INSTANCE_ALIASES to resolve these. | Asset Permission & License Validation: Pre-separation audits must verify library/withheld.json and copyright gates. Materializing or mounting a separated catalogue without verified asset clearance causes 404s and broken links on published documentation. | NPM Manifest in the KG: package.json is an authored pre-packaging asset in the Knowledge Graph (role: "package-manifest"), and .tgz release tarballs are tracked as folio-binary-release/v1 state documents with SHA-256 integrity digests. | No Relative Directory Climbing Across Repositories: Once separated into standalone checkouts, climbing ../.. escapes the repository boundary into .claude/worktrees/ or the parent filesystem and fails with Cannot find module. All cross-repository imports MUST be authored as package imports (e.g. @litlfred/cat-harness/... or via package exports), or resolved through package specifiers / tsconfig paths, NEVER through escaping filesystem ../.. traversals. | No Fixed-Depth Repository Root Assumptions (REPO): const REPO = resolve(import.meta.dir, "..", "..") points at the checkout root in a monorepo and above it in a standalone repository, so the script cannot find <instance>.json or scans sibling worktrees. Resolve the root dynamically — search upward for <instance>.json, index.config.json, or .git. | Clean Standalone Manifest (package.json) and Tooling Scaffolding: When extracting a layer to an upstream repository, package.json must be normalized: . | Operational commands must live under "scripts", not leftover monorepo "checkoutScripts". | Script definitions must NOT hardcode monorepo subdirectory paths (e.g. "bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/..." -> "bun run scripts/..."). | A standalone tsconfig.json must be present to prevent tsc from walking up to the monorepo root. | Explicit dependencies and devDependencies must be declared. | . | Fan-Out Recursion Guard in declaringInstances: When a mounted dependency carries its own nested remoteMounts, consumer remote fan-out must not mount sub-layers into roots that are already locked mounts of the parent checkout (!lockedMountPaths(checkout).has(rel)). Otherwise remoteFanOut mutates the child checkout’s tree and treeDigest verification fails. | Relative Directory Symlink Handling in Staging & Tarball Scripts: Recursive copies (cpSync(..., { recursive: true })) of trees with internal symlinked directories can recurse forever. Staging, site compilation, and packaging scripts must copy symlinks with { dereference: false } or use archive utilities (such as tar or rsync -a) that preserve symlink references. | Purely Declarative Ontologies vs. Companion Toolsets (FR-7): Purely declarative base repositories (such as litlfred/bootstrap) contain zero runtime execution code, zero test suites, and zero package.json manifests (FR-7). All graph compilation (JSON-LD export, BPMN diagram rendering, site staging, and schema validation) is executed by the companion tooling repository (bootstrap-tools). The declarative repository marks its render exemption (renderExemption: true) in its root manifest, and tooling scripts accept an explicit target repository argument (--repo <dir>). | Toolchain Decentralization (package.json, tsconfig.json, bunfig.toml): Tools and harness subgraphs must possess full standalone toolchain autonomy. package.json must be a standalone package manifest (e.g. @litlfred/<tools-layer>), bunfig.toml defines test preloads per layer, and tsconfig.json must set "noEmit": true and omit rootDir/outDir to prevent error TS6059: File is not under rootDir when cross-subgraph schemas or utilities are imported. See bun-use. | Monorepo Coordinator Demotion: Once tools and code are extracted to their respective packages, the root package.json is demoted to a private coordinator ("private": true) with narrowed tsconfig.json (test/**/*.ts). The root platform coordinates development workspaces, mounts, and integration tests, but never directly exports or publishes tool implementations. | Ephemeral File Purging and Root Hygiene: Ephemeral generated directories (_kg/, build/, test-results/) must NEVER be committed to the root repository or left unignored. Build outputs belong to the tool that produces them. | Layer Memory Preservation: Root directories beans/, todos/, and fsh-guts/ are the layer’s own durable working memory (the agent’s plan, the user’s todo queue, and the archival store). They are never overlaid across layers, never extracted to downstream packages, and stay at root by design. | A cutover is not done until the layer has re-pointed and can publish itself: livesAt is not a comment — remote-mount.ts takes livesAt.path as the mount path and seed-ready reads it as “still staged”. A path that was only ever a mount inside the parent’s site build serves nothing on its own, and generated pages keep absolute links to the parent’s paths, which 404 once the bytes move. Before stage 13: livesAt is gone, iriBase is declared, and the layer’s own site builds from its own repository. | The replayer must never live inside a layer it replays: if every workflow (and every downstream folio’s staging build, through a reusable workflow) bootstraps by running a script inside the directory being retired, the cutover breaks the first step of every job. Before stage 13, grep every workflow the parent ships for paths into the directory being retired, and give the parent a bootstrap entry point that lives in the parent and needs nothing mounted (a dependency-free .github/mount-from-lock.sh that fetches the pinned replayer). | A downstream’s CI is part of “green” for a cutover: a reusable workflow called @main (uses: litlfred/folio-assistant/.github/workflows/folio-staging.yml@main) runs the PARENT’s current workflow in the DOWNSTREAM’s repository. A cutover that is green in the parent can therefore be red in every folio at once, and the red lands on whatever pull request the folio author opens next — it reads as their failure. Stage 12’s “green” includes one dispatched staging run of at least one downstream folio after the cutover commit. | A separated checkout must run its own tests and type-check its own subgraphs: run them in a fresh standalone clone. A test that reads <checkout>/../package.json fails with ENOENT outside the composed tree (lesson 6 by another route), and a tsconfig.json whose include omits named subgraphs (openapi/, archimate/) is green while never reading them. A test or type-check that silently depends on the composition, or silently skips part of the repository, is not evidence the separated repository works. | The kinds a declaration is judged against come from the checkout being read, not from where the harness module sits: the graph-typology registry reads the checkout under inspection first (defaultTypologyRoots; $REPO_ROOT still overrides), then its own; a kind both declare is shadowed and reported, never merged. Otherwise two layouts give two answers about one correct declaration. Every path a declaration names is resolved in one run by check:declaration-resolution, and separation:cutover:check uses it as its declarations condition. | .

1133.title: After a move lands — the post-move sweep
1133.content: Moving files between the pair is one reviewed commit in each repository; making the repositories that consume the move work again is most of the work. Run the sweep after a move lands and before the parent re-pins (stage 11), and do not call the move done until every gate in this table is green in a composed checkout at the matched pins. When another layer links into the moved path, declare the move first, so the layers can re-pin in any order: two-phase-move. | what still names the old home | the gate that catches it | the fix | . | A Tool node’s invoke.shell | kg:audit criterion tool-invoke-path-resolves (CRITICAL) | rewrite the invokes in each tools/<id>/<id>.json | . | Prose and commands in skills, guides, READMEs, BPMN documentation, workflows | check:command-paths | the rewrite rule below | . | A script’s own usage string | check:usage-paths | rewrite it in the receiving layer | . | Printed and RUN commands: “Run: …” remedies, generated banners, shell hooks, an e2e global setup | check:published-instance-exports, check:invocation-parity, security:gate (all three match paths by text), and the unit tests | rewrite the strings in the receiving layer | . | A wrapper generator’s list of the scripts it wraps | bat:sync / bat:sync:check (the writer errors on the first missing file) | update the list | . | Partition rules naming moved files | check:partition (“exact rule(s) name a file that is not in …”) | remove the dead rules | . | A kind-validator node pointing at a moved module | check:kind-validators:require-all | open: how a node in one layer names a module in the other | . | A writer’s claims in qa-refresh: files the writer used to rewrite became output it writes | qa:refresh (“N file(s) no declared writer claims”) | update the writer’s claims | . | A visualiser route a generator computed by hand | uml:overview inside skill:register (“no glossary page at …”) | use the declared route (declaredRoute(<core>, "glossary-page")) | . | A browser bundle importing a node-only module through a package import | navbar:assets (“Browser polyfill for module node:url …”) | move the constant into a node-free module | . | A directory declared inside another declared directory in the receiving layer | check:layout-norms (it stops qa:refresh) | move it out of the enclosing declared directory | . | A file left in BOTH layers | slice:sqlite / slice:sqlite:check (the KG export mints the same IRI twice and the slice dies on a UNIQUE constraint); node-kinds:check and kg:export do not refuse a duplicate on their own | delete the copy in the layer that no longer owns it, archived to fsh-guts/retired/ | . | Paired artefacts a move split across repositories | skills:docs (“page(s) produced by NO source”), check:declared-dirs (“absent — declared and not on disk”) | pin the receiving commits WITH the removing one (below) | . The rewrite rule . Rewrite a path only where the file exists in the destination and not in the source, and never in a record. The first half keeps a placeholder or a typo from turning into a different wrong path; the second keeps a file that moved and was later re-created from being redirected. Records say what was true when they were written, so they stay as written: proposals, todos, agent memory, work items, provenance (library figures, terminologies), upstream pins, vocab mappings, QA results and test fixtures. Generated files are rewritten by re-running their generators, never by hand. The rule is a Tool: rewrite-moved-paths (bun run cat paths:rewrite-moved --from-name <old> --from-root <dir> --to-name <new> --to-root <dir> --prefix <moved dir> … [--keep <glob>]). It reports with file and line by default, applies with --write, and with --check is the gate for a sweep that should be finished. Its test proves it never opens a proposal, a memory or a fixture. Pin the pair together, and record each consent first-hand . A move that removes files from one repository must be pinned together with the commit that adds them to the receiving one. A parent that pins the new source with the OLD pin of a receiving repository has the moved artefacts in neither, and the gates say so only indirectly. Before a re-pin, list what each new commit removes and confirm the receiving repository’s pin contains it. Every pin is a trust decision with its own consent (rule H8, remote-mount): trust.consent names who, when, the exact ref and the evidence, and mount:remote refuses a ref nobody consented to. A consent relayed by another agent is not the owner’s consent, so it is not recorded from the relay alone; record it when the owner’s answer to a question naming the exact SHAs is relayed verbatim with its time. A standing consent (“pin any main commit of these repositories that includes a fix merged in this session, listed in the PR”) covers only the repositories and the window it names, and each pin made under it is listed where the owner will read it. When a consented ref turns out not to do (a consented main with no declaration of the layer), do not substitute another ref: keep the previous pin and report it. The order that worked, and the rules for several sessions at once . | Fix the tools (the receiving layer): paths, the checks that matched paths by text, bundles, layout. | Fix the content (the source layer): prose, Tool invokes, declarations, partition rules. | Regenerate the content at matched pins, in a composed checkout laid down from the parent’s lock, to a fixed point (qa:refresh COMPLETE, then bun run cat regen, then every --check green on a fresh lay-down). | Re-pin the parent to those commits. | Run bun run cat gates on a fresh lay-down of the parent. | . When several sessions work on one separation at once: . | Hold pushes on a branch another session is superseding; hand over what is unpushed instead of racing it. | Announce which gates each session takes before starting, and re-check the open PRs and recent merges of a repository before opening one there. | Verify on the lock of the PR that will land, in a fresh scratch copy, never on another session’s checkout. | A measurement-only workaround stays local (for example a baseline entry needed to run qa:refresh while a decision is pending), is never committed, and is deleted once the real fix lands. | .

1134.title: Rollback
1134.content: Until the parent is green with the extraction declared, the extraction is additive and the parent keeps its copy; the cutover commit is the one unit worth reverting, and since the copy is ARCHIVED in the parent’s fsh-guts rather than deleted, the archive restores the exact tree that was removed. After a release, a tagged version is never reused: roll back with a new patch release and move the parent’s pin back.

1135.title: Worked examples
1135.content: 1. bootstrap + bootstrap-tools . | Stages 1–5: wrong facts, folio-only names and root-relative paths removed; graph typologies, $schema tags and QA moved out; IRIs under https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/ with semver. | Stage 6: bootstrap-tools/ created as a sibling; the Zod source moved down; the import cone cut to zod only; check:tools-closure and check:node-iris added, each watched failing on a planted violation. | . 2. cat-harness + the tools layer . | cat-harness (litlfred/cat-harness): owns the knowledge graph, declarative schemas, content adapters, and BPMN/DMN processes. | The tools layer: owns the MCP server (src/server.ts), concrete tool implementations (src/tools/), ambient moddle type definitions (types/), standalone package.json, tsconfig.json, and bunfig.toml. | Consumed through an index.config.json remote mount, locked in index.lock.json. The move of the harness’s remaining code into the tools layer is the case the post-move sweep was written from. | .

1137.title: Subscribing to a knowledge graph
1137.content: Skill kg-subscription: Subscribing a folio or harness to an external knowledge graph — a substrate — and walking its parts from referenced to materialised, one at a time and only through the shared materialisation gates. When to subscribe, what makes a repository a substrate, choosing subgraphs, assets and harnesses, the five gates, instantiating a harness so it reaches the navbar, moving the pin, and what never to do. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . A folio layer, or any harness, can subscribe to an external knowledge graph: choose to materialize some or all of its subgraphs and assets locally, and instantiate one or more of its harnesses so they appear in the navbar. A subscription is not a new mechanism. It is the relation that joins pieces this repository already has: the materialisation record, the shared Process_MaterializeRemote, the refresh, and the harness tile. This skill is the walk between them; each piece keeps its own rules, and where this file and one of them disagree, that one wins. |   | where | . | the process | subscribe-kg.bpmn | . | the entry | SubscriptionSchema in cat-harness/schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts | . | the held-bytes record | the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer) | . | the gates | materialize-remote and its process | .

1138.title: When to subscribe — and when not to
1138.content: Subscribe when your graph consumes another repository’s graph and you want to hold some of it, or just to pin exactly which version you are reading. | you want | relation | . | to load a layer fully, with its skills overlaid | needs | . | to point at a harness and never load it | associatedHarnesses | . | to consume a remote graph, holding the parts you choose | subscriptions | . A subscription sits between the other two and moves: every part starts referenced and becomes materialised only when chosen and let through the gates. The schema refuses an id that is also in needs or associatedHarnesses, because two relations to one layer is two answers to “do we hold it”.

1139.title: The substrate rule
1139.content: You can subscribe only to a substrate: a repository whose root declaration . | parses as bootstrap’s KnowledgeGraphDeclarationSchema (bootstrap-tools/schemas/graph.ts), and | declares at least one instantiated harness. | . Both are answered by the declaration file alone, so validate with a sparse, shallow fetch of that one file — never a full clone. “Could not fetch” is a third answer, never “conforms”. A repository that fails either point is not subscribed; record the reason and the pin you asked at, and write no entry. Known substrates are derived from each staged layer’s repository and each associated harness, with hand rows (knownSubstrates, schema KnownSubstrateSchema) only where no declaration names one. Start from that registry before asking the person for a repository name.

1140.title: Pin, always
1140.content: ref is a full 40-character commit SHA. Never a branch, never an abbreviated SHA, never “latest”. An unpinned subscription is how two subscribers see two different graphs under one name, and the schema refuses anything else — the same rule sync-remote-skills.ts enforces for remote skills. A tag replaces the SHA only once the substrate publishes releases.

1141.title: The entry holds the choice, never the state
1141.content: "subscriptions": [{ "id": "<iris-replica>", "repository": "litlfred/<iris-replica>", "ref": "<40-char sha>", "subgraphs": ["catalogue"], // CHOSEN; everything else stays referenced "assets": { "policy": "on-demand" }, // none | on-demand | all "harnesses": ["<iris-replica>"] // CHOSEN for instantiation }] . Whether catalogue is held is answered by its materialisation record, not by this list. Writing “materialised: true” on the entry would be a second answer free to disagree with the record — so do not add one, and do not read subgraphs as “what arrived”. A subgraph not listed is referenced, not absent: the visualizer still shows it.

1142.title: Choosing parts
1142.content: Show the person everything the cached declaration offers — every subgraph, asset class and harness, each with its state — before asking what to hold. A reader who sees only what was chosen cannot tell “not offered” from “not taken”. Then follow interaction-modality: context, options, recommendation, question. | Subgraphs — by the substrate’s directories[].id. Choose the smallest set that serves the folio; each is a separate trip through the gates. A nested subgraph is chosen by its parent’s id and materialised by its path (next section). | Assets — none, on-demand (each asset through the gates when first asked for), or all (every referenced asset walked now). on-demand is the sensible default for a large binary library; all on a catalogue the size of IRIS is a size-gate refusal waiting to happen. | Harnesses — only those whose needs are held here, locally or by another subscription. The process checks this before any byte moves and sends the choice back if not: subscribe the missing dependency first, or leave that harness referenced. | . Choosing nothing is legitimate. A subscription with no parts chosen is a pinned reference.

1143.title: Materialising: the five gates, via the shared process only
1143.content: Every chosen subgraph or asset goes through Process_MaterializeRemote, called — never re-implemented. Purpose first (working or archival), then the five gates in order: . | size — what fraction, and what the whole costs; refuse when you cannot tell | restrictions — “none known” is a state, not a green light | copyright — per bitstream, and separately for the derived work | retention — what expires this copy | source loss — what survives if the origin goes; only an archival copy discharges it | . unknown on any gate keeps the part referenced. That is the process working, not failing: record the refusing gate’s basis and continue with the next part — one part refused is not the subscription refused. The bytes that do arrive carry a materialization.json with fixity, and check:materialized-fixity covers them. A nested subgraph: chosen by its parent, materialised by its path . Some subgraphs are declared from within another directory. skills/voices, for example, is declared in skills/skills.json. To hold only that part, choose its parent’s id in subgraphs and ask for the part by path: . bun run cat kg:materialize <subscription> skills/voices # `skills` is chosen . The snapshot is not changed and nobody re-subscribes. The snapshot holds the root declaration only, so a nested id cannot be checked against it offline. The parent’s id can be, and the path is checked against the parent’s declared path. The part goes through the same five gates and its record names the parent’s id and the nested path. It is held beside the parent’s own part, which it never disturbs. A path under no declared directory is refused, and so is a path whose parent is not chosen.

1144.title: A subgraph’s nodes without its bytes: metadata mode
1144.content: To know what is in a subgraph — every node of sdlc/skills, typed, labelled and linked — you do not need its files. Ask for its published index.hydrated.jsonld instead (kg-export §”Named subgraphs”): . bun run cat kg:materialize --nodes <subscription> <subgraph-path> # e.g. --nodes cat sdlc/skills . | It fetches one file at the pin, <docs>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/<path>/index.hydrated.jsonld. Here <docs> and <HARNESS> come from the cached declaration. The file is validated against SubgraphHydratedSchema, and its root @id must be the subgraph you asked for. | It is held under <snapshot dir>/<subscription>/nodes/<path>/, beside a nodes.json record with its sha256. kg:materialize:check re-hashes it. | The root is refused. A harness root publishes index.jsonld only, so read that for the child subgraph IRIs, then ask for a child. | Only size applies, as a measured cap (--max-bytes). The four person gates guard copies of somebody else’s content. This is published graph metadata, with every body left as a pointer, and it can be fetched again from the pin at any time. The reasoning is in the header of the content core’s scripts/kg-materialize.ts. | It is not a substitute for the byte copy. When you need the files themselves, choose the subgraph and run it through the five gates above. | .

1145.title: Instantiating a harness
1145.content: kg:instantiate writes the state directories the harness declares and its config. The state directories go under the subscriber’s own subscribed-harnesses directory (graph typology subscribed-harnesses, holds: state), at <state dir>/<subscription>/<harness>/; a subscriber that declares none is refused, with what to declare. They never go at the repository root, where a harness named after a staged layer would write into that layer’s directory, and never under the snapshot directory, which holds upstream’s bytes and is declared readOnly. Where the checkout has a root index.config.json, the config goes INLINE in a new instances[] entry and no <harness>.config.json is written: the index is the one config, and it is then what reads as instantiated. Only a checkout with no index gets a root <harness>.config.json. The rule is index-config’s. Instantiation is what harness-tiles reads, and what puts the harness in the navbar’s bottom region. check:instance-render must be green afterwards; a config that renders nothing is a navbar entry pointing nowhere. A harness already instantiated at this pin is skipped, not rewritten.

1146.title: Moving the pin is refresh, not re-subscribe
1146.content: To move ref: validate the substrate at the new commit, then run every held part through Process_RefreshMaterialized — what changed upstream, what changed locally, what to do when both did; an archival copy is fixity-checked and never re-fetched. Only then rewrite ref and re-cache the declaration. Moving the ref first leaves the records of parts not yet refreshed describing a commit the entry no longer names. Afterwards, review again: the new pin may offer subgraphs the old one did not.

1147.title: Do not
1147.content: . | Materialise without the gates. No copying a subgraph by hand, no git archive into the tree, no “it’s only a few files”. Every byte arrives through Process_MaterializeRemote, or it is an unrecorded fork of upstream. Metadata mode (--nodes) is not an exception to this, because it copies none of the subgraph’s bytes: only the graph description that the substrate publishes. | Subscribe unpinned. No branch, no short SHA, no follow-latest. | Record state on the entry. State lives on the materialisation record. | Treat a refused part as failure and retry it with the gate relaxed. The refusal is the answer until the fact behind it changes. | Instantiate a harness whose needs are not held. Subscribe them first. | Subscribe to a non-substrate because its content looks useful. Without a conforming declaration there is nothing to pin subgraphs against — reference it instead. | Delete a materialised part to “unsubscribe” it on your own initiative. It is a durable artefact; report what would go and wait (deletion-requires-confirmation). | Skip a step because its tool is missing. Perform it by hand following the process — least of all the gates. | .

1149.title: L1 coverage — nothing normative goes missing silently
1149.content: Skill l1-coverage: Check that an L1 extraction accounted for every normative sentence in its source publication — captured as a node, or excluded for a fixed-list reason a person signed off. Per-page counts, captured %, accounted-for %, and a non-zero exit below 100 % accounted-for. Generic: three input files, nothing folio-specific. Implements smart-kg’s docs/COVERAGE.md contract. Named by: DTH authoring . Any L1 extraction SHALL produce a coverage QA report: every normative sentence in the source is captured, or excluded for a reason from a fixed list; the target is 100 % accounted for. The report’s fields and what its numbers mean are fixed by smart-kg’s docs/COVERAGE.md; this is the implementation that contract says core owns.

1150.title: Why
1150.content: An extraction — by hand or by a tool — fails silently: a recommendation that never became a node leaves no trace in the graph. For example, a label-based extractor finds 0 recommendations in a WHO position paper (WER 92(17), measles, 2017) because position papers print no “Recommendation N” labels. Only a check that reads the source catches that.

1151.title: Run it
1151.content: bun run cat l1:coverage --text pages.json --captured captured.json \ [--exclusions exclusions.json] [--out report.json] . | input | shape | . | --text | the BODY text, page-tagged: {"pages":[{"page":3,"text":"…"}]}, or plain text with a form feed between pages (what pdftotext writes). Strip references, running headers and the table of contents first — the script cannot tell a header from a sentence. | . | --captured | [{"id":"rec-1","text":"…"}] — every captured statement, verbatim | . | --exclusions | [{"location":"p3:s7","reason":"background-fact","signedOffBy":"…","signedOffAt":"…"}], or text in place of location | . Exit 0 only at 100 % accounted-for (or when nothing in the source is normative — the percentages are then null, never 100); 1 below target or on an exclusion with an unknown reason; 2 on unusable input. The per-page table goes to stderr, the report to --out or stdout.

1152.title: Reading the numbers
1152.content: . | Accounted-for is the target, captured is beside it. A publication legitimately holds normative-looking sentences that are not recommendations (“all regions should have eliminated measles by 2020” is history). A 100 % accounted-for made mostly of exclusions is visible as a low captured %. | A proposed exclusion is not an exclusion. Without signedOffBy the sentence stays unaccounted. An agent may PROPOSE an exclusion; only a person signs it off (req:agent-workflow → judgement-stays-human). | The reasons are fixed: background-fact, manufacturer-statement, editorial, research-question, duplicate-of:<captured id>. A sentence that fits none is either a missing capture or a missing reason, and both go to a person — never to a sixth string. | Matching is normalised substring (case, quotes, dashes, whitespace). A paraphrased capture reads as unaccounted on purpose: a near match is a judgement, and the report does not make it for you. | The marker list is closed and English (contract §1): should, shall, must, recommend*, should not, is not a reason, are not a contraindication, and may be + given/administered/offered/considered/ used/co-administered/implemented. Bare may does not count. | .

1153.title: Where --captured comes from in a DAK or DTH
1153.content: From the entry’s own candidates.json. The requirements aspect proposes every sentence carrying one of the markers above (l1-document-ingestion), verbatim, so jq '[.candidates[] | {id: (.number // .section_file), text: .statement}]' over it is a --captured file. A sentence the aspect proposed matches. One it missed (split across a page or a table cell) shows as unaccounted, and goes to a person.

1154.title: Where it sits
1154.content: After l1-document-ingestion has produced the entry and an extraction has produced the captured statements; before the extraction is reviewed or promoted. check:l1-complete asks whether an L1 entry is structurally complete; this asks whether its normative content was all accounted for. They are different questions and neither implies the other. Once the extraction is reviewed, its statements are published with links to their sources by publish-extracted-statements: coverage says everything was captured, publication makes what was captured readable and traceable.
