1156.title: L1 document ingestion
1156.content: Skill l1-document-ingestion: The detailed method for turning a DOCUMENT in uploads/ into a complete L1 entry in library/<bib-slug>/ — which rung reads it and why, what a complete L1 entry holds, why an inferred structure is refused rather than guessed, and the archive, dataset, narrative, image and vector-label arms. Refines the harness’s basic library-ingestion flow; one entry point: bun run cat ingest. Named by: DTH authoring . This is a refinement, not the entry point. The harness’s library-ingestion skill carries the basic flow every asset takes — an upload is accepted, its metadata goes into the knowledge graph, and the asset lands in library/ if it is materialized — together with the two entry points, the upload’s retirement to fsh-guts/, and the remote half. This skill is what happens next when the asset is a document whose text and structure are wanted as L1 source content: reading it into sections, blocks and sidecars that check:l1-complete can judge. The rung code — scripts/ingest-document.ts, the pdf-*.py rungs, notebook-structure.ts and OCR — lives in the harness. This skill is the METHOD that chooses among them; invoking harness code from here is a downward edge. The executable form is processes/library/l1-document-ingestion.bpmn, which calls the harness’s basic Process_Ingestion first and then the four ingest-* phases beside it.

1157.title: The whole path is two commands
1157.content: bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> # rung + every derived arm, into ingest-staging/ bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> --promote # the L1 gate, then into <lib>/<slug>/ . Staging prints the second line for you, built from your own arguments. --promote writes the entry’s JSON-LD nodes, for that entry only, with the same buildEntryNodes the corpus generator uses. They are minted for the destination, not for staging: an entry’s layer is read off where it sits, and ingest-staging/ belongs to whichever layer holds it. You do not need gen-library-jsonld or check:l1-complete --write after promoting — the first is done, and the second’s verdicts live on the qa-reports branch rather than on main.

1158.title: Which rung, and why there is more than one
1158.content: | rung | when | what it produces | . | pdf-structure.py | any PDF with a text layer | the outline’s chapters; with no outline, the inferred contents when it is trusted, else one section per page | . | pdf-pages.py | a page tree by hand: --first-page-label, or --from-ocr text | one section per page | . | pdf-ocr.py | text extraction yields almost nothing | a text layer to then page-split | . | pdf-tables.py | tables or figures matter | what pdf-structure/v1’s Section does not carry | . | slides-structure.py | the package declares a PPTX or ODP deck | one section per slide, images.json, accessibility.json | . | referenced-source.py | --reference given: the licence forbids a copy | referenced.json only — identity, sha256, outline; no text | . | text-structure.ts | the source is text files — Markdown, MDX, XML — usually fetched from a repository at a commit | text-structure/v1: a Markdown file divided by its own ATX headings outside fenced code, any other file one verbatim section, located by file and line range; images recorded by digest, never sectioned | . | notebook-structure.ts | the file is JSON with a numeric nbformat and a cells array — a Jupyter notebook, decided by content, never by the .ipynb name | notebook-structure/v1: one section per markdown heading, located by cell range; code kept as fenced code and never run; outputs not kept, and structure_note says so | . A notebook is a variant, not a PDF with odd pages. structure.json has a shared base (cat-harness-tools schemas/content/document-structure.ts): the PDF format is one variant, unchanged, and the notebook format is the other. A reader that needs only sections reads either through structureOf(), which says where a section is as {pages} or {cells}. A page-aware reader gets nothing from a notebook, rather than a cell index mistaken for a page number. The decision is mechanical: . | toc_source: outline → pdf-structure (9789241548960-eng, 250 sections) | toc_source: none, source.text_source: embedded → pdf-structure, which keeps its inferred contents only when they pass the trust tests and otherwise writes pages (wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng lands on pages that way) | a junk outline (milnorlink) → pdf-pages: pdf-structure would read the outline it found rather than infer one | toc_source: none, source.text_source: ocr → pdf-ocr then pdf-pages --from-ocr (who-pub-tps-931) | .

1159.title: Slide decks — PPTX and ODP
1159.content: A deck is a zip that declares its type ([Content_Types].xml, or ODF’s mimetype member), so it routes on the sniff, before the archive rung, exactly as a workbook does. slides-structure.py writes the same pdf-structure/v1 shape a paged PDF gets — one section per slide, page_start == page_end == <slide>, granularity: "slide" — so l1-blocks.ts, the manifest and check:l1-complete read it unchanged. Two differences from the PDF rungs: . | A slide’s title is its title placeholder, or it is Slide N. Never the largest text box: that is the inferred-TOC failure below in a new format. It is also an accessibility finding, because a slide with no title placeholder cannot be navigated to by name, so the two questions share one answer (title_source: placeholder | none in each section’s front matter). | No image is a page-scan. A full-bleed picture alone on a slide is the slide’s content, not a scan of text already extracted. | . accessibility.json reports, per check, what the package can answer — slide titles, alt text (with editor auto-captions such as “Description automatically generated” counted as failing, since nobody wrote them), decorative marks, language tags, document title, speaker notes — and says undetermined for the three it cannot: reading order, images of text, contrast. It gives no overall score. A single number would weigh a missing title against a missing alt text, and nothing supports that weighting. Two copies of one deck? Compare before you choose which to ingest: . python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/slides-structure.py --a11y-only DECK.pptx DECK.odp . Prefer the copy that wins the per-check comparison. An export can lose what the author wrote (an ODP export of Google Slides can drop all alt text and keep the language only on the default style), and the format’s reputation does not tell you which way a particular export went. Image descriptions go in the library’s image-verdicts.json as for a PDF. Put the inspector in attribution.<doc-id> when they are not the file’s inspected_by; without it the deck inherits the first inspector’s name and date.

1160.title: A source whose licence forbids a copy — record it, do not ingest it
1160.content: Some sources may be read but not reposted. The OMG BPMN and DMN specifications permit use on condition that a copy “will not be copied or posted on any network computer or broadcast in any media”. A normal ingest commits every section’s text to a public repository, which breaks that condition. It does so silently, because nothing in the text layer says so. bun run cat ingest FILE.pdf --reference IDENTITY.json --library <name> . IDENTITY.json holds the title, version, document number, date, publisher, URL and the licence clause, read off the document. A missing field is refused, never guessed. The entry holds referenced.json — the exact bytes’ sha256, the embedded outline (clause titles and pages, so a citation can still name a clause), a folio-materialization/v1 record in state referenced, and why the text is withheld — plus a manifest with an empty contains, and a licence.json quoting the clause. The choice is the caller’s, never inferred. Whether a licence permits posting is a reading of the licence, not of the bytes. check:l1-complete knows the kind, and refuses a referenced entry that holds sections/, blocks/ or images/. That would be the copy this kind exists not to make. A publication, not a file — an external reference. A FHIR implementation guide is a website and a package, not one PDF, so there are no bytes to hash. Its referenced.json takes the published variant of source (schemas/referenced-source.ts): kind: "published", url, canonical, package_id, version, and read_from / read_at naming the local record the identity was read off — no sha256, rather than a made-up one. links names where a reader goes instead (the publisher’s page, and a site_path on this site such as the layer’s artefact index), and the library viewer shows them on the entry’s row. Write it by hand — there is no file to run referenced-source.py on — then gen-library-jsonld.ts --entry for the manifest. The licence follows the usual rule: stated only with a basis, else unknown with where you looked. Example: the WHO SMART Trust IG’s entry in the DAK layer’s library/.

1161.title: A source published as text in a repository — read it at a commit
1161.content: The Gherkin reference, the MCP specification, the hmans/beans README and FHIR R5’s TestPlan resource are published as Markdown or XML in git repositories. Printing one to PDF so a PDF rung can read it makes the recorded sha256 identify a rendering nobody published, so they take their own rung instead: . bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.md --text --library <lib> # rung + l1-blocks, into ingest-staging/ bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.md --text --library <lib> --promote # the L1 gate, then the entry and its KG nodes . --text is the CALLER’s statement that the file is text: text has no magic bytes, so the extension is never read, and a binary handed in as text is refused as undetermined. Through cat ingest it takes the notebook’s derived arm (l1-blocks), and --promote writes the entry’s JSON-LD nodes, as for every rung. Do not stop at the rung. Run alone, text-structure.ts leaves an entry with no manifest.jsonld and no section or block nodes. A source read at a commit, with its upstream.json and several files, still runs the rung directly: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/text-structure.ts -o <library> --doc-id <slug> \ --base <checkout> --upstream upstream.json [--title T] [--image F]... FILE... and then, without fail, l1-blocks.ts -o <entry> and gen-library-jsonld.ts --entry <entry>, as for a notebook. What it decides: . | Divided by the author’s headings, or not at all. A Markdown file splits at its own ATX headings, outside fenced code. A # comment inside a gherkin block is not a heading. Any other text, and anything that opens with <, is one section, fenced verbatim. Nothing is rendered: shortcodes and JSX stay as written, and structure_note says so. | upstream records the exact revision: repository, 40-hex commit, ref, path, and in words whether that revision is the published text or a working copy. A default branch is often neither, and a reader cannot tell which from a URL. Keep the clone out of the repository tree. The bytes can be fetched again from the commit, so none go to uploads/ or fsh-guts/. | Several files are one source when the publisher ships them as one, as with a specification version that is a directory of pages. Each file keeps its own sha256. The source’s sha256 is the sha256 of their sha256sum listing, so sha256sum -c against a checkout verifies the entry without this code. | .

1162.title: From a library entry to a folio document — seed it, and its graph comes with it
1162.content: A folio whose working document starts from a source (an outline, a draft, a report) is SEEDED from the library entry, not from the raw file: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/seed-folio-from-library.ts \ --entry library/<doc-id> --slug <folio-doc> [--title T] [--author A]... [--force] . Any structure.json variant works. The top heading level becomes the chapters, deeper levels nest as sections, and a section’s own text becomes one prose block. No kind is guessed: a persona or a requirement is the folio’s own enrichment step. Every block carries meta.source (library, section, locator, method: "library-seed"), and the seed ENDS by writing each block’s .jsonld with gen-block-jsonld’s own code. A folio-specific seed script that writes blocks must end the same way, or its site publishes no graph. A seed is one-time: an existing document is refused unless --force, which discards hand edits. The original is never touched: the library entry and the folio’s nodes are DERIVED, and both are checked (gen-library-jsonld --check, gen-block-jsonld --check) so neither can drift unseen.

1163.title: A source’s glossary and abbreviations — candidates, read by one tool
1163.content: Every L1, DTH and DAK source reads its glossary the same way, with the Tool glossary-from-source, never with a script of its own: . bun run cat glossary:from-source --out glossary/<scheme>.glossary.json \ --id <scheme> --title "<title>" --from library/<doc-id>/sections . --from reads every section whose title names a glossary, definitions, terms, abbreviations or acronyms, and each numbered section under a glossary section (a specification that prints one term per heading). A folio block can be named with --terms or --abbreviations. Each row becomes a candidate term, verbatim, with source: <file>#L<line>; an acronym becomes the notation of the term it expands. The scheme is merged: a term a person has adopted or edited is never changed. Only a person moves a term to authored (glossary-terms). --check keeps the candidates in step with the L1 entry.

1164.title: Requirements and normative statements — every DAK and DTH source
1164.content: Requirement extraction is a general part of L1 ingestion for DAK and DTH sources, as a Stage B aspect: cat ingest runs extract-candidates.py --aspects-only on every staged entry, and each requirement the source states becomes a typed node in the entry’s graph, derivedFrom its L1 section. A folio’s requirement block then CITES that node. It does not restate it with an id of its own. The mount is the gate. The requirements aspect lives in the DAK layer (its scripts/extractors/dak-requirements.py), so it runs in DAK and DTH repositories and nowhere else. With no aspect mounted the arm writes nothing. No new schema: the existing kind that fits the source. Requirement schemas come in more than one style, some core and some the DAK layer’s: . | the source prints | kind | layer | . | a DAK requirement row, <CODE>.FXREQ.<n> / .NFXREQ.<n> | functional-requirement / non-functional-requirement | DAK layer | . | a system’s shall/must/should in prose (“The registry shall …”) | functional-requirement, no id | DAK layer | . | a row of a table of system functions | functional-requirement, source_kind: function-table-row (by hand today) | DAK layer | . | a row of a table of information needs, an item of a list of reports or functions, a figure caption naming a function | functional-requirement, source_kind: information-need-table-row, function-list-item, figure-caption (by hand today) | DAK layer | . | an indicator | indicator | DAK layer | . | any other normative sentence | recommendation, strength in rfc2119-requirement-level or grade-recommendation-strength | core | . Ids come from the source or there are none. number is the id exactly as printed, and it lands in the node’s meta.source_number. A requirement that prints no id has none. The node’s @id is derived from the section and the order the items appear in (<kind>-<section>-NN), never from a made-up label such as an agent-assigned FR-xx. A requirement from a source is a reference, not a definition: it contributes to a definition but does not make one. The nodes carry provenance: ingested and route_to: l2-dak-authoring. The folio that cites one decides what it means for its own system, and a person promotes it. Then account for everything. Run l1-coverage with the entry’s requirement candidates as --captured. Every normative sentence the aspect did not propose is either a missing capture or an exclusion a person signs off. A requirement written by hand, from a table no extractor reads yet, uses the same candidates.json shape: kind, source_kind, number (or null), name, statement verbatim, section_file, section_title, pages, formalization_candidate: false, route_to. Leave out document_class, validated and disposition. Those describe the WHOLE document, and the manifest reads them as such. Then run gen-library-jsonld --entry.

1165.title: An inferred chapter tree is refused, not guessed
1165.content: The failure this rule prevents is silent. Without an outline, a heading-detector can infer a table of contents — and an inferred TOC is confidently wrong in a way the output does not show. Two cases: . | WPR-RDO-2020-003-eng.pdf — 11 of 13 inferred sections were named after a different publication, because page 22 reproduces a sample table from one as a design example. | WHO_PUB_TPS_93.1.pdf — inferred entries took page numbers from the contents pages, so 26 of 42 sections came out under 500 characters while 37,923 characters landed in one section misnamed 18-usetul-reference-books. | . So pdf-pages claims no chapter tree and says so in structure_note. A page is a determined division; an inferred chapter was not. Same third-state rule the rest of this repository keeps: a structure that could not be determined is never rendered as one that was. The route pdf-structure.py takes itself . With no outline, the inferred contents is used only when it passes all three tests, in order (inferred_toc_trust): . | concentration: at most 60% of its entries may start on the two commonest pages — a list read off a page is not the document’s structure; | mean confidence ≥ 0.6 (TOC_MIN_MEAN_CONFIDENCE), each entry’s confidence being how much independent evidence agreed — a contents page, the body, a heading style, a numbering run; | headings with bodies: from 5 sections up, no more than 25% of the sections the tree would cut may hold under 50 characters (TOC_MAX_EMPTY_SHARE, TOC_EMPTY_SECTION_CHARS), front matter not counted — a tree of empty sections is logo lettering, a sample table’s column heads or a cover’s address block, not chapters. | . Otherwise — refused, or nothing inferred — the entry is split one section per page (page-001, “Page 1”, the shape pdf-pages.py writes), with granularity: "page", toc_source: undetermined or none, toc_undetermined_reason, and a structure_note saying why. Both inputs are recorded whether or not they passed: diagnostics.toc_inferred_entries and diagnostics.toc_inferred_mean_confidence and diagnostics.toc_inferred_empty_share. What the floor does and does not catch. The mean is a weak predictor of quality. A mean of exactly 0.60 means no entry was corroborated by anything but its style, and “at least 0.6” lets it through, so read a font TOC at 0.60 before citing it. The floor’s real work is on the regex fallback, whose entries carry no confidence and count as 0. The third test is the one that catches a poor font tree; a poor tree with an empty share just under 25% is too close to good ones to separate by this measure.

1166.title: What a complete L1 entry holds
1166.content: library/<bib-slug>/ structure.json "$schema": "pdf-structure/v1" — doc_id, toc_source, granularity, sections[], structure_note, source{} (see below; source.text_source says embedded|ocr) sections/ one Markdown file per section, front matter + body blocks/ the block projection consumers read manifest.jsonld @id, @type folio:SourceDocument, contains[], provenance summaries.json agent summaries of prose blocks, a QA sidecar (see below) ocr/ page-NNN.txt, only where the source was scanned . bun run cat check:l1-complete is the gate. It reports three states, never two: a requirement met, unmet, or not yet derivable — the last because the per-format arms (images, audio, tables, archives) are tracked separately and a check that cannot run must not read as a pass. Then publish its statements. Once the entry is complete and promoted, every statement extracted from it is published in the folio’s working artifact and in the shared extraction viewer, each linked to the entry and its section, and CI keeps those pages current. That is a standard step, the same for every content type: publish-extracted-statements.

1167.title: A manifest’s title — the authority order, and never the page-1 parse
1167.content: A library entry’s manifest.jsonld title is the first of these the entry has: . | rank | meta.title_source | read from | . | 1 | dc-record | dc.title of the Dublin Core record that the catalogue node naming this entry (libraryId) points at through metadataRef | . | 2 | referenced | referenced.json identity.title | . | 3 | pdf-info | structure.json metadata.docinfo.Title, the PDF Info /Title, when it is not junk | . | 3 | text-heading | structure.json metadata.title of a text or notebook structure: front-matter title:, --title, or the level-1 heading | . | 4 | slug | the entry id. Nothing better exists, and check:library-qa reports it as title-missing | . The page-1 front-matter parse is NEVER a title. On a pdf-structure/v1, metadata.title is parse_front_matter’s guess at which lines of page 1 are the title, and it guesses wrong (a running head, a repeated word, a status block). A plausible wrong title passes every check that has no second source. A slug is honest about being a placeholder and gets flagged. The parse may still feed search and the section files’ doc_title. text-heading shares rank 3 because it is the same kind of fact as /Title (the source naming itself, in its format’s own metadata). The two are exclusive by variant, so no entry ever has both. A tabular record’s title is its source file name, which is never a title. Junk /Title (pdfInfoTitleJunk): shorter than 3 characters or no letters; untitled and its kin; Microsoft Word - …; an arXiv stamp (arXiv:0909.4061v2 [math.NA] …); anything ending in a file extension; the source’s file name or stem; the slug. A junk value falls through to the next source. It never becomes the title. Records (ranks 1–2) are taken as written, because a cataloguer’s choice is not a program’s default. Record the Info dictionary at ingest. pdf-structure.py and pdf-pages.py write metadata.docinfo. Backfill an older entry with python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-pages.py --docinfo-into <entry> <pdf>. It refuses unless the PDF’s sha256 is the one the entry recorded. One resolver, cat-harness-tools/pipeline/library-title.ts (resolveLibraryTitle, TITLE_AUTHORITY), is used by both gen-library-jsonld.ts and check-library-qa.ts. The manifest records meta.title_source and meta.title_from, and the QA check re-derives the order from the entry’s files. So a manifest that claims pdf-info while a catalogue record exists is reported as title-implausible, not believed.

1168.title: source{} — the technical facts, written by whichever rung ran
1168.content: Every rung writes source on structure.json, from the single definition in scripts/_tech_meta.py: file, full 64-hex sha256, bytes, mtime (the SOURCE’s, UTC to the second — not the ingest time, because what tells you a re-fetch got something new is the file changing), mimetype_sniffed and mimetype_source. Both rungs add text_source, embedded or ocr: ONE field and ONE vocabulary for where the section text came from. pdf-structure also adds pages and extractor. The mimetype is sniffed from the leading bytes and never falls back to the extension. An extension is a claim by whoever named the file; the magic bytes are what the content is, and a .pdf that is really an HTML error page extracts to nothing while every downstream verdict is about the wrong document. Unrecognised bytes give mimetype_sniffed: null with mimetype_source: "unrecognised": a guess that agrees with the filename is indistinguishable from a real sniff. bun run scripts/ingest-document.ts <pdf> --refresh-meta backfills an existing entry. It reads the indent off the file rather than choosing one: the two rungs write at different widths, and hardcoding either reformats every entry the other authored.

1169.title: provenance — who wrote it, and the closed union that makes omission impossible
1169.content: Every block declares how its text came to be. The vocabulary is schemas/attribution.ts, and it is closed: . | the literal "ingested" — verbatim source text. There is no author to name; the document it came out of is recorded by source{} above. | an Attribution — kind (script | agent | human), id, and optionally version, model, session, date, skill. | . An agent must name its model, structurally. “A model described it, version X” is what a reader needs to weigh a narrative, and what makes the set re-generatable when that model is superseded, so AttributionSchema refuses an agent attribution with no model. The vocabulary is the QA reviewer’s, not a second one. block-qa.ts re-exports ATTRIBUTION_KINDS as QA_REVIEWER_KINDS; the same three participants review and author. What is not shared is QaReviewer itself, most of which is about whether a criterion’s cached verdict is stale. What the gate can and cannot enforce . check:l1-complete checks two things per block, and the second is the point: . | provenance parses as a Provenance. An open string, a malformed attribution, an agent with no model — all unmet. | A block of an authored kind must not claim "ingested". | . LIBRARY_BLOCK_ORIGIN classifies each library block kind as extracted or authored, and a test asserts it is total over what actually occurs in library/ — so a narrative arm cannot land a new kind without classifying it, and classifying one authored arms requirement 2 immediately. Closing the union does not stop an arm asserting something false. It makes the omission impossible: a new arm has to choose, and choosing "ingested" for a generated description is a false statement rather than a missing field. A zero narrative count is reported, never silent. The authored branch is proved to fire by fixtures in scripts/tests/attribution.test.ts, not by the corpus, and each of the three branches is mutation-checked — removing it fails a named test.

1170.title: Archives — the entry list is data, and the rung is chosen by CONTENT
1170.content: A tar or zip in uploads/ is opaque to every grep in the corpus: a search for a filename inside one finds nothing, and that absence is indistinguishable from the file not being there. scripts/archive-contents.py writes library/<slug>/contents.jsonld — one schema whatever the container (schemas/archive-contents.ts), so a consumer reads archives without knowing whether it was tar or zip. Per entry: path, bytes, sha256, mtime, mimetype_sniffed, mimetype_source — the source{} vocabulary above, reused verbatim, because an archive entry is not a different kind of thing from a loose file. The mimetype is sniffed from the entry’s own leading bytes, never from its name, for the same reason it is outside an archive. Four entry states, not two: a directory carries no size and no digest (a zero would be a measurement nobody made); an unreadable member is mimetype_source: "unreadable", which is not an empty file; a symlink or special is listed with its kind rather than dropped. Dropping directories would make an archive of empty ones indistinguishable from an empty archive. A file the sniffer does not recognise as an archive is refused — an empty entries[] would read as an empty archive, a different fact. The rung is chosen before anything opens the file as a PDF . planFor sniffs first, so a zip is never reported as a PDF with a missing backend. A file named .pdf that is really a zip takes the archive rung, which is the case only a sniff can decide. What the gate checks, and the determined zero . Which entries the requirement applies to is derived, not guessed: source. mimetype_sniffed is already on every entry, so “this came from a zip” is a recorded fact. An archive entry must carry a contents.jsonld that validates against the declared schema. An entry that is not an archive reports not an archive (<mimetype>) — said out loud rather than passed in silence, because “nothing to check here” and “the check never ran” are different facts. The requirement is proved to fire by fixture archives built in scripts/tests/archive-contents.test.ts, and each of its four branches is mutation-checked.

1171.title: Datasets — findable by their headers, and the narrative nobody wrote
1171.content: scripts/tabular-records.py writes library/<slug>/tabular.jsonld: sheet names, the header row, and the shape of each sheet. header_vocabulary is the union across sheets, and it is the field a grep for a column name lands in — without it a dataset is stored but not findable, and a failed search is indistinguishable from the dataset not having that column. The record is real JSON-LD, and so is contents.jsonld. Both arms emit the published content context (the URL lives once, in scripts/_content_context.py, pinned to CONTENT_CONTEXT_URL by a test), and every key is a declared term. The facts a consumer queries across documents — format, the counts, header_vocabulary — are real terms; the nested structures that are ours — sheets, entries, the technical metadata, the narrative — are @json literals, because that is how their nulls survive: rows: null means “could not be counted” and narrative.text: null means “nobody has written one”, and JSON-LD drops a null anywhere else. The schemas still accept an older record with no @context, since folio repositories hold them. Stdlib only (zipfile + xml.etree, csv). This repository declares no Python dependencies — no requirements.txt, and CI installs only ruff — so a tool needing openpyxl would pass locally and fail there. Everything this arm needs is in xl/workbook.xml and each sheet’s <dimension>. The narrative is a state machine — drafted by an agent, confirmed by a person . cat-harness-tools schemas/content/narrative.ts: not-authored → draft → confirmed, with rejected as a real fourth state. Two attributions, because they are two acts. drafted_by is who wrote the words; confirmed_by is who accepted them. The question a reader most wants answered is not “did a machine touch this” but “has a person agreed to it”. An agent cannot confirm its own draft — confirmed_by.kind must be "human", structurally. Without that, confirmed degrades into “an agent said so twice”. But a rule about who may act cannot be enforced by a rule about what is written. In an agent container git config user.name is the agent’s, so the CLI could record the agent as a human reviewer and the schema could not see it. reviewer() therefore refuses outside a terminal: a person confirming at a prompt has one, an agent’s subprocess and CI do not. This stops accident, not fraud — it makes it impossible to confirm a narrative while going about other work. rejected keeps its reasons. A rejected draft silently re-offered wastes the reviewer’s time; one that vanishes lets the next agent redraft the identical thing. Reviewing: bun run cat narratives . Numbered list, numbered reasons: a review step that demands a typed sentence is one that will not happen, and then confirmed means “nobody got round to objecting”. bun run cat narratives # what is waiting on you bun run cat narratives:confirm 1 bun run cat narratives:reject 1 --why 2 # or --why-text "..." . check:l1-complete’s narrative-review validates every narrative-bearing file. A draft is reported, not failed: it is work waiting on a person, and failing it would make an unreviewed queue indistinguishable from a broken arm. A null rows/columns is likewise not an empty sheet: shape_source says whether the shape was read, counted, or undetermined. Summarising prose blocks — a QA sidecar, drained slowly . The block stays verbatim. A prose block is the source’s text, provenance: "ingested", and re-ingestion regenerates it. A summary is an agent’s account of that text, so it lives beside the blocks in library/<slug>/summaries.json (folio-block-summaries/v1, schemas/block-summary.ts): one record per block, holding block, source (the section file), source_hash and a narrative. That narrative is the state machine above, not a second one: draft, confirmed by a person only, rejected with a reason, and an agent author must name its model. source_hash makes a changed source read as STALE. It is the sha256 of the section text the summariser was shown (proseBody). Re-ingest a document and any section whose text moved puts its summary back in the queue, marked stale. bun run cat narratives shows it and refuses to confirm it. The queue is derived, so nothing enqueues. Every prose block in every declared library is in it until it has a current draft or confirmation. A rejected draft is back in it, and its rejection reason travels with it. bun run cat summaries # the backlog, per entry bun run cat summaries:next -- --n 5 [--entry <slug>] # next K blocks WITH their text, as JSON bun run cat summaries:record -- drafts.json # write drafts; validated, all or nothing . drafts.json is {drafted_by: {kind: "agent", id, model, session}, drafted_at, drafts: [{block, source_hash, text}]}, with source_hash echoed from summaries:next. record refuses a state other than draft, a hash that no longer matches, and a block that already has a current summary. Drain K at a time during ingestion work, not all at once: a thousand unreviewed drafts at once is a buried reviewer. Write in your own words, from the block’s text only, adding nothing from outside it. Length scales with the source: . | source text | summary | . | under ~150 words | 1 short sentence | . | ~150–600 words | 2 sentences, short to medium | . | ~600–2,000 words | 3 medium sentences | . | over ~2,000 words | 4 sentences, medium to long | . If the extraction put the wrong text under a heading, summarise what is there and say so. The backlog is reported by check:l1-complete (block-summaries) and on the library page. It is advisory, never a gate. What the gate does fail is a sidecar that does not parse, names another entry, or holds a record for a block or source that is not there. The Document panel — what a reader browses . Every entry carrying a structure.json gets a Document panel in the library viewer, built from the ingestion schema by cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts and published as assets/library/entries/<id>.doc.json (folio-library-document/v1) by bun run cat library:viz. Tabs: Contents (the TOC as a tree, collapsed below the first level that branches, each inferred entry’s confidence, linking to its section), Pages (physical page, printed label, sections starting, figures), Figures & tables, Sections (the summary, else an extract — the section’s own opening text, labelled as such and cut at a word), Checks (contents vs body, numbering gaps, page-label conflicts). Because it reads the schema, a new field in structure.json reaches every library at once; a field an older ingestion lacks shows “not recorded — re-ingest”, never an empty table. For a withheld entry the panel keeps structure, page labels, figure and table captions (labels, like TOC titles) and our summaries, and omits only section body extracts. Keywords — from the LSI weights, per section and per document . Keywords are extracted content, so they never live in the ingest record (cat-harness#1144). bun run cat library:keywords builds them at publish into the derived keywords graph: one folio-keywords/v2 JSON-LD node per entry under the site’s assets/keywords/<instance>/<slug>.jsonld, with an index.json beside them. Nothing is written inside library/<slug>/; the route is declared builtAtPublish, and derive:publish runs the writer. Up to 12 for the document and up to 8 per section, fewer for a short section (one per ~20 content tokens, at least 3). Each node holds six variants side by side, so they can be compared: . | Variant | Method | Weighting | Terms scored | . | lsi-log-entropy-surface (default) | lsi | log-entropy | the words the text uses | . | lsi-tfidf-surface | lsi | tf-idf | the words the text uses | . | lsi-log-entropy-latent | lsi | log-entropy | latent scores, any term of the library | . | lsi-tfidf-latent | lsi | tf-idf | latent scores, any term of the library | . | lsi-log-entropy-latent-rerank | lsi | log-entropy | latent scores, only the words the text or its headings use | . | ca-latent | correspondence-analysis | raw counts | latent scores, any term of the library | . The default is read from the same log-entropy matrix the LSI index is built from (keywordsOf in pipeline/lsi.ts), so a keyword means “frequent here, rare across this library” exactly as the index does. A latent variant scores terms by the rank-k reconstruction (k = 100), so it can propose a term the text never uses (synonymy, Deerwester et al. 1990); it scores the top 300 candidates. Correspondence analysis tends to favour rare proper names (authors, publishers), which the comparison shows. The Document panel computes the default variant in memory and shows it as chips, green where a heading also names the term (evidence: ["heading"]): the document saying it of itself. Withheld entries show them: they are derived terms, like captions, not the text. The library-keywords check in bun run cat health reports entries without keywords and any legacy keywords.json still committed. What the scoring does: . | Two-word phrases from truly adjacent tokens said at least twice; a stop word, punctuation, or a line break before a capital (a table cell, a heading) breaks the run — “Development” over “Systematic review team” is two cells, not “development systematic”. | A word said once in a text of 100+ tokens is not a keyword, unless the section’s heading names it; heading-named terms score double. | Generic words the index keeps but that say nothing about a topic (“anyone”, “aims”, “take”, “-ly” adverbs) are excluded from keywords only. | Plurals fold: “evidence reviews” does not follow “evidence review”. | . Limits: no part-of-speech tagging, so a rare verb can still surface in a short section; a library of fewer than 3 sections gets none. A WITHHELD entry in the viewer — its summary, else the gate, never “no content” . An entry whose library root’s withheld.json names it is listed but publishes no verbatim text: gen-library-viz reads its blocks with verbatim: false. “Not ours to show” must not look like “nothing was extracted”: . | A row shows the section’s summary when one exists, labelled as a summary and never as the source text. Summaries are our writing and stay published. | Otherwise, a withheld row says the gate: “Withheld — copyright not granted”, naming every gate that refused (“copyright and restrictions not granted”), with a link to the catalogue record — its published page first, its upstream URI second, no link rather than a guessed one. | Anything else with no content keeps the neutral “(no content carried)”, because for those it is true. | A banner tops a withheld entry: why the text is not shown, which gate refused, the record link, and how many sections have summaries (“0 of 121 sections summarised”). No banner on any other entry. | . Withheld is READ, never inferred from emptiness. The flag, the gates and the record come from withheld.json — folio-withheld/v1 carries an optional structured gates[] and record{id, page, uri} beside the reason sentence, which the layer’s generator writes from its own data (the IRIS catalogue: gen-iris-pages.ts, from the catalogue’s publication gates). A list that carries only the sentence still works: the row then says the sentence. The row and banner code is scripts/lib/library-withheld-view.ts, embedded in the page verbatim so library-withheld-view.test.ts runs the same text the browser does; library-withheld-viewer.e2e.ts opens the rendered page. Drafting the summaries is a separate backlog: bun run cat summaries:next -- --entry <slug> serves a withheld entry’s text to the summariser like any other. Describing a document’s images — and why it is an ARM, not a step you run . pdf-images.py classifies by geometry, which answers exactly one question: is this image the whole page, or something on it. It cannot tell a logo from a chart. The finer roles come from LOOKING, and that judgement is data — <library>/image-verdicts.json, one entry per image, reviewable line by line. bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> # stage; reports what is unmet # look at ingest-staging/<doc-id>/images/, write the verdicts into # <lib>/image-verdicts.json, then: bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> # re-stage: the arm applies them bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> --promote . Re-running ingest is the second step, not a separate apply command. --promote refuses an entry whose image-descriptions requirement is unmet, and the stand-alone narrative writers (apply-image-verdicts.ts, narratives.ts) resolve their targets through directoriesForGraph(root, "library"), i.e. only in promoted libraries. Applying the verdicts as an arm in staging is what lets a document be both described and promoted. Applying by hand works exactly once. pdf-images.py opens the sidecar with "w" — no existence check, no merge — so the next ingest overwrites the descriptions, and overwrites them quietly: the file still parses and still validates, it simply has no narratives in it any more. Running the application as the fourth arm, after pdf-images.py, makes a re-run RE-APPLY instead — the sidecar is rebuilt from the PDF and the committed judgement is laid back over it. --staging <entry-dir> --library <lib-dir> is available directly if you need it, and --library is required: a staging directory does not say which library a document is being promoted into (a queue does not determine a library). An absent verdicts file exits 0, because the first ingest necessarily runs before anybody has looked at the images; image-descriptions is the gate that refuses, not that script. An orphaned verdict — one naming an image the sidecar does not have — still fails, in either mode. Every narrative it writes lands as draft. Only a person confirms one. A role threshold is OPTIONAL, and its default is NONE . A coverage cutoff may sort images into roles (figure vs furniture) only when a caller supplies one. | By default nothing is thresholded. With no value supplied, every role call comes from an inspection verdict as above, naming who looked. | A caller may supply one. An image whose role it decides must record that basis: the value, and that the value was caller-supplied rather than inspected. A thresholded role must never be readable as an inspected one. | Ship no number. No config default, and no value in docs, tests or examples presented as recommended. Per-image coverage does not separate the classes, and a cutoff placed in one corpus’s empty stretch is fitted to that corpus and says nothing about others. | . Reading a figure: the text layer is not the figure . Two traps, both of which produce a wrong description: . A diverging axis’s SIGN cannot be read from the text layer. get_text returned 0.2 0.4 0.6 below the zero of a Delta Pass Rate bar with no sign at any codepoint — matplotlib draws U+2212 as a vector path, so the minus exists in the rendering and not in the text. Rendering the region showed -0.2 -0.4 -0.6 plainly. A verdict trusting the extraction would have called a -0.6 endpoint +0.6. And the direction is a fact about the axis, not about the colours. The recorded inspection said a bar ran “blue low to red high”. Its ticks said Pass Rate, 1.0 at the top in dark blue: blue was HIGH. A reader given the original sentence reads every heatmap in the paper inverted — worse than no description, because a missing one is visibly missing. So: render the region and read the ticks. Two images that look alike need the same check each: a third “repeated legend” can be a different, signed scale. The figure that is DRAWN — pdf-vector-labels.py, the other arm . pdf-images.py answers “what does this page PLACE”. A WHO conceptual figure — a framework, a maturity model, a taxonomy, a process flow — is drawn in path operators and text, so it places nothing, and the raster arm is silent about it truthfully. 9789240120747-eng declares six captioned figures, places zero images, and image-descriptions reported “0 image(s), 0 describable and all described” over it: a determined empty that is true about raster and misleading about figures. The vector arm runs beside the raster one in withDerivedArms and writes vector-labels.json — every positioned text line on a page that declares a figure, with its rectangle in the visible frame, its fonts and sizes, and whether it intersects a drawing. Read the sidecar, not a count. Three things it deliberately does not do: . | It does not say which labels belong to the figure. intersectsDrawing is recorded and never filtered on. On 9789240120747-eng page 34 it separates perfectly; on 9789240010567-eng page 25 it is false for thirty labels that are plainly figure content, because they sit in the white space between the drawn boxes. | It does not group above the MuPDF LINE. A block on that same page holds six circled numerals 200 pt apart across three different diagrams. | It does not compare its counts to anything. Declared figures and recovered labels are not commensurable. | . So when you describe such a figure, the labels are your evidence and the grouping is your judgement — which is the same split as image-verdicts.json, one level over. The rule from the section above holds here with more force, not less: render the page and look at it. The arm recovers what the text layer says; it cannot tell you that the arrows run clockwise. The determined empty is still meaningful: who-rhr-1806-eng records zero pages because it contains no Fig. or Figure mention at all. A document with no text layer returns pages: null with a reason instead — the one place this arm could otherwise report a clean run over an unread scan. An .xlsx IS a zip — ask the container . The magic bytes of an OOXML or ODF document say application/zip, which is true and useless: it would send every spreadsheet to the archive rung to be listed as a bag of XML parts. The magic cannot tell them apart, so _tech_meta.sniff_zip_package asks the container, which declares itself — OOXML by [Content_Types].xml plus the part names, ODF by its mimetype member. Same principle as the byte sniff, one level in. sniff_effective_mimetype is the single answer the router (planFor) and the recorder both ask, so they cannot disagree. A CSV has no magic bytes at all, so routing one cannot be a sniff and must not become an extension guess. is_tabular_text asks the only content question available: do the first rows split into the same number of fields, more than one? Prose, a single column and anything ragged all answer no — a one-column “table” is indistinguishable from a list of lines. Proved on fixtures built at test time, all five branches mutation-checked.

1174.title: l2-component-edit-review
1174.content: Skill l2-component-edit-review: How one L2 DAK component is edited by the agent and reviewed by a person: personas and user scenarios, BPMN business processes, DMN decision and scheduling logic, core data elements and glossary with their terminology bindings, indicators and requirements. One subprocess for all of them. The agent edits, checks, renders and stages with a before/after, then hands the component on, and review forks alongside it without blocking. Per component, it lists the authoring skill, checker, renderer and diff, reviewing role, and what the reviewer judges. Read before authoring or reviewing any L2 component, and when an L2 track asks what its reviewer needs to see. Named by: DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring . Skill id: l2-component-edit-review · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Process: l2-component-edit-review.bpmn (Process_L2ComponentEditReview), called by every authoring track of l2-dak-authoring.bpmn . Every step of the subprocess runs an existing skill: review is cat-harness’s Process_Review, the verdict a qa-review/v1 QaReview, the links follow staging-review’s deep-link rule, and the preview follows before-after-preview. Components differ only in the checker, renderer, diff and reviewer, which the table below records.

1175.title: The shape: edit, check, render, then fork
1175.content: edit ─► check ─► render + stage ─┬─► hand on (adjudication: pending) the track continues └─► ask for review ─► Process_Review ─► verdict approve ─► done request-changes ─► edit again reject ─► reopen upstream, flag derived assets . Adjudication is QA, not a gate. The calling track carries on as soon as the component is staged; nothing waits for the verdict. The call still ends only when both branches have ended, and the DAK is not adjudicated until every component’s verdict is recorded (rules 1 to 4 of smart-guideline-end-to-end, applied to one component).

1177.title: Asking for review
1177.content: Task_RequestReview follows staging-review’s deep-link rule: . | the request carries one deep link per changed page, to the anchor (…/branches/<slug>/<path>#<anchor>), beside the same page on main as before; | the pages come from the change (rendered-impact), not from judgement; | if there is no preview yet, the request says so. | . smart-base content reaches staging by a folio-assistant staging re-pin (bun run cat mount:remote --staging). It never goes through /deploy. Send the request where the person will look: this conversation, the issue the work came from, the pull request, or several of them, each with the same links. The question follows interaction-modality. A tagged PR comment becomes a todo (review-comments). Feedback on published content goes through content-feedback.

The agent never records a verdict.

Author the L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the human-readable, machine-processable Digital Adaptation Kit between a narrative guideline (L1) and FHIR artefacts (L3). Sourcing. The DAK component set and the L1–L4 layers are WHO’s, defined in the SMART Guidelines documentation and realised in WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base. This skill says how to work them here (lane, inputs, tooling); what a component must contain is WHO’s, and where they disagree WHO wins.

1189.title: What L2 is for, and the mistake to avoid
1189.content: L2 is structured but not yet FHIR: reviewable by a clinical SME who does not read FHIR, and regular enough that L3 is derived from it. Do not author L2 as if it were L3 (profiles, slicing, invariants). A decision that can only be expressed in FHIR belongs in l3-fhir-authoring; one that can be stated as a data element, decision rule or indicator belongs here.

1190.title: The three activities the process names
1190.content: | step | produces | note | . | Personas and scenarios | the actors and the user journeys they appear in | The DAK’s own personas, not this harness’s scenarios/roles.json. | . | Data dictionary and core data elements | the data dictionary | Data-dictionary authoring is part of this skill (dakComponent: data-dictionary). | . | Indicators and requirements | indicators, functional and non-functional requirements | The DAK’s requirements, not the harness’s skills/requirements/*.json. 1191.title: Every track is edited, then reviewed alongside
1191.content: Each of the six tracks (the three above, BPMN, DMN and terminology) is a call activity into Process_L2ComponentEditReview (l2-component-edit-review). In that subprocess the agent: . | edits the component with the track’s skill; | runs the component’s checker; | renders and stages it with a before/after; | hands it on with adjudication: pending. | . A person in the component’s reviewing role reviews the staged preview at the same time, through cat-harness’s Process_Review; review never blocks the hand-on. Each component’s renderer, checker, diff and reviewer are in that skill’s table. The clinical SME’s Clinical validation after the join reads the whole DAK across components, without repeating the per-component reviews.

1201.title: l2-dependency-choice
1201.content: Skill l2-dependency-choice: Stage 3 of smart-guideline-end-to-end: choose which existing DAKs (WHO’s, or a jurisdiction’s adaptation) the guideline builds on. From the L1 knowledge graph and any known candidates, one decision row per candidate DAK — reuse, adapt, extend or reject, with evidence and a reason — laid out as a decision-comparison table and put to the adjudicators as a DecisionRequest. Also defines the dependency decision row that stage 5 (l3-dependency-choice) uses at L3. Read before choosing, or recording, a DAK dependency. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: l2-dependency-choice · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Stage 3 of smart-guideline-end-to-end, task Task_DepsL2 of smart-guideline-end-to-end.bpmn. Adjudicated by the programme manager and the business analyst.

1202.title: Input and output
1202.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: stage 2’s l1Kg (recommendation-extraction’s output), and the candidate DAKs already known (candidates: packageId, version, uri, publisher). | Out: l2Dependencies: one dependencyRow per candidate, rejected ones included, the gaps, the comparison table and the decisionRequest. Stage 4 (l2-dak-authoring) takes it as its l2Dependencies. | .

1203.title: The decision row
1203.content: | field | from | meaning | . | packageId, version, uri | cat-harness DependsOnRecord (cat-harness-tools/schemas/kg/depends-on.ts), the same three fields as FHIR ImplementationGuide.dependsOn | the candidate DAK (or, at stage 5, IG). A candidate missing one of the three is a DependsOnGap, listed in gaps, not a row | . | publisher, upstream | — | WHO, or the adapting jurisdiction; for an adaptation, the WHO original it adapts | . | evidence | smart-base KG evidence (smart-base/kg/src/graph.ts) | the L1 KG nodes (and, at L3, the L2 assets) that point at it | . | decision | this skill | reuse (unchanged) · adapt (fork and change) · extend (depend and add) · reject | . | reason | this skill | one sentence; required for reject | . | components | — | what is taken, piece by piece: DAK components here, profiles, value sets and libraries at L3 | . | toolchain | this skill | on each component reused, adapted or extended: how the candidate produces it — a Tool id from bun run cat check:tools, or a script in the candidate’s own repository (its source spreadsheet, converter, CQL refresh, test format), found by the search in smart-base-tools §Adapting a DAK. Stages 4 and 6 produce the component with that toolchain. none only after that search came back empty, naming where it looked; the new tool is then a Tool node, never a script in the adaptation repository | . Only decision, reason and toolchain are new. Once adjudicated, a reuse, adapt or extend row becomes an ordinary dependency: the DAK’s own reference at L2, a dependencies: entry in sushi-config.yaml at L3.

1204.title: Steps
1204.content: . | Find the candidates. Start from candidates, and add each DAK whose Component 1 the L1 KG’s implementedBy / realises edges reach. For each, find how it produces each component it would give (smart-base-tools §Adapting a DAK): that is the component’s toolchain, which stage 4 uses. | Reuse first (recommendation-extraction’s precedence): reuse an existing asset, then adapt one, and create only when neither fits, with a WARNING saying none fitted. The same holds for the tooling that makes an asset: an adapted decision table is an edited copy of the upstream’s source spreadsheet run through the upstream’s converter, not a table re-typed in a new format with a new converter. Prefer the jurisdiction’s adaptation over the WHO original for the same scope, since it already holds the local decisions, and record the WHO original as that row’s upstream. | Lay the rows out as a decision-comparison table and ask through a DecisionRequest (cat-harness-tools/schemas/process/decision-request.ts: two to four options, a recommendation, and what happens if nobody answers). | Go on. Under the QA rule the agent proceeds with its recommendation; the adjudicator’s answer is the stage’s review decision. | .

Indexes each candidate IG with ig-artifact-ingestion, matches the L1 knowledge graph and the stage-4 L2 assets against the index, and returns one decision row per IG naming the profiles, value sets and libraries reused, derived from or not used. 1207.title: Input and output

1208.title: Steps

The index is the evidence; an IG whose root was never read has sidecarApi: unknown, which is not absent. | Match. The matches are the row’s evidence; what is taken is its components (reuse, adapt, extend, not-used). 1210.title: l3-fhir-authoring
1210.content: Named by: L2 DAK to L3 FHIR IG, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: l3-fhir-authoring · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Named by l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn (Author FSH profiles, Compile FSH to FHIR JSON) and ig-incremental-build.bpmn (SUSHI on the restricted tank). Derive the L3 layer — machine-readable FHIR artefacts — from an authored L2 DAK, using FHIR Shorthand and SUSHI. Sourcing. FHIR, FSH and SUSHI are HL7’s; the SMART Guidelines L1–L4 model is WHO’s. This skill states how they are wired in this harness — which lane, which inputs, which binaries the package installs — and defers to the FHIR and FSH specifications for what a conformant artefact must look like.

1211.title: Inputs and outputs
1211.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/l3-fhir-authoring/: . | in — artifactType (required), sourceModel (required), fshOutputDir, igRoot | out — fshFiles (required), sushiResult (required), generatedResources | . L3 is derived, not authored from scratch, so sourceModel is required: an L3 artefact with no source behind it is a profile nobody can review against what it was meant to encode. The layer above chooses the source in its own process: that process maps its model and then CALLS l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn (Process_L3Fhir), which starts at “Source model ready”. Neither this skill nor that pipeline names the model, because this layer may not (AGENTS.md). CQL — clinical decision logic — is part of this skill, not a separate one; cql-library is one of the input schema’s artifactType values.

1212.title: The toolchain
1212.content: sushi-compiler and ig-publisher are capabilities this package declares (providesCapabilities in package-manifest.json, defined in scenarios/capabilities/): . sushi --version # sushi-compiler, requires node-runtime java -jar "$IG_PUBLISHER_JAR" --version # ig-publisher, requires java-runtime . If a capability probe fails, the step was not run — never that it passed.

1213.title: Deriving rather than retyping
1213.content: When the layer above carries transforms in the render direction — from its own model to FSH, or to rendered tables — use them rather than hand-writing what a transform already emits, and read that layer’s own tooling skill for how they behave. Whatever they emit is still FSH this skill owns: a collision between two emitted files is a finding to decide (a duplicate input, or two sources legitimately contributing the same thing), never one to let overwrite silently.

1214.title: Validate before you publish
1214.content: Validation is the separate skill fhir-validation, in its own lane: SUSHI compiling is not conformance. A profile can compile and still fail validation against the packages it claims to constrain.

1215.title: Incremental builds
1215.content: ig-incremental-build.bpmn runs SUSHI on a restricted tank — a cone of the artefacts a change touches rather than the whole IG. That is a build optimisation, not a validation shortcut: the full publisher build in that same diagram is what the release is cut from.

1217.title: l3-readiness
1217.content: Skill l3-readiness: The check between stages 5 and 6 of smart-guideline-end-to-end (Gateway_L3Ready): may the agent write L3 assets yet? Yes only when every source of the use case has its L1 extraction, every L2 asset names the L1 node it rests on, every L3 artefact about to be written names the L2 asset it implements, and the review of each extraction and L2 asset has been requested. Returns the answer, every finding with the stage that fixes it, and what was checked. Read before writing any FSH, CQL or other L3 file for a guideline or an adaptation. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: l3-readiness · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · The check before Gateway_L3Ready of smart-guideline-end-to-end, task Task_L3Ready of smart-guideline-end-to-end.bpmn. Run by the authoring agent; it records no verdict on any asset. The order rule as a check with its own contract. It is not a stage: it produces no asset, only the answer the gateway takes.

1218.title: Input and output
1218.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: the l1Kg (stage 2), the l2Assets (every stage-4 l2-dak-authoring pass’s artifacts), the reviews requested so far, one per extraction or L2 asset, and l3Planned, the L3 artefacts stage 6 is about to write, each with its sourceModel. | Out: ready, which is the gateway’s outcome; findings, each naming the asset, the problem and the stage that fixes it; checked, every asset looked at, so that no findings is a determined empty and not a skipped check. | .

1219.title: Steps
1219.content: . | L1. Every source the use case includes has an l1Kg extraction, at library/<bib>/l1-extraction/ (or l1-extractions/<bib>/ when the entry lives in another instance’s library). A source without one is no-l1-extraction, fixed by stage 2. | L2 on L1. Every L2 asset names at least one L1 node in wasDerivedFrom. One that names none is no-l1-upstream, fixed by stage 4. | L3 on L2. Every l3Planned entry’s sourceModel is an l2Assets path. One that is not is no-l2-upstream, fixed by stage 4. Source documents (a schedule poster, a slide deck) are stage-2 input, never a sourceModel. | Review requested. Every extraction and every L2 asset has a reviews entry: its review item opened and staged. One without is review-not-requested, fixed by the stage that made it. The verdict is not awaited. | Answer. ready is true exactly when findings is empty. The gateway then takes «yes» to stage 6, or «no» back to stage 4 (which fills a missing extraction from stage 2). | . A green build and passing tests do not clear a finding.

The application is the requester’s, not the agent’s, as the use case is in stage 0 (guideline-use-case).

1230.title: Library ingestion — the basic flow
1230.content: Skill library-ingestion: The BASIC ingestion flow every asset takes: an upload is accepted, its metadata goes into the knowledge graph, and the asset lands in library/<slug>/ if it is materialized. The two entry points (a drop in uploads/, or materializing an asset a remote graph lists), what happens to the upload afterwards, and why content-type methods refine this flow from above rather than living in it. Command: bun run cat ingest. Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . uploads/ and library/ are two stages of one pipeline. uploads/ is the incoming queue — raw files as dropped, not L1 and not greppable as corpus. library/<slug>/ is where an ingested asset lives, and every knowledge-graph reference to a source resolves through it. Why that bites: the corpus-grep checklist searches library/ only, so a file still in uploads/ makes a clean grep mean “nobody has done this” when the source is right there. That is how a held result gets re-derived.

1231.title: The flow — four steps, and no content-type decision
1231.content: cat-harness holds only the basic, high-level ingestion workflow, with very little process context assumed: the uploaded asset’s extracted metadata goes into the KG, and the asset into library/ if materialized. library/processes/document-ingestion.bpmn (Process_Ingestion) is that flow, executable: . | Accept — the bytes reach the declared uploads/ queue by a declared route (upload-routes; names per upload-naming; arrival noticed by uploads-watch). | Extract metadata into the KG — asset-extraction: a container’s INDEX goes in, its contents do not unless asked for. | Materialized? — the state vocabulary is schemas/kg/materialization-state.ts: referenced, materialized or unknown, with no default. | Place in library/<slug>/ — this skill. A referenced asset is still catalogued: its record says where the bytes are and that we hold none. | . The flow calls no subprocess and decides nothing about content type. Which reader a PDF needs, what a complete L1 entry holds, how images or datasets are described — those are refinements, and they live in a layer above this one. The mechanism is inversion: a higher-layer process CALLS Process_Ingestion as its first step and continues with its own work. Nothing here names a refinement, because there is no BPMN extension point in the corpus and a harness process naming a higher one would be an upward edge. methodology-from-source.bpmn’s Call_Ingest is a harness caller of the same flow.

1232.title: TWO entry points
1232.content: Things enter the library through uploads/ → library/ document ingestion, or through materializing an asset listed in an external KG that a dependent harness declares. |   | drop | materialize | . | the source is | a file somebody put in uploads/ | an asset listed in a remote graph a dependency declares | . | decided first | how it is read (a refinement’s choice) | the five gates, and a purpose | . | entry | bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE | materialize-remote.bpmn | . Neither is a shortcut past the other. A materialized asset still arrives as bytes that have to be read, so it re-enters at exactly the point a dropped file does. Materialization adds what happens before there is a file: may we hold it, what does holding it cost, for what purpose, and what if the source goes away. Entry one is bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE (--dry-run says what it would do, and why). Entry two starts from remoteGraphs in a layer’s declaration (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts, RemoteGraph): assets listed there are referenced — we know they exist and where, and hold none. materialize-remote.bpmn asks purpose (working or archival), then the five gates, then fetches; the asset lands in library/ with its provenance and fixity, and a refusal leaves the node referenced rather than failing. A reference is not a fetch: the KG viewer follows a remote graph to show its hierarchy without materialising anything — navigable without being held. Who owns which half . | This layer owns the basic flow and the reading CODE — the pdf-* rungs, ingest-document.ts, notebook-structure.ts. Reading bytes is platform work, and OCR stays here. The method that chooses among them is a refinement above. The flow itself cannot move up: uploads and library are graph typologies this layer declares, and a flow above would make the harness’s own library writable only from a layer above it — a wrong-direction, and circular, dependency. | The remote half’s gates belong to the content layer above. Only the state vocabulary lives here; the five gates, the purposes and the record binding them stay with the layer that owns content, because each gate is a decision about content. A harness that cannot hold content must not own the vocabulary for deciding to acquire it. | The large-datasets package owns the question before both (library/skills/large-datasets/): how to enumerate a corpus and ask it for a subset (source-descriptor.ts). Neither entry point can start until something says what is out there. | Further down the tree, a dependency’s declared remoteGraphs is what makes the second path reachable at all, inherited the way directories are. | .

1233.title: A held PDF gets its page-1 cover BEFORE the upload is retired
1233.content: The picture of a PDF entry is library/<slug>/cover.png, page 1 rendered by pdf-cover.py — never its first figure, which can be any picture from deep in the document. With no cover, the entry shows the book glyph. | A new ingest writes it: ingest-document’s cover arm runs last. | An entry without one gets it from bun run cat library:covers. Run it in the checkout that holds the PDF (the composed index, whose uploads/ may be another repository’s), and commit the cover into the repository that holds the entry. | Run it before the upload is retired. Once the PDF moves to fsh-guts/uploads/, library:covers no longer finds it and skips the entry as “not held”. | bun run cat library:covers:check fails on a held, unwithheld PDF that has no cover. | .

1234.title: After ingestion the upload is RETIRED — never left, never deleted
1234.content: Three places, and only uploads/ is temporary: queued uploads/FILE; derived library/<slug>/, which may not hold the source bytes (check:l1-complete reports an unexpected child); archived fsh-guts/uploads/FILE beside a folio-fsh-guts/v1 sidecar whose movedFrom and movedOn are load-bearing. Never rm an ingested upload: it is the only working-tree copy of the source. bun run cat check:uploads-retired finds unretired ones by sha256 against every declared library, never by filename, and refuses rather than passes when no library records a hash. It reports and never moves anything. Rename an upload before its first ingest — the slug follows the name. The full rule — why the library cannot be the destination, the sidecar convention, the blocking and advisory families, and renaming — is in library-ingestion/uploads-retirement.md.

1235.title: When an ingested document names what else the library needs
1235.content: Some documents say what they rest on, by number, in a section the content type defines — and then the library is not complete until it holds those too. The flow above is run again for each, and the citing document’s graph is regenerated once they are in, so a cited source the library HOLDS is described from its own metadata rather than from a one-line reference. The content type owns which section that is, how its citations resolve, and how a cited source is acquired (for instance from a DSpace repository); it says so in its own authoring skill. This layer owns only the rule: the flow above runs once per cited source, and the citing document’s graph is regenerated after.

1236.title: A second representation sits DOWNSTREAM of the entry
1236.content: A content type may describe an ingested document a second time, in its own schema — a WHO guideline is also an L1 knowledge graph. The library is upstream of L1: L1 points upstream, never downstream. So that representation is derived from the entry and points at the entry’s nodes (the source document, its sections, its blocks); nothing in the library points back, and the entry is never rewritten for it. It inherits whatever sectioning this flow produced, so a better reader here improves it without a change there. Whether a document gets one is recorded on its intake (classifications), by a person, by the process that acquired it, or by a rule — the content type owns which, and its skill says how.

1242.title: Materialize on demand
1242.content: Skill materialize-on-demand: After bootstrap, a person asks for part of a remote subgraph to be held locally. Check what is already here (cache:index), put a number on the ask before anything is fetched, then run materialize-remote. Eviction is a report, never an act. Named by: DTH authoring . Bootstrap brings an agent to a working harness. It does not bring the corpus, and must not: a remote source such as IRIS runs to about a million files and hundreds of gigabytes. What arrives is the reference; a person asks, as they come to need it, for parts of subgraphs to be materialized. This skill is that ask. The gates are not here; they are in materialize-remote, once.

1243.title: 1. What is already here
1243.content: bun run cat cache:index # summary and eviction candidates bun run cat cache:index --all # every copy . Read the columns for what they are: . | column | values | what it means | . | size | recorded · measured · directory · absent | measured is the file now, not when it landed. A directory is counted through its parts. absent is not zero. | . | fetched | a date, or not recorded | only the record’s materializedAt | . | last read | not recorded, always | nothing records reads; file access times are not used, because they are often off or reset by a checkout. | . | freshness | fresh · expired · no-expiry · permanent | from freshness(). no-expiry is a finding: a working copy nobody gave a lifetime. | . If what they want is already held and fresh, stop: point them at it.

1244.title: 2. Put a number on the ask BEFORE anything moves
1244.content: Asking must not mean hundreds of gigabytes arrive without a number first. Before calling materialize-remote: . | Name the subset in the source’s own terms: its identifiers, or a subset strategy its descriptor (in the owning layer’s declared sources/, e.g. the IRIS replica’s sources/) supports. | Close it over dependencies if the descriptor says the subset is not self-contained (subsetIsSelfContained: false, mathlib). The size that matters is the closure’s. | State the size and its basis: from the descriptor’s enumeration, or a measured listing. If neither gives a number, say that. The SIZE gate refuses on an unknown, and so should this conversation. | Say what it would add to the cache total from step 1. | . Then ask the person, with the number in front of them.

1245.title: 3. Materialize
1245.content: Run Process_MaterializeRemote. Its five gates decide; this skill does not second-guess them. A refusal leaves the content referenced, with the reason recorded. That is the process working, not failing.

1246.title: 4. Eviction is a report
1246.content: cache:index lists candidates: expired first, then no-expiry working copies, largest first. An archival copy is never a candidate. Nothing is removed by the tool or by you. Show the list with sizes and reasons, and let the person decide (deletion-requires-confirmation).

1248.title: Materializing remote content
1248.content: Skill materialize-remote: Landing remote content locally — the five gates, the three states, and the two purposes. One process, shared by catalogue import and harness bootstrap, plus the refresh that is not a re-import. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . One process for every caller that lands remote content locally. | caller | remote source | held locally | refresh | . | the IRIS replica | IRIS | selected items | refresh-materialized | . | bootstrap | a harness | the cat-harness checkout | upstream-pins.json | . bootstrap/workflows/initialize-harness.bpmn fetches a harness that is remote content and lands it locally; upstream-pins.json exists because that copy goes stale. Diagrams: materialize-remote.bpmn and refresh-materialized.bpmn. Schema: the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer above this one — named here, not linked). Nothing here restates either — where they disagree, the schema wins and this file is wrong.

1249.title: Ask the purpose FIRST
1249.content: working or archival, before any gate, because three of the five mean different things under each. |   | working | archival | . | what is kept | derived content — sections, OCR | the original bytes | . | retention | expires; re-fetchable | no expiry, by design | . | sourceLoss | unanswered | discharged | . | fixity | not needed | required | . A process that gated first and asked afterwards would be judging a copy whose obligations it did not yet know.

1250.title: The five gates
1250.content: Each is a decision a person makes; none is answerable from a file. A gate that only warns is a gate nobody fails. | Size — what fraction, and what the whole would cost. Refuse when you cannot tell: “three items” with no denominator is not a size answer. | Restrictions — “no restrictions known in context” is a state, not a green light. unknown is never rendered as permitted. | Copyright — per bitstream, and separately for the derived work. LICENSE-CONTENT.md exists here and the ingestion pipeline does not read it. | Retention — what expires this copy. A copy with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one. | Source loss — what survives if the origin goes. Only an archival copy discharges this. Origins do disappear: a regional repository instance can be merged away, taking its handles with it. | .

1251.title: Three states, and no default
1251.content: referenced (it exists, we know where, we hold no bytes) · materialized · unknown. A node that has not declared one is invalid, not unknown — “the author did not say” and “the author said they could not tell” are different facts, and only the second is actionable. A refusal is the process working. The node stays referenced, the graph still knows it exists, and the refusing gate’s basis is recorded so the next agent does not re-litigate it.

1252.title: Refresh is not re-import
1252.content: Three answers, not one: what changed upstream, what changed locally, and what to do when both. A materialized copy edited in place is not a copy — overwriting it destroys work whose existence was never established; check:materialized-fixity detects it. An archival copy is never refreshed. Re-fetching it discards the state it exists to keep. It gets a fixity check instead — has our copy rotted — which is a different question with a different remedy: restore from backup, never re-download.

1253.title: Before you enumerate anything
1253.content: cat-harness/schemas/library/source-descriptor.ts answers the question that comes before the gates: how to enumerate a corpus and ask it for a subset. Check subsetIsSelfContained first — when it is false (mathlib), close the request over its dependencies before gating, because the size being gated is the closure’s, not the request’s.
