1265.title: Merge to main — a sub-process with its own gate
1265.content: Skill merge-to-main: Merging to main is its own step with its own gate: the merge-to-main sub-process, which every process that lands work CALLS rather than inlines. Covers the evidence read live on the head (CI per owed job, mergeability, review state, Claude Approvals where the repository runs it), why a repository with no CI is never green, who may authorise a merge and what does NOT count as authorisation (“fix all issues until green” does not), how the authorisation is recorded, and the post-merge steps: base green, site republished, downstream re-pins, work item and issue. Use for “merge it”, “land this PR”, “merge the green PRs”, and before any write to a default branch in any repository. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . sdlc/processes/merge-to-main.bpmn (Process_MergeToMain) is the process. Its two gateways are computed by merge-evidence.dmn and merge-authorisation.dmn. Every process that ends in a write to main calls it. Today that is merge-train.bpmn (Call_MergeToMain) and crdm-close.bpmn (Call_MergeToMain, between the recorded sign-off and the issue close). prepare-merge stops before it; prepare-merge-auto Phase 4 runs it. A process that merges without calling it is a process with a hole in it, and the remedy is a call activity, not a paragraph.

1266.title: Why this is a process of its own
1266.content: A merge inlined as the last line of another process cannot refuse, and does not cover a repository with no CI. As its own step it can.

1267.title: The steps
1267.content: CI regenerates the harness projections on the head (harness-projections). The merging session then reads the evidence, runs local gates if there is no CI, finds the authorisation and asks for it if it is missing. The owner answers: merge, hold or refuse. The merging session records the answer (not relaxable), merges pinned to the head, confirms main, republishes the repository’s site, re-pins downstream mounts and reports. Each step’s own text is in the diagram. The merging session is the merge-steward lane. With a Merge Manager active, that is the steward. With none active, the PR’s own session takes the lane (merge-queue §”When no Merge Manager is active”). The gate is the same for both.

1268.title: Evidence — read on the head, live, every time
1268.content: What lands is the head the evidence was read on. Read these facts from GitHub at the time of the merge. Never use a copy from earlier in the session. | fact | values | read from | . | ciState | green, red, pending, none, unreadable | the workflow runs whose head_sha is the PR’s head, per OWED job (merge-queue §”Admission asks which runs are OWED”). Not the PR page, and not the legacy status API. | . | mergeable | clean, dirty, unknown | the PR’s mergeable / mergeable_state. unknown stays unknown after a short re-ask. Only dirty is believed on its own (prepare-merge §Guardrails, step 0). | . | review | clear, blocking, unknown | open CHANGES_REQUESTED reviews, unresolved threads a reviewer marked blocking, a draft PR, a needs-merge-human label, and Claude Approvals where the repository runs it: its required review or check must be present and approving on this head. A repository that runs it and has no approval on the head is blocking, not clear. | . Where the repository has merge:guard (cat-harness and the layers composed with it), its evaluate mode IS this step. Exit 0 means green/clean/clear, exit 1 maps each refused check to its fact, and exit 2 is unreadable, never a pass. Its eight checks are listed in merge-queue §”A PR lands only through merge:guard”. Where it does not exist, read the same facts with the GitHub tools and write each one down with the URL it came from. CI gates a release only (owner, 2026-11-08) . Owner, card Q-CIB-4 A, 2026-11-08, after “CI not gate on non-release merge to main” and “not all CI needs to run unless doing a release build”: . | A non-release merge does not wait for CI. ciState is still read and written into the report, red included, but it refuses nothing. Mergeability, review, the ready: marker, the label and the owner’s authorisation all still decide. Content still needs the owner, and committee content still never merges: those are authorisation rules, and they are unchanged. | A release merge is gated. A merge is a release when the PR carries the release label or the guard runs with --release. Then every owed job must be green, as before. | Main is judged after the merge, by the integration run on main (the full suite on main’s tip, batched; see release-lifecycle §”The release gate”). A red integration run files one fix issue naming the merges in its range. It does not hold the queue. | . This replaces, for non-release merges only: main-green-first (card Q-CIB-1 B, 2026-11-08), the 2026-10-23 ruling that a layer PR merges only on a green index run with it pinned, and “merge non-content when green” in the merge window rules. merge-evidence.dmn then decides, in this order: hand-back on red (a release), dirty or blocking (to merge-refusal, which returns the PR to its owner with the reason); unknown when a fact could not be read (ends, not merged); not-yet while runs are pending or mergeability is uncomputed (ends; re-enter later); no-ci on a clean, clear head with no CI; ready when everything is green, clean and clear, and ready on a non-release merge whose head is clean and clear, whatever CI said (its release input is false).

1269.title: A repository with no CI is not green (STRICT)
1269.content: none means nothing tested this head. It is the third state that ci-health and prepare-merge §”NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN” describe, reached by a different route. There, runs were owed and did not appear. Here, the repository declares no workflow, so no run is owed and none will ever appear. Zero runs, zero failures: “nothing red” is true and tells you nothing. Four consequences: . | No standing waiver covers it. A waiver such as “you may merge green PRs” names green heads, and a head nothing tested is not one. merge-authorisation.dmn routes waiver + none to ask. | The merging session runs the repository’s own gates locally (Task_LocalGates), on the merge result rather than the branch: bun test, the typecheck, and whatever the repository’s README or package.json names. Record each command, its exit code and the SHA it ran on. A local run is evidence the owner can weigh. It is not CI: the container was contended, the tree was yours, and nobody else can re-run it. Say that. | The question to the owner says so in words: “This repository runs no CI. Nothing but my local run tested this head.” An authorisation given without that sentence was given about a different merge. | After the merge, “main is green” is reported as “not verified: no CI”. It is never “green”. | . unreadable is different. It means the runs could not be asked about: no token, an API error, a rate limit. The remedy is to make the read work, not to ask permission, so the process ends there.

1270.title: Authorisation — who, and what counts
1270.content: Only the owner authorises a merge to main. That means the repository owner, or the person the session works for when they own the repository. A sibling session, a Merge Steward, a bot comment, a reviewer approval and the merging session itself are not the owner. A Claude Approvals approval is evidence about the change. It is not authorisation to merge it. Task_ReadAuthorisation classifies what it finds into one value: . | authorisation | what it is | . | explicit | The owner’s own words, naming this merge. Examples: “merge #12”; “yes, merge it” in reply to a question that named the PR and its evidence; “approve all 6” in reply to a list of six. | . | waiver | A node under memory/waivers/ with gate: merge-to-main, in scope and unexpired, carrying all five fields (confirmation-waiver). | . | instruction-only | A broad instruction about the work that does not name the merge. | . | none | Nothing found. | . | unknown | The waivers could not be read, a waiver is malformed, or the conversation the authorisation would be in is not available to this session. | . These are instruction-only, and they do not authorise a merge: . | “fix all issues until green”, “make CI pass”, “get it working”, “finish this”. They authorise the work, not the write to main. | “prepare-merge”, “make it mergeable”, “ship it”. The first two are prepare-merge, which stops before the merge by definition, and prepare-merge lists the third among its own triggers. | Approval of a plan in which merging is a later step. | A message from another agent or session, however it is phrased. No agent message is the owner’s consent. | Your own summary of what the owner wanted. If you are composing the sentence, it is not the owner’s. | . Why the line is drawn there. A merge publishes the change to everyone who reads main, and through index.config.json pins to every layer that mounts the repository. It cannot be taken back quietly: a revert is a second public change. That makes it the same kind of action as a deletion (deletion-requires-confirmation): an outward write that is hard to reverse, owed an explicit yes. An instruction about the goal does not contain that yes, however confident the reading. merge-authorisation.dmn decides merge for explicit (over green, or over none when the question carried the no-CI sentence) and for waiver over green. Everything else is ask, including waiver over none. The authorisation is bound to the head it was given against. A push after it re-opens the question. The one exception is a bot merge of main into the head with no other change. A batch authorisation covers the PRs listed when it was given, not PRs that arrive later (merge-queue §Landing).

1271.title: Asking — evidence before the question
1271.content: Task_Ask follows interaction-modality §4.1: context, options, recommendation, question. The test is whether the owner can answer without opening anything. For a merge, that means one row per PR: . | repo | PR | head | CI on head | mergeable | review | local gates (if no CI) |—|—|—|—|—|—|—| . Then the recommendation, then one question that covers the batch: “Merge these N?” Several repositories are several merges, but one question can authorise all of them, provided every one is a row. Task_OwnerDecides is the owner’s lane and is fulfilled by a person only. Its answers are merge, hold or refuse. hold and refuse end the process with the PR open. Nothing is closed and nothing is deleted.

1272.title: Recording the authorisation (not relaxable)
1272.content: An authorisation nobody wrote down cannot be told from one that was never given. Task_RecordAuthorisation writes it before the merge. The shape already exists: ReleaseSchema in schemas/sdlc/merge-queue.ts, and this step reuses it rather than inventing a second one. Where the repository has the merge queue, record it with the command that validates it: . bun run cat merge:queue:decide --pr <n> --verdict merge \ --by <owner's login> --captured-by <your session URL> \ --quote "<the owner's words, verbatim>" --source <where they said it> \ --sha <the head SHA they approved> [--standing-ruling --ruled-at <YYYY-MM-DD>] . It refuses a --by that is a session (the person who decided is never the agent that wrote it down), a missing quote or source, and a missing SHA. merge:steward then prints the release against the live head (merge@<sha>, none, or VOID when the head moved), which is the explicit / waiver / none reading Task_ReadAuthorisation needs. Elsewhere (a repository with no queue), post the same fields as a comment on the PR, signed with the session link, and append it to the work item: . merge-authorised: verdict: merge decidedBy: <owner's GitHub login> decidedAt: <ISO-8601 date-time> authority: explicit | standing-ruling (ruledAt: <date>) | waiver:<waiver node id> quote: "<the owner's words, verbatim>" source: <session link or comment permalink> releasedSha: <the full head SHA being merged> capturedBy: <your session URL> ci: green | none (local: <command> exit <code> @ <sha>; ...) . These fields match index.config.json’s trust consent one for one (by, on, ref, evidence). A quote that is not verbatim is not evidence: a paraphrase is the thing under suspicion, as confirmation-waiver says of a waiver’s quote. The same rule covers a re-pin’s trust.consent.evidence. It quotes the owner’s consent to THAT pin. A goal instruction in that field (“fix all issues until green”) records a consent that was never given.

1273.title: Merging
1273.content: Through merge:guard <pr> --merge --session <id> where the repository has it (it re-evaluates live and pins the PUT to the head); elsewhere with the merge call pinned to the head SHA, so GitHub refuses if the head moved. A merge commit unless told otherwise. Never delete the branch (prepare-merge §Guardrails).

1274.title: After the merge
1274.content: . | Task_ConfirmBase: read main’s CI on the merge commit. If it is red, fix forward (continual-progress §”Two green PRs can merge into a red main”). With no CI, report “not verified: no CI”. Do not report it as green. | Task_Republish: rebuild and republish the repository’s site. A merge that changes what a published site shows is not done until the site shows it. When the merged repository’s index.config.json declares site.build, build from the merge commit and publish: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/build-instance-site.ts --root . \ --instance <name> --publish --remote https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> . This is agent-run, never a GitHub Actions workflow. The build’s gates stay in force: an unresolved link refuses the publish, and that refusal goes on the issue and is fixed forward, never published over. A repository whose own workflow publishes its site (docs-site-publish.bpmn) needs nothing here. With no site.build, record “no site to republish”. | Task_Repin: re-pin downstream mounts, as PRs, never as part of this merge. Find the layers whose index.config.json names this repository in source.remote.repository. For each, open a PR that moves ref to the merge commit, carries a trust.consent whose evidence quotes the owner’s consent to that pin, and regenerates index.lock.json with mount:remote (remote-mount, index-config). Each re-pin PR is a merge to main in another repository, so it runs this sub-process again. The merge authorisation covers the re-pin only if the owner’s words named the re-pin. When no layer mounts the repository, record “no downstream mounts found” and say where you looked. | Task_Report: a note on the work item with the merge SHA and the authorisation block, and a round summary on the issue (issue-working). Do not close the issue. In CRDM, crdm-close.bpmn closes it after this sub-process returns, and only on the BA’s authorisation. | .

1275.title: What this does not do yet
1275.content: . | Outside the merge queue, no tool prints authorisation. Where the queue exists, merge:steward prints the recorded release against the live head and check:waivers validates the waiver half. Elsewhere Task_ReadAuthorisation classifies it by reading the conversation, the PR and memory/waivers/. That is a judgement, and the record makes it auditable. | merge:guard does not refuse a merge with no recorded release. releaseCovers exists and merge:steward reports it, but the guard’s eight checks are about readiness. Making the guard require a covering release would turn this rule into a gate. That is a change to merge-guard.ts and is not part of this skill. | It does not change merge:guard’s check 5. In a repository with no workflows, check 5 refuses with “no pull_request run names the head”. Read that refusal as ciState: none and take the no-ci path, not hand-back: the PR has no defect for its owner to fix. | .

1277.title: Adopting a methodology, and choosing between them
1277.content: Skill methodology-adoption: How a named external methodology enters the knowledge graph, and how an agent picks which one applies. Read before following a judgement method, before adopting a new one, and before writing a house method instead of adopting one. Named by: DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring, Phase 1: Planning, SMART Guideline end to end . A methodology is somebody else’s work, adopted whole. It is not a house process with a citation bolted on. The graph carries them as a distinct kind so that adopting one, replacing one and removing one are all ordinary operations. Methodologies are parallel ways of achieving the same process, chosen by context; each is formalised on its own and kept independent, so that other skills can incorporate it as a sub-graph.

1278.title: Parallel, not composable
1278.content: Two or more methodologies may answer the same question. Do not blend them. A composite — this one’s vocabulary, that one’s record, a third one’s filter — is a house method that cites nobody, and it inherits none of their authority while claiming all of it. So: pick one per decision, name it, and follow it.

1279.title: Choosing which applies
1279.content: First: is this a judgement, or a process? . Ask before the ladder. The ladder below is about how to decide something; a request for a change is not yet a decision but work needing agreed requirements before anything is built. Sent down the ladder, it lands on the catch-all rung and produces an options analysis for a question nobody has framed yet. Is somebody asking for a change, such that requirements have to be agreed before it is built? . If yes, the question is who is asking, and does the answer depend on what a folio says? . | A change to the platform’s own capability — a tool, a schema, a pipeline, a skill, a gate — raised by somebody building the tooling, whose answer does not depend on any folio’s subject matter → the software-development process methodology. | Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, tied to a folio’s domain → the stakeholder requirements methodology. | . Both answer request → agreed requirements, so they are parallel and must not be blended — the refusal below applies to this pair first and hardest. Which is which is stated in each one’s applies-when, not here, for the reason in §”Why this skill does not name them”. If no — the change is agreed and the question is how to decide something within it — continue to the ladder. Then the ladder . Ask in this order. The first yes decides. | Do the criteria recur, with the same inputs having to produce the same answer? → the computable methodology. A one-off tabled as if it recurs asserts a repeatability it does not have. | Is the question the certainty of a body of evidence behind a recommendation? → the evidence-grading methodology. Note this is about evidence, not about a design choice that happens to be uncertain. | Is the context a work item recording a decision? → the decision-record methodology. It constrains the record, not the method, so it composes with (1) or (4) rather than competing. | Otherwise — a one-off choice among candidate options → the decision-analysis methodology. | . If none fits, that is a finding, not a licence. Say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit: either is how a house method gets in. Why this skill does not name them . Naming each methodology here would couple this skill to the set, and the set is meant to be extractable: a methodology can be lifted out, or replaced, without a prose edit here. So the declared set is the contents of the methodology graph, read from the layer’s declaration. Ask for it; do not remember it.

1280.title: Node, skill, or both?
1280.content: An adopted methodology can produce up to two artefacts: . | you are writing | it is a node in the methodology graph | it is a skill | . | what the method IS — its vocabulary, its constraints, what it refuses | ✅ | ❌ | . | how to PERFORM it here — the extension element, the gate, the procedure | ❌ | ✅ | . | a house process with no external origin | ❌ | ✅ — and do not dress it as an adoption | . Most adoptions produce both, and the split is the same every time: the node is the method, the skill is this platform’s application of it. The skill names the node and does not restate it, because two files carrying one definition is two copies free to drift. Three worked cases: . | raci — both. The four letters and the one-Accountable rule are the method (node); reading R from the BPMN lane, the cat-harness.processes:raci element and check:raci are this platform’s application (skill). | crdm — both (methodologies/crdm.md). PHII’s three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, swimlane Task Flow Diagrams, and PATH’s activity-linked requirement structure are the external method (node, backed by library/phii-2023-crdm, library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, and library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm); agentic facilitation, 7-dimension code impact analysis, work-item decomposition, and pull-request merge sign-off are this platform’s adaptation (crdm-requirements-workflow and crdm-requirements-template). | swot — both. | . A methodology in use with no node is invisible to the graph: check:methodology-evidence and every other reader of the methodology graph count nodes, not skills.

1281.title: Adopting a new one — the ingestion process
1281.content: . | Establish it is external and named. A methodology has an origin: authors, a publication, a standards body. If it has none, it is a house process — write it as a skill and do not dress it as an adoption. | Render it faithfully, and say where the rendering stops. The file carries what the method says, not a summary of what we liked. Where this platform adopts part of a method and refuses part, both halves are stated with the reason — a silent omission misrepresents the standard. | Declare its applicability. applies-when in the front matter, phrased so the selection question above can reach it, and saying what it is not for. | Place it by ownership, not by convenience. A domain-neutral method belongs to the harness; a domain method belongs to the repo that owns the domain. The separation plan decides, and the placement must make extraction literal — the directory lifts out, its declaration entry goes with it, and nothing else moves. | Declare the directory. A methodology outside a declared directory is invisible to every tool that reads the graph. | State its refusals. The part of a method a platform must not do is as load-bearing as the part it follows, and it is the part a later agent will breach first. | Ingest the source and cite it as evidence. origin names the work; evidence: library/<bib-slug> points at a copy a reader can open from this checkout. Use literature-search to find it and library-ingestion to bring it in. Where the source cannot be fetched, that is an outcome to report — a located-but-unreachable document, never a missing one — and the node keeps its origin with no evidence until somebody closes the gap. | .

1282.title: Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools
1282.content: A source that presents a method through an implementation is presenting two things, and only one of them is the methodology. Render the method first, then decide which tools — existing or to be added — this platform should use to perform it. A node that adopted the source’s tool stack would be adopting an implementation and calling it a method, and it could never be falsified: the tools would work and the method would never be examined. hybrid-llm-deterministic is the worked case. Its source demonstrates the method in one tool with one model and one expression language; the node renders the rule/result inversion, the five safeguards and the bounded-truncation technique, and §”Where this rendering stops” names every tool it declined to adopt and why. The method survives replacing all of them, which is the test of whether you extracted a method at all. Ask it as: what would still be true if they had built it differently? What survives is the methodology. What does not is their engineering, and it belongs in the skill if anywhere — where this platform’s own tool choices already live. And say what the source does NOT establish. A demonstration is not an evaluation. Where a paper shows an approach working once, with no baseline and no measurement, the node records that no performance claim rests on it. Doing otherwise manufactures a finding the authors did not make — the same failure as §”Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured”, arriving through a citation instead.

1283.title: An origin nobody can open is not evidence
1283.content: A methodology’s justification is being somebody else’s named, external work, so its origin must resolve to a source a reader can open. bun run cat check:methodology-evidence is the axis that makes this visible, and test/results/methodology-evidence.qa-results.json is where it is recorded. It reports and does not gate on a missing source: whether a methodology whose source nobody can open may still be used is the owner’s call, and a gate failing on the whole corpus at once would be switched off. It does fail on front matter that does not validate, and on an evidence pointing at a bib-slug no library holds, because a citation that claims to resolve and does not is worse than none. The evidence is an input to SELECTION, not only to adoption. options-analysis.bpmn’s A_CheckEvidence reads it before the chosen methodology is applied. Adoption happens once; selection happens at every decision, and a source can stop being reachable in between. A contested origin is recorded as contested. methodologies/swot.md is the worked example: the usual attribution is repeated everywhere and its own source says no academic reference supports it, so the node declines to name an inventor: flattening that into a fact would carry the authority of a citation while resting on nothing.

1284.title: Refusals
1284.content: . | Never blend two methodologies into one procedure. Parallel means parallel. | Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A citation with no rendered method is an appeal to authority that no reader can check. | Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform adopts the structure and refuses the arithmetic: a total reads as a measurement, and the weights were invented. This is the same rule as never quoting a count from prose as though it were evidence. | Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. Whichever methodology was used, the alternatives and why they lost are part of the output — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted. | Never write a method from recall and cite a paper nobody fetched. Read the source, or say you read it through another and mark each attribution second-hand. See literature-search §”Never fill the gap with recall”. | .

1286.title: Does the prose say what the code does?
1286.content: Skill narrative-asserts-code: Judge whether the prose side of a declared prose ↔ code pair still says what the code does, when the machine could not settle it. Reads the two mechanical signals first — staleness and resolvable claims — and settles what is left in one of three ways, sending a disagreement with a checker to adjudication. General: the Lean case is a specialisation with its own skill. Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring, SMART Guideline end to end . A reader acts on what the prose says. When prose and code disagree, the reader either avoids a working feature or rebuilds it. This skill is the judgement step. The machine has already done everything it can, and your job is the rest.

1287.title: The pairs this applies to — declared, never inferred
1287.content: | pair | prose | code | declared by | . | diagram ↔ workflow | a .bpmn diagram’s <documentation> | the .github/workflows/*.yml it draws | # bpmn: <diagram> in the workflow (+ # bpmn-node: <id> per job) | . | skill ↔ code | a skill .md | the same-stem .ts beside it | the file sitting there | . | proof ↔ Lean | a paper block’s .md | its lean.ref | the block manifest — see below, it has its own skill | . A pair nothing declares is out of scope. Do not go looking for prose that “seems to describe” some code: an inferred pair is a guess, and a finding on a guess is how a check gets switched off.

1288.title: Read the machine’s output first — it is already in the sidecar
1288.content: Two kg-qa criteria on the subject’s sidecar tell you what is open: . | prose-reviewed-since-code-changed. fail means the code changed and the prose did not. It says nothing about truth, only that nobody re-read the prose. | prose-claims-resolve. Each claim the prose makes about the code comes out holds, false or undetermined. bun run cat pairs:claims prints the whole list, including what it did not check. | . What you judge is exactly the stale pairs, the false claims and the undetermined claims. A claim that holds and a pair that is not stale need nothing from you.

1289.title: Three outcomes, and each leaves a record
1289.content: . | The prose holds. Say why, in one sentence, and attest the pair: bun run cat pairs:attest -- --sidecar <sidecar> --by agent|human --reason "…". A reason is required because an attestation nobody can review is not evidence. Name what you compared: “the TypeScript step describes the repository gates and bun run cat gates derives its list from this job” is a reason; “looks fine” is not. | The prose and the code really disagree. Raise a finding against the side that is wrong. Usually that is the prose, because the code is what runs, but not always: a skill can state the intended behaviour correctly while the code has regressed. Say which side, and why that side. | You disagree with a checker’s false. The machine says a claim is false and you read it as true, or the other way round. Do not overrule it quietly. That disagreement is exactly what adjudication exists for: call Process_CriterionAdjudication (the QA-criterion specialisation of adjudication, whose outcomes are: the finding stands, the criterion is scoped, or a dispensation is granted), and the checker’s entry is kept beneath the verdict, because a disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information. | .

1290.title: Lean is the specialisation, not the model
1290.content: For a proof ↔ Lean pair, a proof assistant can settle the formal claim mechanically, which no other pair kind allows. That work belongs to proof-narrative-lean-equivalence (the science layer): stub-weakening, overreach, hypothesis mismatch and notation drift. This skill states the question for every pair kind, and that one answers it for Lean. Nothing Lean-specific goes here, so a pair kind added later inherits the general question without inheriting Lean’s machinery.

1291.content: narrative-code-review.bpmn, entered from review-task.bpmn when a change is prose and the code it describes. The review dispatcher’s gateway is exclusive, so a change that is both goes through this branch.

Table 17 in the DAK provides non-functional requirements as general characteristics of the overall system. Edit this page on GitHub .

1294.title: Semantic Ontologist (Ambiguity Detection & Glossary)
1294.content: Skill ontologist: Semantic Ontologist — scans narrative text for ambiguous terms, generates a formal glossary/registry, and produces a mapping linking narrative strings to formal identifiers. Acts as the “Gatekeeper” ensuring every term has a unique type/identity assignment before formalization proceeds. Named by: Classify and code content .

1295.title: Overview
1295.content: The Gatekeeper for definitions: before any narrative-to-formal translation proceeds, every term has a unique identity (and, where the project has a formal layer, a unique type assignment). The Ontologist detects ambiguities, maintains the formal glossary, and produces the machine-readable mapping.

1296.title: Formal-layer tooling (when available)
1296.content: When the project has a formal-proof layer with language-server / MCP tooling, prefer those tools for type checking over re-building: . | Goal | Prefer | Why better | . | Find type mismatches | structured diagnostics tool | per-file error messages | . | Resolve a symbol’s type | hover-info tool | see the resolved type in place | . | Find an existing definition | local search tool | search project + stdlib | . | Check whether a type exists in the stdlib | symbol/type search tool | locate the exact declaration | . | Find where a type is declared | declaration-file tool | jump to source | . | Guess an import path | completion tool | auto-complete import paths | . Consistency loop . When the formal build or the diagnostics tool reports a type mismatch: . | Identify the glossary entries involved and flag them as ambiguous. | Hover the mismatched symbol → see expected vs actual type. | Search for the intended type → find the correct import. | Read the actual definition to understand the mismatch. | Update the glossary with the corrected assignment. | Regenerate the formal glossary, re-run the scan with the error context, and re-check diagnostics. | .

1297.title: When to Use This Skill
1297.content: . | New terms or definitions are added to chapter files. | The formal build fails due to type mismatches (consistency loop). | The formalizer reports an unresolved term. | Reviewing changes that introduce new notation. | Before running the formalizer on any chapter. | .

1298.title: Workflow
1298.content: 1. Scan narrative text for terms . Run the project’s ontologist scanner over the source chapters. It parses for definitions, symbols, and terms and outputs candidates to the glossary. 2. Detect ambiguities . The scanner flags terms that lack a unique assignment. Trigger phrases (require disambiguation) are bare nouns used without their distinguishing structure — “the mapping” without domain/codomain, “the space” without which kind of space, “the group” without which kind of group, and bare single-letter symbols without an annotation. Action: interrupt the pipeline and request a Type/Identity Assignment. 3. Generate the formal glossary . Run the generator. It produces a formal-glossary file with each term as a declaration, docstrings containing the original narrative definition, and any required annotations. 4. Generate the mapping . Run the mapping generator. It produces a file linking narrative strings to formal identifiers.

1299.title: Glossary entry structure
1299.content: Each glossary entry follows this pattern: a docstring with the human-readable definition, the source location of the narrative definition, and (when relevant) the stdlib reference the term maps to, followed by the declaration itself. Bibliographic reference requirement . Every unproved gap (sorry-style stub) in the formal glossary must be preceded by a reference comment linking to the foundational source, whose key matches a citation key in the project’s reference registry exactly. (Auto-generated bibliography files are derived from the registry — never edit them directly.) .

1300.title: Ambiguity Resolution Format
1300.content: Standing disambiguation rulings . The project’s notation / terminology register holds a table of author-resolved terms; agents MUST apply them when scanning. A ruling fixes the canonical term, any banned synonyms or notations, and when a qualifier is required. Banned notations and “always qualify” entries are hard rules. When an ambiguity is detected, the Ontologist outputs a record naming the narrative term, a message describing the ambiguity, the candidate resolutions, and a resolved_to field that is null until the author fills it. The pipeline halts until resolved_to is filled.

1301.title: Output Files
1301.content: | File | Purpose | . | glossary (machine-readable) | glossary with ambiguity flags | . | formal glossary | formal file with definitions | . | mapping | narrative-to-formal identifier mapping | .

1302.title: Blueprint Integration
1302.content: Every glossary entry that has a label in a chapter file must also appear in the project’s blueprint with the matching formal-declaration macro. The Ontologist ensures: . | Label consistency between chapters and blueprint. | Declaration consistency between blueprint macros and the formal glossary. | Dependency edges in the blueprint reference only labels that exist and whose glossary entries are resolved. | Bibliography references: every reference comment in the formal glossary matches a citation key in the reference registry; new terms get a foundational reference added to the registry. | .

1303.title: Content Object Integration
1303.content: Glossary terms should link to content-object labels. Each definition block has a .ts manifest with a label and a .md narrative. | Definitions in .md blocks reference glossary entries by their formal name and cross-ref by label. | New glossary entries record the content-object label they originate from for bidirectional traceability. | The formal-reference URI in a definition’s .ts manifest matches the corresponding formal-glossary declaration name. | Before creating a glossary entry for a term detected in a .md file, check whether a content object already exists, to avoid duplication. | .

1304.title: Glossary Block Policy
1304.content: A dedicated glossary chapter can contain glossary blocks — remark blocks tagged "glossary" — that map project terminology to canonical stdlib declarations. These are the content-object counterpart of glossary entries. When to use a glossary block vs. a definition block . | Criterion | Glossary block (remark) | Definition block | . | Novelty | none — the term is a synonym/light wrapper for a stdlib type | the project introduces genuinely new material | . | Formal file | not required | required | . | Label prefix | rem:glossary-<term> | def:<term> | . | Chapter | glossary chapter | relevant content chapter | . Decision tree for new terms . | Does the term exist in the stdlib under a different name? → glossary block mapping project name to stdlib name. | Is it a lightweight restriction/specialization of a stdlib type? → glossary block with a note about the restriction. | Does the project add new axioms, fields, or structure? → definition block in the relevant chapter. | Ambiguous? → ask the author. | . Glossary block structure . Each glossary block is a .ts + .md pair: the .ts declares a remark with the glossary tag and a rem:glossary-<term> label; the .md gives a 1–3 sentence definition as used in the project plus the stdlib reference (fully-qualified name, kind, and import path). Snippet validation (mandatory after creating .md) . After creating any glossary .md, validate its embedded math/markup snippets with the project’s snippet validator before committing, and fix any errors. Maintaining consistency . | When a new stdlib-equivalent term appears in any chapter .md, check the glossary chapter for an existing entry before creating a definition. | When the glossary is regenerated, cross-check against the glossary chapter’s entries. | The chapter-analysis skill’s glossary-gap analysis should include the glossary-chapter blocks in its coverage check. | . Wrap-every-occurrence . Every term registered in a block’s defines: [...] must appear wrapped at every mention — the canonical-definition directive once at the canonical site, the reference directive everywhere else. The ontologist owns the choice of canonical site: pick the block whose .md carries the most authoritative definition (stdlib synonym → glossary block; new material → the relevant def: block), add the slug to its defines, and rewrite the canonical mention. Backfilling reference mentions across the project is the codemod’s job.

1307.title: Opening brief — brief the topic before you touch anything
1307.content: Skill opening-brief: Brief a work item or a topic BEFORE touching anything: what you are doing and why it is worth doing, what you already know and with what provenance, how you plan to do it and what would falsify the approach. Scales with irreversibility, not line count. Named by: DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring, SMART Guideline end to end . This skill governs what you say before the work; turn-reporting.md governs what you say during and after it; todo-manager.md keeps the work item mechanics.

1308.title: Opening brief
1308.content: Claiming a work item records the work. Briefing it is what makes the work resumable. Both are required, and the brief comes first — before the first tool call, in the chat, not in the commit. AGENTS.md §”Opening a bean or a topic” states the rule and when it applies. This is the shape. When it applies — proportionality, so this does not become ceremony . The trigger is irreversibility and surprise, not line count. | A one-line fix with an obvious route needs no brief. Say what you are doing and do it. | Anything touching a shipped gate, a shared artefact, a formal declaration with consumers, or a number a reader sees — brief it. | Anything where you expect to be wrong some of the time — brief it, and say where you expect to be wrong. Research is the case this is most valuable for and most often skipped, on the grounds that the outcome is unknown. The unknown outcome is the reason to write down the route, not a reason to skip it. | . Why it is a rule and not a style preference . Sessions end mid-thread. Containers are reclaimed, context windows fill, a branch is picked up days later by an agent with none of the reasoning that produced it. The work item body and the commit are durable; the chain of inference that made them sensible is not, unless it is written down at the point where it was still obvious. An agent resuming cold should be able to read the brief and continue — not reconstruct its predecessor’s rabbit hole first. It catches wrong work before it is done rather than after. A route stated in advance can be corrected by the author in one line. The same route discovered in a finished diff costs a review cycle and, often, a revert. It is the same discipline as the question frame in interaction-modality §4.1, applied to work instead of decisions: a terse start, like a terse question, makes the author go and find context the agent already had. The four parts . 1. The problem, stated for someone who was not here. Expand every identifier on first use. Not “fixing qou-93hu” but “bean qou-93hu — the CriticalExponent conjecture carrier, whose only field is (3 * 4 : ℕ) = 12, a closed numeral identity with no exponent variable in it, so the class constrains nothing.” . 2. What you know, and how you know it. Every number with its provenance: . | provenance | how to say it | . | measured this session, on this tree | “measured just now: 22 of 22 seeded, 0 missed” | . | measured this session, on a DIFFERENT tree | “grepped 0 on claude/x before branching — not re-run here” | . | carried from a prior session | “recorded 2026-08-24 as 43 drifted; not re-measured” | . | asserted by a work item or a doc | “bean qou-q7lf says X — unverified” | . The last row is the one that bites hardest. A sibling’s work item is not a primary source, and neither is a source file’s ## Status note; both go stale, and a specific, recent, confidently-worded work item is exactly the kind that gets believed. “Measured this session” is not the safe case. A measurement is scoped to the TREE it was taken on, and git switch invalidates every earlier one without saying so. The number is real, recent, and yours; only the tree underneath it moved. So say which tree, and re-run anything load-bearing after a branch change — the re-run costs one command and it is the same command. Part 2 includes the result of the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work”: the siblings that overlap, or “no overlap found” and what you checked. 3. The route and the gate. How you plan to do it, what you will verify against, and what would falsify the approach. A plan with no failure mode is not a plan; it is an intention. If the gate is a script, name it and its expected output. 4. What you are NOT doing. The adjacent defect you are leaving, the scope you decline to widen into, the thing you will flag rather than fix. Stating it up front is what stops it becoming either silent scope creep or a silent omission — and it puts the scope call where it can still be argued with, which is before the diff. Briefing a sibling or a subagent — pass interaction-modality on (STRICT) . When a coordinating session writes a brief to launch a child session (create_session, send_message) or a background subagent (Agent, invoke_subagent), the brief is the child’s only prompt until it reads the graph. A child whose brief omits how to ask the owner will default to asking in plain prose when it hits a permission wall or a design call. Every sibling brief and subagent prompt written by a coordinating session MUST carry the interaction-modality contract explicitly: . | If the child can reach the person directly (a sibling session with its own chat surface): every question to the owner goes out twice, in order — first the full question in chat (context, what differs, every identifier expanded, at most four numbered or lettered options with pros, cons, downstream impact and reversibility, recommended option first and marked (Recommended), and the stated default on silence), and second the tappable card (AskUserQuestion, request_decision, ask_question, or post_widget) carrying the same option labels. Never ask in prose alone, and never ask the person to type. | If the child is a background subagent or a sibling running beside a live discussion: it does not ask the person in prose either; it returns any owner-facing decision to the coordinating session in the hand-back-to-discussion schema format so the coordinator presents both the full chat block and the tappable card. | Pass it on: if the child itself spawns a helper or a subagent, its brief to that child must carry the same interaction-modality block. | . Before you offer options, check whether it is already ruled (STRICT) . Part two of the brief is what do I already know, with each measurement’s provenance. This is the half that gets skipped, because an unsettled question is more interesting than a settled one and nothing in a checkout announces that a decision exists. Presenting options for a settled question is worse than presenting none. It reopens a decision, spends the owner’s attention on it a second time, and the options offered will not be the ones already weighed. Four places to look, in this order: . | The proposals — the design corpus. They live in the docs/ of the layer whose stub needs them; today that is cat-harness/docs/proposals/, and its index.md is where to start. Resolve the directory rather than remembering this sentence — a stub’s docs/ is where its proposals are, and this path is an example of the rule, not the rule. | The owner’s rulings, in work items and in the declarations that quote them verbatim. A _comment field in a *.json is frequently where a decision was recorded, because that is where it had to be obeyed. | The skill that owns the area — and read it, rather than recalling it. | The commit history — git log -S "<symbol>" over the file you are about to change, and a beans list | grep <topic> that does not filter to open items. A decision that shipped is invisible to every instrument that looks for pending ones — and a recent one is exactly when you are most confident your own reading is current. One git log -S answers it. | . Cite what you read, never what you remember. A half-remembered line used as an authority is the fake-reference failure activity-names-skill exists to prevent, one level up: it is unfalsifiable by the reader, because it sounds like something this repository would say. Worked example . Starting qou-93hu — the CriticalExponent §3b-cond hypothesis class in lean/QOU/AlgebraicSubstrate/ConditionalClasses.lean. The problem. Its single field is alpha_three_eq_four : (3 * 4 : ℕ) = 12 — a closed numeral identity with the values already substituted in, so no exponent variable occurs in it and rfl proves it whatever the physics. Four sibling carriers in the same file are vacuous too, but they are at least the right shape (parameter-quantified inequalities); this one has no quantifier and no free variable at all. What I know. Measured this session: bound as [C] in 5 files; the probe baseline records it proved-vacuous; the class’s own docstring already claims “α = 4/3”, so the target value is not something I need to invent. Not measured: whether any downstream proof depends on the field’s current type. Route. Make α a class parameter — class CriticalExponent (α : ℝ) : Prop where alpha_eq : α = 4/3. A Prop class cannot carry data, so α must be a parameter, not a field. Gate: lean-direct exit 0 on all three affected modules, plus a content probe proving ¬ CriticalExponent 2 — because inhabitability at 4/3 alone would not show the class constrains anything. Falsifier: if ¬ CriticalExponent 2 will not go through, the encoding is not doing what I claim and I stop. Not doing. The other four carriers need analytic setup their docstrings only gesture at — the author’s mathematics, not a cleanup. Also leaving the separate CriticalExponent in core-levi-form.lean, a different carrier in a different namespace. ~200 words, and it would have let a reader stop the work, redirect it, or pick it up cold. What a thin brief looks like, and why it fails . Starting qou-93hu — fixing CriticalExponent. Names the work item and nothing else. It does not say the field is a closed numeral identity with no exponent variable in it, so a reader cannot tell whether this is cosmetic or load-bearing; it does not say the class signature changes, so nobody can warn that every binder in two consumer modules moves with it; and it does not say what “fixed” will be checked against, so the agent is free to declare victory on a compile. Each of those omissions is a place the author could have intervened for the cost of reading one sentence. The failure this prevents . An agent that has spent an hour inside a problem writes in the private vocabulary it built along the way, and a reader — the author, or the next agent — has to reconstruct that vocabulary before evaluating anything. The brief is written at the one moment when the agent still knows which parts are non-obvious, because it has just finished finding them out. Cheapest correct move when you do not want to spend the words: do not start the topic. A task you cannot brief is one you have not understood well enough to begin. The brief’s durable form is the PR description. Once the work exists, pr-description answers the same questions for a reader who arrives after it.

1310.title: Cutting a package release
1310.content: Skill package-release: Cut a release of a repository’s packages: decide the next version, write the release notes, tag, and create the release — for any repository, the platform or a folio. Publishing the built artefact to a registry is a separate, later step that a person starts. Named by: DTH authoring . A release is a version number that one commit keeps from then on: a tag, notes that say what changed, and a record on the host (a GitHub release). Anything that depends on the package names that version and gets exactly that commit. This skill is general: it is for any repository that publishes packages, including a folio that ships its own. It is not the skill for publishing a folio’s content — that belongs to the content layer above this one, where a person supplies the version when the release is authorised. The two share the word “publish” and nothing else: a package release versions code; a content publication versions a document.

1311.title: The four steps, and who owns each
1311.content: | step | what happens | who | . | 1. Decide the version | the next semver triple, from what changed since the last tag | a mechanism proposes it, a person may raise it | . | 2. Write the notes | what changed, grouped the way a consumer reads it — breaking first | a mechanism drafts them, a person edits | . | 3. Tag and create the release | one tag per package, <package>-v<version>, and the host’s release record | a mechanism, after a person approves | . | 4. Publish the artefact | push the built package to its registry (npm, PyPI, …) | a person starts it, separately | . Step 4 is kept apart on purpose. A tag can be deleted; a version pushed to a public registry cannot be taken back or reused. So the one step nobody can undo is the one step no mechanism takes on its own.

1312.title: Step 1 — where the version comes from
1312.content: Two ways to compute a bump. They can disagree, and the rule for that is below. | From commit messages (conventional commits): feat: is minor, fix: is patch, feat!: or BREAKING CHANGE: is major. Cheap, and what release-please does. Its weakness: a commit message is a claim about a change, not the change. A feat: commit that removed something a consumer uses gives a minor bump and a broken consumer. | From the declared surface: diff what the package exports (for an layer, the graph kg-export walks: graph typologies, skill ids, tool ids, block kinds) between the last tag and HEAD. A removal is major; an addition is minor; neither is patch. | . When both are available, the larger bump wins. You may always release a bigger bump than computed; never a smaller one. A version is an exact triple: no ranges, anywhere. A version that has been tagged is never reused, even if its release was deleted.

1313.title: Step 3 — before you tag
1313.content: . | The package must build from the commit being tagged. Check its manifest’s file list: every entry must exist. A release of a package that cannot be built is worse than no release, because it looks like one. | Only a package declared publishable is released. For a layer, that means publishable: true in its <name>.json (check:publishable). An layer that has not declared it is undecided, not no, and is not released. | The configuration names only what exists. A release tool pointed at a config file that is missing either fails or falls back to guesses. Neither is a release. | .

1314.title: Mechanisms
1314.content: Each Tool that can do this names package-release in its satisfies; ask for them with tool_list rather than relying on this list. | release-please — the GitHub Action or CLI. Does steps 1–3 from commit messages: it opens a release PR, and merging that PR creates the tag and the release. In this repository it is declared but not configured: there is no config. Before one is written, the package must build and the layers to release must declare publishable: true. | By hand — git tag, a CHANGELOG entry and the host’s release form. The same four steps and the same rules; slower, and nothing to misconfigure. | pack-tarball (bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pack-tarball.ts) — packages an layer into an npm .tgz tarball using bun pm pack, computing size and SHA-256 digest into a folio-binary-release/v1 release record. See the npm-kg-distribution skill. | package-release-workflow (gh workflow run release-npm.yml) — dispatches the release workflow across any repository (--repo <owner/repo>) via GitHub Actions. Automates tarball building, tagging, GitHub Release asset upload, and publishing to GitHub Packages / npm registries. Satisfies package-release, npm-kg-distribution, and document-publishing. | .

1315.title: What this skill does not do
1315.content: . | It does not publish a folio’s content (the content layer does). | It does not take in an upstream’s release (upstream-version-adoption). That is the other side of the same event: someone else’s step 3 is the start of your adoption. | It does not push to a registry on its own (step 4, above). | .

1319.title: pcf-consent
1319.content: | Skill pcf-consent: Model IHE Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF 1.1.0, Trial Implementation) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use) resources referenced by canonical URL only, translate PCF Basic and Additional PurposeOfUse Consents plus the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets into W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policies (consentToOdrl()), and evaluate three-valued access-control decisions (permit | deny | unknown) across decide() / permits(), odrl:obtainConsent duties, IHE ITI-108 Consent Registry reads, and PROV-O decision records citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. | . Named by: L2 DAK to L3 FHIR IG . Skill id: pcf-consent · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Layer: fhir-harness · Modules: schemas/pcf-consent.ts (consentToOdrl, decide, evaluatePcfPolicy, PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS), schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts (findAccessConsents, Iti108ConsentClient), schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts. Model patient privacy consent directives in FHIR Implementation Guides, translate them into W3C ODRL 2.2 policies, and evaluate three-valued access-control decisions (permit | deny | unknown). Standards and scope: . | Specifications: IHE IT Infrastructure Technical Framework Supplement — Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) 1.1.0 (Trial Implementation, 2023-08-04) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use, FMG maturity level 2). | Profiles: IHE PCF Basic (IHE.PCF.consentBasic) and Additional PurposeOfUse (IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate: extended HL7 PurposeOfUse codes and nested provision exceptions). The translator also handles IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced security-label sensitivity tags when declared. | Referenced by canonical URL only: never copy or re-author IHE PCF StructureDefinitions or ValueSets in an IG; pin the upstream packages in sushi-config.yaml and reference IHE profiles and value sets by their canonical URLs. | No IUA claim: do not claim conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA), and do not profile ITI-71 / ITI-103 OAuth token exchange; HTTP Authorization headers on ITI-108 reads are passed through opaque to the transport. | Trust-anchor neutral: any consent-bearing workflow or verifiable link depends on an abstract trust anchor (a national PKI, a regional federation, did:web, the Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN), …); none is hardcoded. | .

1320.title: 1. Model — Authoring IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent in a FHIR IG
1320.content: 1.1 Package dependencies in sushi-config.yaml . An IG that profiles, instantiates, or references IHE PCF consent directives or Verifiable Health Links pins the upstream IHE packages in sushi-config.yaml and references their artefacts by canonical URL only: . dependencies: ihe.iti.pcf: id: ihe_iti_pcf uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.pcf version: 1.1.0 ihe.iti.vhl: id: ihe_iti_vhl uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.vhl version: 1.0.0-comment . FHIR R4 Consent in an R5 IG (could-not-determine): ihe.iti.pcf@1.1.0 is an R4 (4.0.1) package. When an R5 (fhirVersion: 5.0.0) IG compiles against it and SUSHI or the IG Publisher rejects cross-version R4-in-R5 profile resolution, report that cross-version outcome explicitly as could-not-determine with the exact tool diagnostic rather than silently dropping the dependency or hand-copying the profile. 1.2 Canonical URLs (never re-declared locally) . Reference the IHE PCF profiles, value sets, and HL7 code systems by their canonical URLs exported in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts: . | Artefact | Canonical URL | Constant in schemas/pcf-consent.ts | . | PCF Implementation Guide | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF | PCF_IG_CANONICAL | . | PCF Basic Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic | PCF_CONSENT_BASIC_PROFILE | . | PCF Intermediate Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate | PCF_CONSENT_INTERMEDIATE_PROFILE | . | PCF Advanced Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced | PCF_CONSENT_ADVANCED_PROFILE | . | PCF Basic Purpose ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/BasicPurposeVS | PCF_BASIC_PURPOSE_VS | . | PCF Advanced Security Tag ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/AdvancedSecurityTagVS | PCF_ADVANCED_SECURITY_TAG_VS | . | HL7 v3 ActReason (PurposeOfUse) | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason | HL7_ACT_REASON_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 Confidentiality | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-Confidentiality | HL7_CONFIDENTIALITY_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ActCode | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActCode | HL7_ACT_CODE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ParticipationType | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ParticipationType | HL7_PARTICIPATION_TYPE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 ConsentScope | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope | HL7_CONSENT_SCOPE_SYSTEM | . | LOINC Privacy policy / Consent | http://loinc.org (59284-0) | LOINC_SYSTEM / LOINC_CONSENT_CODE | . 1.3 Required structure of a PCF Consent instance . Every conformant IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent resource carries: . | meta.profile: one of IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, or IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced (detectPcfProfile(consent) inspects meta.profile and falls back to structural inspection). | status: "active" for an enforceable consent directive ("draft", "proposed", "rejected", "inactive", and "entered-in-error" carry no active permissions or prohibitions). | scope: http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope#patient-privacy. | category: includes http://loinc.org#59284-0 (Consent). | patient: reference to the Patient subject (Patient/<id>). | dateTime and performer (the consenting patient or authorized representative, which becomes the ODRL assigner) and organization (the custodian organization). | sourceReference or sourceAttachment: the signed paper/electronic consent artifact or questionnaire response. | policy: policy[].uri naming the overarching privacy policy (such as one of the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit policy URIs). | provision: root provision (type: "permit" or "deny"), purpose codings from http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason (TREAT, HPAYMT, HOPERAT in BasicPurposeVS, or extended PurposeOfUse codes such as HRESCH, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, PUBHLTH, ETREAT, BTG, PATRQT), optional period, actor, action, dataPeriod, data, securityLabel, and optional nested provision.provision exceptions. | . No draft purpose vocabularies: W3C DPV is a Community Group report and is refused (dpv:* or /dpv returns false in isKnownHl7PurposeOfUse). Always use HL7 v3 ActReason PurposeOfUse codes.

1321.title: 2. Translate — consentToOdrl() and the Four Implicit Policies
1321.content: consentToOdrl(consent, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts translates a FHIR R4 Consent into a W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policy (PcfOdrlSet). 2.1 Field-by-field mapping (Consent → ODRL Set) . | FHIR R4 Consent element | ODRL 2.2 Set element | Translation rule | . | id + meta.versionId | uid | consentPolicyUid(consent) → urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId> (or urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id> when unversioned). | . | performer[0] (fallback patient) | assigner | The party granting or withholding consent. | . | status !== "active" | permission: [], prohibition: [] | Non-active consents emit an empty Set, which evaluates to "unknown" (or defers to implicitPolicy). | . | provision.type ("permit" / "deny") | permission / prohibition | Root provision defaults to "permit" when provision.type is omitted, per FHIR R4 Consent.provision.type. | . | provision.purpose[] (v3-ActReason) | constraint (odrl:purpose) | Each HL7 PurposeOfUse code becomes { leftOperand: "odrl:purpose", operator: "odrl:isA", rightOperand: code }, so ontological parent codes (TREAT, HRESCH, ETREAT, …) permit their sub-concepts (CLINTRL, BTG, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, …) via broaderOrSelf over HL7_PURPOSE_OF_USE (IHE PCF Vol 3 §3:5.8.2). Non-HL7 local project codes become odrl:eq. Multiple purpose codings expand into one rule per purpose (logical OR). | . | provision.period (start, end) | constraint (odrl:dateTime) | period.start → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:gteq", rightOperand: start }; period.end → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:lteq", rightOperand: end }. Date-only bounds (YYYY-MM-DD) expand to 00:00:00.000Z (start) and 23:59:59.999Z (end). | . | provision.actor[].reference | assignee | One rule per actor reference; defaults to ANYONE ("*") when actor is omitted. | . | provision.action[] | action | "read" → "odrl:display", "correct" → "odrl:modify", "access" / "collect" / "use" / "disclose" (and default) → "odrl:use". | . | provision.data[] (meaning: "instance") | target | Direct resource references (DocumentReference/ex-doc, Observation/ex-obs) become rule targets. | . | provision.data[] ("authoredby" / "related") | constraint (pcf:author / pcf:encounter) | meaning: "authoredby" → leftOperand: "pcf:author"; meaning: "related" → leftOperand: "pcf:encounter". | . | provision.dataPeriod | constraint (pcf:dataPeriod) | Clinical data creation/effective period (odrl:gteq / odrl:lteq on pcf:dataPeriod). | . | provision.securityLabel[] | constraint (pcf:securityLabel) | Confidentiality / sensitivity tags (R, V, ETH, PSY, SDV, HIV, …) become odrl:eq or odrl:isAnyOf on pcf:securityLabel. | . | Nested provision.provision[] | permission / prohibition + conflict | Child provisions inherit parent period (intersected via mergePeriods). A root permit with nested deny exceptions sets conflict: "odrl:prohibit". A root deny with nested permit exceptions (e.g. dissent except for Break-Glass BTG) sets conflict: "odrl:perm". | . 2.2 The four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets . When a patient has no explicit active Consent on file (or when their explicit Consent has expired), IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 and §1:53.4.2.4 define four overarching jurisdictional baseline policies, exported in PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS and resolved by getImplicitPolicySet(uriOrAlias): . | Canonical URI (PCF_POLICY_*_URI) | Alias(es) | Constant | Semantics | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-basic-normal | "basic-normal" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BASIC_NORMAL_SET | Permit Clinical Treatment: permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA TREAT (including ETREAT, BTG, CLINTRL, POPHLTH); non-treatment purposes return deny. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-all-normal | "all-normal", "opt-out" | PCF_IMPLICIT_ALL_NORMAL_SET | Permit All Authorized (opt-out baseline): permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA PurposeOfUse. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-break-glass-only | "break-glass-only" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BREAK_GLASS_ONLY_SET | Break-Glass Only: prohibits all uses except when odrl:purpose isA BTG (medical patient-safety override). | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-deny | "deny", "opt-in" | PCF_IMPLICIT_DENY_SET | Deny All (opt-in baseline): prohibits all odrl:use until an explicit active Consent permits access. | .

1322.title: 3. Decide — Three-Valued Evaluation, ITI-108 Reads, obtainConsent, and PROV Citations
1322.content: 3.1 decide() and evaluatePcfPolicy() (permit | deny | unknown) . decide(consentOrPolicy, req, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts evaluates a PcfDecisionRequest (actor, actorRoles, actorGroups, action, and scope / top-level purpose, dateTime, target, securityLabel, dataPeriod, author, encounter): . | Active explicit Consent governs: if one or more active, non-expired Consent resources (or translated PcfOdrlSets) are supplied, any deny across them returns "deny" (odrl:prohibit), any "permit" (with no "deny") returns "permit", and unresolved scope operands return "unknown". | Missing Scope Operand is "unknown", never "permit": if a rule constrains odrl:purpose, odrl:dateTime, pcf:securityLabel, target, or assignee and the request omits that dimension, evaluation yields "unknown". Under conflict: "odrl:perm" (such as a root deny with a Break-Glass permit exception), if the exception’s constraint is unresolved, evaluatePcfPolicy() returns "unknown" rather than prematurely denying before purpose is supplied. | Expired or absent Consent: . | If options.implicitPolicy is provided, decide() falls back to the configured implicit-policy Set (IHE PCF Vol 1 §1:53.2.2 & §1:53.4.2.5). | If no implicitPolicy is configured: an expired active Consent returns "deny", and an absent or non-active Consent returns "unknown" — never a silent "permit". | . | . 3.2 Reading consents via IHE ITI-108 (findAccessConsents) . findAccessConsents(query) and Iti108ConsentClient in fhir-harness/schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts implement the IHE ITI-108 (Find Access Consent, [ITI-108]) RESTful search transaction (GET <baseUrl>/Consent) as a Consent Consumer: . | Search parameters (buildIti108SearchUrl): patient / patient.identifier, status (defaults to "active"), actor, purpose, security-label, period, date, data, _profile, and _count. | Client-side validity filtering (evaluateConsentValidity / filterIti108Bundle): every Bundle.entry.resource of type Consent is verified against FhirConsentSchema. Entries whose status !== "active", whose patient does not match the queried patient, or whose provision.period is expired (end < now) or future-dated (start > now) are excluded from consents and recorded in ignored[] with a structured Iti108IgnoredReason ("not-active", "expired", "not-yet-valid", "patient-mismatch", "invalid-period", "invalid-consent"). | Third-state failure handling (status: "unknown"): network failures, DNS errors, request timeouts, non-2xx HTTP responses, malformed JSON, non-searchset payloads, or OperationOutcome errors return { status: "unknown", reason, detail } — never an empty consents: [] that a caller could mistake for “no consent on file”. When passing an ITI-108 result into decide(), check result.status === "unknown" first and propagate "unknown". | . 3.3 Fulfilling odrl:obtainConsent duties on DSAs via injected createPcfConsentEvaluator . cat-harness/schemas/content/odrl.ts holds no FHIR resource types or pcf:* keys. A Data Sharing Agreement (@type: "Agreement") carrying an { action: "odrl:obtainConsent" } duty evaluates consent through an injected consentEvaluator: createPcfConsentEvaluator(consents, options) callback from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts, which returns { verdict, consent: { id, versionId, uid } } to permits() / permitsWithConsent() / decideWithConsent(): . | DSA + no Consent (or unreachable ITI-108 registry) → "unknown": when odrl:obtainConsent is due and no active matching PCF Consent (or consent-verification record) is provided, permits() returns "unknown". | DSA + matching deny Consent (or expired Consent) → "deny": when the patient’s PCF Consent denies the requested actor, action, purpose, or target, the decision is "deny". | DSA + matching active permit Consent → "permit": when an active, in-period PCF Consent permits the request’s actor, action, purpose, and target (and any other DSA constraints and duties hold), permits() returns "permit". | . 3.3a Consent rules for agreements . Four rules govern consent-based agreements. Rules 2 and 4 are enforced here; rules 1 and 3 are authored in the agreement itself (the dsa document kind and its lifecycle process in folio-assistant-core). | Legal basis. An agreement carries odrl:obtainConsent only when consent is its legal basis. Agreements resting on treatment, public-health law or a research waiver carry no such duty, and this evaluator is never asked. | Version pinning. A Consent names the agreement’s fixed-version URL in R4 Consent.policy.uri. createPcfConsentEvaluator counts a Consent only when that URI equals the agreement’s version (the agreement policy’s uid, or agreementPolicyUri); consentsCitingAgreement() is the filter. An amendment that widens use is a new version URL, so the old Consent no longer counts. An amendment that narrows use needs no new consent: pass the agreement’s DCAT 3 version chain as agreementVersions (each version’s ODRL policy and its dcat:previousVersion), and an older Consent still counts while every step back to its version is a narrowing amendment. isNarrowingAmendment() decides that from the ODRL rules alone: every newer permission sits inside an older one (same or narrower action, same target and assignee, each older constraint matched by one at least as tight, each older duty kept), and every older prohibition and obligation remains. A widening step, a missing version or anything it cannot compare (such as inheritFrom) stops the walk, and new consent is needed. | Plain language. Every agreement that needs consent publishes a plain-language summary, hashed with the agreement. That summary is what the person consents to. | Scale. The jurisdiction picks one of PCF’s implicit default policies (opt-in or opt-out) and passes it as implicitPolicy. Registry reads may be cached: new Iti108ConsentClient(base, defaults, { ttlMs }). An entry ends at its TTL, at the earliest provision.period.end of its Consents, or when consentWithdrawn(id) is called for one of its Consents. | . 3.4 Citing Consent.id + Consent.meta.versionId in PROV-O decision records . Every consent-based access decision recorded in the hash-chained W3C PROV-O decision log (cat-harness/schemas/content/prov.ts, cat-harness-tools/src/workflow/prov-record.ts) must cite the exact Consent resource version used: . | Use extractConsentCitation(consent) / consentPolicyUid(consent) from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts to obtain { id, versionId, uid, status, patient, performer, policyUris }. | Include the translated consent policy uid (urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId>) in "cat-harness:underPolicy" on the prov:Activity decision record alongside the governing DSA Agreement uid, and record the Consent’s id and meta.versionId citation so any auditor can verify which version of the patient’s consent directive was in force when the decision hash (cat-harness:recordHash chained via cat-harness:previousHash) was computed. | . 3.5 One-way renderer: ODRL 2.2 Agreement to FHIR R5 Permission (output only) . HL7 FHIR R5 Permission (Trial Use) is output only: W3C ODRL 2.2 is the source of truth and nothing reads Permission back. schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts provides odrlAgreementToFhirR5Permission(agreement, options) and fhirR5PermissionToFsh(permission, options): . | FhirR5PermissionSchema and its required value-set code lists are built from hl7.fhir.r5.core#5.0.0’s StructureDefinition-Permission.json and CodeSystem-*.json (permission-status, permission-rule-combining, consent-provision-type, consent-data-meaning), so no field outside FHIR R5 Permission is ever invented. | Maps conflict (prohibit / perm) to combining (deny-overrides / permit-overrides); assigner to asserter; shared dateTime constraints to validity; the agreement’s fixed-version uid and dcterms:source to justification.evidence / justification.basis; permission / prohibition to rule.type (permit / deny); target to rule.data.resource; assignee, action (consentaction), and purpose (HL7 v3-ActReason PurposeOfUse) to rule.activity; and delete duty roughly to rule.limit (v3-ActCode#DELAU). | Every ODRL 2.2, DCAT 3, or SPDX term with no exact home in FHIR R5 Permission (including @type, profile, inheritFrom, spdx:checksum, isA, exclusive lt/gt bounds, elapsedTime, refinement, and duties or duty constraints) is returned explicitly in dropped: DroppedOdrlTerm[] rather than dropped silently. | .
