1324.title: Generic Personas
1324.content: . This page includes a depiction of end-users and related stakeholders as introduced in the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for Immunizations. The specific roles and demographic profile of the personas will vary depending on the setting, the generic personas are based on the WHO core competencies and credentials of different health worker personas. Illustrative examples of immunization user personas for individuals are included in the Better Immunization Data (BID) Initiative Product Vision. Targeted generic personas . The targeted personas for the Digital Adaptation Kit for Immunizations are health professionals operating in care settings that are able to provide the required essential interventions for immunization delivery. Their key competencies are defined in the following table. Table. Descriptions of key generic personas . | Occupational Title | Description | Alternate Names | ISCO Code | . | Health worker (HW) | Health workers facilitate education sessions, administer immunizations, provide counselling when needed, record vaccinations administered, record stock movements and compile, generate, and submit reports. | Nurse, registered nurse, practical nurse | 3221 Nursing associate professional | . | Community health worker | Community health workers provide health education, referral and follow-up, case management and basic preventive health care and home visiting services to specific communities. They provide support and assistance to clients by reminding them to get their vaccinations, responding to emergencies and reporting births. | Community health volunteer, village health worker, volunteer assistant, volunteer health worker, treatment supporter, health promoter | 3253 Worker, community: health | . | EPI Manager | Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) managers develop annual and multi-annual plans, immunization communication and mobilization, management of cold chain and vaccine logistics, monitoring, supervision and evaluation of immunization services, and coordination of EPI activities at the national and subnational levels. | Programme manager | 1342 Manager, health service | . Related personas . In addition to the targeted personas detailed in Table 2, there may be value in exploring other health worker occupational groups and stakeholders within the context of immunization services, such as caregiver or child. However, these were not identified as the central personas for the data and decision-support content. Additional related personas are listed in the Table 3 of the DAK. Table. Descriptions of related personas . | Occupational Title | Description | Different Names | ISCO Code | . | Caregiver | Mother, father, guardian, carer of the child, infant, elderly or disabled person. | Parent, guardian | N/A | . | Client | In the context of this document, a client is a person who intends to receive immunization services from the targeted health worker personas. A client who is 15 years of age or younger is considered a child. | Vaccinated person | N/A | . | Child | A client who is 15 years of age or younger and who intends to receive immunization services from the targeted health worker personas. | Infant, baby, client | N/A | . | System administrator | A systems administrator, or a dedicated electronic immunization registry (EIR) staff, supervises the operation and storage of electronic health records and makes sure the server functions properly to allow clients and staff to communicate with each other, coordinate their actions and take care of essential tasks. | IT manager, technical support, EIR staf | 2522 Administrator, IT systems | . | Clerical staff | A clerical staff assists in scheduling appointments, answers phone calls, greets clients, keeps/documents medical records and handles medical billing. | Registration clerk | 3252 Clerk, information: health | . Where each persona appears in the business processes . Each generic persona above, with the business processes whose swimlanes name it. A persona with no swimlane is listed too: that is a gap between the personas and the processes, not an omission here. | Persona | Business processes | . | Health worker (HW) | B. 1325.title: Placement — decide where it goes before you write it
1325.content: Skill placement: Establish where a new node belongs BEFORE you create it — which layer, which declared graph, which kind of node, and which of the two “stub” conventions applies. Read before adding a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision table, schema, tool or content object, and before writing any literal that names one folio. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . One question, answered before the first file exists: . Which layer owns this, which of its declared graphs does it go in, and what kind of node is it? . An agent that starts writing and works the answer out afterwards produces a node in the wrong repository, under a hardcoded path, named by a composed string. All three are silent: the tests pass, and the damage lands on the next consumer. This is a decision procedure. Four steps and a stop. Run it in order; the later steps are meaningless if an earlier one is a guess.

1326.title: Step 1 — which layer?
1326.content: folio-assistant is the platform, not the content. It holds skills, schemas, the pipeline and the MCP server an agent uses to author a folio — a paper, a WHO SMART Guideline, an IG — and the folio lives in a separate repository. Ask of the thing you are about to write: . Does this name, assume, or default to one folio? . A paper directory, a document title, a badge URL, an owner/repo, a Lake library prefix, a workflow filename, a simulator path, a licence block, a vocabulary, a constant with a subject-matter value. If the answer is yes, it does not belong in platform code. There are three destinations, not two, and collapsing the third is the common mistake: . | destination | what goes there | test | . | the platform | the mechanism, parameterised | the same code is correct for every folio | . | the folio’s tree | the subject matter itself | a reader of that folio would look for it | . | the folio’s config | the value the mechanism reads | it varies per folio but platform code needs it | . A value that varies per folio and is consumed by platform code is a config field — <name>.config.json, <name>.json, lakefile.toml — never a literal in a script and never a file the platform has to go and find. A Lake prefix, for example, is read from lakefile.toml, and left unprefixed when no lakefile names one, because a wrong namespace is worse than none. Do not infer the layer from the directory you are standing in. Read the declaration at the repository root, carrying name, stub and directories. basename($PWD) is not an identity — a repo cloned into a differently-named directory resolves to nothing, and reports no config rather than an error.

1327.title: Step 2 — which declared graph, and where does that layer put it?
1327.content: A node’s location is not a path you memorise. Every layer declares the directories it scans in <name>.json, and each entry names the kind of graph it holds — cat-harness (skills, roles, workflows, decisions, requirements, permissions), schemas, tools, qa, beans, folio and the rest. The vocabulary is open. | Ask for a skill, do not open a file. skill_list for what exists here, skill_fetch to load one, work_plan_prime for the work plan. With no MCP, resolve the graph from the declaration (readDeclaration in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) and read the directory it names. | In this repository the skills graph’s path is skills/. That is a fact about this layer, not a convention you may carry to another one. Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. | Overrides match on the entry’s id, never on its path. A layer that sites its knowledge graph elsewhere redeclares the same id with a different path. Matching on path makes two knowledge graphs out of one relocation, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | Declare only what exists. A declared-but-absent directory is worse than an undeclared one: every consumer scans nothing and reports a clean run over it. | . Full rules, inheritance order and the three read states: directory-conventions.md. The docs graph, and the filing question it answers . docs is an authorable destination like the others, and the one an agent most often forgets to consider when it derives a destination list: deriving the list is not enough if the derivation drops a declared graph. What goes there: a design-memory asset — something produced while BUILDING, rather than the thing built. kg-contribution-offer carries the one question that identifies the class and why fsh-guts is the tempting wrong answer (its content may be thrown away; a design record’s value is that it survives). WHOSE docs/ comes first, and it is Step 1’s question again. Detailed information, design and planning for a harness, feature or tool go into that harness’s docs/: docs is a declared graph, and the layer that owns the feature owns the record of why it is shaped that way. A feature’s reasoning filed in the wrong layer’s docs/ reads fine and is unreachable from the place that needs it. Then where inside it, which is this skill’s question and not kg-contribution-offer’s: . | the asset is | it files under | . | why a subsystem is shaped as it is — requirements, options, rulings | <instance>/docs/architecture/, with parent: Architecture in the front matter | . | options for a decision not yet taken, with what each costs | <instance>/docs/proposals/, kind: proposal, and a row in its index.md | . | what was FOUND — prior art, a survey, a measurement, a comparison — that informs a decision without proposing one | <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/, kind: research, and a row in its index.md | . | how a person does a task with it | <instance>/docs/guides/ | . | how to REACH a data source the content describes — endpoints, shapes, quirks | <instance>/docs/, beside the subject it serves | . | what a declared thing IS, generated from source | <instance>/docs/reference/ — never hand-edited | . Three rules that catch the usual mistakes: . | A design record is dated and says what it was true OF. It is history, so it carries the commit, PR or issue it describes. A record written in the present tense becomes a claim about today, and goes stale invisibly. | It states what it could NOT establish. A requirement referenced but never defined, a measurement not taken: named as such. A design record that reads complete when it is not is worse than a short one. | It is prose for a person, not instructions for an agent. If you find yourself writing “the agent SHALL”, it is a skill and it is in the wrong graph. | . The line between the two, stated as a test: . A skill carries what a competent practitioner needs IN ORDER TO DO the task. Anything beyond that is documentation. Background, derivations, options not taken, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls: real, worth keeping, and none of it needed to act. Both directions fail silently — a skill that swallows them makes every agent read a chapter to find a rule, and a rule filed in docs/ because it arrived with context is a rule skill_fetch will never serve. Inheritance . A layer inherits its dependencies’ directories and skills, deepest dependency first and root last so the root wins: declarationChain + resolveDirectories for directories, and resolveSkillDirs in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts for the cross-layer skill overlay. So a skill placed in the platform reaches a downstream folio through its declaration; never copy a skill into the folio, which mints a second copy free to drift.

1328.title: Step 3 — which KIND of node?
1328.content: The axes below are distinct. Ask the separating question; do not pattern-match on what the thing resembles. | you are about to write | ask | the two answers | . | a new content type | does it need different code, or only different rules? | different code → an adapter; only rules → a profile plus a subclass | . | something a participant is or does | must the performer know it, or may the participant do it? | know → a skill, on the lane’s role; do → a permission, on the actor | . | a participant | does it persist across processes, or is it a position inside one? | persists → an actor; a position → a role, which is the BPMN swimlane | . | a sequence of steps | does it have actors, activities and a control flow? | yes → BPMN under the workflows directory, not a Mermaid fence and not prose | . | a branch at a gateway | is the answer computed from facts, or chosen by a person? | computed → a DMN table plus a <cat-harness.processes:decision/> ref; chosen → an ordinary gateway | . | a durable fact for one agent | does it govern, or summarise what governs? | governs → a skill; summarises → a memory entry under the memory nodes | . | subject matter | would a reader of one folio look for it? | yes → the folio, as data — never the platform | . Adapter vs profile is the expensive one. Adapters (paper, dak) partition block kinds into disjoint namespaces, and adapterForKind — what QA-criterion scoping reads — must stay total and unambiguous. Profiles (document, paper) nest: every document kind is also a paper kind. Making document a third adapter would make adapterForKind ambiguous on every shared kind. Actor / role / skill / permission. One sentence carries the model — an actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Permissions stay on the actor: moving them onto Role, which looks right, conflicts wherever a permission is held by some but not all actors sharing a role. Resolution rules, how to bind a lane, and how to add a role: role-model.md. Do not re-derive them here. A .md under the cat-harness path that declares its own $schema is not a skill. The audit walks that directory recursively; declaration beats location, the same contract part-of: carries. Adding a graph typology is a registry change, not a new top-level directory. If nothing in the open vocabulary fits, that is a decision to hand over (Step 5), not one to settle by creating a folder.

1329.title: Step 4 — which stub? There are two, and they are unrelated
1329.content: This is the step most often skipped, because “stub” reads as one word. The agent-file stub — a pointer, never a home . AGENTS.md is the agent-generic source of truth. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are thin stubs whose entire content is a pointer to it; scripts/init-folio.ts writes all three for a new folio. | Never put guidance in a stub. It reaches one tool’s agents and nobody else, and the other two stubs are then quietly wrong. | And prefer not to put it in AGENTS.md either. That file’s own banner says it: it is a bootstrap pointer, and the discipline lives in the skills graph. A rule that exists only in AGENTS.md is not in the generated reference, not in the published skill docs, and not found by an agent that went looking for the skill first. | . So: new guidance is a skill. Add a pointer from AGENTS.md if it needs one, and register the skill in its package manifest. The artefact stub — resolve it, never compose it . The declaration carries stub, the filename stem of every artefact this layer publishes. artefactStub() is the one function that answers it (stub when declared, otherwise name), and renderingPath() / siteDir() derive the published paths from it: . <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld <base>/<name>/<stub>.json <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json <base>/<stub>/ docs/<stub>/ . The graph document is under the layer’s own directory, the host’s included: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document (instance-publication §”Which base an @id is minted against”). Compose nothing; resolve everything. A hand-written path such as /kg/ 404s, because the real path comes out of renderingPath. A naive guess is not merely fragile, it is wrong on real layers. WHO’s SMART Base IG publishes under a stub shorter than its repository name, so “the stub is the repo name” fails on the reference implementation the convention was modelled on. The declaration file itself is NOT stub-named: it is <name>.json, found by findDeclarationFile() matching a file’s stem to its own name. Everything it describes is named after the stub, because by the time you fetch those you have read the declaration that names them.

1330.title: Step 5 — when you cannot tell, stop and ask
1330.content: Placement has three states, like everything else here: determined, determined-empty (this layer genuinely has no such directory — a real answer), and could-not-determine. The third is never to be rendered as the first. Do not guess and do not pick the repository you happen to be standing in. A misplaced node is not a typo: it is a second copy of something, free to drift, that a later agent will find and believe. Hand the decision over the way interaction-modality.md §4.1 requires — context → options with what each costs → your recommendation, marked → what happens if they say nothing → the question. The test is one pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . Every identifier expanded on first use. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. I need to place <thing>, which <one sentence on what it does>. Two candidates: A. <instance/graph> — costs <what this makes harder, concretely> B. <instance/graph> — costs <…> Recommend B, because <the property that decides it>. If you say nothing I will do B and note it in the PR body. A or B? .

1331.title: The worked failure this skill exists to prevent
1331.content: A platform script that writes a whole README holding one folio’s title, badges and licence destroys the README of every other folio it runs in, because prose about a folio belongs to that folio. Every step above catches it: Step 1, the content names one folio; Step 2, a helper path is composed rather than resolved; Step 4, published paths are built by convention and checked against nothing. The pattern that replaces it: the folio owns the file; the platform owns the markers, and writes a section only where the README carries its marker pair (readme-sections).

1332.title: Checklist
1332.content: Before you create a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision, schema, tool or content object: . | Layer — platform, folio, or the folio’s config? Does anything in it name one folio? | Graph — which declared entry, resolved from <name>.json by id? Not a path you remember. | Kind — which side of the separating question in Step 3, and can you say why in one sentence? | Stub — if it is guidance, is it a skill rather than a stub or AGENTS.md? If it publishes, does every path come from artefactStub() / renderingPath()? | Registered — bun run cat skill:register (skill-registration), and bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts run, so the published mirror is not stale. | Could not determine? Stop. Ask in the Step 5 frame. Do not default to the repo you are in. | .

1334.title: The platform’s own gates — run what CI will run
1334.content: Skill platform-gates: bun test passing is not the gates passing. What to run before you push, why the list is derived from the CI workflow rather than written down, and what a *:check failure is actually telling you to do. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . One command: . bun run cat gates # the fast set bun run cat gates --all # plus the jobs that need a browser bun run cat gates:list # see them without running them . Run it before you push, not after CI tells you.

1335.title: The CI workflow is the list
1335.content: This skill does not list the gates, because a written list drifts from CI and a stale list reads as authoritative, so nobody checks it. bun run cat gates derives the set from .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml at the moment you run it, so a gate added to CI is in your next local sweep. package.json is not the authority: many of its check: scripts appear in no workflow, and running all of them would fail you on things CI does not gate. The workflow’s own comments name the scripts it deliberately excludes, with a reason beside each (for example check:ci-health is a report about main, not a gate on your diff). Read the reasons there.

1336.title: bun test green is not the gates green
1336.content: The test suite, tsc --noEmit and the *:check gates fail independently. One cause can also fail two gates at once. Run the gate set, not just the tests.

1337.title: …and the gates green is not the PUBLISHED PAGE green
1337.content: Gates read sources. A defect that exists only in a renderer’s output — for example markup that Kramdown escapes because a Liquid whitespace-strip joined two attributes — passes every gate. | Gate coverage is bounded by what a gate can look at. Ask what the gates read, not how many there are. | When your change alters a rendered page, build the page. The site build is not in the fast loop. check:escaped-markup asks one narrow version of “the output is well-formed”, and only in docs-site.yml, where _site/ exists. If the real build will not run locally (the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway; never substitute the thing under test. continual-progress §”A template is not a page” carries the discipline. | .

1338.title: …and a green gate is not a VERIFIED FACT
1338.content: A gate can see the artefact and still answer a different question from yours. A rule that lives only in prose has a compliance ceiling nobody measures. When you write a rule into prose, ask what would fail if somebody ignored it; if the answer is nothing, you have written a wish. The measurable form is a check, a schema field, or a test. A gate’s silence is bounded by its stated scope. check:stale-paths, for example, judges two shapes — an id adjacent to an arrow, and a numbered step under a path heading — and declines everything else. Prose that merely mentions a closed work item passes it while carrying the same defect. Likewise check:ci-health labels workflow files that produced no run unjudged, not green. Green over a narrow rule is worse than red, because red is examined; a gate that does not fire is indistinguishable from one that passed. Before quoting a tick as evidence: . What does this gate say it judges, and is my claim inside it? . Read the check’s own header — every one here states its scope and its declined cases — rather than inferring the scope from the fact that it ran.

1339.title: Fast versus full is job membership
1339.content: The split is read from the workflow at run time. | fast — the typescript job. No browser. This is the inner loop. | --all — adds the jobs that install Chromium. render:bpmn:check is there because bpmn-js renders through a browser, so it can pass locally only because a browser happened to be installed. | .

1340.title: Running “the gates that relate to my change” is not running the gates
1340.content: Pick the gate set by JOB MEMBERSHIP, never by which gates you judge relevant. bun run cat gates --all is the whole point of there being a command. A subset chosen by an author tests the author’s model of the change, and CI tests the change; they differ precisely where the bug is. gates --all takes minutes; a red CI run costs a push cycle. A verification names a tree . A verification names a TREE, not a branch. Anything edited after the run started is unverified, however green the run was. bun run cat gates reads the WORKING TREE, not the commit. An edit made while it runs leaves the change unverified, and can make the run report failures that were never in any commit. Nothing looks wrong when this happens: the run really passed, about a different tree from the one pushed. Run the gates after the last edit, not alongside it — if you edit while they run, the run is spent and needs doing again. A skill edit is the case most likely to produce this, because a skill body has two committed artefacts generated from it. A skill edit is three files: . | file | regenerate with | . | the body, skills/<pkg>/<name>.md | — you edit it | . | test/results/kg-qa/.../<name>.kg-qa.json | bun run cat kg:audit | . | docs/reference/skill-instructions/<name>.md | bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts | . The kg-qa row is a derived QA result whose record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch. While a committed copy exists, kg:audit:check compares against it, so regenerate it. bun run cat skill:register does all of it in one command. A minted term needs a gloss . termIri("X") MINTS a term, and a minted term needs a gloss. Adding a new @type or a new property in kg-export.ts is therefore a TWO-file change: the emitter, and schemas/content/vocabulary.ts (CLASS_GLOSSES for a type, PROPERTY_GLOSSES for a property). ns:check refuses the half done alone. This is a different gate from the export’s own undeclared-term report: one checks that the JSON-LD @context binds the term, the other checks that the namespace DEFINES it. Both must pass, and passing the first is not evidence about the second.

1341.title: What a *:check failure is telling you
1341.content: Most of these gates compare a committed artefact against what its generator would produce now. A red one almost never means “the artefact is wrong”. It means you changed an input and did not regenerate. So the fix is to run the generator and commit its output — never to hand-edit the artefact into agreement, which makes the next regeneration noisy and detaches the artefact from its source. QA gates have a different shape. A gate over the qa graph computes and judges: --check writes nothing, and fails only on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — the committed working copy, or --against <ref> on the qa-reports branch. A missing baseline is UNKNOWN, printed and never a pass, never a fail. The four judge states are ok (0), finding (1), unknown and error (2) — JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. A red one of THOSE is a real finding your change introduced; regenerating does not clear it, fixing the subject does. Which gates have this shape is in each script’s own docblock. Each *:check script has a generator beside it under the same stem; bun run cat gates:list shows the check, and the script it checks is named in the check’s own output when it fails.

1342.title: …and a green gate set is not a CLEAN RUN
1342.content: bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. gate-tree-mutation carries the two causes, the one command that tells them apart, and the question that settles the second: does the churning field describe the subject the artefact is about, or the run that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write.

1343.title: Three things this skill will not do for you
1343.content: It does not replace reading the failure. The runner names the failing command and the CI step it belongs to, so a local failure and a red PR are findable by the same string. Read what the gate printed. It does not tell you a gate is wrong. A gate whose purpose you cannot state gets “fixed” by being made to pass, which turns the check into decoration. Every gate in that workflow carries a comment saying what it catches; if you think one is wrong, that comment is what you are arguing with. It does not make --all optional before a push that touches a diagram. Anything under processes/ changes a rendered SVG, and the check for that is in the browser job.

1344.title: If bun run cat gates reports no gates
1344.content: It fails rather than exiting clean: an empty sweep that exits 0 is indistinguishable from a passing one. If you see that refusal, the workflow was renamed or restructured and the reader needs fixing — not the gate list.

1345.title: Related
1345.content: |   |   | . | .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml | the authority, with a comment per gate saying what it catches | . | scripts/gates.ts | the reader, and the vacuity guard | . | continual-progress | commit early, open the PR at the first commit — this is the step before the push | . | prepare-merge | the pre-merge recipe, which runs these plus content-type gates | . | ci-health | whether the workflows themselves are working — a different question | . | gate-tree-mutation | reading NOT clean — a green gate set over a tree a gate repaired | .

1347.title: pr-description — a PR body a first-time reader can follow
1347.content: Skill pr-description: Write or update a pull request’s description so that someone who has never seen the work can follow it: the problem, why it matters, how it was approached, what constrained it, the solution, how to use it, and what is not done. Read before opening a PR, before rewriting its body, and whenever the PR’s scope changes. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end .

1348.title: What a PR description is for
1348.content: The reader has not been here. A reviewer, the owner coming back a week later, or the next agent opens the PR cold. The description is the one place they can learn what the change is for, without the chat, the work item or the commit log. If they need any of those to follow it, it has failed. It is not a change log of commit titles turned into bullets (“fix fsh-index path”, “one file per key”): every line is true, and only the author can read it.

1349.title: The sections, in order
1349.content: | # | section | answers | test | . | 1 | The problem | what is wrong or missing today, concretely | a reader could explain it to a colleague without reading the code | . | 2 | Why it matters | who it hurts, and what it blocks | names a person, a process or a measured cost, not “improves quality” | . | 3 | The approach | the shape of the solution, and the alternatives set aside | says why THIS shape, not only what | . | 4 | Constraints | what the solution had to respect: owner rulings, invariants, things it must not change | each one is a reason a reviewer would otherwise ask “why not just…?” | . | 5 | The solution | what changed, grouped by idea, not by commit | a table or short list, at most one line per idea | . | 6 | How to use it | the commands, flags or pages a reader runs or opens | copy-pasteable, with prerequisites stated | . | 7 | What is not done | untested paths, known gaps, follow-ups | nothing a reviewer would be surprised by later | . | 8 | Status | the live checklist (continual-progress invariant 3) | CI state on the CURRENT head | . Scale it to the change. A one-file fix can be three short paragraphs: problem, fix, verified by. The order still holds, and so does “why”, because “why” is the section a reviewer cannot reconstruct from the diff. These are the questions opening-brief asks in chat before the work starts. The PR description is their durable form, updated with what the work found.

1350.title: Rules
1350.content: . | Expand every identifier on first use. Not “fixes wnhh” but “bean wnhh: SUSHI and the IG Publisher cannot run locally without packages.fhir.org”. Not “W7”, but “W7, the incremental rebuild”. | Every number carries its provenance: measured on which head, by which command, or carried from where. The table in opening-brief §”The four parts” applies unchanged. | Say what is not verified in its own section. Not as a hedge buried in a bullet. continual-progress §”What to do with the thing you could not verify” is the rule; this is where it goes. | A decision you hand the reader follows interaction-modality §4.1: context, then options, then a recommendation, then the question. The test is whether the reader can answer without opening anything. | Link, never paste. A long log, a full diff or a measurement table goes in a comment, a committed sidecar or a linked page. The description carries the conclusion and the link. | .

1351.title: Updating a PR: comments, not edits
1351.content: A reader who has already read the description must be able to trust that it still says what it said. A change they need to see goes where GitHub shows it as new, which is a comment: a push, a CI round, a review answered, a decision taken. Two exceptions are edited in the description itself: . | Status is updated in place. It has two parts, and both stay current: . | structured: the status checklist (continual-progress invariant 3), with the work item and its epic, each linked, and the CI state on the current head; | narrative: two or three sentences on where the work stands and what it waits on. | . | Scope changes are recorded, never overwritten. Keep the original problem and solution text. Add a dated entry under ## Scope history: what changed, why, who decided, and what it supersedes. Strike through (~~…~~) any original line it invalidates, instead of deleting it. A reader can then see both what was first proposed and what is being merged. | . Anything else, such as a better phrasing or a fact found later, goes in a comment.

1352.title: Cross-reference everything
1352.content: Every identifier is a link: . | thing | link to | . | work item | its file, beans/defs/<id>--<slug>.md, on the PR’s head branch | . | epic or milestone | the same, plus the work items dashboard at <site>/beans/ (for this repository, https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/beans/) | . | issue or PR | a full owner/repo#N link, never a bare #N across repositories | . | skill or process | its file, or its page under <site>/reference/ | . | a measurement | the committed sidecar or the CI run that produced it | . The dashboard has no per-bean deep link, because its epic scope lives only in page memory. A link opens the whole board, so link the work item’s file for the work item, and the dashboard for the overview.

1353.title: What never goes in it
1353.content: . | Credentials, tokens, internal hostnames, or anything outside the diff. The same rule as for PR templates. | Model identifiers. The footer carries the session link, not the model. | Chat shorthand that only the session understood: “per the 2y ruling”, “Q4”, “round 3”. Say what the ruling was. | .

1354.title: Worked example
1354.content: A PR adding an incremental-build library to the FHIR IG Publisher, before and after. | Before: “What’s in it”: twelve bullets, one per commit (“W1:”, “W2:”, “-fsh-users:”, …), then “Housekeeping”. Accurate, and unreadable to anyone who did not write it. | After: . | The problem: the Publisher is all-or-nothing, and what a build knew is thrown away. | Why it matters: folio-assistant needs a structured record of a build to detect staleness, review changes and eventually rebuild part of an IG. | The approach: a library on top of the Publisher, staged W1 to W7, with a table of what each stage adds and its state. | Constraints: the Publisher is not modified; an AST is a cache, never an authority; “cannot tell” means a full build. | How to use it: three commands. | What is not done: W7 has never run end to end, and a stray .pyc was committed. | . | .

1355.title: Relationship to other skills
1355.content: . | continual-progress owns the status checklist and the rule to open the PR at the first commit. This skill owns everything above that checklist. | opening-brief asks the same questions in chat before the work starts. The description answers them for a reader after it. | prepare-merge records gate results in the body, in the gate’s own terms, and adds them under Status. | issue-working: the issue holds the request and its sign-off, and the PR description links it in the first line rather than restating it. | .

1356.title: Staging links
1356.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: staging-review §”The deep-link rule”.

1358.title: /prepare-merge-auto — Autonomous merge pipeline
1358.content: Skill prepare-merge-auto: Full prepare-merge → resolve → merge pipeline. Coordinates with sibling PRs, resolves review comments, asks structured questions only when blocked, then hands the merge to the merge-to-main sub-process, which merges only on the owner’s authorisation. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . Runs the full /prepare-merge workflow PLUS: . | Sibling coordination (before starting) | Review-comment resolution (after reviews land) | Structured user questions (only when genuinely blocked) | Merge (after all comments resolved), through merge-to-main: “autonomous” covers the preparation, never the authorisation | .

1359.title: Workflow
1359.content: Phase 0: Sibling coordination . Before starting the merge pipeline, identify sibling change proposals (pull requests, PRs) whose scope overlaps this branch’s files: list the open ones with the list change proposals forge-operation Tool. For each sibling PR that touches the same files or content domain: . | Post a brief coordination comment: “Starting prepare-merge on # | ; touches . Review welcome if you'd like to check for conflicts before merge." | | Do NOT wait for responses — this is a courtesy notification, not a blocking request. | . Phase 1: /prepare-merge (steps 1–6) . Execute the full /prepare-merge skill (rebase, integrate, one-voice, build, final rebase, request reviews). All steps must succeed before proceeding. Phase 1b: Wait for reviews + status briefing . Wait for Copilot and Gemini reviews to land before proceeding. Do NOT skip ahead — the reviews are the input to Phase 2. Wait protocol (15-minute window): . | After requesting reviews in Phase 1, poll for Copilot’s check-run status every 30 seconds (up to 15 minutes) — the github Tool, read change proposal (check runs). Look for the copilot-pull-request-reviewer check run: . | "status": "queued" or "status": "in_progress" → reviewer has noticed the PR; keep polling every 30s | "status": "completed" → reviews are in, proceed immediately | No check run after 2 minutes → reviewer did not trigger for this file type (e.g. skill-only PRs with no code); proceed with 0 comments | . | For Gemini: check the PR’s issue comments with the read change proposal forge-operation Tool (comments). If a gemini-code-assist[bot] comment contains “daily quota limit”, note “Gemini: quota exhausted” and proceed without waiting further. | 15-minute hard cap: if neither reviewer has completed after 15 minutes, proceed with whatever comments have landed. Note “Copilot: timed out (15 min)” in the briefing. | . Once reviews arrive (or the 15-minute cap is reached), give the user a concise status briefing: . | PR identity: “#N — title” with clickable URL | Branch: branch-name → main | Scope: files changed, additions/deletions, commits | Review comments received: total count, by reviewer, with 1-line summary of each thread: ``` Review comments (5 total — Copilot: 3, Gemini: 2): . | [Copilot] line 42 engine.py — threshold mismatch | [Copilot] line 98 engine.py — unused variable | [Copilot] line 173 engine.py — spelling fix | [Gemini] line 15 table.md — missing citation | [Gemini] line 88 table.md — ambiguous wording ``` | . | Disposition plan: for each comment, state the planned action (accept / modify / reject / escalate) BEFORE making changes — so the user can redirect: Plan: accept 1,2,3; accept-with-modification 4; reject 5 (reason: standard term per §7a) . | CI status: green / failing / pending | . The user can reply with overrides (e.g. “reject 4”, “skip 2,3”). If no override within ~30 seconds, proceed with the stated plan. Phase 2: Resolve review comments . After the briefing (and any user overrides), triage each thread: . | Classification | Action | . | accept | Apply the suggested fix, commit, push. | . | accept-with-modification | Apply a modified version, commit with explanation. | . | reject-with-reason | Reply on the thread with the reason (e.g. “intentional — see §X”). | . | escalate | Cannot resolve autonomously — proceed to Phase 3. | . For each resolved thread, commit the fix with message: fix(PR #N): address <reviewer> thread r<id> — <1-line summary> . Push after each batch of resolutions. Phase 3: Structured user questions (only when blocked) . If any review comment requires a judgment call (ambiguous intent, architectural decision, multiple valid approaches), use AskUserQuestion with: . | Rich context per interaction-modality: . | Quote the exact comment + file path + line number | Show the current code vs proposed change (preview) | State trade-offs for each option | Default to multiSelect: true unless choices are mutually exclusive | Prefix with 🟡 | . | Batch questions — collect ALL blocked items into a single AskUserQuestion call (up to 4 questions) rather than asking one at a time. | . Phase 4: Merge . After all review comments are resolved (or the user has answered all escalated questions): . | Run bun run scripts/run-validate.ts content/<paper> one final time. | Run the merge-to-main sub-process (sdlc/processes/merge-to-main.bpmn). In order: read the head’s evidence live (CI per owed job on the head SHA, mergeability, review state and Claude Approvals where the repository runs it); a repository with no CI is none, never green; find the owner’s authorisation for THIS merge, and ask with the evidence when there is none; record it; then merge pinned to the head, with merge_method: "merge" unless told otherwise. Having invoked this skill is not the authorisation, and neither is a broad instruction such as “fix all issues until green”. | CRITICAL: DO NOT DELETE THE BRANCH EVER! If using the GitHub CLI, DO NOT pass --delete-branch. If using the GitHub API, ensure the branch is preserved. | Report the merge SHA + URL, and the authorisation it was made under. | . Phase 5: Post-merge coordination . After merge: . | Post a brief update on any sibling PRs that were notified in Phase 0: “PR # merged; updated on main. Please rebase if needed." | Unsubscribe from the merged PR’s activity. | .

1360.title: Error handling
1360.content: . | If /prepare-merge fails at any step, STOP and report the blocker. Do not request reviews on a broken branch. | If CI fails after pushing review fixes, investigate and fix before merging. | If the user doesn’t respond to Phase 3 questions within the session, leave the PR open with a summary comment listing the unresolved items. | .

1361.title: Anti-patterns
1361.content: . | Do NOT merge without resolving review comments (even if CI is green). | Do NOT merge without the owner’s authorisation for that merge, recorded (merge-to-main). Green CI is evidence, not permission. | Do NOT read “no checks” as “nothing red”. A PR with ZERO check runs renders identically to one whose checks have not started. Match the PR’s head_sha against the branch’s workflow-run list before calling it green, and re-run the workflows by dispatch when no run exists for that sha. Same rule, with the procedure, in prepare-merge.md §Guardrails; change one and change the other, because a rule kept in only one of the two is missed by agents following the other. | Do NOT squash unless the user explicitly says “squash”. | Do NOT skip sibling coordination — it prevents post-merge conflicts. | Do NOT ask trivial questions in Phase 3 — only genuinely ambiguous decisions warrant user input. | Do NOT delete the branch after merging — and not at any other time either, without explicit assent from the user or the repository owner. Same rule, same wording, in prepare-merge.md §Guardrails; change one and change the other. | .
