1404.title: quality-control
1404.content: Named by: DTH authoring . Skill id: quality-control · Package: content-lifecycle-ext · Named by draft-to-publication.bpmn here, and by the QC gates of processes in the layers built on this one — which bind it from above, so this skill names none of them. Apply the publication quality gates to an aggregate of QA output, and decide whether it clears.

1405.title: Inputs and outputs
1405.content: folio-assistant-core/schemas/skills/quality-control/: . | in — checkType (required), targetPath (required), checklistSections | out — overallResult, findings, checklistResults | .

1406.title: Two of the three lanes are human, and that is the design
1406.content: A QC gate is a decision, and the processes put it in a reviewer’s lane — QC reviewer, PR reviewer / QC reviewer — not the build’s. The build’s lane runs the checks; the reviewer’s lane rules on them. The qc-reviewer role holds qa-reporting as a permission, and qa-reporting is also held by ci-pipeline and ig-publisher-service. That a build system and a human share a permission is deliberate: emitting a QA report is mechanical, ruling on it is not. editing-hci-validation.bpmn marks Task_ReviewFindings and Gateway_EditorDecision relaxable="false": the editor seeing the findings, and the decision itself, are the gate.

1407.title: Compute the gate, do not assert it
1407.content: Where a gateway carries <cat-harness.processes:decision/>, pass the facts — e.g. { failCritical: 0, failMajor: 2 } from qa_sweep totals — and let the DMN table return the branch. workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome at such a gateway. decisions/draft-qa-gate.dmn is the table; dmn-authoring is how to change it.

1408.title: Severity is the gate’s vocabulary
1408.content: The corpus-wide convention, and what the tables read: . | critical — a broken reference: something names a thing that does not exist, and a consumer following it gets nothing. Blocks. | major — a missing join: intact, but a question has no answer. | minor — coverage. Has legitimate instances, so it must not gate; forcing a fake entry onto a real step is worse than the gap. | . unknown is never counted as a pass, and it is not promoted either — it counts at its own criterion’s severity: a check that did not run has not cleared.

1409.title: What to run
1409.content: qa_sweep for content, bun run cat kg:audit for the process/role/skill graph, and the content type’s own conformance validator where its layer provides one (for a FHIR IG, that layer’s validation skill). checklistSections narrows the pass; findings and checklistResults are what the reviewer reads — not overallResult alone, which is a summary of them rather than a substitute.

1411.title: RACI — involvement, over the graph that already exists
1411.content: Skill raci: RACI over this repository’s processes — who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each activity. Three declared edge kinds over the roles and BPMN activities that already exist, not a new party registry. Use it to work out involvement when a project is initiated, and to sketch its breakdown. Named by: Phase 1: Planning . The method is not in this file. It is the raci node in the methodology graph — methodologies/raci.md — which carries the four letters, the exactly-one-Accountable constraint, and what RACI is not for. This file carries how this platform applies it (methodology-adoption’s split): the method’s text lives once, so two skills quoting it cannot drift apart. Read the node first; everything here assumes it. R is already declared, and that is this platform’s contribution. A BPMN lane says who performs an activity; that IS Responsible, so the overlay does not restate it and declares only the other three: . | letter | where it comes from HERE | . | Responsible | read from the BPMN lane, never declared | . | Accountable | cat-harness.processes:raci, exactly one per activity, gated | . | Consulted | cat-harness.processes:raci | . | Informed | cat-harness.processes:raci | . <bpmn:task id="A_Entities" name="Identify entities"> <bpmn:extensionElements> <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="crdm-data-model"/> <cat-harness.processes:raci ref="business-analyst" involvement="accountable"/> <cat-harness.processes:raci ref="stakeholder" involvement="consulted"/> </bpmn:extensionElements> </bpmn:task> . bun run cat raci prints the chart across every declared process; bun run cat check:raci enforces the rule and is a gate.

1412.title: Why an overlay and not a registry
1412.content: RACI needs tasks and parties. This repository already declares both — BPMN activities under the declared workflow directories, and roles in scenarios/roles.json. RACI adds only the relation between them, and only three quarters of it. A RACI implemented as its own table of names would be a second answer to “who is the reviewer”, free to disagree with roles.json. Every letter names a ROLE, not an actor. role-model.md’s rule is that nothing IS a reviewer — somebody acts as one for the duration of a lane — and naming a concrete actor would bind a process to one participant. That holds for informed too, where the temptation to name a person is strongest.

1413.title: Exactly one Accountable — the method’s rule, ENFORCED here
1413.content: The constraint itself is the node’s; what this section adds is that check:raci fails on a breach rather than advising against one. Zero is also a breach, once an activity declares any RACI at all. An activity declaring nothing is n/a, because annotation is incremental: the gate is on what a diagram CLAIMS, never on how much it has claimed so far. That is the platform’s choice; RACI says nothing about partially annotated corpora. A role cannot be both accountable and consulted on one activity, and the gate enforces that too.

1414.title: Using it to initiate a project
1414.content: The chart is the second half. The first is a conversation, and the order matters: . | Enumerate the activities. From the BPMN if a process exists; from the breakdown if it does not. An activity nobody can name is a gap in the breakdown, not a gap in the chart — finding those is the point. | Ask who is Accountable, one activity at a time. Not a list: one question per row. The answer “the team” means the activity is not yet decomposed far enough, and that is the most valuable finding this produces. | Then Consulted, then Informed. In that order, because C is the expensive one — every name added is a round trip before the work can proceed — and a long C list is a signal to re-read step 2. | Read the columns, not the rows. A role that is C on everything is a bottleneck; a role that appears nowhere was not a stakeholder after all, and saying so is cheaper than discovering it late. | . The agent enumerates; the person decides. CRDM states this for stakeholder identification — “the BA knows the domain, the agent does not guess” — and it applies here with more force, because a wrong A is invisible until something goes wrong and somebody has to answer for it.

1415.title: What this is NOT — the platform’s half
1415.content: The method’s own refusals are in the node. These three are about the overlay, and each names the declaration RACI must not be mistaken for: . Not an approval mechanism. Gates are BPMN — a userTask in a lane, with the fulfilmentKindsForBpmnType rule that a system actor cannot fill one. Not permissions. What an actor may DO is an ODRL rule in policies/ (actions in skills/permissions/permissions.json), and cross-cuts roles. Being R for a task says who is expected to do it; performing it also needs a rule that permits perform-task there. Not a substitute for the lane. If the chart and the lane disagree about who performs something, the lane is right and the chart is stale — which is why R is read rather than declared.

1417.title: recommendation-extraction
1417.content: Skill recommendation-extraction: Extract the recommendations of an L1 source as L1 3.0 recommendation and remark nodes, then describe each one’s scenario: the persona (role) who acts on it, the business process they act in, and the user story, as smart-kg L2 user-scenario candidates that reuse the target guide’s own vocabulary. Read before extracting recommendations from a WHO guideline or position paper with no printed “Recommendation N” labels, before linking a recommendation to a DAK persona or process, and whenever a recommendation has to say who does it and where. Covers the hybrid extraction (mechanical candidates, agent structuring, verbatim and 100 % coverage gates), the reuse-first precedence for personas and processes, the WARNING format, and sign-off. Named by: Classify and code content, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: recommendation-extraction · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Follows dak-l1-library, which builds the library and the layout graph this extracts from. A recommendation that does not say who does it, and during what, cannot be implemented. This skill extracts each recommendation verbatim and records, per recommendation, the persona who acts on it, the business process they act in, and whether the guideline is clinical, public-health or health-system-strengthening, before any L2 asset is drawn. It reuses existing vocabulary and processes first, and warns when none fits.

1418.title: Input and output
1418.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: l1Sources, dak-l1-library’s output, and the targetGuide whose personas and processes the scenarios reuse first. | Out: l1Kg: per included source, its extractionPath (library/<bib>/l1-extraction/), sourceVersion, the recommendation, remark, practice and scenario-candidate counts, the coverage and every WARNING. Stages 3 (l2-dependency-choice), 4 and 5 take it as their l1Kg. | . As stage 2 of smart-guideline-end-to-end, a source is skipped only when it is already in a KG: its extraction directory exists, is declared, and is at the same source version (skipped: true). A library entry with no extraction still needs it, after bun run cat ingest and dak-l1-library’s generic-document layer have put it in library/. Skipping is per source.

1419.title: The two halves
1419.content: | half | produces | layer | schema | . | extraction | recommendation and remark nodes, verbatim — or, for implementation guidance, implementation-practice nodes | L1 | L1 3.0, smart-base/kg/src/l1.ts (KGRecommendation); implementation-practice is the l1-library extension, smart-base/kg/src/l1-library.ts (KGImplementationPractice); not smart-kg 1.0 | . | scenario | one user-scenario candidate per recommendation, joined to persona and business-process | L2 | smart-kg ontology/l2/l2.json, unchanged; smart-base UserScenario.fsh | . No L1 field carries the scenario: L1 holds what WHO says; who does it, and during which process, is adaptation, which is L2’s. Implementation guidance prints practices, not recommendations . A recommendation is a GRC-approved normative statement made by a guideline. A publication whose publicationType is implementation-guidance or methodology (a “how to” document, such as a digital transformation handbook with its own “Best practices” lists) makes no recommendations of its own (handbook for guideline development §1.9). What it prints as normative is an implementation-practice node, never a recommendation with a new kind code. | Record the type in the curation as publication.publicationType. With implementation-guidance or methodology, every as: recommendation decision emits an implementation-practice node at <publication>/implementation-practice/<key>, and the graph names l1-library.context.jsonld so the validator scopes L1 + the extension. | The class lives in smart-base/kg/src/l1-library.ts; l1.ts stays the L1 3.0 layer, unextended. | It carries identifier, statement (verbatim) and contentHash; no kind, direction, strength or certainty. A kind on such a decision is refused. | No remark. L1 3.0’s remark is minted under a recommendation, so a remark decision in such a publication is refused: exclude the sentence or make it its own practice. | smart-base/kg/src/validate.ts refuses a recommendation defined in an implementation-guidance or methodology publication. | The output graph is l1.json. | .

1420.title: Part 1 — extraction (hybrid)
1420.content: Candidates are mechanical, structure is the agent’s, and the gates are mechanical. | Ingest the source (see dak-l1-library steps 1–2): bun run cat ingest uploads/<doc_id>/<doc_id>.pdf --library <lib>. | Fast path — a guideline that prints labels. When the source prints Recommendation N: labels, bun run smart-base/scripts/extract-smart-kg-l1.ts --entry smart-base/library/<id> extracts them by label (it writes L1 1.0). A source with no labels, such as the measles position paper, takes the hybrid path below. | List the normative sentences. Run core’s l1-coverage with an empty capture list; every sentence carrying a marker (should, shall, must, recommend*, should not, may be given/administered/offered/…) comes back as unaccounted, with its page: . echo '[]' > captured.json bun run cat l1:coverage --text pages.json --captured captured.json --out candidates.json . --text is body text only, page-tagged; strip references and running headers first. | Structure them. The agent turns each candidate into an L1 3.0 recommendation (identifier, statement, kind, population, intervention, setting, …) or a remark (text, remarkType) attached by hasRemark: . | statement and text are verbatim: the printed words, line breaks joined, nothing else changed; | a sentence that is history, background or a manufacturer’s statement is proposed for exclusion (step 5), not forced into a node; | GRADE strength and certainty are set only where the source prints them; | every node is inferred, with a note and evidence (page and quote). | . | Gate: 100 % accounted for. Re-run with the captured statements and the exclusions: . bun run cat l1:coverage --text pages.json --captured captured.json \ --exclusions exclusions.json --out coverage.json . Exit 0 only at 100 %. An exclusion counts only with signedOffBy: an agent may propose one, only a person signs it, and the reason is one of background-fact, manufacturer-statement, editorial, research-question or duplicate-of:<id>. | Gate: the graph’s shape. Validate the L1 3.0 document with the Zod port: npx tsx src/validate.ts <graph.json> from smart-base/kg/. | . Part 1 as a tool: l1-recommendation-candidates . Steps 3–6 are the named skill recommendation-candidates, satisfied by the Tool smart-base/tools/l1-recommendation-candidates/, run twice around the agent’s judgement: . # 1. mechanical: the work list — every normative sentence, with hints; nothing decided bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-recommendation-candidates.ts --entry smart-base/library/<id> --out <dir> # 2. agent: write <dir>/curation.yaml (l1-recommendation-curation/v1), one decision per location # 3. mechanical: the gates, and the L1 3.0 graph bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-recommendation-candidates.ts --entry smart-base/library/<id> \ --curation <dir>/curation.yaml --out <dir> [--check] . The curation is the agent’s step. The script hints (licence-or-imprint, glossary-page, layout-fragment) and proposes the publication’s identity from the printed ISBN; it never decides. Per candidate location (p<page>:s<n>, l1-coverage’s own), the agent records one of: . | as | means | fields | . | recommendation | an L1 recommendation node | key; statement only to narrow a joined list to one bullet, or to join a split sentence; kind only where printed | . | remark | a remark of a recommendation, by hasRemark | of, remarkType | . | part-of | inside another recommendation’s statement | of | . | exclude | a PROPOSED exclusion, one of the fixed reasons | reason; signedOffBy is a person’s acting as l1-extraction-reviewer, never an agent’s | . Every decision carries a basis. A location may carry a list of recommendation decisions: the splitter reads a bulleted list as one sentence. It refuses a statement not printed in the entry (normalised), an override that neither contains nor is contained in its candidate, a location the entry does not hold, a reused key, and a remark of an undeclared key, then checks the graph with smart-base/kg/src/validate.ts. It writes recommendation-candidates.json (the work list), l1.json, exclusions.proposed.json, extraction-warnings.md and run-context.json. Who signs an exclusion. Each record in exclusions.proposed.json names its signer as a role-graph RoleRef (cat-harness-tools/schemas/process/role-graph.ts): "signerRole": {"role": "l1-extraction-reviewer"}, declared in smart-base/scenarios/roles.json (a person, inheriting the harness’s reviewer). It stays unsigned until a person in that role reads the sentence against the printed page and signs it in Lane_ExtractionReviewer of classify-and-code-content.bpmn, following classify-and-code-content and terminology-coding. Provenance. Each run of either tool writes a cat-harness folio-run-context/v1 (cat-harness-tools/schemas/sdlc/run-context.ts) as run-context.json beside its output: the platform commit, the mounts, the script and its hash, and the inputs’ hash basis, as pdf-ocr.py writes at ingest. The work list cites it by reference. --check ignores it, as it ignores generatedAt. Declare every output directory, in the same commit. Each --out directory in or beside a library (library/<entry>/l1-extraction/, a sibling such as library/l1-recommendation-scenarios/ that Part 2 writes, or l1-extractions/<entry>/) is declared in the instance’s <name>.json with "graphTypologies": ["l1-extraction"], one entry per directory, never a wildcard (smart-base’s l1-extraction-9789240116191-eng is the pattern). An undeclared one fails folio-assistant’s check:l1-complete, and with it the QA working copy, every test shard and gate reading it, and the staging build. When the entry lives in another instance’s library, hold the output at l1-extractions/<entry>/, never in a library/<entry>/ folder: that reads as a duplicate of the entry, which the library ingest refuses. Before staging, run bun run cat check:l1-complete in a folio-assistant checkout that mounts the instance at the commit being staged; it must exit 0.

1421.title: Part 2 — the scenario
1421.content: Its mechanical step is the named skill recommendation-scenarios (Tool l1-recommendation-scenarios). The shape: L2 nodes, reused unchanged . Per recommendation, one user-scenario (smart-base UserScenario: title, id, description, personas[]) joined by three edges smart-kg L2 already licenses: . recommendation implementedBy user-scenario user-scenario involves persona business-process realises user-scenario . The description is a user story: . As a <persona>, during <process>, I <act> so that <outcome>. Each link records its source, as an intake classifications entry does (cat-harness-tools/schemas/library/intake.ts): . | source | meaning | smart-kg derivation | . | declared | a person said so; names by | decided | . | context | the section the statement is printed under settles it | inferred | . | inferred | an agent’s reading of the statement | inferred | . and a status: candidate until a person reviews the entry. Reuse first, stop at the first hit . Persona, business-process and guideline-domain coding apply the terminology-coding methodology (backed by classify-and-code-content, the terminology-lookup Tool, and glossary-terms): . | what | 1st | 2nd | otherwise | . | persona | the target guide’s own personas | smart-base’s generic DAK.Persona.* (input/fsh/actors/, ISCO / CDHI) | a glossary candidate, and a WARNING | . | process | the target guide’s own processes | a domain process catalogue — none exists yet (smart-base-clinical holds no processes): report “catalogue absent” | could-not-determine, and a WARNING | . | domain | clinical | public-health | health-system-strengthening, per scenario, with its source |   |   | . Never invent a process. A process not in the guide is could-not-determine, and the warning says why: it is the evidence that the guide (or a catalogue) is missing one. Choose the persona who acts on the statement, not the one it is about: “Vaccine should be offered to travellers” is acted on by the health worker. A persona a guide’s description does not cover (an immunization DAK’s health worker treating measles) falls to the next rung rather than being stretched. Read the statement, not its section: “Countries should achieve ≥95 % coverage” sits under WHO position and is acted on through coverage analysis (IMMZ.I), while “MCVs should not be given to individuals with … severe immunosuppression” is a per-client check (IMMZ.D, IMMZ.D5). A national policy, schedule-design or programme decision is not a per-client process. Run it . | The vocabulary. For the target guide, read its business-processes.md and personas.md from a guide checkout; for the generic rung, read smart-base’s ActorDefinitions: . bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-scenario-vocabulary.ts --guide <guide checkout> --out guide-vocabulary.json bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-scenario-vocabulary.ts --fsh-actors <smart-base checkout>/input/fsh/actors --out smart-base-generic-personas.json . Each file records the repository, the commit, and the file and line of every entry. The guide’s name, namespace and repository come from the checkout’s <name>.json and sushi-config.yaml canonical. Persona ids are slug(title) where the guide prints none (as smart-kg kgid.mjs mints a persona IRI); process ids are the printed Process IDs. | The mapping (l1-scenario-mapping/v1, YAML), authored: per recommendation, its personas (an id, or a candidate term), its process (an id, or could-not-determine), act, outcome and domain, each with a source and a basis quoting the statement, the vocabulary row or the person’s ruling. | The candidates: . bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-recommendation-scenarios.ts \ --l1 <recommendations.yaml | l1-graph.json> --vocabulary guide-vocabulary.json \ --generic smart-base-generic-personas.json --mapping mapping.yaml --out <dir> [--check] . It writes scenario-candidates.l2.json (an L2 graph document) and scenario-warnings.md, and refuses: . | an id the vocabulary does not hold; | a recommendation with no mapping entry (coverage is 100 %); | a mapping entry for a recommendation the source does not hold; | a declared link that names nobody. | . | Tier 2. node tools/validate.mjs <l1-graph.json> scenario-candidates.l2.json in a smart-kg checkout; give it the L1 document too, or every implementedBy edge reads as dangling. | . The WARNING format . One line per warning, greppable, in the report and on stderr: . WARNING process-not-determined <key>: no <guide> process (<ids>) realises this; domain process catalogue absent. <basis> WARNING persona-glossary-candidate <key>: persona "<term>" is a glossary candidate — … <basis> . A warning is not a refusal: the run succeeds, and the warnings are the work list for whoever owns the guide’s processes or the glossary. Review and sign-off . Everything this skill writes is a candidate. A person reviews an entry and records it in the mapping (review: {by, at}); the run then marks that entry’s links reviewed. A person may also turn a link declared (with by). An agent never writes either. Part 1’s exclusions are signed only by a person acting as l1-extraction-reviewer.

1422.title: What smart-kg L2 could not hold
1422.content: user-scenario declares only id, title, description, sourceKind, source and resolutionStatus, and tier 2 refuses any other node property. So domain, each link’s linkSource and the reviewStatus go on the edges’ open properties; the act and outcome live only inside description.

1423.title: What it feeds, later
1423.content: The scenarios are the hinge to L2. Each realises edge names the process, and so the BPMN whose lane is the persona, a scenario will be drawn in; the recommendation’s conditions become DMN rules (for measles, the IMMZ.D2.DT.Measles.* and IMMZ.D5 tables); and the user story becomes a functional requirement (functional-requirement fulfilledBy persona). None of that is drawn here. could-not-determine scenarios have no process to draw into yet.

1424.title: The worked examples
1424.content: An ingested handbook, end to end. smart-base/l1-extractions/9789240116191-eng/ is the Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue (WHO, 2025; its sections are in who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/) run through both tools: 48 normative sentences. It is implementation guidance, so the curation took 22 implementation practices and proposed 30 exclusions (licence text, glossary definitions, background on SMART Guidelines, chapter checkpoints, and the definition of the data owner on page 26), each naming l1-extraction-reviewer as signer and none signed, so coverage reads 18/48 until a person signs them. The scenarios reuse the handbook’s own roles (data owner, custodian, steward, project manager, solution architect: 18 links), one generic DAK.Persona.DataManager, and 3 glossary candidates (the national regulatory authority, twice, and the master data governance group). The handbook prints no business process with an id and no health-system catalogue exists, so all 22 are could-not-determine: 26 warnings, one of them practice-implementedBy-unlicensed (smart-kg’s L2 licenses implementedBy from a recommendation only, so from a practice it is a proposal for L2). The test l1-recommendation-candidates.test.ts keeps it current. An authored L1, scenario half only. The 75 recommendations of the WHO measles position paper (WER 92(17), 2017), mapped against the immunization guide’s personas and processes, with the vocabulary, mapping, output and warnings, live in that guide’s library with the check that keeps them current: https://github.com/litlfred/smart-immunizations/tree/main/library/l1-recommendation-scenarios/measles. smart-base holds no guide’s example. The generic rung it was run with is smart-base/scripts/fixtures/l1-recommendation-scenarios/smart-base-generic-personas.json, shared with the handbook example. An authored L1 from pictures. When the source prints its recommendations only as images (a schedule poster, a slide deck), Part 1 finds nothing and the L1 is authored from the inspected image narratives and transcriptions of the rendered page. Its check is the step skill transcription-verbatim (Tool l1-transcription-verbatim): every statement verbatim in the narrative or transcription it names, every transcription word corroborated by the text layer unless listed under inspectionOnly with its basis. The Uganda schedule poster and UNEPI deck (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-immunizations-uganda/tree/main/library/l1-recommendation-scenarios/uganda) are the worked example.

1431.title: Related work: find it, sort it, ask
1431.content: Skill related-work-coordination: Before new work takes shape, find the work it touches. Search work items, issues and open PRs for relevance; categorize and summarize every hit; then ask the user whether and how to coordinate. Judgement decides the categories and the recommendation, and the user decides the coordination. Called by CRDM when a requirement is initiated or updated in chat, and by methodology adoption. Process: sdlc/processes/related-work.bpmn. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end .

1432.title: When
1432.content: . | CRDM: a requirement is initiated or updated in a human-agent chat. crdm-issue-linking.bpmn calls Process_RelatedWork before it scans for an issue to link. | Methodology adoption: methodology-from-source.bpmn calls it after ingesting the source. | Anywhere else a new piece of work is about to start and could collide with work in flight. | .

1433.title: Search (all three, every time)
1433.content: | where | how | why | . | work items | beans list --json, then match on titles and bodies; include recently completed work items | a completed work item is a decision already made | . | issues | the repository’s issues, open and closed | an open issue may already own the requirement | . | open PRs | the repository’s open pull requests | a PR touching the same files is the collision worth finding first | .

1434.title: Categorize and summarize (judgement)
1434.content: Every hit gets exactly one category and a one-line summary giving its state and why it is in that category: . | category | meaning | . | overlaps: coordinate | the same thing, or changes the same files or process; left alone, the two will collide | . | affected by | this work will change what that item sees or does | . | out of scope | related, but deliberately not part of this work; say why | . | unrelated | a false match; list it only if a reader might assume otherwise | . This is judgement, not keyword matching. A title match is a lead, and the body decides the category.

1435.title: Ask
1435.content: Put one question to the user, in the order context, then options, then recommendation (interaction-modality §4.1). Typical options: . | work in parallel and follow the other item’s conventions; | wait for it to land; | build on its branch; | note only. | . Recommend one of them. Do not link, block, merge or comment on another item before the answer. Coordinating is a commitment made on behalf of that item’s owners.

1436.title: Record
1436.content: . | Write the choice where it will be found: work item links (--blocked-by, --parent), a section in the issue or PR body, or “note only”. | A declined coordination is recorded too. | .

1438.title: Release epic planning
1438.content: Skill release-epic-planning: Plan and track releases using work item epics. Covers epic creation, story/task decomposition, release readiness tracking, and the relationship between epics and GitHub milestones. Applies to code releases, paper publications, and project milestones. Named by: DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring, Phase 1: Planning . A release epic groups all the work for a specific release version. This skill governs how to create, structure, and track them.

1439.title: Epic structure
1439.content: The work items hierarchy for a release: . epic: "Release v0.2.0" ├── feature: "CRDM Phase 4b prioritization" │ ├── task: "Add Phase 4b to crdm-requirements-workflow.md" │ └── task: "Update phase table" ├── feature: "Release lifecycle skills" │ ├── task: "Create release-lifecycle.md" │ ├── task: "Create code-review-process.md" │ └── task: "Create branch-freshness.md" └── bug: "Fix 7 BPMN isMarkerVisible attributes" └── task: "Add isMarkerVisible to 5 files" . Bean types in a release context . | Type | Role in release | Granularity | . | epic | The release itself | 1 per release | . | feature | A capability area / user story | 1 per feature | . | task | A single PR-sized implementation unit | 1 per PR | . | bug | A defect fix included in the release | 1 per fix | . | milestone | A session-scoped work container | Not release-scoped | . Creating the hierarchy . # 1. Create the release epic beans create "Release v0.2.0" --type epic # 2. Create features under it beans create "CRDM Phase 4b prioritization" --type feature beans update <feature-id> --parent <epic-id> # 3. Create tasks under features beans create "Add Phase 4b to workflow" --type task beans update <task-id> --parent <feature-id> . Always check before creating — beans create is not idempotent. See todo-manager.md §”Check before you create”.

1440.title: Ordering within a release
1440.content: Apply the Phase 4b formalize-first rule from crdm-requirements-workflow.md: . | Structural/organizational work first | Process/policy formalization second | Implementation third | Visualization/UI last | . Within the epic, number features by dependency order. The first feature completed should not depend on any later feature.

1441.title: Release readiness
1441.content: Tracking readiness . The work items visualizer (<base>/beans/) shows open work items grouped by epic. A release is ready when its epic shows 0 open work items. Readiness checklist . Before moving from draft to pre-release: . | All must-have features resolved (all child work items completed) | All should-have features either resolved or deferred to next release | CI green on main (bun run cat gates) | All changed BPMN diagrams re-rendered | All changed docs pages regenerated | Changelog written (see release-lifecycle.md) | BA has reviewed accumulated changes | . Deferring to next release . If a should-have or nice-to-have feature won’t make the release: . # Move the feature bean to the next release epic beans update <feature-id> --parent <next-epic-id> . Record the deferral reason in the work item body: . beans update <feature-id> --body-append "Deferred to v0.3.0: not blocking v0.2.0" .

1442.title: GitHub milestone integration (optional)
1442.content: A GitHub milestone can mirror the release epic for stakeholder visibility: . # Create milestone gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/milestones --method POST \ -f title="v0.2.0" -f description="Release v0.2.0" # Assign PRs to milestone gh pr edit <number> --milestone "v0.2.0" . The milestone’s completion percentage gives stakeholders a progress view without needing access to the work items store.

1443.title: Cross-domain applicability
1443.content: | Domain | Epic title | Features | . | Code | “Release v0.2.0” | Skills, schemas, pipeline changes | . | Paper | “Publication: Chapter 3 revision” | Section rewrites, figure updates | . | Project | “Deliverable: Phase 1 report” | Analysis sections, appendices | . The hierarchy and readiness tracking are identical.

1444.title: Rules
1444.content: . | One epic per release — if scope creeps, split the epic | Features are independently reviewable — each can be a PR | Tasks are PR-sized — one task, one PR, one review cycle | Never close an epic without BA approval — the epic is the release | Deferred features move to the next epic — they are not deleted | .

1448.title: Semver policy
1448.content: folio-assistant follows Semantic Versioning 2.0.0: . | Version part | When to bump | Examples | . | Major (X.0.0) | Breaking change to MCP tools, schema types, or public API. Requires downstream folios to update. | Rename a block kind, remove a pipeline stage | . | Minor (0.X.0) | New backward-compatible capability. New skills, tools, block kinds, BPMN workflows. | Add a skill, add a docs page | . | Patch (0.0.X) | Bug fix, typo, documentation correction, CI fix. No new capability. | Fix a BPMN marker, fix a broken link | .

1449.title: Release types and their gates
1449.content: | Type | Gate | Who decides | . | Draft | First PR for a planned release merges | Agent creates, BA approves | . | Pre-release (RC) | All must-have work items resolved, the full suite green on the candidate (§”The release gate”) | BA decides when to test | . | Named release | Stakeholder sign-off on the RC | BA + stakeholders | .

1450.title: The release gate: the full suite runs for a release
1450.content: Owner, card Q-CIB-4 A, 2026-11-08: “not all CI needs to run unless doing a release build”, “you can merge to main and not be release build”, “CI not gate on non-release merge to main”. So CI has three lanes, and only the last one gates: . | lane | what runs | gates? | where it shows | . | Pull request | the fast tier: types, lint, and the tests and gates the change can reach; no re-run of main | no: shown on the PR, advisory | a preview at branches/<slug>/, on request, and always for content PRs | . | main | the integration run: the full suite on main’s tip, batched (one run per repository per hour, not one per merge) | no: a red run files ONE fix issue naming the merges in its range | the staging root of the site, not the live root | . | Release | the full tier as an absolute gate: every test, every gate, derive:publish, e2e, the standalone measure, the index at released layer pins | yes: nothing publishes from a red release candidate | the live site, the registry, the GitHub release | . What makes a merge a release: the PR carries the release label (or merge:guard runs with --release). The guard’s check 5 then gates the merge on green owed CI, as it did for every merge before 2026-11-08. A release candidate is cut from main after that merge, and only a green candidate is published (package-release step 3). What does not change: content still needs the owner’s authorisation; committee content never merges; the WHO repositories are not changed without the owner; CodeQL keeps its schedule. Those are authorisation and security rules, not CI tiers. What it replaces: for non-release merges, main-green-first (card Q-CIB-1 B, 2026-11-08), the 2026-10-23 ruling that a layer PR merges only on a green index run, and “merge non-content when green” in the merge window rules. Rollout (phased, owner’s choice A): 1. these skills, the merge DMNs and merge:guard (check 5 advisory unless a release); 2. cat-harness-tools’ layer checks (PR fast tier, the hourly integration run, the release run); . | folio-assistant’s Code-quality gates, previews on request, the site’s staging root; 4. the other layers and the re-pin train. Until a phase lands, its workflows still run in full: they are simply no longer a merge gate. | .

1451.title: Release planning with epics

1452.title: Where code review sits
1452.content: Code review happens at the PR level (before merge to main). Release approval happens at the RC level (after many PRs merge). PR → code review → merge → accumulate in draft release ↓ draft → RC → stakeholder test → named release . See code-review-process for the review detail.

1458.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
1458.content: Skill render-kg-to-cdn: Render a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a publication root URL, and report a status and one message. The same step for a staging preview and for a release — only the root URL and the target differ. Names the target’s Tool, never its steps: GitHub Pages (gh-pages) is one Tool, and it carries its own subprocess. Named by: DTH authoring . Render the content of a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a given publication root URL, independent of staging or release, and report the status of the push with a message. GitHub Pages is one Tool for this general step. Drawn as render-kg-to-cdn.bpmn.

1459.title: Inputs and output
1459.content: | input | what | . | Knowledge Graph | a layer root — or a tree the caller has already rendered and verified | . | Subgraphs | optional: declared directory ids; absent means the whole graph | . | publication root URL | where the rendering is served | . | CDN target | which Tool performs the push — a Tool that satisfies: ["render-kg-to-cdn"] | . | output | what | . | status | pushed, not-pushed, or could-not-determine — a check that could not look is never pushed | . | message | one line, postable as it stands: what is live (a commit), where, and the QA result | .

1460.title: Staging and release are the same step
1460.content: A preview is this with a root under the release root; a release is this with the release root. What differs belongs to the caller: who may start it, what must be reviewed or verified first, what else lives on the same host and must survive the push. That is why feature-staging and docs-site-publish both call this process rather than restating it, and keep their own steps — the slug, the render log, restoring the open previews, the publication-manager alert — around the call.

1461.title: Name the Tool, not its steps
1461.content: The general process has one call activity, bound by the Tool: the activity names this skill, the Tool for the chosen target satisfies it, and the Tool lists its own subprocesses — the diagram of its steps (skills-and-tools, bpmn-processes). The general skill never lists them. | target | Tool | its subprocess | its message | . | GitHub Pages | gh-pages | bootstrap-tools processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn | the commit merged onto gh-pages + the QA of what is staged and what is served | . A target may need provisioning before it accepts a push; the Tool’s subprocess owns that. For GitHub Pages a gh-pages branch has to exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it, so the gh-pages subprocess creates it first — the general step does not. Another CDN is another Tool with its own subprocess, and nothing here changes. A CDN in front of an origin is a layer, not a publication host (kg-to-portal): the publication root URL stays the origin’s canonical one even when a CDN serves it.

1462.title: What this is not
1462.content: Not the verification of what a build produced — that is publish-verification, and it runs before a caller hands its tree over. Not the decision to release — the content layer’s publication step and release-lifecycle. This step renders, pushes, and says whether the push landed.

1464.title: Rendered impact — which rendered files a Change Set changes
1464.content: Skill rendered-impact: The list of rendered files a Change Set alters, and how a reviewer approves against it. Each renderer maps the input files a change touched to the rendered files of its site through its dependency cone, before any build; a build diff then confirms the prediction. Use when opening or reviewing a Change Set PR, when asked “which pages does this change”, when a prediction and a build disagree, or when adding a renderer. Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: rendered-impact · Package: sdlc-core . A Change Set’s PR is approved against what it does to the rendered site, not only against its source diff. A one-line FSH edit can re-render one page of 722 or all of them, and a reviewer cannot tell which from the diff. So every renderer answers one question, and the PR shows the answer.

1465.title: Scope
1465.content: . | Every renderer maps a list of changed input files to the list of changed rendered files, from its dependency cone. | The public-comment Change Set (changeset/1.0.0) is the Change Set for ANY folio change, and the rendered list is one of its fields. | The original stays in library/; a Change Set applies to the folio materialised in folio/, never to the library source. | .

1466.title: The contract: rendered-impact/v1
1466.content: Declared in cat-harness/schemas/ui/rendered-impact.ts. A renderer takes the changed input files and returns: . | field | says | . | files[] | each rendered file the change alters: path in the built site, change (changed, added, removed), role (content, data, index) and via, the chain that reached it | . | files[].anchors | for a page that assembles many units (a document page), the fragment ids the change alters; the review list links path#anchor | . | undetermined[] | each input the renderer could NOT place, with its reason, and scope: all when it can change any page | . | method | cone (predicted before a build) or build-diff (measured after one) | . Three rules, each one a refusal: . | Could-not-determine is never “no change”. An empty files with a non-empty undetermined is “not known”, and the PR says so in those words. A renderer that drops an input it cannot map is broken. | Index files are listed and marked, not dropped. The reviewer’s list (reviewList) leaves out role: index (search data, sitemaps, an artefact index) because review is of content, not indexes. The renderer marks the role; the reader filters. | A page whose bytes do not change can still change. An AST artefact page loads its resource in the browser, so the cone names the page AND its data file, and a build diff sees only the data file. That is unconfirmed, not a defect. | .

1467.title: Checking a prediction: the one comparison that matters
1467.content: comparePrediction(predicted, measured) sorts every file into three groups: . | missed: the build changed it, the cone did not predict it. A cone defect, never a pass. Report it on the PR and fix the renderer: the next Change Set relies on the same cone to tell the reviewer what to open. | confirmed: predicted and measured. | unconfirmed: predicted, not measured. Expected for content pages that load their data (rule 3). For anything else it means the cone is too wide: it is safe, but say so. | .

1468.title: The renderers today
1468.content: | renderer | maps | how | status | . | fhir-ig-pages | .fsh, .cql, input/pagecontent/*.md | fsh-cone forward cone → SUSHI’s fsh-index.json → AST artefact page + served JSON; a page → itself and every page that includes it | in the FHIR layer, documented with its AST tooling (skill_fetch ig-ast-delta) | . | document-site, public-comment-site, library-site | a block, a document/chapter/section manifest, media/*, the public-comment store, a file in a declared library entry or a folio review-anchors.json naming one (the entry’s Document view and doc.json; its structure.json also the library index) | loaded from the published changeset.json (each changed block’s label and file) and outline.json (the documents), never from source: a block lands on its document’s page, anchored at its label (anchors) — on a LAZY page (outline.json lazy) on its blocks/NNN.json chunk and index.hydrated.html instead, and a block added, removed, renamed or moved reshapes the shell and every chunk from its position on; a file no builder of the site reads is an input with no page: each builder in the folio’s build command exports siteReads (the folio; the comment store; every directory of a typology holding a kind it renders), and a file outside all of them, the submodules, .github/ and the root’s non-Markdown files reaches nothing — so beans/ reaches no page, while todos/, whose pages are rendered, still may. A step that exports no siteReads excludes nothing; never decide it from the layer’s declaration, which also declares what no builder reads | in the document layer, with the ChangeSet Tool | . | docs-site | any file | a file in the COMPOSED Jekyll tree (docsLayers, composedInstances) → its page (permalink, or .md → .html) or asset; an include → the pages that include it, transitively; _data → the pages and includes that read it; a layout, a THEME include (read from the installed theme; unreadable means every include) or an include nothing calls → any page; any page change → the search index; a file outside the tree → undetermined when the staging cone carries any directory, nothing when it reaches none | cat-harness-tools/scripts/docs-rendered-impact.ts | . | published-provenance | a mounted layer’s skill, process or schema (anything a generator renders) | the published root’s own record of what each page was generated from — the “Generated from <path>” note and data-src on the edit link — read back as source → pages; a new source has no page yet and an index names no source, so both stay for the QA diff | cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts (predictByProvenance) | . Two builds of one commit differ in every page by a ?v=<build time> cache-buster, so diffBuiltSites blanks BUILD_STAMPS before hashing; without that, every page reads as missed. A renderer’s command line belongs to the layer that owns it; this layer names none above it.

1469.title: In the review process
1469.content: content-change-review.bpmn: . | Produce: the staging build writes rendered-impact.json beside the preview and puts the review list in the PR comment. Each entry links to the preview and to main’s copy of the page. | Read: at Compare main vs staging, the reviewer opens every file on the review list, not only the pages the author mentions. Use before-after-preview for the pairs, and visual-diff for figures. | Measure: the staging job diffs its build against main’s published site (measure-rendered-impact.ts, before the banner goes on) and writes rendered-measured.json: what changed, and what the prediction MISSED. Only when that site was built from the PR’s base does it count (status: known); otherwise main’s own changes would read as misses (not-base). No published main site, no file: “not measured”, never “nothing missed”. The review page shows it under the list, as the PR comment does: a run started by dispatch finds its PR from the branch, so the comment is not lost when no pull_request event started the run. | Show: every docs-site preview also carries branches/<slug>/changes/ (cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts): the changed sources, with a re-pinned mount in index.lock.json expanded into the files its repository changed between the two pins (a re-pin handed to a renderer as one JSON line predicts nothing); the cone’s files and its undetermined inputs; and the build diffed against the site at the gh-pages root, its missed files listed as changed, not in the cone. That diff folds the preview’s base URL to the root’s, blanks BUILD_STAMPS and compares a page’s <main>, because a preview’s chrome differs on every page; a removed file is listed apart, by directory, since most are parts of the site the preview does not carry. The root records its build commit in build.json; a root not built from the PR’s base is said on the page, never read as this branch’s change. | Gate: review-coverage-gate.dmn reads three page counts beside the block counts, each with a status fact so an uncomputed count is never 0: . | unreviewedPages: review-list files nobody has reviewed at their current pin. A page is reviewed by a page: verdict, or block by block when every block anchored on it has a verdict; a data file goes with a reviewed page that shares its pin. | undeterminedInputs: inputs no renderer placed, until an input: verdict or waiver (with a reason) says somebody looked. | missedPages: measured but not predicted, until a page: verdict. | . A pin is the hash of the git blobs of the changed inputs on a file’s via (pinImpact), never the built bytes, which carry a per-build banner. An edit after review reopens exactly the pages it touched. The tag is in review-comments. | .

Decide that from what the layer declares, never from a list of names here. | Test it against a real build with comparePrediction: 0 missed is the bar. | .

1472.title: /repo-conversion — folio-assistant over a repo that already has a life
1472.content: Skill repo-conversion: Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Process: the content core’s processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn, Task_ScanRepo, Task_ChooseHarnessed and Task_ConfirmImport (both non-relaxable). Scanner: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts.

1473.title: 0. The one rule
1473.content: Scan, show, ask, then move — and never in any other order. The author’s repository is the thing of value; the scaffolding is replaceable. A wrong import is not fixed by a git checkout, because the author has to work out what the agent did. Task_ConfirmImport is marked relaxable="false" in the BPMN, and a content package may not declare it away.

1474.title: 1. Scan — read-only, and honest about its limits
1474.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts # human-readable report bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts --json # same, as facts . It walks the working tree (respecting .gitignore) and sorts what it finds into three buckets: . | bucket | means | typical | . | library | external source material — something somebody else wrote, that the folio will cite or ingest | PDFs, papers, scans, datasets, references/, papers/, sources/ | . | content | material authored here, that could become folio blocks | Markdown prose, docs/, notes/, drafts/, .tex | . | unclassified | it could not tell | everything else, and it is reported, not hidden | . unclassified is reported, never forced. A two-bucket scanner’s mistakes arrive as moved files; this one reports what it could not place, and the author disposes of it. The classification is by path convention and extension only. It does not read file contents or call a model, so the author can disagree with any row of it in one word. Outside-content candidate scanning — preserving evidence and refutations . In repositories with formal, analytical, or domain-specific content, crucial verification scripts, macros, and counterexamples often live outside the primary content tree (content/ or folio/); a conversion that carries only that tree drops the evidence that some claims are false. scan-repo-content.ts scans outside the content tree and classifies these artifacts into read-only candidate classifications (defined by the content-type layer’s conversion refinement skill), reporting source location, rationale, and linkStatus (linked when referenced by at least one content block, or unlinked when orphaned). Like the general scan, candidate scanning never writes, moves, or modifies files; it presents the candidates to the author and agent so decisions can be made before importing.

1475.title: 2. Show, then ask — three questions, all as selections
1475.content: Present the scan as counts and a handful of examples per bucket, never as a 1,400-line file list. Then three questions, each answerable by picking. Load interaction-modality first. Q1 — import at all? . | Import everything the scan found (recommended) | Import only the library bucket — sources now, prose later | Import nothing; just set up folio-assistant | Let me pick bucket by bucket | . Q2 — where does each group go? Only for groups the scan was not confident about, and only when Q1 was not “nothing”. Offer library/ vs content/ per directory, not per file (a per-file interrogation is the accessibility failure in interaction-modality §0). Q3 — leave in place, or reorganise? . | Leave everything where it is (recommended) — the folio references the files at their current paths. Nothing moves, every existing link still works, and the decision stays open. | Reorganise into library/ and content/ — tidier, and it rewrites paths. Offer this only on a clean working tree, do it in its own commit, and use git mv so history follows. | . Recommend leave in place by default: a broken relative link in somebody’s README is a defect.

1476.title: 2a. Markers — choose what the harness reads (declare, don’t slurp)
1476.content: A harness declares what it reads in a repository; it does not take all of its content. The principle is directory-conventions §”A marker declares what is read, and nothing else is”. The scan’s fourth section, markers, lists the content a harness COULD be told to read: a sushi-config.yaml (an IG: contentTypes.ig), a legacy dak.json (contentTypes.dak), .bpmn processes, a work items store, library/, uploads/, Lean (contentType: paper) and folio manifests (contentType: document). For each it gives the paths, whether it is already declared — declared, not-declared, or unknown when there is no readable index.config.json to ask — and the snippet that would declare it, with where it goes (index.config.json#contentTypes, or a local layer’s <name>.json#directories). Content types come from the registry (defaultContentTypes; an { indexSection } type is checked against contentTypes.<id>), directory facets are checked against the registered graph typologies, and only the evidence the registries cannot state is a short table in cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/content-markers.ts. Where each kind of content lives is directory-conventions. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers # the list bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers --json # same, as facts . A plain command: any agent host (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot) or a person at a shell runs it, with no MCP server. It writes nothing. Q0 — which of these should the harness read? (Task_ChooseHarnessed, non-relaxable). Ask it the interaction-modality way — the full question in the chat, then a tap card where the host has one, otherwise a numbered pick-list with its default stated. Never a typed reply. Offer only the markers that are not-declared (or unknown), one option each: . | None of these for now (the default) — nothing is declared; the scan can be run again any time | contentTypes.ig — sushi-config.yaml, input/fsh/, … (the FHIR IG) | directories: processes — processes/ (7 BPMN files) | Let me pick several — the same options as a multi-select | . The default declares nothing, and the agent never declares a marker the person did not pick. Declare exactly the picks — the scan’s suggestion snippet, at its suggestion.at — in the scaffolding commit, or in its own commit on a layer that already exists. After setup, too. The same question fits any layer at any time: “what else could this harness declare?” is --markers on the layer’s repository, then Q0. Rows already declared are shown for context and are not offered. A content type registered by a higher harness layer appears as a hint when that layer is not loaded, with a note saying where the type lives. Declaring a scoped content type is not a boolean flag: its include list states everything that layer’s readers will read, so confirm the list with the person and consult that layer’s build-pipeline skill for how additional paths are added later.

1477.title: 3. Dispatch the ingestion
1477.content: Ingestion proper is library/processes/document-ingestion.bpmn (and the content layer’s document-intake refinement skill when converting into a content folio). What this skill decides is how much parallelism, and it is a question for the author because it spends their tokens: . | scale | when | how | . | inline | under ~10 documents | do it here, no subagents | . | one agent | tens of documents, one kind | a single background agent, reporting per document | . | small swarm | hundreds, or several distinct kinds | dispatch-agent — 2–4 agents partitioned by directory, never by file count | . Partition by directory because a per-file partition puts two agents in the same manifest, and the conflicts cost more than the parallelism saves. Open one work item per ingestion front before dispatching — running the existence check in todo-manager.md §”Check before you create” first — so a session that dies mid-import leaves a plan behind rather than a half-full library/.

1478.title: 4. The conversion itself
1478.content: Once Q1–Q3 are answered, folio_init against the existing directory. It refuses rather than overwrites where a file is already present, which on this branch is the common case (README.md, .gitignore, a docs/). Read its report rather than assuming; the files it declined to write are the ones you now merge by hand: . | AGENTS.md — if one exists, merge; do not replace. It is the most valuable file in the repository for the next agent. | README.md — never replaced. readme-sections.ts only writes inside marker pairs the author has opted into, so offer to add markers rather than content. | .gitignore — append the folio entries; keep theirs. | . If the remote is empty, push main first. A repository with work locally can still have an empty remote, and GitHub makes the first branch pushed to an empty repository its default. Run init-folio or push main before any feature branch. If main has no harness yet, land a setup-only PR first. A fork or an existing repository whose main has no index.config.json and index.lock.json gives the full PR checks nothing to compare against: the base side fails before any test runs, and the PR’s own gates are skipped. So open one small PR with only what folio_init writes and the pins, merge it, and only then branch for content. Draft-tier checks never build the base, so this does not show until the content PR leaves draft. The setup-only PR has a Tool: instantiate-harness. It pins the harness and every layer it needs, mounts them, commits the setup on harness/<harness>, opens that PR, and renders the branch’s preview at gh-pages:branches/<branch>/. On a repository with nothing mounted yet, run it from a fresh clone of the tools layer: . git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools /tmp/cht echo "<where the author consented>" | bun run /tmp/cht/scripts/instantiate-harness.ts \ --repo . --harness <owner/repo> --consent-by <who> [--plan | --local] . The setup also writes .github/cat.ts and .github/mount-from-lock.sh and sets the root’s cat script to bun .github/cat.ts, so after the merge a fresh clone needs no mount step: the first bun run cat … mounts the layers. --plan prints the closure and every step and writes nothing; --local commits on the branch and pushes nothing. The harness’s own adoption steps are its checkout scripts instantiate:<harness> (files it declares, committed with the setup) and prepare:<harness> (what the site is built from, never committed). For an IG on a FHIR harness these declare contentTypes.ig and build the IG’s first AST. A harness built on this platform may add adoption steps of its own for its kind of repository, for example about CI that already publishes a site on every push. Ask skill_list for the skill governing that kind before calling the conversion done.

1479.title: 5. Publishing — provision gh-pages first; an overlay needs it too
1479.content: An overlay never reaches getting-started §5 by itself, so this section repeats the one step a publishing route cannot skip: provision gh-pages before GitHub Pages is switched on. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in getting-started.bpmn, on the shared path after scaffolding and before the Pages build, and it carries the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. The tool is pages-bootstrap: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts # reports `unprovisioned` (exit 3) and the exact command when gh-pages is absent bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision # pushes an orphan gh-pages: placeholder index.html + .nojekyll . --provision is idempotent and never forces a push, and nothing creates a remote branch without it. Then switch Pages on with Source: “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — the script prints the source it expects. When the repository’s publish workflow pushes gh-pages, “GitHub Actions” is the wrong source: the workflow would push a branch Pages was never told to serve. The same holds for an overlay that remote-mounts its dependencies. A mount brings layers in; it does not provision anything on the downstream’s remote.

1480.title: 6. Anti-patterns
1480.content: . | Moving a file before Q3 is answered. | Reporting a two-bucket classification. If unclassified is empty on a real repository, suspect the scanner rather than celebrate it. | A per-file confirmation loop. See §2. | Swarming a 12-document import. The dispatch overhead exceeds the work. | Replacing an existing AGENTS.md or README.md. Merge, or leave. | Treating the scan as ingestion. It reads; it never writes. Ingestion is a separate process with its own diagram and its own gate. | Switching Pages on before gh-pages exists, or choosing “GitHub Actions” for a workflow that pushes gh-pages. See §5. | Dropping outside-content math artifacts or unlinked audit refutations. Carrying only the primary content tree (content/ or folio/) drops outside proofs, computations, and refutations showing that some paper claims are false. See §1. | .

1482.title: User Scenarios
1482.content: . Component 3 in the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for Immunizations includes user scenarios, which are narratives that describe how the different personas may interact with each other. The user scenarios are only illustrative and are intended to give an idea of a typical workflow. How to interpret user scenarios . User scenarios can be helpful tools not only to better understand the context in which a digital tool would operate, but also for some insights into what key data elements would need to be recorded and accounted for in the database. Additionally, the context in which the tool would operate, illuminated by the user scenarios, provides insight into some functional and non-functional requirements that the system would also need. As examples, the scenarios identify: key data elements that need to be recorded and/or calculated; decision-support logic that can be automated in the system; key functional and non-functional requirements that should be included in the system, and adolescent-specific considerations that should be accounted for. 1486.title: Session context
1486.content: Skill session-context: What a state machine tracks across a session, as against one process instance. What the record carries, why actor is required and the rest are not, why the session’s view of a node is advisory, and what a sibling session reads it for. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . A session is one actor working, from the moment it picks up until it stops. A process instance is a token’s position in one diagram. They are not the same object and the difference is load-bearing: . A session starts before any instance, may open several, switches between them, and outlives each. A session with nothing open is the commonest state there is. Model the session as a field on an instance and the first process opened owns facts that belong to the actor — and the idle session, which is most of them, becomes unrepresentable. So it is its own record, referencing instances rather than containing them. Shape: schemas/sdlc/session-context.ts. Graph typology: session-state, layer state — a session writes its own record as it goes, which is exactly what content-context-and-state-graphs means by live state.

1487.title: The fields — read them off the schema, never off this page
1487.content: SessionContextSchema in schemas/sdlc/session-context.ts is authoritative. A field list in prose beside a Zod object is a second answer, wrong the first time somebody adds a field, so this page gives no field count; the sections below say what the main fields are for.

1488.title: actor is required, and it is the point of the record
1488.content: Every other field can be recovered by looking at the repository. Open instances are in the work item graph; claimed work items carry their own status; timestamps can be reconstructed from commits. WHO is acting cannot be derived from anything. The machine keeping the session cannot infer it, which is also why log-message takes actor. A sibling session needs to know who is answerable before it touches the same work item. It is a reference with a declared flag, not an ActorDefinition. An agent may act without a node under the actors graph, and requiring one would make the field unfillable in exactly the cold-start case the record is most useful for. The two facts — an id that resolves and a name nobody declared — are kept apart because a consumer acts differently on each: an audit can follow the first to a role and a permission set, and can only quote the second. And declared is written, not inferred at read time. A reader resolving it themselves gets a different answer than the writer did if the node was added or removed in between, and the record says what was true when the session acted.

1489.title: The rest of the fields, and what each is for
1489.content: | field | for | notes | . | id | naming this session | stable for its life | . | startedAt / updatedAt | telling a live session from an abandoned one | ISO-8601 UTC | . | open[] | which instances this session is inside | empty is normal, not a gap | . | claimed[] | which work items this session announced | by reference, never copied | . | waitingOn | why nothing is moving | what + since, together | . open empty is the normal state. An agent answering a question, reading, or deciding what to do next is in no process at all, and process-state calls that idle rather than broken. A record that treated empty as a defect would report every reading session as one. claimed is by reference because a claim announces rather than reserves. The work item is the authority on its own status (bean-coordination); a status copied here would be free to contradict it, and a sibling reading the copy would act on a claim that had already been released. waitingOn carries since or it carries nothing. A wait with no start cannot be told from abandoned work — the same argument bean-blocking makes for requiring an expiry. what is free text on purpose: a human answer, a CI run, a sibling’s PR is an open set no enum would survive.

1490.title: The session’s view of a node is ADVISORY
1490.content: open[].atNode is what the session believes. The instance wins. The instance is the authority on its own token; this can be stale by exactly one step — the gap between a step completing and the session noticing. It is recorded anyway for two reasons. The commonest question about a session (“what is it doing”) should not need a second file read. And a disagreement between the two is itself worth seeing: a session whose view has drifted from the instance is a session that lost track, which is one of the detectors process-state names for being out of process.

1491.title: Who reads it, and why it is parsed rather than trusted
1491.content: A sibling session, deciding whether a work item is genuinely being worked or was claimed by someone who stopped. A person, asking what is in flight. The session itself on resume, in a fresh container, where the alternative is starting a second session beside the one that already exists. The writer may be an LLM playing the part of a state machine, so the shape cannot be assumed from the writer’s care. parseSessionContext() parses at the boundary, which is what makes a non-deterministic writer safe to read from. The general rule: where a machine may be played rather than executed, the schema is the contract and the parse is where it is enforced.

1492.title: What this is NOT
1492.content: Not the work plan. A work item says what is being worked on and survives the session; this says who is working and where they are right now. Delete every session record and the plan is intact. Not a log. log-message records what an actor DID at a moment, append-only. This is the current position, overwritten as it moves. A log tells you how you got here; this tells you where you are. Not interaction preferences. cat-harness/memory/interaction.json holds how a person wants to be asked — durable, read at session start, never written by a process. That is context, and this is state: the two are on opposite sides of the layer line and must not be merged, however adjacent they look. Not a store yet. The kind is registered and the shape is defined; nothing writes one, so no directory is declared for it: a declared-but-empty directory makes a consumer scan nothing and report a clean run.

1494.title: Playing a state machine
1494.content: Skill session-state-machine: An agent PLAYING a state machine rather than an engine executing one. Where the non-determinism actually lives, why the diagram stays strict, the cat-harness.processes:judgement marker that makes a judgement point countable, and what the machine must never do on the actor’s behalf. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . An agent can play a non-deterministic state machine as a tool, managing state during a human and agentic discussion. The diagram is processes/process/session-state-machine.bpmn. It keeps a session’s context current across a discussion: establish who is acting, open the record, and on each turn decide whether anything changed.

1495.title: The non-determinism is in the TRANSITIONS, not the shape
1495.content: A machine whose shape were non-deterministic could not be drawn here. The interpreter supports nine BPMN element types and throws on the rest, on purpose: skipping an unrecognised element yields a process that runs, reports progress, and is silently not the process on the diagram. So the shape is strict and enumerable. What varies is which enabled branch the agent takes, and what it writes. An exclusive gateway carrying <cat-harness.processes:decision> is computed and workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome; one without it means the caller supplies the answer.

1496.title: Saying that a judgement is deliberate
1496.content: A gateway with no decision table can be two different things: . | somebody’s call, which no table can make, and | a table nobody has written yet. | . <cat-harness.processes:judgement reason="…"/> declares the first, with the same three rules as cat-harness.processes:no-skill on activities: the reason is required and a declaration without one does not load; it is refused on anything but an exclusive gateway; and it is refused alongside cat-harness.processes:decision, because a gateway claiming both that a table decides it and that a person does leaves a reader unable to tell which the author meant. Why this matters more than the activity case. A step with no skill is a documentation gap. A gateway with no table is a point where an LLM decides the branch — and how many of those there are, and which, is exactly the question the deterministic-to-agentic spectrum is about (deterministic-and-agentic), and a mechanism that cannot enumerate its own judgement points cannot answer it. check:workflow-refs prints the three-way split (computed, declared judgement, undeclared) from the models. Ask the checker, not this page. An undeclared gateway is a backlog entry rather than a defect: every gateway that predates the marker lands there, and a gate that failed on an un-annotated corpus would be turned off.

1497.title: What the machine must never do
1497.content: It claims nothing. No cat-harness.processes:bean appears anywhere in the diagram. The process RECORDS that an actor claimed a work item; it does not claim one. A machine that claimed on the actor’s behalf would make the claim’s owner unrecoverable — and a claim announces rather than reserves precisely so a reader can tell who announced it. It closes nothing but itself. A_CloseSession records that the actor stopped. It does not resolve work items or complete instances: those outlive the session by design, and a machine that tidied them away on exit would be asserting that work finished because somebody went away. It is advisory, not strict. An agent keeping its own session record must never be refused. A missing update is a gap in a record, not an unauthorised write — and the base content processes are the ones that gate.

1498.title: The two judgement points, and why each is safe to be one
1498.content: Gateway_ActorKnown — only the discussion says who is acting, and it rarely says so in a field. A table would need a name to read; this branch is the reading. Gateway_TurnEffect — whether a turn changed the session’s state is a reading of intent. “I might look at X later” and “start X” differ by nothing a table can key on. Both are safe to be judgement for the same reason, which will not hold everywhere: getting one wrong is recoverable. The next turn corrects it, and nothing downstream has been authorised in the meantime. Contrast the steps the base processes mark relaxable="false" — the editor seeing the findings, the decision, the write, the release authorisation — where a wrong branch authorises something that cannot be un-authorised. Recoverability is one candidate criterion for where judgement is admissible; whether it is the right one is open research (deterministic-and-agentic).

1499.title: Writing state a non-deterministic machine produced
1499.content: The record’s shape cannot be assumed from the writer’s care, because the writer is an LLM playing a part. parseSessionContext() parses at the boundary. Where a machine may be PLAYED rather than executed, the schema is the contract and the parse is where it is enforced — at the point the value crosses in.

1502.title: smart-base Toolchain
1502.content: Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: smart-base-tools · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines . Run WHO’s DAK toolchain from a smart-base checkout. Load it; never vendor it. smart-base/tools/ holds Tool nodes: declarations of what each upstream capability consumes, produces and satisfies, so a BPMN activity can bind it. A Tool node duplicates no code. The Python stays in WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base, which the DAK repositories’ GitHub Actions run in place; a copy here would be a second, drifting toolchain. Declare here, execute upstream, until the execution moves as one migration with a cutover (toolchain-ownership). strip_library_binaries.py and strip_library_content.py are not declared here: they are not DAK-shaped and belong to fhir-harness (smart-stack-layering).

1503.title: Before you start
1503.content: export SMART_BASE_HOME=/path/to/smart-base # default: /opt/smart-base python3 smart-base/scripts/smart-base-transform.py --check . --check exits non-zero and names what is missing. Without a checkout the skill degrades to skip — it does not report a clean run over a toolchain it never had.

1504.title: Transforms
1504.content: Both render an authored source artefact into a published representation (the extractors go the other way). # BPMN → FHIR Shorthand python3 smart-base/scripts/smart-base-transform.py bpmn2fsh <file.bpmn|dir> -o OUTDIR # DMN → HTML python3 smart-base/scripts/smart-base-transform.py dmn2html <file.dmn|dir> -o OUTDIR . Omit -o for a dry run that reports counts and writes nothing.

1505.title: Two things to expect
1505.content: bpmn2fhirfsh.xsl emits many files per input. Its output is an envelope, <files><file name="…">…</file>…</files>, and each entry is a separate artefact at the path the transform names. Measured on smart-dak-immz: 8 business processes → 313 files, one process alone accounting for 157. Paths collide across inputs. Those 313 land at only 201 distinct paths, because shared actors and near-duplicate processes name the same outputs. The runner counts and names every collision on stderr instead of overwriting silently. Decide for each whether it is a duplicate input to remove or two processes that legitimately contribute the same actor.

1506.title: What else is in there
1506.content: smart-base carries ~54 Python scripts: extractors (dd_extractor, dt_extractor, req_extractor, extractpr), generators (generate_jsonld_vocabularies, generate_*_schemas, dmn_questionnaire_generator), a translation subsystem, and IG build/CI orchestration. The two transforms above are wrapped, and extract_dak.py (which runs dd_extractor, req_extractor and dt_extractor) is declared as the Tool extract-dak. The IG build and CI scripts want no skill: GitHub Actions is their caller.
