1603.title: translations/ directory rules
1603.content: The translations/ directory contains only three file types: . | .pot — POT templates (extractable strings) | .po — PO translated strings | .ts — TranslationNode manifests (KG nodes) | . Do not put .md, .qa.json, or status.json files in translations/. Rendered output lives in docs/<locale>/; QA and status are properties of the TranslationNode manifest. A layer with no translations directory of its own is hosted. translationsHomeFor (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) puts its templates in the extracting harness’s translations/<locale>/<stub>/ — cat-harness/translations/<locale>/bootstrap/processes/*.pot for bootstrap’s three diagrams — rather than inside the layer, which holds no translation machinery. 1604.title: A layer that defines its own translator
1604.content: A layer built on this one may define its own translator actor and translation subsystem. Then the rule is load it; never vendor it: the subsystem is invoked from that layer’s checkout, not copied here, and that layer’s skills say how. This skill names no layer above it.

1605.title: IG Publisher i18n
1605.content: For FHIR IG folios, the IG Publisher’s own i18n system is used in parallel: . | i18n-default-lang in sushi-config.yaml — source language. | i18n-lang — target languages. | translation-sources — path to input/translations/{lang}/ containing per-resource .po files. | Run with -generation-off -validation-off flags for fast translation-only builds. | . The prose translation pipeline (this skill) and the FHIR resource translation pipeline (IG Publisher) are complementary and independent.

1606.title: Do not
1606.content: . | Do not manually add badge includes. docs-ui.js renders them automatically from front matter. The include it replaced is deleted, not deprecated — an include that still exists is one somebody adds back. | Do not publish a semantic-QA number a script cannot establish. A back-translation from this repo’s own PO map, or from a word-substitution table, scores the table rather than the translation — and a string with no back-translation at all scores 0 and reads as drift. If no independent back-translator has run, the criterion has no verdict, and saying so is the honest output. | Do not infer a locale from a directory name. docs/fr/index.md is French because it says lang: fr. A subtag match is wrong in both directions and neither failure announces itself — see The navbar filters by locale. | Do not add a graph typology for translated content. It is the same kind of thing as the page it translates, differing by a field the file declares. Translatability is a property of a FORMAT within a content type — schemas/library/translation-tools.ts and isTranslatable — not of a directory. | Do not leave a translated page in the static nav. nav_exclude: true is what keeps it out, and no amount of client-side work substitutes for it: the nav is built once, for every reader, before anybody has chosen a locale. | Do not put non-PO files in translations/. Only .pot, .po, and .ts manifests belong there. Rendered .md goes in docs/<locale>/. | Do not vendor SMART Base translation scripts. Load from checkout. | Do not translate math, labels, or code. Exclude in extraction. | Do not auto-sign-off. Official status requires a human. | Do not re-extract per locale. Templates are extracted once, merged to main in one source PR, and every locale starts from them. | Do not open a locale PR into the source branch, and do not push to a branch whose PR has merged. Each locale is its own PR to main. | Do not fix the source in a translation. Report it as one issue. | Do not edit a FHIR resource to translate it. Its terms go into the locale’s CodeSystem supplement. | Do not re-translate a term a lower layer fixes in the same subject area. Translate with the locale term base, and fix a violation where the term is fixed. A use in another subject area is enforced once an adjudicator rules it in sense; until then it is pending, not a violation. | Do not treat staleness as “wrong”. A stale translation is still useful; it just needs re-review. | Do not conflate FHIR resource translation with prose translation. They are different pipelines with different tooling. | Do not auto-remove staging previews. Require staging:cleanup label. | .

1607.title: Content-type-specific translation tools
1607.content: Each content type declares what formats it can translate and what scripts handle each format. The declaration belongs to the layer that OWNS the content type, under contentTranslations in its <instance>.json; schemas/library/translation-tools.ts collects every present layer’s profiles and refuses a content type declared twice. A module or diagram path in a profile resolves from the declaring layer, then down its needs chain. The profiles: . | Content type | Formats | RTL | . | document | Markdown | ✅ | . | paper | Markdown + LaTeX | — | . | dak (WHO L2) | Markdown + PlantUML + SVG + ArchiMate + Excel + BPMN | ✅ | . | ig (WHO L3) | Markdown + FSH + FHIR JSON | ✅ | . The generic pipeline (pot-extract.ts, po-inject.ts) handles Markdown. Adapter-specific tools extend it with format-specific extractors. The Python originals from SMART Base live in scripts/translation/ and are referenced in the registry. RTL support . Arabic (and Hebrew, Farsi, Urdu) pages are detected at load time by docs-ui.js and get dir="rtl" on <html>. The CSS in docs-ui.css provides smooth 0.4s transitions for sidebar and content layout: . | Sidebar slides to the right side | Content flows RTL | Mermaid diagrams and badges stay LTR | BPMN diagrams need re-rendering with translated labels | . Staging review . When presenting translated content for review, use the staging-review skill to provide before/after URL comparison tables. See schemas/sdlc/staging.ts for the StagingComparison schema.

1614.title: Upload naming — the name is normalised, not the link escaped
1614.content: Skill upload-naming: What an ingested file may be CALLED. Read before adding anything to an uploads or library graph, before writing a generator that links to one, and before “fixing” a broken link in a generated README. Covers which characters break what, why the name is normalised as well as the link escaped, how a sidecar stays paired with its source, and the one case the fixer refuses. Named by: DTH authoring . A file in an uploads or library graph is named by whoever uploaded it, and that name reaches a generated Markdown link. So the name is an interface, not a label. It is a library-core skill, beside uploads-watch and library-ingestion, because what an ingested file may be called is a question about acquiring and ingesting sources. bun run cat check:upload-names reports; check:upload-names:check gates; check:upload-names:fix renames with git mv.

1615.title: The rule
1615.content: A name may not contain any of . space , ( ) [ ] { } # ? & % ' " ` < > | . Everything else is left exactly as uploaded. The fixer replaces a run of those with a single -, trims, and preserves the extension and any sidecar suffix. A name with no unsafe character is returned untouched. Collapsing and trimming happen only to names that were going to change anyway; a double dash, a leading dash or a trailing dash is not this check’s business. Case is not a defect either: README.md stays README.md, because renaming it breaks every link to it and every generator that writes one. Rewriting a name that was already safe breaks whatever looks it up by that name, such as a generator that lists a section file. Both are pinned by tests.

1616.title: What each character breaks
1616.content: | character | what it breaks | . | space, (, ) | a Markdown link target ends at the first ) | . | [ ] | the label half of the link | . | < > \| | the angle-bracket link form, and tables | . | # ? | a fragment and a query to every URL parser | . | & % quotes backtick | escaping in a shell, an href, or both | . | , | nothing — included for the stub convention | .

1617.title: Why the NAME as well as the link
1617.content: uploads/X (2).pdf produces the link target X (2).pdf, which resolves to X (2. Two layers answer this, and neither subsumes the other: . | layer | reaches | fails when | . | linkTarget (in subgraph-readmes.ts) / decodeLinkTarget (in check-subgraphs.ts) | every generated README link, in every graph typology, including directory names | never — it percent-encodes every segment of what the generator writes (parentheses included, because an unbalanced one ends a CommonMark destination as surely as a space), and the check decodes before asking the filesystem | . | this check | uploads and library names, before anything links them | a name reaches something that is not that generator | . The encoder keeps generated READMEs valid. This check keeps a filename usable in a shell, an href, a CI log line, a curl, and any later generator. Escaping is per-generator; a name is per-file, so a name that is safe everywhere is safe once. A rename churns downstream references, and that is accepted: they are repaired, not abandoned. After a rename, repoint the hand-maintained path fields (files[].path in intake.json; container and assets[].path in *.extraction.json; provenance.source in catalogue records; file and source_file in structure.json and manifest.jsonld; hardcoded paths in tests and scripts). Leave a hand-authored wireframe alone: what it depicts is a design decision, not a consequence of the rename. Then regenerate in dependency order: library:graph → library:viz → library:readmes → readme:subgraphs, then skill:register. Out of order, a later writer stales an earlier one’s output, which reads exactly like a real failure. Build the old-name list for a reference sweep from git diff --name-status -M split on tabs (awk -F'\t'), not on whitespace: the filenames being renamed contain spaces. A sweep that finds nothing must be shown to have had something to look for.

1618.title: A sidecar suffix is not an extension
1618.content: X.pdf pairs with X.pdf.extraction.json. Two ways to break that: . | rename the source and not the sidecar → the extraction is orphaned | normalise the sidecar by a different rule than its source → same | . So the fixer strips the sidecar suffix first, normalises the remaining name by the one rule, and restores the suffix. The pair moves together by construction. The stem is normalised and the extension left alone, because a whole-filename slug destroys the extension (…(2).pdf → …-2-pdf).

1619.title: Findings are not the size of a rename
1619.content: The check reports only what is still unnormalised, so once part of the corpus has been renamed its count is the tail of the work, not its size. Measure a rename from git diff --name-status -M.

1620.title: The one case it refuses
1620.content: Two files that normalise to one name. The fixer reports the collision and renames neither: picking a winner silently destroys an upload, and an upload is somebody’s source material. Rename one by hand. That is deletion-requires-confirmation applied to a rename — a git mv that overwrites is a deletion with a friendlier name.

1621.title: What this does NOT cover
1621.content: . | Directory names. The check reads files; a directory with a space in it is not graded. | Content. It reads names and never opens a file, which is why it is harness-layer rather than folio-layer in the repo partition. | Whether a file should be there at all. That is ingestion’s question, not naming’s. | .

1623.title: Adopting an upstream version bump
1623.content: Skill upstream-version-adoption: Watch a pinned upstream dependency for a new release, and take a candidate version through impact analysis, an MVP build, review and a person’s adopt/hold/decline decision. Reusable per pin — the theme is the first tenant, not the only one. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . An unpinned dependency is an unreviewed commit from a stranger, merged on every build. A pinned one is a commitment that somebody has to revisit. This skill is the second half: what happens between upstream cut a release and we are running it. It implements two diagrams, and the diagram is the source of truth for ordering: . | Diagram | What it is | . | upstream-pin-watch.bpmn | The watcher. Scheduled, mechanical, ends at either “every pin is current” or “one tracking issue says which is not”. | . | upstream-version-adoption.bpmn | The reusable subprocess, entered once per stale pin. Scope → impact → MVP → review → decide. | . The second is called, not copied: calledElement="Process_UpstreamAdoption". Any pinned upstream dependency enters it the same way, and a new tenant is a registry row plus a call activity — never a second diagram that says the same thing in different words.

1624.title: The registry is the tenant list, and it does not hold the version
1624.content: upstream/upstream-pins.json — in this harness’s declared upstream/ directory — declares each pinned dependency, with each pinnedIn resolved against the harness root: the upstream repo, the file the pin literal actually lives in, the pattern that reads it, what of ours binds to it, and the commands that constitute its MVP. It deliberately does not store the pinned version. The version lives in exactly one place — site-chrome/_config.yml for the theme — and the registry says how to read it from there. A registry that carried its own copy would be a second answer to “what are we running”, free to disagree with the build. bun run cat check:upstream-pins reads the literal out of the declared file; a pattern that matches nothing is reported as an error, not as “no pin”. binds and mvp are the reason the registry exists at all rather than the check simply grepping for version strings. They are what turn impact analysis and MVP from words in a box into a list somebody can work through.

1625.title: 1 — Watch
1625.content: bun run cat check:upstream-pins, weekly from .github/workflows/upstream-pins.yml and on demand. For each row: read the pinned ref out of its declared file, list the upstream tags that match tagPattern, and compare. Exit codes, and the middle one is the point: . | Exit | Meaning | What the workflow does | . | 0 | every pin is at the newest matching release | closes the tracking issue if one is open | . | 1 | at least one pin is behind | opens one issue labelled upstream-pin, or edits the existing one | . | 2 | could not determine — upstream unreachable, pattern did not match | leaves the issue untouched and fails the job | . Three rules it inherits from check-ci-health.ts, and they are not optional: . | “Could not check” is never rendered as current. An unreachable upstream is exit 2, not exit 0. A watchdog that goes blind must not read as good news. | One issue, edited in place. An edit does not notify, so a pin that stays stale for months stays one unread item rather than many. | The job fails on exit 2, which makes this workflow itself red on the default branch, which check:ci-health reports. The watchdog is watched. | .

1626.title: 2 — Impact analysis
1626.content: Scope the delta first, and scope it to what reaches our output. The upstream changelog is the claim; the diff is the evidence. For a Jekyll theme that means _sass, _includes, _layouts and assets — a change to upstream’s own docs, CI or tests cannot reach us: . git -C <upstream-clone> diff --stat <pinned>..<candidate> -- _sass _includes _layouts assets . Then ask what of ours binds to it, from the row’s binds list. This is the half that a changelog cannot tell you, because upstream does not know what you reached into. For the theme it is concrete and small: site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js moves the theme’s own search markup into the action launcher, binding .search, #search-input and .search-label; site-chrome/assets/css/docs-ui.css overrides .side-bar, .site-header and .main-header; and three e2e specs assert the structure the theme emits. An upstream rename of any of those is not a build failure — it is a shipped feature that quietly stops working, which is the failure mode a pin exists to convert into a decision. Write the analysis down as the work item’s note before building anything. A candidate that touches nothing we bind to is a different conversation from one that renames a selector we depend on, and the reviewer needs to know which they are looking at before they look.

1627.title: 3 — MVP
1627.content: An MVP is a deployed build, not a description of one. Move the pin on a branch, let feature-staging.yml publish it under branches/<branch-slug>/, and run the row’s mvp commands. For the theme: . rm -rf _kg _site bun test # unit tests CI=1 bun run cat test:e2e # a11y, action tiles, sidebar panels, qa panel bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/site-links.ts --site ./_site # every navbar tile resolves in the BUILT site . site-links.ts checks the tiles against the real _site rather than against the attribute, which is what catches a tile that 404s. A red gate is evidence, not an exit. It does not end the process and it does not loop on its own — it goes to the reviewer with everything else, because “this version breaks us” is a finding the decider needs, not a reason to stop before they see it.

1628.title: 4 — Review
1628.content: Post the staging URL, the gate results and the impact analysis on the PR, then hand it over. The reviewer’s question is narrower than “is the new version good”: it is does anything in binds still hold, checked against the deployed page rather than against a screenshot. Findings the agent can fix — our overlay adapting to a renamed class, a test fixture updated to the markup the theme now emits — loop back into impact analysis on the same branch. Findings that are upstream’s behaviour rather than ours go to the decision as they are.

1629.title: 5 — Decide
1629.content: A person decides, and the diagram says so. PM_Decide is a bpmn:userTask in the publication manager’s lane, and that role admits person only, so activity-fulfilment-kind fails the moment somebody tries to make an agent the accepting party. It also carries <cat-harness.processes:policy relaxable="false"/>: no package may relax it. The lane is the publication manager’s rather than the editor’s because the pin is not a change to the corpus — it is a change to what the published artefact is built from, and that role is the one “accountable for what is live”. The gateway is not DMN-backed, and that is deliberate. Every other computed gateway in this repository reduces to arithmetic over tool output; this one weighs a rendering nobody can score against the cost of staying behind. A table here would look authoritative and would not be. Three outcomes: . | Adopt — move the pin, open the PR, and say in the body what the version range changed in rendered output. Record the evidence you used, not just the verdict. | Hold — record it as a block with an expiry and a revisit trigger (bean-blocking.md). A hold with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work, and the next watcher run will re-raise the same pin with no memory of why it was left. | Decline — record the reasons on the work item and scrap it. A scrapped work item is what stops the next agent re-entering the same dead end; a deleted one leaves them unable to tell a decision from an accident. | . In every case the decision is written down before the process ends. The work item is resolved from the terminal step, so a run that stops at “we looked and said no” is as finished as one that moved the pin.

1630.title: Adding a tenant
1630.content: . | Pin the literal wherever the tool reads it, with a comment saying which process governs moving it. | Add a row to upstream-pins.json: repo, pinnedIn, pattern, tagPattern, binds, mvp. | Run bun run cat check:upstream-pins and confirm it reads your pin back. A pattern that does not match is exit 2 — “could not determine” — and the row is not watched until it does. | . No diagram changes. That is what reusable means here.

1631.title: How to pick the pinned version when you first pin something
1631.content: Pin what is running, not what is newest. Those are different changes, and doing both at once means neither is reviewable — a regression cannot be attributed to the pin or to the bump. Establish what is running by fingerprint, not by assumption. For the theme that meant finding a declaration in the deployed CSS on gh-pages (text-wrap: balance, in _sass/navigation.scss) that entered upstream after the newest release, which proved the live site was tracking the default branch rather than any tag. The newest release at or below that point is the pin, and the PR states the residual delta — one CSS declaration — rather than claiming there is none. If no fingerprint discriminates, say so and pin the newest release anyway; an unverified pin is still strictly better than an unpinned dependency, and “could not determine” written down is worth more than a confident guess.

1633.title: Visual diff — see a figure change
1633.content: Skill visual-diff: Pictures of a changed figure, diagram or table, before and after, and how much of it changed. Says when to use it, what the percentage means and must NOT be read as, what a missing picture means, and how the staging job and the review process call it. Use when a reviewer asks “what does this figure look like now”, when a table’s markup diff is unreadable, or when a staging preview’s pictures are missing. Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: visual-diff · Package: sdlc-core . For a figure, a diagram, a table, an equation or a simulator, the change a reviewer must judge is how the block LOOKS. The Markdown or SVG diff of a recoloured bar chart is noise. So the staging job pictures each such block on both sides, and the review page shows the pictures. For a before/after of anything the staging job does not picture (page chrome, scroll behaviour, a PDF page, an IG page, a slide), and for the rules every reviewer-facing pair follows, see before-after-preview.

1634.title: Design rules
1634.content: . | A Skill and a Tool, built into the processes. The steps live in the folio-block-screenshots Tool and in this skill. The staging workflow and the review process CALL them; nobody copies them. | No new dependency. The pictures are taken with Playwright, which the platform already uses, and the comparison runs in Chromium’s own canvas, so nothing new needs a licence. | One key or one click; never a drag. The page offers four views as radio buttons, not a slider. | .

1635.title: What the reviewer sees
1635.content: On the review page, a visual block opens on “Pictures, before and after”. It shows: . | a sentence stating how much changed: “12.3% of the block’s pixels changed”, or “No pixel changed beyond anti-aliasing”, or “Only one side could be pictured”; | four views, each one click (or an arrow key): | . | view | shows | . | Changed pixels | the after picture faded to grey, with every changed pixel marked in magenta | . | Before | the block on the published site | . | After | the block on this preview | . | Both | before and after side by side | . When a build published no pictures, the block opens side by side (the live pages in frames) instead, because the page takes the first view that can run and lists the block’s kind.

1636.title: What the percentage means, and must NOT be read as
1636.content: | it is | it is not | . | the share of the block’s pixels, in the larger of the two pictures, that differ by more than a small tolerance (24 of 255 per channel, to absorb anti-aliasing) | whether the change is right. A one-pixel line through a chart can be the whole point | . | counted over the larger picture, so a block that grew counts the new area as changed | a measure of text change: a reworded caption moves many pixels | . | of the light theme only | a check of dark mode | . Zero means nothing changed that the eye would see. A block the ChangeSet lists as changed with 0% is still worth a look at its markup: the change may be in alt text, a label or a link.

1637.title: When a picture is missing
1637.content: A missing picture is said, never drawn blank: . | message | means | what to do | . | “Not on main: this block is new.” | an added block has no before | nothing: there is nothing to compare | . | “Its page is not in the published site” | the before side has no page for the block’s document | the document is new, or main was never published. A folio publishes main when its staging caller lists push to main; the build log warns when _main-site.json is absent | . | “Its anchor is not on the … page” | the page exists, but has no <a id="<label>"> for the block | the block was renamed without renamedFrom, or the build dropped it. Check the id-stable QA criterion | .

1638.title: How a picture is taken
1638.content: The site build writes an empty <a id="<label>"> before each labelled block. There is no element that wraps the block. So a block’s picture is the region from its anchor down to the next anchor, as wide as the anchor’s container. A page with anchors out of order pictures the wrong region, so if a picture looks wrong, check the anchors first.

1639.title: The Tool
1639.content: # how many blocks would be pictured (no browser needed) bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/scripts/block-screenshots.ts --changeset _site/changeset.json --count # picture and compare bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/scripts/block-screenshots.ts \ --changeset _site/changeset.json --base pages --head _site --out _site . It writes visual-diff.json (folio-visual-diff/v1) and visual/*.png next to the site. The review page reads ../visual-diff.json.

1640.title: Where it runs in the processes
1640.content: . | folio-staging.yml, step “Picture changed figures, diagrams and tables”. It runs after the step “Choose the before side”, which picks: . | main’s site, at the publish branch’s root, published by the same workflow’s publish-main job on every push to main; | for a stacked PR, its base branch’s preview, branches/<base-slug>/, so the pictures and the ChangeSet compare with the same branch. When the base has no preview, main’s site is used and the banner, the review page and the PR comment all say so. | . It installs Chromium only when --count is above zero. | publish-main (same workflow) deletes only files its own manifest, _main-site.json, lists. branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are never touched, and the first publish removes nothing. | content-change-review.bpmn, task Compare main vs staging. The reviewer’s comparison names this skill beside staging-review, so a reviewer handed that task is told the pictures exist. | .

1641.title: Tests
1641.content: . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/block-screenshots.test.ts: the pixel compare, the tolerance, a size change, block selection, and page paths (including .. being refused). | the tools layer’s test/block-screenshots.e2e.ts: the whole Tool in Chromium. It covers a recoloured block, an unchanged block, a new block, and a missing anchor. | the tools layer’s test/review-visual.e2e.ts: the renderer, keyboard only. | .

1643.title: Vocabulary authority — one fact, one home, N renderings
1643.content: Skill vocabulary-authority: One vocabulary is authoritative for one kind of fact, and every other is a derived rendering reached by a declared mapping. Which vocabulary owns what here, the pros and cons behind each ruling, how DC and SKOS overlap and what stops them drifting, and the normalisation-first rule for any modelling or mapping exercise. Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . Skill id: vocabulary-authority · Package: folio-core .

1644.title: The rule
1644.content: A fact has ONE authoritative vocabulary. Every other vocabulary that carries it is a RENDERING, reached by a declared mapping with stated equivalence — never a second copy of the fact. | the fact | authoritative | why not the others | . | what a term MEANS | SKOS | the only candidate here whose subject IS a meaning | . | a resource’s metadata | Dublin Core | a document has a title; a concept has a preferred label. Different subjects | . | a clinical code’s operational semantics | FHIR CodeSystem / ValueSet / ConceptMap | versioning, designations with a use, expansion-as-release. SKOS has none of these | . | a release of any of the above | DCAT (held, not built) | it is not a term model at all; it describes a published dataset | . ┌──────────────────────────────┐ AUTHORITATIVE ──▶ │ skos:Concept = the MEANING │ └───────────────┬──────────────┘ skos:exactMatch / closeMatch / broadMatch / relatedMatch │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ FHIR Code- Dublin Core schema.org TBX DCAT System (resource DefinedTerm termbase (release of (clinical metadata, (SEO / (CAT-tool any of these operations) bib records) discovery) exchange) as a dataset) . SKOS is the hub because its mapping properties exist for exactly this, and because it is the only one of the five whose subject is a meaning rather than an artefact, a record, or a distribution.

1645.title: Pros and cons, as ruled
1645.content: The reasons are measured against this corpus, not read off the specs. SKOS — adopted, authoritative for meaning . |   |   | . | Pro | Native JSON-LD. Multilingual labels first-class. notation is the code — TermGloss’s prefixed names. Mapping properties with stated equivalence. Carries the vocabulary terms and swimlane roles here | . | Con | No versioning model at all. No designation use. No post-coordination. Mapping properties carry no provenance | . The con is why convergence STOPS at SKOS. The failure this exists to prevent: reading “one glossary mechanism” as “one terminology mechanism” and binding an ICD-11 code to a skos:Concept with a notation and no version. That graph validates, publishes, and is wrong the next release. Dublin Core — kept, authoritative for resources . |   |   | . | Pro | ISO 15836. Qualified, repeatable and language-tagged as IRIS actually uses it — the content core’s schemas/dublin-core.ts is shaped by one measured record that does all three | . | Con | Two predicates overlap SKOS (below) | . schema.org — kept at 3 predicates; never a source of truth . |   |   | . | Pro | Search engines consume it. Native JSON-LD | . | Con | A publishing vocabulary, not a terminology one. DefinedTerm has name + description and stops: no versioning, no designation concept at all, no mapping semantics, no deprecation-with-successor | . It has no definitions to speak of. Used for 3 predicates (softwareVersion, codeRepository, text). Measuring usage: a naive grep for schema.org mostly matches json-schema.org (JSON Schema’s $schema keyword) and the schema:viz npm script. Never cite that count. TBX — not closed, and still not adopted . ISO 30042:2019 is published both as an ISO standard and as a free open industry standard; dialects and schemas are public. So “closed” is false and the ruling does not rest on it. |   |   | . | Pro | Genuinely open. Purpose-built for multilingual term entries | . | Con | Its niche is CAT-tool termbase interchange. This repo translates through gettext .po, not a termbase. XML-only | . Legitimate as an export if translators ever ask for a termbase. Rejected outright . SKOS-XL — it reifies labels to fix part of the designation gap and nothing else; the gap it does not fix is the one that matters. OWL — overkill: prose definitions, no reasoner in the pipeline. DCAT — held, for the render of whatever is landed on.

1646.title: DC ↔ SKOS: the overlap, and what stops the drift
1646.content: | pair | relation | . | dcterms:title ↔ skos:prefLabel | real overlap | . | dcterms:description ↔ skos:definition | real overlap | . | dcterms:subject → skos:Concept | not overlap — the designed JOIN. DC points at a concept | . | dcterms:hasPart, dcterms:source | no SKOS equivalent | . DC describes a RESOURCE. SKOS describes a CONCEPT. One object, one type, one naming predicate. They collide only where a node is genuinely both — such as the glossary document, which is a file and a skos:ConceptScheme, carrying both skos:prefLabel and dcterms:title. Two predicates for one fact, with nothing declaring which is authoritative, drift apart. The node is a concept scheme, so skos:prefLabel is the source and dcterms:title is the derived copy for resource-metadata consumers.

1647.title: Guidance for schema and data modelling
1647.content: . | Model in an open standard. Not a proprietary or house schema that happens to be convenient. | Proprietary input is mapped, not adopted. A mapping is a declared artefact with stated equivalence — not a rename in a loader. | Normalise FIRST. The first step of any mapping exercise is data normalisation. Mapping un-normalised data encodes the source’s accidents into the target and they are invisible afterwards. | The exercise runs as a defined process, not as a one-off script. | .

1648.title: Where the pins live
1648.content: cat-harness/external-schemas/ — one record per specification, pinning the edition and carrying the operative terms derived from the corpus, never hand-listed. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/external-schemas.ts --check. A vocabulary can be used in more than one syntax (a BPMN file, a JSON-LD @context); a usage check that reads only one reports the other as absent.

1649.content: . | schema-management — the registry’s own discipline. | terminology-management (the FHIR IG layer) — the FHIR half, for a folio’s clinical terminology. | The content core’s schemas/kg/external-schema.ts — the record contract, and why conforms / reads / cites are different answers. | .

1651.title: Voice authoring guidance
1651.content: Skill voice-authoring-guidance: Load the active voices’ rules BEFORE writing, so a block is drafted in the register it will be reviewed against. The authoring half of the voice overlay; voice-overlay-review is the half that runs after. Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end .

1652.title: Read the voices before the first sentence, not after the first review
1652.content: A voice is an editorial register — spelling, punctuation, terminology, how a normative statement is phrased. Get it right while drafting; correcting it afterwards means rewriting prose somebody has already reviewed. bun run cat check:voices # what this instance ships, and how many rules each carries . The active set is in the layer’s config, its index.config.json entry: . { "voices": { "active": ["milnor"] } } . An empty or absent list means no voice, and that is a real answer. The platform’s own documentation activates none. Do not add one because a voice exists.

1653.title: What to load, and what to do with it
1653.content: Each voice’s rules carry three things you need while writing: . | terminology — preferred/deprecated pairs. Apply these as you type; a terminology change ripples into every sentence built around the old word. | patterns — what the mechanical check will look for, i.e. which constructions will be questioned. | judgementOnly: true — no lexical check can decide it, so nobody will catch it for you. These are the rules to hold in mind rather than fix on a later pass. | .

1654.title: The rules most often broken by drafting on instinct
1654.content: The rules worth knowing in advance are the ones where instinct is wrong. For example, under the science layer’s milnor voice, “clearly” is fine in a mathematical block when it routes the reader away from a routine verification; do not write around it to appease the checker. This skill restates no voice’s rules: each rule belongs to the layer that derived it, with the publication, page and verbatim quote it was read from, and a copy here would lose that citation — and the uncited copy is the one a reader meets first and nothing can check. To learn which of your voices’ rules are counterintuitive, open the voices.

1655.title: When two active voices disagree
1655.content: Rules are unioned, not merged, and both stand. If honouring one would break the other, that is a finding for the author and not something to resolve silently in the prose — say which two rules and which voices, and let the editor decide. A silent choice hides a genuine conflict between two documents the folio has adopted.

1656.title: Do not
1656.content: . | Do not apply a voice the folio has not activated. An unasked-for register produces confident findings against prose never written to it. | Do not treat a voice as a substitute for the base house voice. Voices overlay one-voice-style-guide.md; they do not replace it. | Do not add a rule to a voice while drafting. A voice rule needs a citation that resolves (check:voices enforces it) — a rule you inferred from the prose you are writing is circular. | .

1658.title: Voice overlay review
1658.content: Skill voice-overlay-review: Review a block against the active voices’ rules and record the verdict on its QA sidecar. The human/agent half of the voice overlay; the mechanical half is whatever patterns and terminology a rule carries. Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring, SMART Guideline end to end .

1659.title: What you are reviewing, and against what
1659.content: One block, against the rules of the voices the folio has activated — not every voice it ships. The layer’s config (its index.config.json entry) holds the list; an empty list means there is nothing for this skill to do and that is a pass, not a gap. bun run cat check:voices # the voices, their rule counts, and that every citation resolves .

1660.title: The rule’s citation is the argument, so open it
1660.content: Every voice rule carries a source that resolves to a real file — a library/<doc>/sections/<section>.md for a rule read from an ingested document, or a path for a house standard. It also carries the quote the rule was read from. Open the citation before upholding a finding. | A reviewer who has read the source can say why the rule applies to this block. | The rule may be wrong. A rule derived from a document can misread it. If the quote does not support the rule, the rule is the defect and the work item goes against the voice, not against the block. | .

1661.title: Three outcomes, as with the house voice axis
1661.content: Identical to voice-editorial-review: . | The finding stands — the register is wrong for this block. Fix the prose. | The rule does not apply to this content — record it, and consider whether the rule needs appliesTo scoping on the voice. One scoping edit beats many per-block overrules. | The rule applies and this block is an exception — a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached and nothing is silently rewritten. | .

1662.title: A mechanical match is a question
1662.content: A pattern is a regex over text; it does not know what the block is about. Examples of non-defects it matches: . | voice-scholarly-default on documentation pages whose register is correctly second-person. | voice-editorializing on merely inside a comparative, where the contrast is the block’s claim. | voice-editorializing on clearly used as proof economy. | . Verify before upholding, and when a rule fires repeatedly across a corpus on the same non-defect, that is evidence about the RULE.

1663.title: Recording the verdict
1663.content: Voice findings go on the block’s QA sidecar like any other, through the same writer, so the icon and the published witness agree with what you decided: . bun run pipeline/qa-merge-findings.ts --file findings.json . insertAdjudication places your entry ahead of the script entry, because list[0] is a criterion’s effective verdict. The script’s entry is kept beneath yours, because the disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.

1664.title: Do not
1664.content: . | Do not uphold a finding you have not traced to its quote. A rule that misreads its source is the failure this design exists to prevent. | Do not review against a voice the folio has not activated. | Do not delete a script finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one returns with no record that anyone looked. | Do not resolve a conflict between two active voices in the prose. Both rules stand: name them and let the editor decide. | .

1666.title: /watch — background watcher with integration check
1666.content: Skill watch: Background-watch a branch (default origin/main) or a GitHub PR for new activity while you work, and on every event report whether to integrate / whether it conflicts with the current branch / whether it lets you simplify exposition / proofs / computations . Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . A unified watcher that handles branches (poll git ls-remote) and change proposals — pull requests, PRs — (subscribe to their activity through the session platform; subscribing is not a forge operation). On every event, walk the §3 integration checklist and either act, defer, or flag the user.

1667.title: Invocation
1667.content: The user’s request maps to one of three modes; pick the right one without asking: . | user phrase | mode | how | . | “watch main” / “watch upstream” / no target | branch:main | poll origin/main every 5 min | . | “watch PR 516” / “watch the PR” / “watch this PR” | pr:N | subscribe to its activity — the session platform’s subscription (event-driven) | . | “watch branch foo/bar” / “watch claude/x-y” | branch:foo/bar | poll origin/foo/bar every 5 min | . | “watch foo/bar PR 42” | pr:42 + maybe branch | subscribe + poll | . If ambiguous, default to branch:main.

1668.title: 1.  Stash the baseline
1668.content: Before arming anything, record the current state so the §3 review compares cleanly: . # Explicit refspec, ALWAYS. `git fetch origin <BRANCH>` writes FETCH_HEAD and # refreshes refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH> only when the clone's configured # refspec covers it — and exits 0 either way. A baseline read from a tracking # ref that was never updated is not a baseline. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null # Sanitize branch name for use in a file path: replace `/` with `_` # (e.g. `feature/foo` → `feature_foo`). Without this, branches with # slashes silently land in non-existent directory trees. SAFE_BRANCH=$(printf '%s' "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') git rev-parse "origin/<BRANCH>" > "/tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE_BRANCH}.sha" . For PR mode, instead capture the latest PR head SHA: read PR N with the read change proposal forge-operation Tool and stash its head commit SHA.

1669.title: 2.  Arm the watcher
1669.content: Branch mode — Monitor with poll loop . Use the Monitor tool, persistent: true, 5-minute poll: . Monitor: description: "origin/<BRANCH> new commits" persistent: true command: | BRANCH="<BRANCH>" last=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" | cut -f1) while true; do cur=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1) if [ -n "$cur" ] && [ "$cur" != "$last" ]; then git fetch origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null # one line per new commit, oldest first git log --reverse --oneline "$last..$cur" | head -20 last=$cur fi sleep 300 done . Each new commit becomes one notification line. PR mode — activity subscription . Subscribe to the PR’s activity through the session platform (in a Claude Code remote session, its PR-activity subscription). This is not a forge operation, so no forge Tool node offers it. Already event-driven — no polling needed. The harness delivers <github-webhook-activity> events for comments, CI status, reviews, and merges. See the existing PR-subscription guidance in the system prompt for handling.

1670.title: 3.  Per-event integration checklist
1670.content: For every notification (branch commit or PR event), run through these four questions in order — stop at the first “no” or “no action”: . Q1 — Should we integrate? . | Is the change on a file we touch in this branch? Quick check: git diff --name-only HEAD <NEW_SHA> -- $(git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD). | If yes and the change is small, rebase / pull now. | If yes but large, defer until the immediate task ships and add a TODO. | If no overlap, skip Q2/Q3/Q4 and acknowledge with a one-liner. | . Q2 — Does it conflict? . | Try a dry rebase in a fresh worktree. Use mktemp -d so the path is unique (avoids collisions with previous failed runs and with parallel /watch invocations) and clean up unconditionally via trap: . PROBE=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rebase-probe.XXXXXX) trap 'git worktree remove --force "$PROBE" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$PROBE"' EXIT git worktree add "$PROBE" HEAD >/dev/null ( cd "$PROBE" && git rebase "origin/<BRANCH>" ) status=$? # trap fires on EXIT . | Conflicts (status != 0) → first attempt auto-resolve for the recurring drift-conflict pattern (see §2a below); only flag the user if auto-resolve fails or the conflict is non-trivial (overlapping logic edits, schema rewrites, etc.). | . §2a — Auto-resolve drift-conflict pattern (CI-regenerated artifacts) . Some artifacts (*.witness.json sidecars, generated caches, derived reference files) are routinely regenerated by the CI validate job and frequently conflict on rebase against fast-moving main. These conflicts are always the same shape: our branch’s committed artifact was regenerated against an older main; main now has a fresher version. Resolution is mechanical: regenerate against current main and recommit. The recipe (run on the real branch, not the probe worktree): . # When `git rebase origin/<BRANCH>` halts with a regenerated artifact # in the conflict list, do NOT hand-merge the JSON. Instead: # 1. If the conflicting commit was a pure regen of these generated # artifacts (no other changes), skip it — main already has the regen: git diff --name-only --cached | grep -qE '\.witness\.json$' && \ ! git diff --name-only --cached | grep -vE '\.witness\.json$' && \ git rebase --skip # 2. Otherwise, abort the rebase, regenerate the artifacts # on the rebased branch, then re-rebase. This produces a clean # apply because the regenerated artifact now matches main. git rebase --abort git rebase origin/<BRANCH> # re-rebase, skipping bad commits as above # regenerate the affected artifacts via the project's generator(s), e.g. bun run cat regen git add <regenerated-artifact-paths> git commit -m "Regen generated artifacts post-rebase against latest main" git push --force-with-lease . Only flag the user if: . | The conflict is in a source file (.py, .lean, .ts, .md) — those are real semantic conflicts that need human judgment. | The conflict is in a generated artifact whose regenerated content differs substantively from a simple drift (e.g. a numerical value changed, not just a timestamp/hash) — that means a CI-run generator on main produced different output, which deserves a closer look before blindly accepting. | The auto-resolve recipe itself fails (regen script errors out, push rejected for non-fast-forward reasons, etc.). | . For generated artifacts specifically: if upstream regenerated files our branch also touched, prefer rebase-and-regenerate over hand-merging. Drift is structural; merging is fragile. Q3 — Can we reuse? . Apply four reuse questions: . | Definitions / lemmas / helpers / witnesses — does the new commit add something our branch is duplicating, paraphrasing, or reinventing? Replace with uses[] / a citation and delete the local stand-in. | Proofs — does a new lemma or tactic discharge a hypothesis, collapse a chain, or close a gap? Apply via the project’s proof-simplification / build-fix skills. | Exposition — does our .md re-derive what main now defines upstream? Replace with a forward-reference; route through the project’s accuracy / readability skills. | Computation — does a new script or witness supersede a hand-rolled loop or stale witness in our branch? Swap in and regenerate the artifact. (See §2a for the routine drift-conflict pattern.) . | When the upstream commit adds or modifies a prop: / thm: / lem: / cor: block (or its sibling formalization), delegate to the project’s compute-integration watcher to check whether the new claim is wired into the production compute chain. Capture the verdict here and feed it into Q4. | . | . Q3a — Did upstream land a new skill file? . For each main-refresh, check whether a skill directory the layer declares in its kg graph (skill_list names them) gained a new file between this branch’s prior baseline and the new origin/main: . git diff --name-only --diff-filter=A "$LAST_BASE..origin/main" -- <skill-dirs> . For each new skill file: . | Read its frontmatter — extract name, roles, description, and any inherits field. | Match against branch scope — does the skill’s description overlap with what this branch is doing? Heuristics: . | skill description mentions a file kind / domain / pattern that appears in this branch’s git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only, OR | skill is a new integration-watcher child (inherits: local/integration-watcher) and your branch is itself an integration-watcher PR, OR | skill is a content-block QA skill (e.g. one-voice-*, proof-*, compute-*) and your branch touches .md / .ts / .lean content blocks. | . | Surface to the user via AskUserQuestion with the standard 3-chip pattern: . New skill <name> landed on main: . <one-line description from frontmatter> . This branch’s scope overlaps because <one-line match rationale + file paths>. 1) Adopt now — invoke the skill on the relevant subset of this branch’s diff before continuing. 2) Defer to follow-up branch — record the decision and note for the next branch; don’t change this branch. 3) Not relevant — record so the watcher doesn’t re-prompt on future main-refreshes. | Record the decision as a note on the watcher’s work item (or in chat for the bare /watch flow) so subsequent main-refreshes don’t re-prompt for the same skill. | . This rule applies to skill files only. Skills landing on sibling PRs that haven’t merged yet do NOT trigger this check — only main commits count, mirroring the §2 “watch origin/main” scope. Q4 — Report or act? . | Acted (made the change): one-line summary + the new commit SHA. | Will act after current task: add a TODO with what + why. | Skipped: one-line reason (“no overlap”, “blocked on $TASK”). | .

1671.title: 4.  Stop the watcher
1671.content: Stop when the branch ships (PR merged, or you switch branches): . | Branch mode: call TaskStop on the Monitor task ID. | PR mode: the harness auto-unsubscribes when the PR merges/closes; otherwise unsubscribe through the session platform. | .

1672.title: 5.  Common upstream patterns (heuristics)
1672.content: . | Artifact drift: upstream regenerated generated artifacts (*.witness.json, caches) while we also modified them → rebase-and-regenerate, never hand-merge. | Toolchain version bumps: a dependency/toolchain hash changed → check our branch’s toolchain pin aligns before continuing a build. | Schema or generator changes: run bun run cat regen before continuing. | Routine review-cycle commits (Gemini/Copilot fixes on unrelated PRs): almost always Q1 = no overlap = skip with one-liner. | .

1673.title: 5b.  Monitor-timeout recovery (MANDATORY when re-arming)
1673.content: Background Monitors time out ([Monitor timed out — re-arm if needed]). Do not just re-arm and continue — between the last event and the timeout, main may have moved substantially. Mandatory steps on timeout-recovery: . # Compare the stashed baseline against the WATCHED BRANCH's actual head. # # This fetched `main` and then measured `origin/<BRANCH>` — a different ref # from the one it refreshed. The recovery step that exists to catch what was # missed while the watcher was down therefore compared the baseline against a # tracking ref nothing had updated, found them equal, and reported 0 missed # every time. Fetch the ref you are about to read, with an explicit refspec so # the tracking ref is actually written. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null SAFE=$(echo "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') LAST=$(cat /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha 2>/dev/null || echo "") CUR=$(git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH>) if [ "$LAST" != "$CUR" ]; then MISSED=$(git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" 2>/dev/null | wc -l) echo "MISSED $MISSED commits while watcher was down" git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" | head -10 # Update baseline AFTER reporting git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH> > /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha fi . If MISSED >= 5 OR any missed commit touches a file in your branch’s diff, run the §3 integration checklist on the missed range BEFORE arming a fresh monitor. This catches main moving many commits ahead during a long focused session while the watcher is timed out.

1674.title: 6.  Output style
1674.content: Follow interaction-modality: . | One sentence per commit / event by default | Numbered choices when integration is non-obvious | Run small fixes proactively; flag big ones | .

1676.title: Wireframe design review
1676.content: Skill wireframe-design-review: Design a user interface (a page, a visualiser, a navbar) by the WireGen methodology: a written design intent, at least two mid-fidelity HTML candidates, each with a web AND a mobile layout, mechanical checks at both viewports, a blind per-criterion review, adjudication where reviewers disagree, and a recorded choice. Also how an EXISTING visualiser is wireframed as-is, so that every declared visualiser has a wireframe with a QA sidecar. Process: processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn. Called for Design use from CRDM (Process_CRDM_Requirements, Call_Wireframe) whenever a requirement changes a rendered surface, before anything is built. Named by: DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 component edit and review, L2 DAK authoring, SMART Guideline end to end . Method: wiregen. Process: processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn.

1677.title: Where wireframes live
1677.content: | use | directory | . | As-is | <instance>/docs/wireframes/<topic>/, in the layer that declares the visualiser: cat-harness/docs/wireframes/<topic>/ for this harness’s own pages, and a content layer’s own docs/wireframes/<topic>/ for a page it declares | . | Design, from a CRDM request | docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/, beside the request’s proposal docs/proposals/<slug>.md: the candidates are assets of the proposal. When the proposal is filed (git mv to docs/requirements/, crdm-requirements-workflow), its asset directory moves with it in the same commit. | . Either directory holds: . | intent.md | one HTML file per candidate | authors.json, which reviewers are not shown | checks/: screenshots and the checker’s report | reviews/: one file per reviewer | . Each layer’s docs/wireframes/index.json maps the visualiser refs that layer declares to the wireframe that covers each. bun run cat check:wireframes reads every such index in the checkout, writes the QA sidecar (test/results/wireframes.qa-results.json) and fails on any gap. A wireframe sits with its page because an index naming another layer’s page reads as an undeclared ref wherever that layer is not mounted; another layer’s wireframes are reported as <instance>/<topic>.

1678.title: Input and output
1678.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: the use (design or as-is), the topic (for CRDM, the proposal slug), the surface, and, from CRDM, the requirements that change it, the proposal path, the humanReviewer (requester or BA), the channels the candidates are shown in, and the branch. | Out — the renderings: assetDir, intent, and one candidates[] entry per candidate: its source HTML path, its screenshots.web and screenshots.mobile paths (from wireframe-check), their staging deep links, its per-criterion entries, and its outcome with the reason. chosen names the candidate, who chose it and the comment that records it; it is absent until a person chooses. | Out — as changed assets: changedAssets[] lists every wireframe file the branch adds, changes or removes (candidate HTML, screenshots, intent, reviews) in the record shape a staging preview’s graph carries (change, kind, title, before, after, source, pages or pagesUnknown; ChangedAsset in cat-harness-tools scripts/kg-changed-assets.ts). The review therefore lists the drawings the same way it lists every other changed asset. | Out — staging links: stagingLinks, the shape every request for feedback carries (staging-review), copied inline as definitions.stagingLinks. | .

1679.title: Two uses
1679.content: | use | candidates | review | . | Design: a new or changed UI | at least two, compared blind | per-criterion, then adjudication, then options analysis | . | As-is: an existing visualiser, drawn as it renders on main | exactly one, marked as-is | the same criteria. A finding becomes a work item against the visualiser, not a redesign | .

1680.title: 1. Intent
1680.content: A few sentences: who the screen is for, what they need to do, and what it must show. For an as-is wireframe, the intent is read off the visualiser’s own declaration and generator, not invented.

1681.title: 2. Candidates
1681.content: . | Mid-fidelity HTML: monochrome, real content from the graph it shows, semantic icons, and no placeholder text. | Web and mobile in every candidate, through responsive CSS or two layouts. A candidate with one layout does not enter review. | .

1682.title: 3. Mechanical checks (wireframe-viewport-check)
1682.content: bun run cat wireframe:check --use as-is --topic <topic> --surface <visualiser ref> bun run cat wireframe:check --use design --topic <slug> --surface <surface> . The three flags are this skill’s input. --topic picks the directory in the table above and every candidate in it (name candidates to check fewer; one outside it is refused), and the report goes to its checks/. --use design needs at least two candidates; --use as-is needs each marked as-is in its file name, and a --surface that is the topic or a ref index.json says it covers. The use, topic and surface are recorded in report.json. This renders each candidate at web (1280×800) and mobile (390×844) sizes. It records script entries for renders, no-overflow and no-placeholder, each pass or fail with a note, and writes a screenshot per viewport. Any fail sends the candidate back to step 2.

1683.title: 4. Blind review, per criterion
1683.content: Reviewers include at least one agent that did not author the candidate and one human. For Design use called from CRDM, the human is the requester or the BA who owns the request: the person who will accept the delivered feature chooses its design. They see the intent, the screenshots and the HTML, without the authors. For each criterion they record pass, warn or fail, with a reason: . | criterion | question | . | intent-fit | Does it do what the intent says, for the person it names? | . | web usability | Can the task be done at desktop width? | . | mobile usability | Can the task be done at phone width, by touch? | . | accessibility | Contrast, a non-colour channel, accessible names, keyboard, reading order | . | alternatives | Do the candidates differ in the ways that matter? (Design use only) | . There are no scores and no averages (methodology-adoption, Refusals).

1684.title: 5. Adjudication and choice
1684.content: . | When entries for one criterion disagree, call Process_Adjudication. The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and a dispensation needs its reason. | The choice between surviving candidates is Process_OptionsAnalysis. Rejected candidates stay, each with the reason it lost. | .

1685.title: Staging links
1685.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: staging-review §”The deep-link rule”.

1686.title: Showing it to the requester
1686.content: Design use from CRDM ends in a person’s choice, so the candidates must be in front of that person before implementation starts: . | Commit the candidates, intent.md, checks/ (screenshots) and reviews/ under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, so feature-staging publishes them with the rest of the branch. | Show them where the requester will look, chosen from context: the conversation, the issue the request came from, the pull request, or more than one of these. Where it goes is a judgement (staging-review, the deep-link rule, point 5); every place chosen carries the same content: a short narrative of what each candidate does differently; branches/ deep links to each candidate’s HTML (not the site root); and its web and mobile screenshots shown as images, not only linked. Say which could not be linked or rendered, and why. | Ask the requester or BA to choose, with the comparison (one row per candidate, from A_CompareOptions) and a recommendation, per interaction-modality where it applies. | Record their choice in the proposal and in the output’s chosen. An agent never chooses on their behalf. Implementation (CRDM Phase 6) builds against the chosen candidate, and the delivery summary links it beside the after-screenshot. | .

1689.title: The work plan’s contract
1689.content: Skill work-plan-store: The contract the work plan (work items) keeps as a data store, as operations any Tool must provide: get, list, create, update with ifMatch, note, history, and where a work item is in its processes. Give back a work item exactly as written, keep ids unique and links whole, keep status and type to their closed lists, lose nothing to concurrent writers, and answer a work item’s history. A mechanical Actor plays this Role through whichever Tool the deployment names. Named by: DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . The work plan is a data store, and this is its contract. work-plan in scenarios/roles.json is a mechanical Role with a store block: what it holds, and how it is reached. This skill is the other half, what it must do. How an agent USES the plan is todo-manager; this file says what the plan promises back. This contract names no Tool. A process or skill that touches the work plan says which operation below it performs (“note the bean”, “claim it”), never which command does it. How one Tool performs an operation belongs on that Tool’s page, listed in §”Tools”. The Tool in use is chosen by the deployment description, per checkout. A diagram draws the store as a data store, never a lane: a dataStoreReference with dataStoreRef="work-plan", declared once in processes/global-tasks.bpmn. A task that opens or closes a work item writes to it with a dataOutputAssociation; a task that reads the plan has a dataInputAssociation from it. The task sits in the lane of whoever does it.

1690.title: What it holds
1690.content: | Kind | What | . | bean-defs | work items ($schema: bean/1.0.0), shaped by schemas/kinds/bean-defs.schema.json | . | bean-notes | addenda to a work item, one per writer, never rewritten | . | workflow-state | running and finished BPMN instances (folio-workflow-instance/v1) | .

1691.title: Operations
1691.content: Every Tool provides these. Each line says what a caller can rely on. | Operation | Guarantee | . | get(id) | the work item as last written, or “none”. A short id resolves to exactly one work item or to none | . | list(filter) | work items by status, type, tag or parent; archived work items only when the filter asks for them | . | create(bean) | the id is unique; the work item is readable by get once create returns | . | update(id, change, ifMatch) | refused when ifMatch names a version that is no longer current; a retry on the current version lands. archived: true archives the work item | . | note(id, text, by) | appended to the work item’s notes, never rewriting earlier ones | . | history(id) | every change to the work item, oldest first: when, by whom, what changed, and which process step made it when one did | . | positions(id) | every workflow instance that names the work item: process, step(s), instance status, last move | . | beansAt(process, step?) | the work items with a token at that process (and step) | . Archiving is a field, not an operation. update(id, { archived: true }, ifMatch) is refused unless the work item is completed or scrapped, and the work item keeps its status. get still finds an archived work item; list leaves it out unless asked. Where an archived work item lives is the Tool’s choice, stated on its page. A work item’s position lives only in the workflow instances. The work item records no process or step of its own; positions and beansAt read the instances the store holds. A tag such as process:code-change-review may label a work item for people, and is never read as its position.

1692.title: Responsibilities
1692.content: Each line is something a test can check against any Tool. | Give back what was written. get after create or update returns, byte for byte, the work item written. | Keep ids unique. No two work items share an id. | Keep links whole. parent, blocking and blocked_by name work items that exist. | Keep the lists closed. status and type take only the values the schema declares. | Lose nothing to a race. Two writers at once both land: the second update with a stale ifMatch is refused, retried on the current version, and lands. Nothing is overwritten unread. | Keep the history. history(id) answers who changed what and when, and which process step did it. | Archive only what is finished. archived: true on a work item that is not completed or scrapped is refused. | Know where a work item is. positions and beansAt agree with the instances the store holds. | .

1693.title: Tools
1693.content: | Tool | Backed by | Page | . | git state branch | a branch per graph (cat/<harness>/beans), mounted at beans/, written with the beans CLI (beans-cli) or by hand (beans-manual), read with bean-query | work-plan-store-git-branch | . | work items server | beans-serve GraphQL (schema); its mutations already take ifMatch | proposed | . | MCP service | an MCP server over the same operations | proposed | . | run-scoped store | in memory or a scratch branch, one per benchmark run, never the real plan (req:model-benchmark) | proposed | .

1694.title: Tests
1694.content: The conformance suite lives in the tools layer (scripts/tests/sdlc/work-plan-store-conformance.ts, one describe per responsibility above) and runs against both of the git Tool’s access modes. Until this file carries a tested-by: line, kg-audit reports this role as mechanical-role-untested.

1695.title: Not its responsibility
1695.content: Deciding what to work on, who claims a work item, or whether work is done. Those are judgements made in the lanes of the people and agents who read and write the plan.

1697.title: State in a running process
1697.content: Skill workflow-state: Where a running process keeps what it knows, and which store answers which question. The three records a step may touch, the one it may not, what <cat-harness.processes:bean op> actually performs, and why an instance and a work item must be one answer rather than two. Named by: Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . A process instance is not self-contained. It walks a diagram that lives somewhere else, records its position somewhere else again, and reads facts it must not change. Five stores; confusing any two of them is how a work plan comes to disagree with itself.

1698.title: Which store answers which question
1698.content: | question | store | graph typology | layer | . | what does this process DO? | processes/**/*.bpmn | cat-harness | content | . | where did this instance GET TO? | the workflow-state node of the work item graph | workflow-state | state | . | what is being worked on? | the bean-defs node of the work item graph | bean-defs | state | . | what does a PERSON still owe? | todos/ | todo-items | state | . | what do I already know? | agent memory | memory | context | . The layer column says what a step may do. A step may write to a state graph; that is what state is for. A step that writes to context is a defect, not an update: memory changes when a human directs an authoring act, outside any instance. content-context-and-state-graphs carries the axis; processMayWrite() is the predicate.

1699.title: The diagram is content and the instance is state, and that is the whole model
1699.content: A .bpmn is authored, reviewed, versioned and read by anyone — it stands on its own. An instance is a token position in that diagram plus a history: it means nothing detached from the file it walks. That is why the two live in different graphs and why an instance names its process rather than embedding it. Two consequences: . An instance is never edited by hand. It carries "$schema": "folio-workflow-instance/v1" and the interpreter owns it. Hand- editing a token is asserting a step happened, which is precisely what the gate exists to refuse. A diagram change does not rewrite history. An instance records where it got to under the diagram as it stood. If a step is renamed, the honest answer is that the old instance names a node that no longer exists — not that it retroactively took a different path.

1700.title: Beans and instances are ONE answer, not two
1700.content: bean-defs says what is being worked on; workflow-state says where it got to. Those must be one answer or they diverge, and a work plan that disagrees with itself is worse than one that is merely coarse. The loop is closed by <cat-harness.processes:bean op="…"> on an activity. A bean-marked step is not a step about the work plan — it IS the work-plan operation, so completing the step performs it: . | op | on completing the step | . | claim | status → in-progress, idempotent | . | note | append the caller’s note to the body | . | resolve | status → completed, only if the instance itself finished (or only archive steps are left) | . | archive | move a completed or scrapped work item into the archive, only once the instance finished | . claim is drawn only in Process_BeanOpen, and resolve and archive only in Process_BeanClose; every process that works on a work item calls both (check:bean-calls). note is drawn where the work happens. resolve is the careful one. A work item is never closed on somebody else’s judgement, so it does not fire on the caller’s say-so: the work item completes only when the instance tracking it has completed, which is a fact derived from the process rather than asserted by the agent calling it. A still-running instance gets a note. An op the build does not implement fails at process load. A step that says it resolves a work item and quietly does nothing is exactly the divergence the extension exists to close.

1701.title: What state does NOT buy you
1701.content: Ordering is not quality. A completed instance means the gates ran in order and a person saw the findings. Whether the content is correct is what the QA axes, the build and the validators are for. A green process must never be read as a reviewed artefact, and any dashboard built on this has to say so. A position is not a claim. An instance at Task_Commit says the token arrived, not that the commit is good.

1702.title: Where running instances live — the state graph on the branch store
1702.content: Running instances are part of the work-plan store (workflow-state graph typology; positions in work-plan-store). Where the deployment uses the git state-branch Tool, the store is mounted and pushed as described in work-plan-store-git-branch. The container is ephemeral and a work plan only one agent can see is not a work plan. Instance state lives in the shared work-plan store for the same reason work item definitions do: a sibling session, or the same session resumed in a fresh container, reads the store to find the position that exists rather than starting a second one beside it. When an instance advances, its state is written through the store’s Tool (bun run cat state:push when backed by the git state branch). This keeps instance state globally visible without cluttering code PR diffs on main. Instance ids are derived from the subject rather than random, so re-entering a step finds the instance that is already there: beans create is not idempotent and dedupes on nothing, so an id you can recompute is what prevents duplicates.

1703.title: Reading the state you did not write
1703.content: Before acting on an instance you did not start, ask what it is waiting on. A work item’s status defaults to non-blocking; a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff — because a block with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work. bean-blocking carries that, and bean-coordination carries the rule that a claim announces rather than reserves until your PR exists.
